1. Administration
1.1. Purpose: The purposeof thisprocedure is to identify the Incident Priorities for the Columbus Division of Fire.

1.2. Responsibility: It shall be the responsibility of each member to know, understand, and utilize these procedures as they apply to the situation at hand. It shall further be the responsibility of all Division Officers to train their subordinates in the proper application of these procedures and to implement and enforce the use of these procedures.
2. Incident Priorities
1.3. Incident priorities are the first items the Incident Commander considers at any emergency scene.
2.1. The incident priorities for all incidents shall be:

1.3.1. Life Safety – The Incident Commander must consider life safety of all firefighters, other emergency responders, occupants and bystanders at an incident. No property is worth the risk of even one life. Life safetymust come before all other considerations.

1.3.2. Incident Stabilization – The Incident Commander must develop the command structure and strategy to stabilize the incident. The command structure must match the complexity of the incident, not the size.

1.3.3. Property Conservation – Property conservation at an incident means achieving our goals and objectives while minimizing property damage. No incident can be considered successfully managed if property conservation is not given proper consideration and implemented in a timely manner.
1.4. While these priorities are always considered in the order listed, they may not be accomplished in order. For example, the incident may need to be stabilized in order to affect life safety.
3. Benchmarks
1.5. The objectives of each priority are reflected in the following benchmarks of completion:
3.1.1. Life Safety/Rescue – “All Clear” (primary search)
3.1.2. Incident Stabilization – “Situation Contained”
3.1.3. Property Conservation – Salvage and Overhaul

1.6. In order for the Incident Commander to satisfy the objectives of each benchmark in its priority order he/she must, in many cases, overlap the activities of each in order to achieve the current benchmark. Notable examples are the frequent need to achieve interior tenability with active/extensive fire control efforts before beginning primary search, or the need to initiate salvage operations while fire control efforts are being extended.
1. Administration
1.1. Purpose: The purpose of this procedure is to identify factors affecting rescue priorities.

1.2. Responsibility: It shall be the responsibility of each member to know, understand, and utilize these procedures as they apply to the situation at hand. It shall further be the responsibility of all Division Officers to train their subordinates in the proper application of these procedures and to implement and enforce the use of these procedures.
2. General

1.3. The Incident Commander must make the basic rescue decision: Do we remove victims from the fire or do we remove the fire from the victims? In some cases, occupants are safer in their rooms (Sheltered in-place) than moving through contaminated hallways and interior areas. Such movement may also impede interior firefighting.

1.4. The Incident Commander must evaluate the resources required to remove victims and then treat their injuries. In cases involving multiple victims, the Incident Commander should call for additional resources early and quickly develop an Incident Action Plan that will both stabilize the fire and provide for the removal and treatment of any victims.
1.5. The most urgent reason for calling additional alarms is for the purpose of covering Life Safety.
3. RescueSize-Up and Activities
1.6. The Incident Commander must consider the following factors in developing a basic rescue size-up:
3.1.1. Number, location and condition of victims
3.1.2. Effect the fire/incident has on the victims
1.6.1. Capability of the control forces to enter the building, remove/protect victims and control the fire/incident
3.2. Rescue efforts should be extended in the following order:
3.2.1. The most severely threatened
3.2.2. The largest number (groups)
3.2.3. The remainder of the fire/incident area
3.2.4. The exposed areas

1.7. The Incident Commander must make primary search assignments to specific companies to cover specific areas of large, complex occupancies, and must maintain on-going control of such companies until the entire area is searched and a primary “All Clear” is obtained.
1.7.1. When primary search companies encounter and remove victims, the Incident Commandermust assign other companies to continue the search of the interior positions vacated by those companies.

1.8. All initial attack efforts must be directed toward supporting rescue efforts. Hose lines must be placed in a manner to control interior access, confine the fire, and protect avenues of escape. Hose line placement becomes a critical factor in these cases and the Incident Commander and all operating companies must realize that the operation is in a Rescue Mode. It may be necessary to operate in a manner that writes off the structure in order to obtain an “All Clear”.

1.9. Normal means of interior access (stairs, halls, doorways, etc.) should be utilized to remove victims whenever possible. Secondary means of rescue (platforms, ladders, fire escapes, helicopters, etc.) may be utilized in their order of effectiveness.
1.10. The Incident Commander must provide for the treatment of victims after removal. Victims should be removed to one location for more effective triage, treatment and transport.
1.10.1. The Incident Commander should coordinate and utilize medics and assign treatment companies as required to the Emergency Medical Group.
1. Administration
1.1. Purpose: The purpose of this procedure is to define the search benchmark, “All Clear”.

1.2. Responsibility: It shall be the responsibility of each member to know, understand, and utilize these procedures as they apply to the situation at hand. It shall further be the responsibility of all Division Officers to train their subordinates in the proper application of these procedures and to implement and enforce the use of these procedures.
2. Search Operations
2.1. Search operations are defined as Primary and Secondary.
1.3. It is the standard operating procedure to extend a Primary Search in all involved and exposed occupancies that can be entered.
1.3.1. Primary search means companies have quickly gone through all affected areas and verified the removal and/or safety of all occupants.
1.3.2. The Incident Commander must structure initial operations around the completion of the Primary Search.
1.3.3. Time is the critical factor in the primary search process. Successful primary search operations must be extended quickly during initial fire stages.
1.4. Secondary Search means that companies thoroughly search the interior of the fire area after initial fire control and ventilation activities have been completed.

1.4.1. The Secondary Search should preferably be completed by different companies than those involved in Primary Search activities. Thoroughness, rather than time, is the critical factor in Secondary Search.
3. All Clear
1.5. The completion of thePrimary Search is reported utilizing the standard radio reporting term “Primary All Clear”.

1.6. It is the responsibility of the Incident Commander to coordinate Primary Search assignments, secure completion reports from interior companies, and to transmit the “All Clear” report to the fire alarm office. The fire alarm office will record the time of this report.
4. Obtaining an All Clear
1.7. The stage of the fire becomes a critical factor that affects the rescue approach developed by the Incident Commander.
1.8. In nothing showing situations or in very minor fire cases that clearly pose no life hazard, the Incident Commander must structure a rapid interior search and report ‘All Clear’.

1.9. In smoke showing and working fire situations, fire control efforts must be extended simultaneously with rescue operations in order to gain entry and control interior access to complete primary search. In such cases, the Incident Commander and operating companies must be aware the operation is in a rescue mode until the Primary Search is complete, regardless of the fire control required.
1.9.1. In working fire situations, the Primary Search must be followed by a Secondary Search.

1.10. In cases of fully involved buildings or sections of buildings, immediate entry and primary search activities become impossible and survival of occupants is improbable, the Incident Commander must initially report a working fire that is fully involved and that we “will not have an ‘All Clear’ on the structure”.
1.10.1. As quickly as fire control is achieved, the Incident Commander must structure what is in effect a Secondary Search for victims to include the exterior.
1.11. The Incident Commander and operating companies should not depend upon reports from spectators to determine status of victims.

1.11.1. Fire control forces should utilize reports as to the location, number, and condition of victims as supporting primary search efforts and must extend and complete a primary search wherever entry is possible.
1.12. A Secondary Search should be conducted on non-fire incidents such as Haz Mat, airplane, bus or auto accidents with ejection.
1. Administration
1.1. Purpose: The purpose of this procedure is to identify the incident commander’s considerations when determining the appropriate fire control strategy.

1.2. Responsibility: It shall be the responsibility of each member to know, understand, and utilize these procedures as they apply to the situation at hand. It shall further be the responsibility of all Division Officers to train their subordinates in the proper application of these procedures and to implement and enforce the use of these procedures.
2. Risk Management
1.3. Prior to committing to a fire control strategy, the incident commander shall conduct a risk assessment to determine the most appropriate method of fire control.

1.4. The acceptable level of risk is directly related to the potential to save lives or property. Where there is no potential to save lives, the risk to fire department members should be evaluated in proportion to the ability to save property of value.
1.5. During emergency operations, a risk analysis shall be utilized on the basis of the following principles:
1.5.1. Activities that present a significant risk to the safety of members shall be limited to situations where there is a potential to save endangered lives.
1.5.2. Activities that are employed to protect property shall be recognized as inherent risks to the safety of members, and actions shall be taken to reduce or avoid these risks.
1.5.3. No risk to the safety of members shall be acceptable when there is no possibility to save lives or property.
1.5.4. In situations where the risk to fire department members is excessive, activities shall be limited to defensive operations.
3. FireControl Strategies
1.6. The Incident Commander must determine the appropriate fire control strategy after considering the following critical factors:
1.6.1. Extent and location of the fire
3.1.1. Structural conditions
3.1.2. Entry capability
3.1.3. Fire Dynamics
3.1.4. Impact on ventilation and fire flow path
3.1.5. Survival profile of any victims
3.1.6. Resources
1.7. The two fire control strategies that the incident commander should consider are:
3.1.7. Offensive Strategy
3.1.8. Defensive Strategy
1.8. Offensive Strategy – A fire attack initiated from the interior of the building or started from the exterior and transitioned to an interior position to complete the extinguishment process.
1.8.1. The normal steps taken in the offensive attack are:
3.1.8.1. Establish the Command Post
3.1.8.2. Initiate the Primary Search
3.1.8.3. First line - fast, aggressive offensive attack
3.1.8.4. Provide support activities
3.1.8.5. Second line – back-up the first line and/or protect egress
3.1.8.6. Quickly evaluate effectiveness and react
1.9. Defensive Strategy – Exterior attack directed to first reduce fire extension and then bring the fire under control.
3.1.9. The normal steps taken in the basic defensive attack are:
3.1.9.1. Establish the command post
3.1.9.2. Evaluate fire spread/write-off lost property
3.1.9.3. Establish collapse zones
3.1.9.4. Identify key tactical positions
3.1.9.5. Prioritize fire streams
3.1.9.6. Provide big, well-placed streams
3.1.9.7. Quick determination of additional resource needs
3.1.9.8. Surround and drown

1.9.1. When there is no ability to save lives or property, there is no justification to expose fire department members to avoidable risk, and defensive fire suppression operations are the appropriate strategy.
1. Administration
1.1. Purpose:The purpose of this procedure is to identify offensive operations.

1.1. Responsibility: It shall be the responsibility of each member to know, understand, and utilize these procedures as they apply to the situation at hand. It shall further be the responsibility of all Division Officers to train their subordinates in the proper application of these procedures and to implement and enforce the use of these procedures.
2. General
1.2. While offensive (interior) fire attack is still the most common and important fire attack method, emphasis must be put on controlling ventilation openings and cooling fire gases.

1.3. Prior to initiating an offensive attack, a 360 survey should be completed to determine whether first water should be applied from the exterior, prior to entry (transitional attack); or first water should be applied from an interior position (direct interior attack).
1.3.1. If a transitional attack is appropriate, SOP 02-03-02 (Transitional Fire Attack) shall be followed.
1.4. Passing fire (either interior or exterior) withoutapplying water should be avoided.
2. Command Responsibilities

2.1. The Incident Commander must structure whatever operations are required to put water on the fire. Many fireground concerns, (control, extension, exposures etc.) can be controlled by a fast, well-placed attack.
2.2. Effective fire control requires that water be applied directly to the fire. The Incident Commander must establish an attack plan that overpowers the fire with water application.
2.3. The Incident Commander should develop an effective Incident Action Plan (IAP) that includes the following:
2.1.1. Fire attack plan
2.1.2. Search plan
2.1.3. Coordination of tactics
2.4. Clear and direct communication between Incident Command and companies assigned to ventilation, fire attack, search, and other tactical functions that take place inside the structure is required.
1. Administration
1.1. Purpose:The purpose of this procedure is to identify Defensive Operations.

1.1. Responsibility: It shall be the responsibility of each member to know, understand, and utilize these procedures as they apply to the situation at hand. It shall further be the responsibility of all Division Officers to train their subordinates in the proper application of these procedures and to implement and enforce the use of these procedures.
2. General

1.2. The decision to operate in a Defensive mode indicates that the Offensive attack strategy has been abandoned for reasons of personnel safety or inadequate resources,and the involved structure has been conceded as lost (written off).
3. Defensive Operations
3.1. Defensive operations fall under one of two categories:
3.1.1. Defensive from the onset:
1.2.1.1. Structures with advanced fire showing without the potential of savable victims
1.2.1.2. Structures with a low probability of extinguishment in a salvageable condition
1.2.1.3. Low value and/or high-risk structures with advanced fire conditions and low life hazard (e.g., vacant or lightweight buildings)
3.1.2. Offensive operations that transition to Defensive operations:
3.1.2.1. An offensive fire attack that is not making progress on the fire
1.2.1.4. A lack of on-scene resources requires the strategic shift to defensive operations
3.2. Defensive from Onset
1.2.2. The I/C will give the initial radio report and state “This will be a defensive operation”. The I/C shall then direct incoming companies’ tasks and positioning.
3.3. Offensive to Defensive
1.2.3. The announcement of a change to a Defensive attack will be made over the Fireground All-Call Talkgroup (ATG) and repeated by the FAO on ATG.
1.2.4. All personnel shall withdraw from the structure and maintain a safe perimeter. Officers will account for the safety of all personnel. A PAR shall be conducted per SOP 02-01-01.
1.2.5. Interior lines will be withdrawn and repositioned when changing to a Defensive attack. Lines should be backed away to positions which will protect exposures.
3.3.1. The first priority in defensive operations is life safety.

1.2.6. The second priority is exposure protection. All exposures, both immediate and anticipated must be identified and protected.Extinguishing the main body of fire may assist in the protection of exposures but does not replace it as the second priority.
1.2.7. Once exposure coverage is established, attention may be directed to knocking down the main body of fire.

1.2.8. The change from Offensive to Defensive Strategy is not to be confused with Emergency Evacuation (SOP 02-01-04).An Emergency Evacuation is the immediate emergency evacuation of all fire personnel from the hazard zone accompanied by air horn blasts.
4. Situation Contained

1.3. When the fire is under control it is reported utilizing the standard radio reporting term "Situation Contained". It is the responsibility of the Incident Commander to transmit this report to the fire alarm office.

1.4. While "Situation Contained" officially indicates the incident is contained or stabilized,meaning the forward progress of the fire has been stopped and the remaining fire can be extinguished with the on-scene resources, it does not mean the fire is completely out.
1. Administration
1.1. Purpose: The purpose of this procedure is to identify Property Conservation factors.

1.2. Responsibility: It shall be the responsibility of each member to know, understand, and utilize these procedures as they apply to the situation at hand. It shall further be the responsibility of all Division Officers to train their subordinates in the proper application of these procedures and to implement and enforce the use of these procedures.
2. General

1.3. It is standard procedure to commit whatever fireground resource is required to reduce property loss to an absolute minimum. The activities that relate to effective property conservation require the same early and on-going command functions and aggressive action as both rescue and fire control. All members are expected to perform in a manner that continually reduces loss during fire operations.
3. Property Conservation

1.4. When the fire is out, shut down the fire streams. Early recognition that the forward progress of the fire has been stopped is an important element in reducing loss. The earlier the salvage operations begin, the smaller the loss.
1.5. When basic fire control has been achieved, the Incident Commander must commit and direct companies into loss prevention activities; such activities generally include:
3.1.1. Evaluating damage to overall fire area
3.1.2. Evaluating the salvage value of various areas
3.1.3. Determining the manpower and equipment that will be required
3.1.4. Committingthe required companies to salvage functions
3.1.5. Redirectinghose lines from fire control functions to salvage functions

1.6. In cases where there is an overlapping need for both fire control and salvage to be performed simultaneously and where initial alarm companies are involved in firefighting while salvage remains undone, call for additional resources to assign to salvage functions.
1.7. The Incident Commander must be willing to commit adequate resources to property conservation activities.

1.8. Be aware that personnel involved in rescue and fire control operations are generally fatigued by the time property conservation functions must be completed. This can result in sloppy work and many injuries. Evaluate the conditions of personnel and replace with fresh crews as needed.

1.9. Salvage and overhaul functions must be integrated with investigative efforts. When fire control becomes stable, efforts should be made to protect and preserve evidence. Beware of personnel who want to quickly shovel out the interior and go home, they will generally shovel out the evidence with the debris.

1.4. Hose lines should be advanced inside fire buildings in order to control access to halls, stairways, or other vertical and horizontal channels through which people and fire may travel.

"Assure" in this case does not mean they must necessarily lay the line to the water supply, but that it is their responsibility to get water into their pump, by whatever means are appropriate.
3. FireStreamManagement
3.1. The following items relate directly to the effectiveness of hose lines:
3.1.1. Size
3.1.2. Placement
3.1.3. Speed
3.1.4. Mobility
3.1.5. Supply
4. Support Activities

1. Administration
1.1. Purpose:The purpose of this procedure is to identify factors and considerations affecting ventilation timing and techniques.

1.2. Responsibility: It shall be the responsibility of each member to know, understand, and utilize these procedures as they apply to the situation at hand. It shall further be the responsibility of all Division Officers to train their subordinates in the proper application of these procedures and to implement and enforce the use of these procedures.
2. General

1.3. The importance of understanding the impact of ventilation decisions on the fireground cannot be overstated. Fire growth and development are impacted by both the amount of air entering the fire area and by the amount of fire gases exiting the fire area. Opening a door or window provides oxygen to a ventilation- limited fire.

1.4. During offensive operations, the ventilation openings must be controlled by coordinating ventilation tactics with the fire attack. Before any ventilation is performed, the firefighter must understand its impact on fire growth and spread.
2.1.1. Ventilation factors affecting fire growth and development include:
2.1.1.1. Wind speed and direction
2.1.1.2. Other ventilation openings
2.1.1.3. Progress of the fire attack
1.5. Uncontrolled forcible entry may result in firefighter or civilian injury and death, and unnecessary property loss.
1.6. The guiding principle before performing any ventilation should be to ‘vent with purpose’… always consider the effect of the action.
2.2. Flow Path

1.6.1. The flow path of a fire is how a fire moves through a structure as determined by inlet and exhaust vents for air, since air allows fire to sustain and grow. Every new ventilation opening provides a new flowpath for the fire.
2.2.1. Principles of Fire Flow Path
1.6.1.1. Enlarging or creating openings (inlet and/or exhaust openings) will result in fire growth and spread.
1.6.1.2. Interrupting the fire flow path by limiting or controlling openings can limit fire growth.
1.6.1.3. Controlling the door – keeping doors closed aids firefighters by limiting the oxygen feeding the fire and results in lower temperatures.
1.6.1.4. Anyone in the exhaustportion of the flow path - between where the fire is and the direction of its travel – is in a high hazard location.
2.2.1.1. Controlling the flow path improves victim survivability.
3. Horizontal Ventilation

1.7. Forcing the door is ventilation and must be thought of as such. While forcing entry is necessary to fight the fire, it must also trigger the thought that air is being fed to the fire and that the fire may increase in size and intensity until water is applied. The clock is ticking (on firefighter and occupant tenability) before either the fire gets extinguished or it grows beyond control, jeopardizing the safety of everyone in the structure.
1.8. Once the front door is opened, attention should be given to the flow through the front door. A rapid rush of air or a tunneling effect could indicate a ventilation- limited fire.

1.9. Every new ventilation opening provides a new flow path. This could create very dangerous conditions when there is a ventilation-limited fire. You never want to be between where the fire is and where it wants to go withoutwater or a door to close.
1.10. Fire showing does notmean the fire is adequately vented. Additional vent points will grow the fire if water is not applied in a timely manner.
1.11. Horizontal ventilation must take place in coordination with fire attack. Openings should be controlled until the ‘water on the fire’ benchmark is announced.

1.12. Operations at commercial buildings may require horizontal openings be accessed or created for potential egress. Personnel should consider the effects of these openings and control inlets whenever possible.
4. Vertical Ventilation

1.13. Vertical ventilation is the most effective type of natural ventilation, but it does not guarantee positive results. It allows for the hottest gases to exit the structure; however, it also allows the most air to be entrained into the structure.

1.14. Vertical ventilation creates an exit flow path for hot fuel and will accelerate air flow into the fire as well as spread the fire along the flow path. This significant increase in oxygen combining with the hot, fuel-rich environment of a ventilation- limited fire can result in rapid fire growth.
1.15. Vertical ventilation must be coordinated by the Incident Commander along with fire attack.
1.16. Personnel shall not operate over top of a truss roof system that has been impacted by fire unless an inspection of the trust loft has been performed and indicates no or minimal fire damage.
5. Wind-Driven Fires

1.17. Wind is a powerful force influencing the direction of a flow path. Any time a window or door is opened on the side of a building that faces the wind (windward side) a huge amount of oxygen will be introduced into the fire. This sudden increase in oxygen combined with hot flammable gas from the fire can result in rapid fire growth but can also produce a sudden change in the direction of the flow path due to the pressure imposed by the wind.
1.18. Personnel performing fire attack or ventilation during wind conditions should consider the following:
5.1.1. Keep the wind at your back during fire attack
1.18.1. Ventilation prior to fire control should be limited to the downwind (leeward) side of the fire building
6. Positive Pressure Ventilation
6.1. Positive pressure ventilation shall be coordinated by the Incident Commander.
1.19. Positive pressure ventilation shall never occurprior to the ‘water on the fire’ benchmark being announced.
7. Vent, Enter, Isolate, Search (VEIS)
1.20. VEIS is an effective tactic when there is a good potential for savable victims that can be accessed more readily via a window.

1.21. When performing VEIS, care should be taken to reduce the potential of creating a new flow path and drawing fire towards a victim. The following actions should be incorporated into the VEIS tactic:
1.21.1. Do not use the ladder to vent the window.
1.21.2. Delay venting the entry window until just prior to entry.
1.21.3. Upon entry into the room, immediately take steps to control the door (flow path) to the room.
1. Administration
1.1. Purpose: The purpose of this procedure is to identify forcible entry factors.

1.2. Responsibility: It shall be the responsibility of each member to know, understand, and utilize these procedures as they apply to the situation at hand. It shall further be the responsibility of all Division Officers to train their subordinates in the proper application of these procedures and to implement and enforce the use of these procedures.

1.3. Prior to entry, be aware of the possibility the business or residence has a Rapid Key Entry System. Accomplish this by checking the MDC for remarks or a red sticker on the front door. Refer to SOP 02-03-18 for more details.
2. Forcible Entry
2.1. Fire Forced Entry

2.1.1. Forcible entry is used to gain entry to, and more importantly, egress from a building. The methods used to force entry are determined by the urgency and nature of the incident. Forcible entry involves a trade-off in time versus damage; the faster you force the more damage you do. If the fire is progressing and you must gain access to control the fire, don't waste time, gain entry by the most direct means possible.

2.1.2. Forcing entry is ventilation and must be thought of as such. While forcing entry is necessary to fight the fire, it must also trigger the thought that air is being fed to the fire and the clock is ticking before either the fire gets extinguished or it grows until an untenable condition exists, jeopardizing the safety of everyone in the structure.

2.1.3. Consideration must be given to the effect entry methods will have on the fire flow path. It is better to force a door at the latch than at the hinges, allowing control of ventilation and the ability to close the opening for crew protection.
2.2. Investigation Medical Run Forced Entry
2.2.1. Companies on the scene of fire alarms/medic runs may need to force entry. In these cases, entry should be gained with the least damage possible (e.g., through the lock or unlocked window).
2.2.2. Forced entry is appropriate when it is objectively reasonable to believe a person is in immediate need of emergency medical care. Those incidents include third- party calls and medical alarms.

2.2.3. The decision to force entry must be based upon the circumstances presented and a need to act. All of the circumstances presented and the decision to force entryor not force entry must be thoroughly documented in the electronic health record (EHR).
1.1. Forcible Entry Service Run, Vehicle Lockout – No Emergency Exists

2.2.4. When no reasonable person would conclude that an emergency exists, CPD or other law enforcement agency shall be requested by Division personnel priorto making entry or entry may be refused. This is to ensure the individual requesting assistance has a legal right or authority to be on the premise prior to making entry.
2.2.5. When a CFD company forces entry into a structure and no occupant or responsible party is on scene to maintain security of the structure, CPD must be notified via the FAO.
1.2. Documentationof forced entry shall be documented in the NFIRS report.
1. Administration
1.1. Purpose: The purpose of this procedure is to identify factors that should be considered when determining the need for additional resources.

1.2. Responsibility: It shall be the responsibility of each member to know, understand, and utilize these procedures as they apply to the situation at hand. It shall further be the responsibility of all Division Officers to train their subordinates in the proper application of these procedures and to implement and enforce the use of these procedures.
2. General

1.3. The decisions requiredto provide foradequate resources are an important factor in effective fire forecasting. The Incident Commander must develop strategic goals and obtain the resources required to stay ahead of the situation. Beware of "Crisis Management": this happens when a situation grows at a rate faster than the response rate to that situation. The Incident Commander ends up with a rapidly advancing situation and inadequate resources to control it.

1.4. Many times, the Incident Commander will reach a point where he/she begins to debate whether to call another alarm or not. In such cases call for it. If the extra resources are not needed, they can easily be put back in service.
1.5. In most cases, the Incident Commander should utilize the greateralarm mechanism in lieu of asking for extra companies.

1.6. It is the continuing responsibility and function of the Incident Commander to determine the resources required to control the situation and to provide for the timely call for any additional resource required.
1.7. The Incident Commander must be aware of both the capability and response time of additional resources and effectively integrate these facts into calls for additional resources.

1.8. As the Incident Commander calls for additional resources, he/she must expand the ICS as necessary to manage the number of additional resources. The Incident Commander cannot encounter a big fire situation, call additional alarms and then expect to effectively manage that additional resource in a single alarm command situation.
3. Additional Resources
3.1. Additionalresources should be requested for the following situations:
1.8.1. The number, location, and condition of actual victims exceeds the rescue/removal/treatment capabilities of companies.
1.8.2. There is evidence of significant fire but companies are unable to determine location and extent.
3.1.1. Conditionsbecome more severe or the situation deteriorates significantly.
3.1.2. All companies have been committed and the incident is not controlled.
1.8.3. Command runs out of a critical resource (e.g., personnel, apparatus, water, equipment, command, etc.).
1.8.4. The situation becomesso complex that the Incident Commander can no longer control the incident without a larger command structure.
1.8.5. An actual or potential situation exists and the property protection demand exceeds the fire control capabilities of available resources.
3.1.3. Companies cannot effectively perform early salvage operations.
3.1.4. Theweather conditions and or fatigue factor require additional manpower.
1.8.6. The use of SCBAs during salvage and overhaulrequires additional manpower.
1.8.7. The Incident Commanderinstinctively feels the need to summon additional resources (don't disregard fireground “hunches”).

1.2. Responsibility: It shall be the responsibility of each member to know, understand, and utilize these procedures as they apply to the situation at hand. It shall further be the responsibility of all Division Officers to train their subordinates in the proper application of these procedures and to implement and enforce the use of these procedures.
2. General
1.3. The radio designation “Code One” will be used to indicate that a person(s) is/are found Dead on Arrival (DOA) or to indicate any other death in the field, regardless of the circumstances.

1.4. In all cases, if the Police are not on the scene, the appropriate law enforcementagency will be requested through the Fire Alarm Office. The scene shall be secured until the arrival of the Police.

1.5. The procedure will be to notify the FAO that there is a “Code One”. The FAO will acknowledge Code One and give a Code One time. This will be the time used by the Police as the discovery time or in the case of EMS situations, as the time that resuscitation attempts were halted.

1. Administration
1.1. Purpose: The purpose of this procedure is to identify proper personal protective clothing and equipment to be used by personnel operating at emergencies.

1.2. Responsibility: It shall be the responsibility of each member to know, understand, and utilize these procedures as they apply to the situation at hand. It shall further be the responsibility of all Division Officers to train their subordinates in the proper application of these procedures and to implement and enforce the use of these procedures.
2. General
1.3. Personal protective clothing and equipment shall be used whenever the member may be exposed to the hazards for which it is provided.
2.1. Protective clothing shall be maintained in accordance with SOP 01-04-07.
1.4. Respiratory protection equipment shall meet the requirements of SOP 01-04- 02.
3. Protective Clothing
3.1. Station/Work Uniforms
1.4.1. Station/work uniforms are a component of the protective ensemble and shall be worn while on-duty.
1.4.2. Station/work uniforms shall meet the requirements of NFPA 1975, Standard on Station/Work Uniforms for Emergency Services, where possible.
1.4.3. The use of non-approved station work uniforms is strictly prohibited while engaged in emergency response activities.
3.2. Protective Clothing for Structural Firefighting
1.4.4. The following items constitute a complete set of protective clothing for firefighting:
3.2.1.1. Fire helmet
3.2.1.2. Turnout coat with liner
3.2.1.3. Turnoutpants with liner
3.2.1.4. Nomex or PBI hood
3.2.1.5. Structural fire gloves
3.2.1.7. SCBA mask
1.4.5. All PPE shall meet the applicable requirements of NFPA 1971, Standard on Protective Ensembles for Structural Fire Fighting and Proximity Fire Fighting when purchased.
3.2.2. Unless otherwise stated, all items must be worn together.
1.4.6. Thermally unstable materials (e.g., polyester, Dri-Fit, Under Armor, etc.) shall not be worn at any time while engaged in fire suppression activities.
1.4.7. No one shall be allowed in hazardous locations, such as the fireground hazard zone, unless they are properly wearing appropriate protective clothing and equipment.
1.4.7.1. Company officers may allow the removal of various items of protective clothing only after conditions no longer present a hazard.
1.4.7.2. In complex situations, the Safety Officer should be consulted about the advisability of removing articles of protective clothing.
1.4.8. Protective clothing for firefighting and ensemble elements shall be retired no more than 10 years from the date the ensembles or ensemble elements were manufactured.
3.3. Protective Clothing When Operating in The Roadway

1.4.9. Personnel operating at roadway incidents, who are not engaged in suppression activities, shall wear a Division issued high-visibility retroreflective vest or jacket and a fire or rescue helmet.
1.4.10. Personnel engaged in emergency operations that may directly expose them to flame, fire, heat, and/or hazardous materials shall wear protective clothing for firefighting.
1.4.11. Personnel engaged in non-emergency activities on or near the roadway (e.g., checking hydrants, training, etc.) shall wear a Division issued highvisibility retro- reflective vest or jacket.
3.4. Protective Clothing for Rescue and Special Operations
1.4.12. Whenever head protection is needed, personnel shall wear a fire or rescue helmet.
1.4.13. Appropriate protective clothing for rescue and special operations incidents shall be determined by the Incident Commander, with input from the Incident Safety Officer.

1.4.14. Where the potential for flash fire exists, personnel shall wear PPE meeting the requirements of NFPA 1971, Standard on Protective Ensembles for Structural Fire Fighting and Proximity Fire Fighting.
3.5. Protective Clothing for Violent Incidents / Unknown Emergencies
3.5.1. Ballistic helmet and vest shall be worn for the following:
3.5.1.1. Shootings
3.5.1.2. Stabbings
1.4.14.1. Unknown emergencies or when forcing entry into premises unannounced (this does not apply to fireground operations).
3.5.1.5. At the discretion of the company commanderor IC
1.4.15. The member can wear the ballistic vest or helmet in addition to above emergencies.
1.4.16. Ballistic helmet and vest shall not be worn under or over turnout gear during structural firefighting.
2. Eye Protection

2.1. When operating in a hazardous area at an emergency scene without the fullface piece of respiratory protection being worn, members shall wear primary eye protection that is designed to protect the member’s eyes from the expected hazards.
2.2. Personnelengaged in activities that may subject their eyes to projectile hazards shall wear eye protection.
2.3. Eye protection shall meet the requirements ofANSI Z87.1.
3. Modificationto Personal ProtectiveEquipment for Structural Firefighting
3.1. The Laundry Technician shallmaintain a list of approved modifications to PPE that do not require higher authorization.

3.2. The addition of patches, logos, emblems shall not be permitted without required NFPA “Transmitted and Stored Thermal Energy” Testing of the affected areas (when appropriate) and approval by the Fire Chief.
3.3. If a cost is associated with the required testing, the requester will be required to obtain certified testing at their cost prior to final approval.
3.4. When applicable, requests to modify or add patches, logos, or emblems to any article of PPE should be submitted along with the item to the Fire Chief using Form PI-32e.
3.5. Upon approval of the Fire Chief, a patch, logo, or emblem not exceeding 4” across may be applied to the upper shoulder of the turnout coat by the Laundry Technician.
3.6. Modificationsto turnout gear shall only be permitted through this process.
4. Non-Division-Issued Personal Protective Equipmentfor Structural Firefighting
3.7. Personnelmay wear non-division issued PPE that meet the following criteria:
4.1.1. The PPE meets the current or previous edition of the applicable NFPA Standard
3.7.1. The PPE was manufactured within the past ten years
3.7.2. Same or similar style or design as that of current CFD PPE
3.7.3. Approval by the Fire Chief
4.2. Requests to use non-division issued PPE should be submitted through the chain of command to the Fire Chief using form PI-32e.
3.8. Ballistic vests and helmets must be Division issued.
4.3. Members are not permitted to wear ballistic vests or helmets that are not Division issued.
5. Apparatus Operators
5.1. Minimum PPE to operate a pump or aerial device shall be helmet and utility gloves.
5.2. When working in the hazard zone, apparatus operators shall don full protective clothing for structural firefighting.
1. Administration

1.1. Purpose: The purpose of this procedure is to define the minimum respiratory protection requirements for personnel who may be exposed to respiratory hazards during the performance of their duties.

1.2. Responsibility: It shall be the responsibility of each member to know, understand, and utilize these procedures as they apply to the situation at hand. It shall further be the responsibility of all Division Officers to train their subordinates in the proper application of these procedures and to implement and enforce the use of these procedures.
2. Use of Respiratory Protection

1.3. Because there is no way to predetermine hazardous conditions such as the presence of fireground toxic contaminants, lack of oxygen, chemical spills, etc., the following unknown atmospheres should be assumed to be Immediately Dangerous to Life and Health (IDLH) and shall require the use of a Self- Contained Breathing Apparatus (SCBA) while operating in the hazard area:
1.3.1. Structure fires where the fire is beyond the stage where it can be controlled by the use of a hand-held fire extinguisher
2.1.1. Dumpster and vehicle fires
2.1.2. Confined-space and/orbelow grade responses
2.1.3. Gas leaks
2.1.4. Hazmat, Bomb, and WMD responses
1.4. Whereappropriate, a supplied air breathing apparatus (SABA) system may be utilized in place of an SCBA when supplied-air is required.
1.5. An appropriate air-purifying respirator (APR) may be used in place of an SCBA when the requirements of SOP 01-04-05 are met.
3. Respiratory Protection Requirements
1.6. Personnel using respiratory protection shall pass an annual quantitative fit test.
1.7. Members may only wear a facepiece or mask size and model that they have passed a fit-tested for.
1.8. RespiratoryProtection shall be worn according to the manufacturer’s requirements.
1.9. Unapproved devices, or approved devices that have been modified in a manner that voids their approval, shall not be used.

1.10. Members using SCBA shall not compromise the protective integrity of the SCBA for any reason when operating in IDLH, potentially IDLH, or unknown atmospheres by removing the facepiece or disconnecting any portion of the SCBA that would allow the ambient atmosphere to be breathed.
1.10.1. The only exception to this policy will be when providing an emergency air supply using the regulator from the low-pressure side of the RIT Pack.
1.11. A quantitatively fit-tested facepiece ensures a proper seal. This seal must not be compromised by any means including, but not limited to, the following:
1.11.1. Facial Hair: Beards, sideburns, mustaches, long hair, or bangs that pass between the sealing surface of the facepiece and the face of the wearer are not permitted.

1.11.2. Head coverings: The protective hood, or any other head covering, must be worn over the tightening straps of the facepiece so as not to break the seal between the facepiece and the face of the wearer.
1.11.3. Protuberances: Eyeglass temple bars, or any other accommodative device, must not pass through the seal of the facepiece and the face of the user.
1.11.3.1. Members needing to wear eyeglasses must have an approved spectacle kit, obtained from the Mask Repair Section, to accommodate corrective lenses. Contact lenses may be worn.
1.12. Members using SCBAs shall operate in teamsof two or more and shall be in close physical proximity with each other.
1.13. Members must be aware of their heads-up display in their SCBA’s facepiece, and use the 50% warning as an indicator to begin to exit the hazard zone (SOP 01-04-08).
1.14. Anytime a member must exit the hazard zone,anothermembermust accompany them.

1.15. Members using respiratory protection shall be monitored by company officer, incident safety officers, incident commanders, and medic personnel on the scene for signs of fatigue or other factors that could result in medical compromise.

1.16. All personnel required to wearSCBA’s shall be evaluated at least annually on their knowledge and proficiency in SCBA operations, including safety, policies, procedures, maintenance, and inspection.

1. General

1.3. It is the goal of the Division of Fire to reduce exposures to fireground toxic contaminants,ultra-fine particulates, oxygen deficient atmospheres, and other respiratory hazards found within the hazard area of various emergencies to which we respond. In order to achieve this goal, SCBA use should be maintained and monitored throughout operations.
2. Structure Fires
1.4. Personnel shall wear SCBA during all phases of suppression, salvage, and overhaul while operating within any portion of the structure that had been exposed to fire.
1.5. An air-purifying respirator (APR) with an appropriate chemical cartridge may be used in place of an SCBA during fire cause determination when the requirements of SOP 01-04-05 are met.
3. Below-Grade and Confined Space

1.6. SCBA/SABAs will be used in these situations until the ambient atmosphere can be continuously ventilated monitored and sampled (per OSHA 1910.146 specifications) to prove that the atmosphere is no longer Immediately Dangerous to Life and Health (IDLH) AND there are no other permit entry hazards present.

2. General

1.3. The following procedures will provide for the compliance of facets of the Respiratory Protection Program mandated byNFPA 1500,Standard on Fire Department Occupational Safety and Health Program, and NFPA 1852, Standard on Selection, Care, and Maintenance of Open-Circuit SelfContained Breathing Apparatus (SCBA). These procedures define the standards the Columbus Division of Fire has adopted, and must be followed.
3. Daily Inspections
1.4. Clean and disinfect the second stage regulatorusing only an approved disinfectant cleaner for SCBA.
3.1. Ensure cylinder is registering to full capacity.
1.5. Check both the Vibra-alert (tactile low-air alarm) and the heads-up display to ensure proper activation and adequate battery power.
3.2. Verify facepiece-to-face seal.
3.3. Check the exhalation valve function.

3. Cleaning
3.1. The external surfaces of the SCBA shall be cleaned and disinfected according to the manufacturer's instructions using a mild detergent such as soap and water.

3.2. The facepiece shall be cleaned after each use and disinfected as needed. Facepiece cleaning and disinfecting shall be performed according to the manufacturer's instructions using only those agents indicated by the manufacturer (i.e., Scott Multi-Wash).

3.3. The second stage regulator shall be thoroughly cleaned and disinfected if the internal components have been exposed to bodily fluids, exhaled breath, dirt, or debris. The cleaning and disinfecting shall be performed according to the manufacturer's instructions using only an approved disinfectant for SCBA (i.e., Scott Multi-Wash).
3.4. Caution shall be taken to prevent water or cleaning materials from entering the connection between the cylinder valve and the mating SCBA inlet connector.
3.5. All SCBA components shall be thoroughly airdried prior to storage in a compartment that does not allow for air circulation.
3.6. Under no circumstances shall chlorine bleach ever be used to clean straps and harness assemblies.
6.4. Appropriate inspections shall be performed after cleaning.

1. Administration
1.1. Purpose: To explain and provide guidelines for the use of an Air-Purifying Respirator (APR) for respiratory protection.

1.2. Responsibility: It shall be the responsibility of each member to know, understand, and utilize these procedures as they apply to the situation at hand. It shall further be the responsibility of all Division Officers to train their subordinates in the proper application of these procedures and to implement and enforce the use of these procedures.
2. General
1.3. An air-purifying respirator (APR) provides a lower level of respiratory protection than an SCBA. The use of an APR is limited to the situations contained in this SOP.
1.4. A risk assessment shall be conducted to determine whether a full or halffacepiece APR is appropriate.
1.5. When a half-face respiratoris worn, appropriate eye protection shall be utilized.
1.6. Personnelmay only use an APR for which they have passed an annual quantitative fit test.
1.7. An APR may only be utilized with a filter or cartridge appropriate for the environment where it is being used.

1.8. When the facepiece is properly donned and adjusted, detection of odor or taste, or irritation to eye, nose or throat may indicate that the filtration element is exhausted or compromised. If this occurs, return to fresh air immediately, check facepiece fit, and replace filtration element as needed.
2. APR Use During EMS Operations

2.1. A fit-tested P-100 air-purifying respirator shall be the minimum level of protection against viral, bacterial or otherairborne inhalation hazards when respiratory protection is deemed appropriate during an EMS response.
3. APR Use During Overhaul
2.1. The use of an APR while performing overhaul is strictly prohibited.
3. APR UseDuringFire CauseDetermination Activities
3.1. An APR with an appropriate chemical cartridge is permitted when all of the following conditions are met:
3.1.1. ≥ 30 minutes post-extinguishment
3.1.2. No active overhaul is taking place
3.1.3. Positive pressure ventilation is in place
3.1.1. Continuous air monitoring is in place and levels are within acceptable short-term occupational exposure limits:
3.1.3.1. Hydrogen Cyanide (HCN) ≤ 4.7ppm
3.1.3.2. Carbon Monoxide (CO) ≤ 35 ppm
3.2. The chemical cartridge shall be NIOSH-approved to provide protection against atmospheres containing particulates, acid gases, organic vapors, and formaldehyde.
4. Hazmat Operations

3.3. When determined to be appropriate by the Incident Commander, with input from the Hazmat Officer, personnel may be assigned a chemical-level protection canister and adapter to be fitted onto their facepiece and used in place of their SCBA.
5. Other Uses
3.4. The air-purifying respiratoris being recommended for protection from the following when working in or around the station:
5.1.1. Asbestos fibers or lead dust
5.1.2. Nuisance dusts or particulates
5.1.3. Pollen or other allergen particulates
5.1.4. Liquid or oil-based particles from sprays
5.1.5. Metal fumes produced from welding and cutting
5.1.6. Mold spores
5.1.7. Biological Pathogens
4. Care and Maintenance
4.1. Air-Purifying Respirators and filtration elements shall be maintained and used according to the manufacturer’s requirements.
4.2. Clean the facepiece ormask assembly and check the overall condition after each use.
5.2. P-100Particulate filters can be ordered from Mask Repair.

1. Administration
1.1. Purpose: The purpose of this procedure is to identify the procedure to be utilized for managing one’s air supply in an IDLH environment.

1.2. Responsibility: It shall be the responsibility of each member to know, understand, and utilize these procedures as they apply to the situation at hand. It shall further be the responsibility of all Division Officers to train their subordinates in the proper application of these procedures and to implement and enforce the use of these procedures.
2. General

1.3. The air supply carried in an SCBA is intended for entry, work and exit from an IDLH atmosphere. It is difficult to gauge the appropriate amount of air necessary to exit from a structure. This has resulted in firefighters becoming lost, trapped, and disoriented inside of structures, and is responsible for a large percentage of firefighter fireground deaths.

1.4. In an effort to improve safety on the fireground, it is necessary to allocate some air as an emergency reserve for unintended events that may otherwise lead to a firefighter exhausting their air supply before exiting the hazard zone.
2. Air Monitoring
2.1. In all cases, firefighters should monitor their air consumption and the environment in order to allow for an adequate air reserve and ensure a safe exit.
2.2. Firefighters shall monitor air consumption through their Heads-Up Display (HUD) and shall begin to exit the structure when the 50% yellow LED begins to flash except as noted below:

2.2.1. If initial attack personnel find a known rescue situation where immediate action could prevent the loss of life, deviation from the air management policy may be permitted. The exception is not for standard search and rescue activities.
2.2.2. In no instance shall a firefighter be permitted to remain in the hazard zone following the activation of the 75% red LED or the Vibra-alert.
3. PolicyDeviation
3.1. Any deviation must be an exception and not standard practice.
2.3. If a deviation occurs, the occurrence must be reported promptly to the Incident Commander.
2.4. A thorough investigation and written report must be submitted in a timely manner to the Division Safety Officer.
4. High Risk Environments

2.5. The following situations are considered extremely high risk. Deviation of this policy in these environments should only occur in very rare circumstances after a thorough and conservative risk/benefit analysis is performed:
4.1.1. Fires in commercial buildings
4.1.2. Fires below grade
4.1.3. Fires in occupancies with center hall construction
2.5.1. Fires in occupancies with mazelike configurations (e.g., office cubicles, stockrooms, etc.)
2.5.2. Fires in multifamily or non-residential structures with lightweight construction features (e.g., restaurants, strip malls, large single-story structures)
3. Division Inspection Program
4.2. Prolonged SCBA use has the following associated risks:
3.1.1. Increased cardiac work stress
4.2.1. Increased thermal stress
4.2.2. Increased depth of entry into the hazard zone
4.2.3. Increased degradation of structure if fire is not contained
3.1.2. Inadequate margin of error for unintended events (e.g., lost, trapped, disoriented, structural failure, etc.)
4. Out of Air

4.1. In the event that a firefighter depletes his/her air supply prior to exiting a structure, the firefighter should resist the impulse to remove their facepiece, unless a clean air source is available.
4.2. Superheated air or air that is highly contaminated with fire gases is more likely to result in death than suffocation resulting from no air source.
1. Administration
1.1. Purpose: To provide a written procedure for the use and testing of all Personal Alert Safety System (PASS) Devices.

1.2. Responsibility: It shall be the responsibility of each member to know, understand, and utilize these procedures as they apply to the situation at hand. It shall further be the responsibility of all Division Officers to train their subordinates in the proper application of these procedures and to implement and enforce the use of these procedures.
2. PASS Usage
1.3. The PASS unit shall be turned ‘ON’ for any entry into a potential hazard area, including, but not limited to:
2.1.1. Atmospheres that could be IDLH.
2.1.2. Incidents that could result in entrapment.
2.1.3. Structural collapse of any type.
2.1.4. Investigation mode.
2.1.5. As directed by the Incident Commander or Incident Safety Officer.
2.2. The PASS ‘Alarm’ shall be activated in the following situations:
1.3.1. Any time a memberfeels that they have become lost, trapped, or disoriented.
2.2.1. When a member is out of air or may not have enough air to safely exit.
1.3.2. Any time a member becomes incapacitated or seriously injured in the hazard zone.
1.3.3. When a member feels threatened, or deems it appropriate to activate the alarm.
1. Administration

1.1. Purpose: To provide the opportunity for a review of emergency operations at the scene while all involved members are present and the incident is still fresh in everyone’s mind. Allows Incident Commander and Safety Officer opportunities for training and review (with emphasis on Standard Operating Procedures). Other members may contribute observations and experiences as relevant.

1.2. Responsibility: It shall be the responsibility of each member to know, understand, and utilize these procedures as they apply to the situation at hand. It shall further be the responsibility of all Division Officers to train their subordinates in the proper application of these procedures and to implement and enforce the use of these procedures.
2. Implementation

1.3. The Incident Commander shall provide the opportunity for an “on-scene” post-incident safety review of any emergency operation in which more than one company was committed. The review may be no more than the Incident Commander inquiring of the Safety Officer if he has any issues to discuss, or it could involve a detailed discussion of an operation that did not work as planned. This “on-scene” review does not preclude a more formal, intricate critique at a later time, if so warranted. The following situations will apply:

1.3.1. Structure Fires: All residential or commercial structure working fires must be reviewed (garages and out buildingsneed not be critiqued unless a problem needs to be addressed, or SOPs need to be emphasized).
1.3.1.1. Incident Safety Officer(or Incident Commander if SO-2 is not on the scene) will address safety related SOPs for compliance:
2.1.1.1.1. Accountability
2.1.1.1.2. Two-in / two-out rule; and use of the “buddy” system
1.3.1.1.1. Personal Protective Equipment including, but not limited to turnouts, PASS devices, SCBAs, Thermal Imaging Cameras (TICs), etc.
2.1.1.1.3. Structural monitoring for CO levels
1.3.1.2. SO-2, orIncident Commander, will discuss hazard identification and communications on the fireground, if appropriate.
1.3.2. Rescue Operations: All technical rescue operations, especially confined space, high-angle, and rapid water rescues by in-charge rescue personnel.
2.1.2. HazMat Operations: All operations by HazMat Team Leader and SO-2.
3. Procedure

1.4. The Incident Commander, sometime after the situation is contained, but before all companies are returned to service, must provide an “on- scene” post-incident safety review using the following guidelines:

1.4.1. Only those companiesactually involved in the operation will be included in the review. Any companies called as extra company, stand-by, or multiple-alarm that are not actively engaged in the operation will be excluded. This will prevent keeping companies out of service unnecessarily (do not exclude those companies that played a part in the operation, however minor, just to rush them back to service).

1.4.2. If another “working” incident occurs requiring a company attending the review, and they are able to respond, the Incident Commander will excuse them (e.g., HazMat Team and/or Technical Rescue Teams, etc.).
1.4.3. Remember, these reviews, like the more formal critiques, are for training and review and are to be conducted as such for everyone’s benefit.
1. Administration

1.1. Purpose: The purpose of this procedure is to ensure the Department of Building and Zoning Services (BZS) is notified of structural damage that may affect public safety. This damage may be the result of age, neglect, weather, fire, a vehicle hitting a structure, explosion, or other unspecified circumstances that renders a structure unsafe.

1.2. Responsibility: It shall be the responsibility of each member to know, understand, and utilize these procedures as they apply to the situation at hand. It shall further be the responsibility of all division officers to train their subordinates in the proper application of these procedures and to implement and enforce the use of these procedures.
2. General
1.3. BZS is charged with the responsibility of ensuring that structures are safe for occupancy.

1.4. The Division of Fire is often the first to become aware of structural problems and it is our duty to notify the proper authority. Suspected or potential nonemergent structural problems as well as emergent hazards shall be reported to BZS, previously known as “Building One”.
1.5. BZS will then classify this information into two response categories: Emergent and Non-Emergent. The reported information should also include the following:
2.1.1. Address of involved structure(s)
2.1.2. Number of stories
2.1.3. Type of construction
2.1.4. Residential or commercial
2.1.5. Occupied or vacant
2.1.6. Building owner’s name and phone number
2.1.7. Occupant’s name and phone number
3. Emergent Hazard
1.6. The on-scene Incident Commander shall request the immediate response of BZS when there is a strong possibility that any of the following three dangers are present:
3.1.1. Immediate danger of the structure collapsing onto another building
3.1.2. Immediate danger of the structure collapsing onto a roadway
3.1.3. Immediate danger of the structure collapsing onto a sidewalk
1.7. Upon request by the Incident Commander, the Fire Alarm Office will complete the “Structural Damage Notification Form” and notify BZS at the appropriate 24-hour number.

1.8. The on-duty Safety Officer (SO-2) will be dispatched to all Non-Residential properties where an Emergent Hazard exists. SO-2, with the assistance of Prevention 18 if needed, is responsible for posting the building if conditions warrant. The posting of the building could vary depending on the severity of the situation. This posting could range from securing the area with scene tape and stickers to requesting CPD standby to ensure no one enters the hazard/collapse zone.Prevention 18 is also to complete a Building Inspection Report for any fire code violations as a result of the structural damage (e.g., blocked exit(s), fire sprinklers systems OOS, etc.).

1.9. In the course of conducting Emergency Services Operations or inspections and an Emergent Hazard is found, contact the FAO and have a minimum of a Battalion Chief dispatched to your location. The Battalion Chief will follow
Section 3 of this policy if conditions warrant.
4. Non-Emergent Hazard

1.10. In the course of conducting Emergency Services Operations or inspections and a non-emergent hazard is found, this damage and the accompanying requested information listed above will be reported to the FAO. The FAO will notify BZS and the Fire Prevention Bureau, via e-mail, using the “Structural Damage Notification Form”.
4.1. This includes the following types of damage but not exclusive to the following:
1.10.1. Damage in buildings such as holes in the roof or floor, weakened or missing studs, damaged stairs, etc. Buildings that have been weakened by age, neglect, or fire.
1.10.2. A vehicle hitting a building, or other damage, not defined under Section 3 for Emergent Hazard.

1.11. Non-emergent hazards will be surveyed by a designee from BZS as soon as possible during regular business hours. Upon notification, the Fire Prevention Bureau will assign the appropriate Inspector for proper processing.

1. Administration
1.1. Purpose: To establish notification guidelines for the American Red Cross in the event of a fire or other emergency.

1.2. Responsibility: It shall be the responsibility of each member to know, understand, and utilize these procedures as they apply to the situation at hand. It shall further be the responsibility of all division officers to train their subordinates in the proper application of these procedures and to implement and enforce the use of these procedures.
2. Definition

1.3. Dwelling: For response purpose the American Red Cross defines a dwelling as “a structure, no matter the type of construction, which is intended to house one or more persons.” This could include a campsite along a waterway and railroad right-of-way, and it could also include a vehicle used as a residence.
3. Notification Needed

1.4. Fires and other emergencies of all sizes can be traumatic to the residents and the American Red Cross is available to respond and provide a place to stay, comfort and other immediate needs until other resources are available.
1.5. The Columbus Division of Fire should contact the American Red Cross when any of the following situations occur:
1.5.1. When the dwelling unit is damaged to the extent it is uninhabitable, whether for safety or health reasons, without repairs.
1.5.2. When there is noticeable damage / loss, whetherfrom fire, water, smoke or by salvage and overhaul.
3.1.1. When there is a death or injury, with or without transport, to any resident.
1.5.3. When the resident exhibits emotionaldistress, caused by the fire or otherwise.
1.5.4. When the resident reports loss of medicines ordurable medical goods, including glasses and dentures.
1.5.5. When there are children, elderly, or person with disabilities living in the home.
3.1.2. When the structure houses multiple residential units.
3.1.3. When the utilities have been disconnected.
1.5.6. When the resident asks for Red Cross presence or says “yes” when asked if they need assistance regardless of the amount of damage.
4. Notification NOT Needed
1.6. Notification of the American Red Cross may not be needed under these conditions:
1.6.1. When the damage is minimal (minor stove fire; trash can fire) with little or no disruption in normal routine.
1.6.2. When the incident is the result of a maintenance problem (e.g., sewage backup, ruptured water pipes, gas leak, etc.).
4.1.1. When the structure is obviously uninhabited.
4.1.2. When the structure is not residential, unless canteening is requested.
5. Contact Numbers

5.1.1. Preferred: 614-253-8888 (First Responder use ONLY)
