1. Administration
1.1. Purpose: The purpose of this procedure is to identify the method of personnel accountability at incidents.

1.2. Responsibility: It shall be the responsibility of each member to know, understand, and utilize these procedures as they apply to the situation at hand. It shall further be the responsibility of all Division Officers to train their subordinates in the proper application of these procedures and to implement and enforce the use of these procedures.
2. Hardware
2.1. Personal Accountability Tags (PAT)
1.2.1. Each firefighter and officer will be issued color-coded plastic tags (PAT) containing their name and ID number:
2.1.1.1. Firefighters – 4 yellow with black print
2.1.1.2. Lieutenants – 4 red with white print
2.1.1.3. Captains– 3 red with white print, and 1 black with white print
2.1.1.4. Chief officers – 3 black with white print
2.1.1.5. Safety officers – 4 green with white print
1.2.2. PAT’s will be attached to underside of the rearof the helmet brim when not on a passport.
1.2.3. Each company will be issued blank yellow tags (PAT) on which to write the names of non-uniformed and auxiliary riders.
2.2. Passports
2.2.1. Plastic cards approximately 3” x 4” with Velcro on front and rear.
2.2.2. Two passports are assigned to all engines, ladders, rescues, and medics.
2.2.3. One passport for most single person companies.
2.2.4. The passports will be attached to the passenger side dash with Velcro.
1.2.4. A Personal Accountability Tag (PAT) for each member of the crew shall be placed on/off each Passport whenever members move on or off the apparatus for any time frame.
1.2.4.1. The top name will always be the crew leader (e.g., company officer, I/C rescue, etc.).
1.2.4.2. The second name will be the driver. On Engines, Ladders and Rescues this nametag will be placed on the Passport upside down.
1.2.4.2.1. Upside down PAT’s will indicate that the person might not actually be in the hazard zone.
1.2.4.3. On tiller ladders, the third name will be the tillerman. This name tag will be placed on the Passport upside down.
1.2.4.4. Only the name tags ofmembers actually responding with the company shall be on the Passport.
1.2.4.5. All members shall be responsible for placing orremoving their name tags as appropriate.
1.2.5. Crew leaders shall visually check the Passports following any change in personnel assigned to the crew ensure accuracy.
1.2.6. Crew leaders shall enter the name of any non-division person responding with their company on blank name tags and attach these name tags to the Passports.
2.3. Small Status Boards
1.2.7. Plastic boards approximately 12” x 8” with Velcro on front and rear with positions for eight Passports (4 on the front and 4 on the rear).
2.3.1. One Small Status Board is carried on all apparatus.
1.2.8. A Small StatusBoard should be used for accountability on small incidents.
1.2.9. The Small Status Board should be mounted on the inside of the driver’s door on engines and ladders.
2.4. Large Status Boards
1.2.10. Plastic boards approximately 12” x 24” with Velcro on front and rearwith positions for 24 passports (12 on the front and 12 on the rear).
2.4.1. One Large Status Board is carried on each battalion chief vehicle.
1.2.11. The Large Status Board should be used for accountability on larger incidents.
3. Rules of Accountability
1.3. The Incident Commander shall be responsible for accountability on all incidents, but may delegate the responsibility within the incident command structure.
1.4. The Passport Accountability System shall be utilized any time that personnel are operating at an incident.
1.5. All crews shall work within the Incident Command System. Freelancing is not permitted.
3.1. All crews shall remain intact as much as possible.
1.5.1. Personnel must work in teams of at least two while in the interior “hazard zone”.
3.1.1. No one may enter, work in, or leave an interior “hazard zone” alone.

1.5.1.1. A “hazard zone” is any area that requires a SCBA or in which a firefighter is at risk of becoming lost, trapped, or injured. This will include entering a structure to search for a fire, operating in close proximity to the structure during exterior operations, confined space or trench rescue, etc., or any other situation deemed appropriate by the Incident Commander.
3.2. Passportsmust never enter the hazard zone.
1.6. Passports should be maintained at the Command Post or at another designated location outside of the hazard zone.
3.3. Passports should reflect all personnel operating at the incident.
1.7. Personnel not operating in the hazard zone must still be accounted for when a Personnel Accountability Report (PAR) is requested.
1.8. Crew leaders shall leave their Passports at thedesignated Accountability location prior to entering a hazard zone.

1.9. The first arriving vehicle to each side of the incident shall become the initial accountability location for that side of the incident. The identity and location of this vehicle shall be transmitted as part of the initial radio report.
1.10. There will be only one accountability location for each point of entry.
1.11. If the first vehicle is not an engine, the first engine to each side of the incident shall assume the responsibility of becoming the accountability location for that side of the incident.

1.11.1. The pump operator, if not accompanying their crew, shall retrieve the Small Status Board from the first arriving vehicle and maintain accountability for that side of the incident until relieved by a Division or Group Supervisor.
1.12. Any change of the Accountability location shall be announced over all talkgroups.
4. Level I Accountability – SingleCompany Incidents
1.13. For single company incidents, the Passports shall remain on the apparatus and the driver will assume accountability responsibilities.
5. Level II Accountability –MultipleCompany Responses
1.14. All companies shall leave one Passport on their vehicle and place their second Passport on theStatus Board at the designated accountability location prior to entering the hazard zone.
1.15. The first vehicle to each geographic side of the incident becomes the initial accountability location for all later arriving companies to that side of the incident.

5.1. As the incident escalates, Division and Group Supervisors shall assume the responsibility of collecting Passports and maintaining accountability for all crews under their control in the hazard zone.

1.16. If Division or Group Supervisors are operating within the hazard zone, Passports must remain outside the hazard zone with a designated accountability officer. The Division or Group Supervisor should assign someone this responsibility.
6. Level III Accountability –High Rise Accountability
6.1. All companies shall bring both Passports and status board to the lobby.
6.2. There are two accountability locations in a high-rise incident:
6.2.1. Lobby Control Accountability
6.2.2. Forward Accountability
6.3. Lobby Control Accountability
1.16.1. The first company to arrive at the lobby shall place their small status board in the lobby.
1.16.2. The initial incident commander will designatewho is in charge of accountability.
1.16.3. All companies that enter the lobby shall place a passport on the lobby accountability board.
1.16.4. Chief Officers shall bring their large accountability boards to use as the incident escalates.
6.4. Forward Accountability
1.16.5. Forward Accountability is located at least one floor below the hazard zone, and records personnel operating in the hazard zone.
1.16.6. Forward accountability shall record the names of individual actually in the hazard zone.
1.16.7. The hazard zone at a high-rise incident is defined as the fire floor and subsequent floors above the fire floor.
1.16.8. The second engine assigned to the Fire Attack Group shall bring their small status board to the forward accountability point near the standpipe hookup on the floor below the fire.
1.16.9. Any company advancing beyond the floor below the fire floor shall leave a Passport at the forward accountability location.
2. Personnel Accountability Report (PAR)
2.1. A Personnel Accountability Report is a roll call of personnel assigned to the hazard zone.
2.2. For a crew leader, a “PAR” is a confirmation that members assigned to their crew have been visually or verbally accounted for.
2.3. For a Division or Group Supervisor, “PAR” is an accounting for all crew members of all companies in the hazard zone assigned to their division or group.
2.4. For the Incident Commander, “PAR” is an accounting for all personnel in the hazard zone.
2.5. When a Personnel Accountability Report is called for, each crew leader will account for all members of their company and notify the next level of supervision that they have “PAR”.
2.5.1. On small incidents, crew leaders will report “PAR” directly to the Incident Commander.

2.5.2. If Divisions or Groups have been established, crew leaders will report “PAR” to their Division or Group Supervisor. Division and Group Supervisors will report “PAR” to the Incident Commander once all companies assigned to them have reported “PAR”.
2.6. Crew leaders must account for all personnel who have name tags on the passport whether they are actually working directly with the crew leader or not.
2.7. The Incident Commander shall initiate a personnel accountability report for the following situations:
2.7.1. Any report of a missing or trapped firefighter.
6.4.1. Any change from offensive to defensive modes.
2.7.2. Any sudden hazardousevent at the incident - flash over, backdraft, collapse, etc.
6.4.2. At least every thirty minutes.
6.4.3. At a report of Situation Contained.
2.7.3. Any othertime the Incident Commanderor Safety Officer feels is necessary.
6.5. Lost, Missing, or Trapped Firefighter
2.7.4. An absent memberof any crew will automatically be assumed lost or trapped in the hazard zone.
2.7.5. Crew leaders must immediately report any absent members directly to the Incident Commander.
2.7.6. Upon receiving a report of a lost, missing or trapped firefighter the Incident Commander must initiate the following:
6.5.1.1. Request the next greater alarm.
6.5.1.2. A roll call (PAR) of all companies assigned in the hazard zone.
2.7.6.1. Send the Rapid Intervention Team to the last reported working area of the lost firefighter to begin a search.
2.7.6.2. Adjust on-scene strategies to a priority search and rescue effort.
2.7.6.3. Move operating companies not involved in the rescue effort to the appropriate “CHANGE” talkgroup (SOP 01-02-02).
7. Terminating the Passport System
2.8. Passport Accountability must be maintained through a report of Situation Contained, at which time a Personnel Accountability Report (PAR) for all crews must be obtained.
2.9. After the situation is contained, the Incident Commander will determine when to terminate Accountability, and will announce it on all talkgroups being utilized.
2.10. Upon release from the incident, crew leaders will ensure that Passports are returned to their vehicles and the Passport is accurate.
1. Administration

1.1. Purpose: The purpose of this procedure is to provide for the safety of firefightersby requiring a rapid intervention component any time firefighters are operating in an Immediately Dangerous to Life or Health (IDLH) atmosphere.

1.2. Responsibility: It shall be the responsibility of each member to know, understand, and utilize these procedures as they apply to the situation at hand. It shall further be the responsibility of all Division Officers to train their subordinates in the proper application of these procedures and to implement and enforce the use of these procedures.
2. General
2.1. Compliance with this procedure will require a minimum of four firefighters to be present prior to any entrance in an IDLH atmosphere.

1.3. This procedure must be followed by all Division personnel prior to entry into any structure fire, as well as other emergency response operations in any IDLH, potential IDLH, or unknown atmosphere.
1.4. If four firefighters are not initially present, some other activities that may be performed include: exterior or transitional attack, exposure protection, equipment setup, and water supply.
3. Two-In/Two-Out
1.5. The “initial stages” refers to the tasks undertaken by the first arriving fire companies operating in the hazard zone.

1.5.1. In the “initial stages” of an incident where only a few companies are operating in the hazard zone, a minimum of four firefighters are required, consisting of at least two firefighters working as a team in the hazard zone, and at least two firefighters present outside the hazard zone for assistance or rescue of the firefighters in the hazard area (“Two-In/TwoOut”).
1.6. The standby members shall be responsible for maintaining a constant awareness of the number, location, function, time of entry, and identity of the members operating inside the hazard zone.
1.6.1. One of these members shall remain in radio, visual, voice, or signal line communication with the crew operating inside the hazard zone.
1.7. One of the standby members shall be permitted to perform other functions such as apparatus operator or Incident Commander.
1.8. The standby members shall be utilized to perform a rescue of the operating crew, or mitigate other life-threatening situations if necessary.
1.9. If the standby members are utilized for any reason, the Incident Commander shall announce this on the B# FG talkgroup.
1.9.1. The Fire Alarm Office shall relay this message to all responding companies.
1.10. If the incident is not quickly stabilized, a Rapid Intervention Team (RIT) Group shall be established.
1.10.1. Initially, the RIT Group may be staffed by one company; it should be staffed by a minimum of two companies as soon as possible.
3.1. Exception
1.10.2. If initial attack personnel find a known life-hazard situation where immediate action could prevent the loss of life, deviation from the twoin/two-out policy is permitted.
1.10.3. This exception is for a known life hazard only, not for standard search and rescue activities. Any such deviations must be exceptions, and not standard practice.

1.10.4. Any deviation from the Two-In/Two-Out policy shall be reported to incoming companies by radio immediately. A thorough investigation and written report must be submitted in a timely manner to the Division Safety Officer.
2. Rapid InterventionTeam (RIT) Group

2.1. On all working incidents beyond the initial stages, at least one Rapid Intervention Team (RIT) Group shall be established and maintained by the Incident Commander. This shall include all incidents where an interior fire attack is made, or whenever an operation places personnel in a hazard zone.

2.2. The RIT Group shall be maintained at least until a “Situation Contained” is reported. After the situation is contained, the Incident Commander will determine when the RIT Group is no longer necessary.

2.3. If the RIT Group is utilized, the Incident Commander must immediately make arrangements to replace them. If on scene resources are not adequate to accomplish this, additional companies must be requested.

2.3.1. If a company assigned to the RIT Group is assigned other duties on the fireground, the Incident Commander shall ensure adequate companies are responding or available to establish a two company RIT Group.
2.4. On multiple alarms and complex incidents, more than one RIT Group may be appropriate. The Incident Commander shall determine the appropriate number of RIT Groups for the incident.
2.5. The initial RIT Group may consist of an Engine, Ladder, or Rescue company. It should be transitioned to at least two companies as soon as possible.
2.6. The RIT Group composition should be flexible and its structure shall be at the discretion of the Incident Commander based on the type and complexity of the incident.
2.7. The RIT Group should be made up of personnel who are not performing other fireground functions.
2.8. The RIT Group shall be fully dressed and standing by with the appropriate equipment, ready for immediate deployment.
2.9. The standby location of the Rapid Intervention Team shall be at the discretion of the Incident Commander, but close to the Command Post is usually appropriate.
2.10. The RIT Group Supervisor should attempt a 360 of the structure, review personnel accountability, and function as the initial safety officer until relieved by SO-2.
2.11. The crew should stretch and charge an attack line to be deployed if necessary.
2.12. The Incident Commander may designate a RIT Group Supervisor. If none is designated, the senior ranking officer of the RIT Group shall assume this responsibility.
2.13. The location and assignment of the RIT Group shall be announced on the appropriate radio talkgroup by the Incident Commander when a Fixed Command is established.
4. Equipment
2.14. The minimum equipment that should be assembled in the staging area shall be:
4.1.1. ResidentialStructures
4.1.1.2. Chain saw and circular saw with metal cutting blade
4.1.1.3. Attic ladder
4.1.1.4. RIT pack
4.1.1.5. Two (2) thermal imaging cameras
4.1.1.6. Hand tools
4.1.1.7. Charged hoseline
4.1.2. Commercial Structures
4.1.2.1. 200’ search rope
4.1.2.2. Chainsaw and circular saw with metal cutting blade
4.1.2.3. Two (2) thermal imaging cameras
4.1.2.4. Hand tools, rabbit tool, battering ram
4.1.2.5. Stokes basket
4.1.2.6. RIT pack
4.1.2.7. Charged hoseline
2.15. Powered equipment shall be started and brought to operating temperature while standing by.
2.16. This list is a minimum requirement and by no means is the only equipment that may be assembled. Additional equipment may be required depending on the situation.
5. Use of theRIT Universal Air Connection (RIT UAC)
2.17. In some instances, membersmay have to replenish the air supply of a down firefighter. Air supply may be replenished using the RIT Pack.
2.18. The preferred method of air replenishment is the use of the high-pressure quick fill line (RIC UAC).

2.19. If this method is not feasible, or more than one firefighter is in need of air, rescuers may choose to utilize the regulator from the low-pressure side of the system to provide an emergency air supply (aka “Hot Swap”).
1. Administration
1.1. Purpose: The purpose of this procedure is to identify Emergency Evacuation procedures.

1.2. Responsibility: It shall be the responsibility of each member to know, understand, and utilize these procedures as they apply to the situation at hand. It shall further be the responsibility of all Division Officers to train their subordinates in the proper application of these procedures and to implement and enforce the use of these procedures.
2. General
1.3. The Emergency Evacuation Signal will be transmitted whenever ALL PERSONNEL are required to IMMEDIATELY leave the Hazard Zone due to personal safety.
1.3.1. When an Emergency Evacuation is initiated, personnel should not remain in the hazard zone to reposition lines or retrieve equipment.
2.1. Examples of reasons to use the Urgent message are, but not limited to:
2.1.1. Drastic change in fire conditions
2.1.2. Collapse Potential
2.1.3. Backdraft or Explosion Potential
3. EmergencySignalon Radios
3.1. Follow Urgent or Mayday Communication SOP 01-02-04.
4. Air Horn Blast
1.4. The Air Horns of all apparatus in proximity of the Hazard Zone will be activated for a period of 10 seconds. This will be followed by 5 seconds of silence and another blast of 10 seconds.
5. Accountability
5.1. A PAR will be conducted per SOP 02-01-01.
1. Administration
1.1. Purpose: The purpose of this procedure is to identify functions and responsibilities of a rehab area at emergency incidents.

1.2. Responsibility: It shall be the responsibility of each member to know, understand, and utilize these procedures as they apply to the situation at hand. It shall further be the responsibility of all Division Officers to train their subordinates in the proper application of these procedures and to implement and enforce the use of these procedures.
2. General
1.3. Proper rehab of firefighters at an emergency incident allows for better efficiency and productivity, and above all, a higher degree of safety for firefighting forces.
3. Initiation
1.4. A“Rehab Group” will be initiated under the following circumstances:
3.1.1. At the request of the Incident Commander
3.1.2. At the request of the Safety Officer
3.1.3. At all 2ndAlarm and Higher Incidents
3.1.4. At all Working HazMat Incidents where an entry will be made
4. Rehab Group
4.1. Command/Staff
1.4.1. The Rehab Group will report directly to the Safety Officer or the Incident Commander in the absence of a Safety Officer.
1.4.2. The Rehab Group will be directly supervised by the Second EMS Supervisor assigned to an incident or any member directed by the Incident Commander.
1.4.3. At least one Transport vehicle with a crew of two medics will be assigned to rehab.
1.4.4. Other companies maybe assigned as the Incident Commander deems necessary.
1.4.5. The Rehab Group Officer will work with the members of Box 15 in order to avoid duplication of efforts and increase rehab effectiveness.
4.1.1. The ICS Structure would be as follows:
4.2. Location
4.2.1. Should be as free from the stresses of the incident as possible.
1.4.6. If it is cold or wet, the rehab should be warm ordry; if it is hot, rehab should be cool and moist.
1.4.7. Garages, nearby building lobbies, and shaded areas make good rehab areas.
1.4.7.1. In high rise fires, the Rehab Group will be located on the appropriate floor below the fire per High Rise SOPs.
1.4.7.2. COTA buses, school buses, or other commercial vehicles may be used if necessary.
4.3. Functions
1.4.8. Hydration
4.3.1.1. Drinking water shall be made available at the rehab group.
1.4.8.1. At least 8 oz. will be given to each member upon entering rehab.
1.4.8.2. Other drinks may include:
4.3.1.1.1. Commercially prepared rehab drinks
4.3.1.1.1.1. Gatorade, Sportade, etc.
4.3.1.1.1.2. These will be mixed 50/50 with water
4.3.1.1.2. Coffee, tea, or hot chocolate
4.3.1.1.3. Soft Drinks
1.4.8.2.1. These drinks will only be given after the initial 8 oz of water is consumed.
4.3.2. Nourishment
1.4.8.3. At all incidents longer than four (4) hours in length, or during the normal mealtime hours, food should be considered.
4.3.2.1. Foods that maybe used are as follows:
4.3.2.1.1. Broth or Soup
1.4.8.3.1.1. These are much faster digested than solid foods.
1.4.8.3.1.2. These provide replacement of nutrients not available elsewhere.
4.3.2.1.3. Sandwiches or snack
4.3.2.1.4. Fatty and/or salty foods should be avoided.
1.4.8.3.2. Rotation of companies in order for them to return to quarters to eat is another option.
4.3.3. Rehab
4.3.3.1. Members shall be sent to rehab after:
1.4.8.3.3. They have used two consecutive SCBA cylinders until the 50% yellow LED activates
1.4.8.3.4. They have used 75% or greater of one SCBA cylinder (as indicated by activation of the Vibra-alert or the HUD’s red LED)
4.3.3.1.1. They have worked for forty-five minutes
4.3.3.2. Memberswill stay in rehab until released by the rehab supervisor.
4.3.3.2.1. Rest periods will be no less than ten minutes.
1.4.8.3.5. No crew or membermay leave rehab unless released by the rehab supervisor.
1.4.8.4. When members are released from rehab theymay be reassigned or released as designated by the IC.
4.3.4. Medical Evaluation
1.4.8.5. Medical personnel shall evaluate all members entering for rehab. The following items shall be documented:
4.3.4.1.3. SpO2 (pulse ox)
4.3.4.1.4. Temperature
4.3.4.1.5. EKG (if indicated)
4.3.4.1.6. Other signs and symptoms noted by rehab staff
1.4.8.6. If medical treatment is provided, it shall be documented in an EMS incident report.
2. Accountability
4.4. Passports
2.1.1. Passportswill be turned in to the Rehab Staff upon entering.
4.4.1. Passports will be picked up upon release.
1. Administration
1.1. Purpose:The purpose of this procedure is to identify functions of “Staging”.

1.1. Responsibility: It shall be the responsibility of each member to know, understand, and utilize these procedures as they apply to the situation at hand. It shall further be the responsibility of all Division Officers to train their subordinates in the proper application of these procedures and to implement and enforce the use of these procedures.
2. General
1.2. The objective of the staging procedure is to provide a standard system of initial placement for responding apparatus, personnel, and equipment.
2.1. Effective utilization of this procedure:
2.1.1. Will prevent excessive apparatus congestion at the scene.
1.2.1. Will allow time for the Incident Commander to evaluate conditions priorto assigning companies.
1.2.2. Places apparatus in an uncommitted location close to the immediate scene to facilitate more effective assignment by the Incident Commander.
1.2.3. Produces more effective communications by virtue of reducing radio traffic during the critical initial stages of fire operations.
3. Staging Levels
3.1. LevelI Staging applies to all multiple company responses on the First Alarm.
1.3. Level II Staging applies to greater alarm responses and large, complex- type incidents requiring an on-scene reserve of companies that will require a formal staging area.
1.3.1. Level II Staging includes a Staging area and the Staging Area Manager functions (SOP 02-02-06).
1. Administration
1.1. Purpose: The purpose of this procedure is to identify the response areas for first alarm companies at an “A” Assignment.

1.2. Responsibility: It shall be the responsibility of each member to know, understand, and utilize these procedures as they apply to the situation at hand. It shall further be the responsibility of all Division Officers to train their subordinates in the proper application of these procedures and to implement and enforce the use of these procedures.
2. Level I Staging
2.1. Arrival of First Engine
1.2.1. The first Engine shall place itself in a position to use its hose line to the best of their ability.
1.2.2. Location of hydrants, obstructions, and hard surfacesmay dictate other than ideal placement.
2.2. Arrival of First Ladder
1.2.3. The first Ladder will generally take the front of the structure or a position that will be most suitable for the use of the aerial.
1.2.4. Obstructions such as overhead wires, trees, or unstable ground may require other than ideal placement.
2.3. Arrival of Second Engine

1.2.5. The second Engine will place itself at a hydrant in order to assist with water supply. If no water supply is needed, the second engine will move closer to the scene to be used should the first engine fail. The two Engines should be positioned so that supply is set up in series (either the engine at the hydrant pumping to the other on the scene, or a line laid from a hydrant to one of the engines on the scene who will then pump to the other engine on the scene), this procedure will create a backup should one engine fail.
2.4. Arrival of First Rescue
1.2.6. The first Rescue will generally place itself in a position as close to the Structure as possible without interfering with incoming companies.
2.5. Arrival of Battalion Chiefs
1.2.7. Battalion Chiefs will position themselves as close to the incident as possible without interfering with incoming companies.
2.6. Arrival of Medics

1.2.8. First Medic will be responsible for supporting the First Engine or First Ladder. They shall don all full PPE in accordance with SOP 01-04-01 while working in the hazard zone. If victim care is needed upon arrival to the scene or at any time prior to the arrival of the second medic, the first medic will cease all other operations and assist the victims.
1.2.9. Second Medic will be responsible for victim care, rehab, and care of the firefighting crew.
2.7. Other Companies

1.2.10. All other companies will stage their apparatus in a way so as to not impede any other companies or traffic, unless for safety purposes. Their apparatus will only be brought to the scene if equipment is needed the IC deems necessary.
1. Administration
1.1. Purpose: The purpose of this procedure is to identify assignments and placement for a Fire Response.

1.2. Responsibility: It shall be the responsibility of each member to know, understand, and utilize these procedures as they apply to the situation at hand. It shall further be the responsibility of all Division Officers to train their subordinates in the proper application of these procedures and to implement and enforce the use of these procedures.
2. Fire Response Assignment
1.3. The Fire Alarm Office will dispatch a ‘Fire Response’ to all reports of a fire in a structure.
1.3.1. The Fire Response assignment will consist of three (3) Engines, two (2) Ladders, one (1) Rescue, one (1) Medic, and one (1) Battalion Chief.
1.3.2. All companies dispatched on a Fire Response shall initially respond in the “emergency” mode.
1.3.2.1. The initial on-scene Incident Commander should consider downgrading the response mode forany company still responding if conditions warrant.
1.4. The arrival sequence ofcompanies will determine their Level I Staging responsibilities.
3. Incident Command
1.5. It shall be mandatory for the first arriving company or division member to establish command, give the radio report, and direct incoming companies.
1.6. The initial Incident Commander shall be responsible for developing and implementing the Incident Action Plan that will include either:
3.1.1. An investigation plan, or
3.1.2. A fire attack plan and a search plan
1.7. The command post ordinarily should be situated at the front or address side of the incident.
1.7.1. The Incident Commander shall announce the location of the Command Post over the radio.
1.8. All companies shall bring their Passport to the designated accountability location and follow Level II Accountability procedures formultiple company responses (See SOP 02-01-01).
4. Level 1 Staging: Nothing Showing/Investigation Mode
1.9. At single and double family residential structures the first engine and ladder should investigate the situation.
1.10. On all sprinklered buildings the first company to arrive shall send a person to locate and check the annunciator.

1.11. On large buildings where the floor is not designated and nothing is showing, the Incident Commander shall use, with the exception of the pump operator, the personnel on the first arriving engine company and the first arriving ladder company to search the inside of the building.
1.12. Companies shall conduct a reconnaissance of the building or incident scene for information.
1.12.1. If smoke is encountered, the officer should direct teams of two people to search that area and move at least one firefighting company into position to fight fire when it is discovered.
1.13. Companies not assigned as part of the initial investigation shall stage in a place that provides the best position to deploy if assigned by the Incident Commander.
1.13.1. The second engine company shall stage at hydrant with crew intact, and report their placement to Incident Command.
2. Level 1 Staging: Smoke or Fire Showing
2.1. First Engine
4.1.1. The first engine is responsible for initiating fire attack.

2.1.1. If fire or smoke is showing, and there is any doubt about the ability to control the situation with the engine’s tank, or it will be some time before the next engine company will be able to lay a line, a supply line should be laid going in.
2.1.2. The first engine company should proceed to the area that will facilitate the quickest and most direct attack on the fire.
2.1.2.1. Placement of the engine should consider ladder company access to the building.

2.1.3. On large buildings, if the floor is designated, the first engine company should go to the floor below and advance via the stairs to the fire floor. If the building is equipped with a standpipe system, they shall take their standpipe kit and hose with them.
2.1.3.1. If the fire is above the third floor and it is known the standpipe system will be used, the first arriving engine company may be used to lay lines to the standpipe connection.
4.2. First Ladder
2.1.4. The first ladder company should proceed to the scene and take a position that will best facilitate rescue, ventilation, roof access, and/or fire control.
2.1.5. The first ladder shall be responsible for rescue, ventilation, and to determine if the fire is extending.
4.3. Second Engine
2.1.6. Unless orders are received from the Incident Commanderprior to orafter arrival, the second engine company shall be responsible for:
2.1.6.1. Establishing a water supply to the first engine and/or sprinkler and standpipe system.
4.3.1.1. Establish a backup line.
4.4. Second Ladder

2.1.7. The second arriving ladder company should take a position that will enable them to operateat the rear of the incident. This company should remain flexible so if the aerial is needed in other areas, it will be able to respond with a minimum of delay.
4.5. Third Engine
2.1.8. The third arriving engine company will make up part of the Rapid Intervention Team (RIT) Group.
2.1.9. The company commander shall ensure their vehicle does not block access to the scene and are in position to use their equipment if necessary.
2.1.10. They shall assemble close to the command post in full PPE with SCBA and RIT equipment (SOP 02-01-03) and be ready for immediate deployment.
2.1.11. The officer should attempt a 360 of the structure, review personnel accountability,monitorall talkgroups in use, and function as the initial safety officer until relieved by SO-2.
2.1.12. The crew shall stretch and charge an attack line to be deployed if necessary.
4.6. Rescue Company
2.1.13. The rescue company shall be responsible for search and rescue, utilities, and other tasks as assigned by the Incident Commander.
2.1.14. Care should be taken that their apparatus does not block access to the incident scene or does not become blocked in at the scene.
4.7. Battalion Chief
2.1.15. TheBattalion Chief shall assume command when arriving with the initial companies.

2.1.16. If the Battalion Chief has been preceded to the scene, upon arrival he/she shall conduct a transfer of command briefing with the officer being relieved (SOP 01-03-05), followed by a Status Report transmitted on the appropriate talkgroup(s).
2.1.17. The Battalion Chief shall monitor“B# CFD FG” and “B# CFD IC” talkgroups.
4.8. Medic

2.1.18. The medic vehicle and crew should, if possible, be located near the command post, and beprepared to care for injured personnel or citizens. They should remain flexible so that if needed in other areas they will be able to respond with a minimum of delay.
2.1.18.1. Care should be taken that their apparatus does not block access to the incident scene or does not become blocked in at the scene.

2.1.19. If no victims are present or expected, the first arriving medic may don full protective equipment and assist with firefighting duties as assigned by their company commander or the Incident Commander.
2.1.19.1. If assisting a fire company, they shall follow Accountability procedures (SOP 02-01-01) and report their intentions with the Incident Commander.
5. Working Fire
5.1. Working Fire Assignment

2.1.20. Unless otherwise directed by the Incident Commander, the Fire Alarm Office will automatically dispatch an Engine, Ladder, Medic, Battalion Chief, EMS Supervisor, and Safety Officer to all working incidents.
2.1.21. The Incident Commander should conduct an ongoing needs assessment to determine if these, or other, resources will be necessary.
2.1.22. The Fire Alarm Office shall notify the IncidentCommanderof any company unavailable to respond (e.g., SO-2, Rescue).
5.2. Arrival of the Fourth Engine
5.2.1. Stage approximately 200 feet from incident orin a safe location.
5.2.2. Await assignment by the Incident Commander.
5.3. Third Ladder
2.1.23. The third arriving ladder company will make up part of the Rapid Intervention Team (RIT) Group.
2.1.24. The Company Commander shall ensure that their vehicle does not block access to the scene and are in a position to use their equipment if necessary.
2.1.25. They shall assemble close to the command post in full PPE with SCBA and RIT equipment (SOP 02-01-03) and be ready for immediate deployment.
2.1.26. If a RIT company is assigned other duties on the fireground, the Incident Commander shall ensure adequate companies are responding or available to establish a two company RIT.
5.4. Second Medic
2.1.27. The second medic on the scene of a working fire shall standby for patient care.
2.1.28. The second medic shall bring all ALS equipment, backboard, and cot to a location near the Command Post and standby in a ready position.
2.1.29. The medic vehicle should be positioned so asnot to impede access in to or out of the scene.
5.5. Second Battalion Chief
2.1.30. The second arriving Battalion Chief will report to the Incident Commander for assignment.
2.1.31. The second Battalion Chief should generally take a position that allows him/her to see the opposite side of the structure as the Incident Commander.
2.1.32. At large or complex incidents, the Incident Commander should consider assigning the second Battalion Chief as a Division or Group Supervisor.
2.1.33. The second Battalion Chief shall monitor “B# FG” and “B# IC” talkgroups.
5.6. Arrival of the EMS Supervisor
2.1.34. Unless otherwise assigned, the EMS supervisor will standby with the second medic.
2.1.35. If needed, the EMS supervisor may be assigned as the EMS Group Supervisor.
2.1.36. If an EMS Group is established, the “BN# EMS” talkgroup should be utilized.
5.7. Arrival of the Safety Officer
5.7.1. The Safety Officer shall monitor overall scene safety.
5.7.2. The Safety Officer shall monitor the “B# FG” and “B# IC” talkgroups.
6. Additional Alarms
2.2. Additional alarms are called at the discretion of the on-scene Incident Commander.
2.3. If the incident goes to a multiple alarm, the on-duty Deputy Chief (ES-2) shall be dispatched by the Fire Alarm Office.
6.1.1. Upon arrival, the Deputy Chief shall assume command of the incident.
2.4. Level2 Staging (SOP 02-02-05) will be an automatic procedure when dispatched to a multiple alarm.
1. Administration
1.1. Purpose: The purpose of this procedure is to identify the response to an “Alarm” assignment.

1.2. Responsibility: It shall be the responsibility of each member to know, understand, and utilize these procedures as they apply to the situation at hand. It shall further be the responsibility of all Division Officers to train their subordinates in the proper application of these procedures and to implement and enforce the use of these procedures.
2. Fire Alarm Classifications
2.1. Fire Alarm “A” (FA)

1.2.1. Occupancies included in this category are: double- and single-family residence, small apartment buildings, strip malls, and small mercantile; and other occupancies not classified as high life hazard.
2.2. Fire Alarm “B” (FAB)

1.2.2. High life hazard occupancies including multi-family apartments, hospitals, hotels, nursing homes, big box stores, warehouses, large industrial/manufacturing facilities, industrial complexes, schools, churches.
2.2.1. A Fire Alarm “B” will be sent on all water flow alarms.
2.3. Fire Alarm “High Rise” (FAH)
1.2.3. Commercialand residential occupancies greaterthan six stories above ground.
2.4. Modified Alarm Response
2.4.1. A modified response based on potential limited resource availability.
1.2.4. Initiated by the Fire Alarm Office with the approval of the Emergency Services Deputy Chief (ES-2).
2.4.2. Modified Alarm Response applies to all occupancy types.
1.2.5. Assignmentmay be modified by the Fire Alarm Office or first-due company officer based upon additional information.
3. Fire Alarm Assignments
3.1. Fire Alarm “A” (FA)
3.1.1. (1) Engine and (1) Ladder
3.2. Fire Alarm “B” (FAB)
3.2.1. (1) Engine, (1) Ladder, and (1) Battalion Chief
3.3. Fire Alarm “High-Rise” (FAH)
3.3.1. (2) Engines, (1) Ladder, and (1) Battalion Chief
3.4. Modified Alarm Response
3.4.1. Closest appropriate company
3.4.2. Company responds on Emergency
4. Upgrading/Downgrading/Canceling Alarm Assignments
1.3. After dispatch, alarm assignments can be upgraded to a fire response by the Fire Alarm Office or responding companies based on additional information received.

1.4. After dispatch, alarm assignments can be cancelled or downgraded to a single company response by the responding Battalion Chief (on “B”Alarms) or first in company officer (on “A” Alarms), based on additional information received from the Fire Alarm Office or information gained from a previous response to the same address.
1. Administration
1.1. Purpose: The purpose of this procedure is to identify the response procedures for Level II Staging.

1.2. Responsibility: It shall be the responsibility of each member to know, understand, and utilize these procedures as they apply to the situation at hand. It shall further be the responsibility of all Division Officers to train their subordinates in the proper application of these procedures and to implement and enforce the use of these procedures.
2. General
1.3. Level II Staging applies to greater alarm responses and large, complex-type incidents requiring an on-scene reserve of companies that will require a formal staging area.
1.3.1. The staging area should be away from the Command Post and from the emergency scene in order to provide adequate space for assembly and for safe and effective apparatus movement.
1.3.2. When the Incident Commander announces a formal staging area, all responding companies will report to and remain in the staging area until assigned a task by the Staging Area Manager.
3. Level II Staging
1.4. Level II Staging will be an automatic procedure when dispatched to a multiple alarm incident.

1.5. The Incident Commander may designate a staging area and a Staging Area Manager who will be responsible for the activities outlined in this procedure. If this occurs the companies dispatched on the multiple alarm will respond to the designated staging area, report to the Staging Area Manager in person and be guided by his/her directions.
1.5.1. If a staging area is designated but no Staging Area Manager is assigned, the Fire Alarm Office will assign the first-due engine as the Staging Area Manager.
1.5.2. If no staging area or Staging Area Manager is designated, the Fire Alarm Office shall announce the Staging Area Manager, who will then designate the location of the staging area.

1.5.3. If the initial Staging Area Manager is a ladder or Mutual Aid company, the first arriving Columbus engine company shall assume the role of the Staging Area Manager. MutualAid command officers may be used as the Staging Area Manager at the discretion of the Incident Commander.

1.6. After the staging area is designated, the Fire Alarm Office will notify all future incoming companies to respond on the specific battalion Staging Talkgroup. (e.g., If the fire is assigned to “B1 FG” talkgroup, staging will be on the “B1 Staging” talkgroup).
1. Administration
1.1. Purpose: The purpose of this procedure is to identify the roles of theStaging Area Manager.

1.2. Responsibility: It shall be the responsibility of each member to know, understand, and utilize these procedures as they apply to the situation at hand. It shall further be the responsibility of all Division Officers to train their subordinates in the proper application of these procedures and to implement and enforce the use of these procedures.
2. General
1.3. When a formal staging area will be established, the first company commander to arrive at the approximate location will automatically become the Staging Area Manager.
1.3.1. The Staging Area Manager shall notify the Incident Commander of his/her arrival over the “B# IC” talkgroup, and the exact location of the staging area.

1.4. Due to the limited number of ladder companies, if the first arriving officer is in charge of a ladder company, he/she will transfer command of the staging area to the first arriving engine company officer.
1.5. The radio designation for the person in charge of staging area will be "Staging Area Manager."
1.5.1. Communications between the Staging Area Manager and the Incident Commander shall be conducted on the “B# IC” talkgroup.
1.6. All responding companies will respond directly to the designated staging area, and report in person to the Staging Area Manager on the “B# Staging” talkgroup.
1.6.1. Companies will remain by their apparatus; crew intact; with warning lights off, unless warning lights are needed to protect the crew or apparatus.
1.7. All communications from companies dispatched on the multiple alarm from the time of dispatch until assigned a task on the fireground will take place on the “B# Staging” talkgroup.
3. Staging AreaManager Role
1.8. When requested by theIncident Commander, the Staging Area Manager will assign companies to report to specific Divisions or Groups, telling them location, radio talkgroup, and supervisor.
1.8.1. The Staging Area Manager will advise the Incident Commander of the specific companies assigned. The Division orGroup supervisormay then communicate directly with the company.

1.9. The Staging Area Manager will give the Incident Commander periodic reports of available companies in the staging area. If requested to do so by the Incident Commander, the Staging Area Manager may utilize the Staging Talkgroup to communicate directly with the Fire Alarm Office for additional resources.
4. Staging Area Responsibilities
1.10. Coordinate with the police to block streets, intersections, and other access required for the staging area.

1.11. Assure that all apparatus is parked in an appropriate manner. The parking can be arranged to keep company types in specific areas in order to help the Staging Area Manager keep better track of companies. The diagonal, headout, parking method is advised in orderto keep companies out of the way and organized while allowing for response of vehicles out of the staging area when necessary.

1.12. Maintain a list of companies available in the staging area and inventory all specialized equipment that might be required at the scene. This shall include Accountability for all staged resources.
1.13. Review with the Incident Commander what resources must be maintained in the staging area and coordinate the request for these resources with the Fire Alarm Office.
1.14. Assume a position that is visible and accessible to incoming and staged companies. This will be accomplished by leaving the emergency lights operating on his/her apparatus.
1.15. In some cases, the Staging Area Manager may have to indicate the best direction of response and routing for responding companies to get into the staging area.
5. Staging Area Resources

1.16. Unless otherwise instructed, the Staging Area Manager will advise the Incident Commander when the level of resources in the staging area is depleted to two engines and one ladder or less. The Incident Commander will make a decision whether or not to call for additional units or to call for an additional alarm.

1.17. The Incident Commander may instruct the Staging Area Manager to maintain a base level of resources until further advised. In such circumstances, the Staging Area Managerwill communicate directly with the Fire Alarm Office to request additional units.

1.18. Medics and EMS Supervisors responding to incidents when Level II Staging has been established will be dispatched to the staging area. The Staging Area Manager will acknowledge the arrival of the medics with the Fire Alarm Office and will give instructions to the medic personnel as requested by the Incident Commander.
1.18.1. AnEMS supervisor should assist the Staging Area Manager, when necessary, in organizing EMS personnel and vehicles.

1.19. A major medical emergency may require a separate staging area for medics. In such cases, the Staging Area Manager will so designate and relay this information to the Incident Commander and the Fire Alarm Office. Columbus Columbus Division Division of Fire | S.O.P. 02-02-07

02-02-07.t: Staging for Behavioral Health (BH) and Attempt
p: 1 Administration
1.1 Purpose: The purpose of this procedure is to identify the response procedures for EMS Staging Tiers I,II, and III.

1.2 Member safety is our absolute priority. This directive establishes a standardized Tiered EMS Response Model for all Behavioral Health (BH) and Suicide Attempt incidents. No CFD unit shall enter an unknown or unverified scene blindly. Units must wait for Columbus Division of Police (CPD) clearance or Fire Alarm Office (FAO) risk verification as outlined below.

1.3 Responsibility: It shall be the responsibility of each member to know, understand, and utilize these procedures as they apply to the situation at hand. It shall further be the responsibility of all Division Officers to train their subordinates in the proper application of these procedures and to implement and enforce the use of these procedures. 2 General
2.1 EMS Tier Level Staging applies to responses to Behavioral Health (BH) and Suicide Attempts.
2.2 Staging areas should be away from and not in direct view of the scene. 3 Fire Alarm Office (FAO) Risk Triage Criteria
3.1 The FAO will use a holistic evaluation based on caller type (patient, family, PD, healthcare) and diagnostic questioning.
3.1.2 Patient speech capabilities (complete sentences vs. confusion).
3.1.3 History of BH, previous suicide attempts, or psychiatric medications.
3.1.4 Presence of, or immediate access to, weapons.
3.1.5 Physical injuries or active threats of harm to self/others.
3.1.6 Scene atmosphere (chaotic background noise, alcohol or drug involvement). Columbus Columbus Division Division of Fire | S.O.P. 02-02-07 4 Tier I: Respond to Scene Behavioral Health (BH)

4.1 Criteria: Low-risk controlled environments. No immediate threat identified through specific call-taker criteria to the caller on patient history for violence, weapons, aggressiveness displayed or history, medicines for BH, alcohol or substance use or abuse, and many other criteria.
4.2 Action: Units are authorized to enter the scene immediately upon arrival.

4.3 Response Mode: Typically, “emergency” response. Signal “X” should be utilized, when appropriate based on specific FAO direction and messaging on patient injury and illness. 5 Tier II: Stage Near Scene Behavioral Health (BH)
5.1 Criteria: Potential risk is identified, or safety unverified, but suspicion of patient injury/ medical need is high or confirmed.
5.2 Action: Units must wait at a safe distance, out of line-of-sight. Do not enter until CPD explicitly confirms the scene is secured.
5.3 Response Mode: An emergency response shall be utilized. 6 Tier III: HOLD (non-dispatched) Behavioral Health (BH)
6.1 Criteria: Incident details are unknown or insufficient to determine scene safety.
6.2 Action: Run is placed on "HOLD" in CAD and routed to CPD for initial investigation.
6.3 CFD Dispatch: CFD units will not be dispatched unless CPD arrives, secures the scene, and requests medical assistance. 7 Tiers and Mandatory Actions: “Attempt” responses.
7.1 FAO risk assessment questioning based on the type of caller (patient, family, healthcare, PD, other PSAPS, etc.). 8 Tier I: Suicide Attempt-Respond to Scene = Medic
8.1 Criteria: Run Type indicates an actual suicide attempt that has been made.
8.2 Action: Low risk scene where crews respond immediately. This is a scene with a non-life-threatening patient in a controlled environment.

8.3 Response Mode: A Signal “X” response should be utilized. Response mode can be changed based on updated scene intelligence received from the FAO or other responders on the scene. 9 Tier II: Suicide Attempt-Stage near Scene = Medic and EMSO
9.1 Criteria: Run type indicates an actual suicide attempt has been made.

9.2 Action: HIGH RISK scene where crew will stage near the scene and wait on CPD to arrive and advise when scene is secured. This is a scene with a potentially threatening patient in an unsecured environment. Columbus Columbus Division Division of Fire | S.O.P. 02-02-07

9.3 Response Mode: Signal “X” response should be utilized when responding to the “staging” location. An emergency response into the scene once secured, is appropriate. 10 Tier III: Suicide Attempt-HOLD (non-dispatched)
10.1 Criteria: This is a typical call where the details of the scene are unknown or not enough information to arrive at a safe Run Type.
10.2 Action: This call gets put on HOLD and sent back to CPD for a Unit to be dispatched and investigate.

10.3 Response: When CPD arrives on scene they will advise the FAO when the scene is secured and provide more information on the current situation. The CFD response will be based on “condition” found and relayed to us by on scene CPD units. 11 Crew Authority & Dynamic Safety Upgrades
11.1 Criteria: Dispatch Instructions represent a baseline. Responding crews maintain full authority to upgrade response levels based on real-time field intelligence.
11.2 Dynamic Staging: If dispatched as a “respond to scene” but scene sizeup suggest a threat, units must switch to “staging” immediately.

11.3 Retreat: If a scene becomes unsafe after arrival, crews should, if possible and safe to do so, retreat, upgrade the assignment to a “BH”-Stage or “attempt” stage, and request immediate CPD assistance (10-57).

11.4 Emergency Assistance: If a situation escalates to a direct threat after patient contact, call for immediate CPD response (10-3). The FAO will immediately upgrade the incident to Firefighter in Trouble (FIT) and dispatch emergency backup.

11.5 Safety: Better questioning from the call-taker position allows for more robust scene safety assessment than past triaging. Crew members have the autonomy to change their status to “stage” or back-out of situations where crew safety is threatened or at risk.
1. Administration
1.1. Purpose: The purpose of this procedure is to identify the responsibilities of companies working at one- or two-family residential fires.

1.2. Responsibility: It shall be the responsibility of each member to know, understand, and utilize these procedures as they apply to the situation at hand. It shall further be the responsibility of all Division Officers to train their subordinates in the proper application of these procedures and to implement and enforce the use of these procedures.
2. Responding
1.3. Officer will develop a preliminary action plan for his/her company based on information available.
2.1. Officerwill clearly assign duties that deviate from standard practice.
2.2. Radios will be changed to appropriate talkgroup.
3. Arrival
1.4. The action plan for all fires should be based on the RECEO VS acronym as outlined below. These functions are to be performed in order of priority as below (except Ventilation and Salvage).

1.4.1. Rescue – This will be the primary concern on all fires in residences. If persons are reported trapped or it is a possibility, hose crews should be positioned in order to protect occupants and crews performing rescue.
1.4.2. Exposure – Protection of exposures, whether internal or external, shall be the next concern for the IC.
1.4.3. Confinement – Containing the fire to an area or building shall be the next concern for the IC.
1.4.4. Extinguishment – Total extinguishment of the involved fuels will be the next concern for the IC.
1.4.5. Overhaul – Searching for hidden fire or rekindle possibilities will be the next concern for the IC.
1.4.6. Ventilation and Salvage – These can be inserted and performed at any point in the order of priority above as deemed necessary by the IC based on the conditions present.
4. Operations
4.1. Fire Attack
4.1.1. Suppression devices will be determined by the officer in charge.
4.2. Backup Lines
4.2.1. Willbe in place as soon as possible after an interior attack is initiated.
4.3. Supply Lines
1.4.7. Should be laid and charged whenever interior crews are expected to use more than 25% of the vehicles water tank capacity.
4.3.1. Supply Lines for Residential Fires should be 5” LDH.
1.4.8. 3” Supply lines can be used for the purpose ofrefilling the tank or to maintain a water supply for overhaul and mop-up operations.
4.4. Ground Ladders
1.4.9. Shall be place in service when any floor of thebuilding is above ground level or when companies are working on the roof.
1. Administration
1.1. Purpose: The purpose of this SOP is to identify the procedure to be used when a transitional fire attack is determined to be appropriate.

1.2. Responsibility: It shall be the responsibility of each member to know, understand, and utilize these procedures as they apply to the situation at hand. It shall further be the responsibility of all Division Officers to train their subordinates in the proper application of these procedures and to implement and enforce the use of these procedures.
2. General
1.3. A transitional fire attack will be initiated on structure fires that have fire venting from openings that are readily accessible upon arrival.
1.4. The IC shall determine if flowing water through an opening is the quickest means of applying water to the fire.
1.5. The IC will announce over the assigned talk group when a transitional attack is being used.
2. Transitional Fire Attack
2.1. Procedure
2.1.1. Direct a straight or solid stream at a high angle through the bottom half (air inlet) of the opening to deflect water off the ceiling of the fire compartment.
2.1.1. Flowwater long enough to darken down and cool the fire area.
2.1.2. Do not rotate or whip the nozzle as this may impede the exit flow of hot gases from the top halfof the window and cause a shift in the flow path.
2.2. If conditions permit, immediately following the knockdown, an interior advance to the seat of the fire (direct attack) should be conducted.
2.3. Consider keeping the exterior line in place in the event that a second exterior application of water is necessary.
2.4. If resources permit, consider deploying multiple lines simultaneously to allow a direct attack to commence in coordination with the transitional attack.
1. Administration
1.1. Purpose: The purpose of this procedure is to establish the operation procedures for below grade fires.

1.2. Responsibility: It shall be the responsibility of each member to know, understand, and utilize these procedures as they apply to the situation at hand. It shall further be the responsibility of all Division Officers to train their subordinates in the proper application of these procedures and to implement and enforce the use of these procedures.
2. General
1.3. Life safety and information obtained during the initial 360 survey shall be used to determine the presence of a basement fire and the appropriate tactics to be used.
1.3.1. If the approximate location of the fire is identified during the 360 survey, it shall be announced over the radio (B# FG) along with attack strategy being implemented.

2.1.1. Example: “All companies from E14, the fire is in the basement near the CharlieDelta area; E14 will be applying water from the Bravo side basement window prior to advancing through the Alpha side entryway.”
1.4. Basement fires often quickly involve the floor system and may result in an early collapse of the floor system above the fire.
1.4.1. A thermal imaging camera may be helpful in determining the presence and location of a basement fire, but cannot be relied upon to determine structural integrity of the floor above the fire.
1.5. If heavy smoke or fire conditions exist upon arrival, implement tactics that do not place firefighters above the involved area of the basement prior to the application of water on the fire.
1.6. A charged hoseline must be in place prior to entry into the structure at any basement fire.
3. Basement Fire Tactics
1.7. If a basement fire is suspected after the 360 survey, a Transitional Fire Attack (SOP 02-03-02) shall be attempted.
1.7.1. When possible, the transition line shall be maintained at the vent opening and ready to be placed back in service if necessary while a second attack line is stretched to the seat of the fire.
1.7.2. Firefighters should avoid operating directly over the fire area prior to the application of water on the fire.
1.8. If no fire is visible from the exterior and basement exterior access is available, the attack shall be initiated from the exterior basement access.
1.8.1. When a basement exterior access is uncontrolled, ventilation from above should not be initiated until after ‘water on the fire’ is announced.

1.9. If no fire is visible upon arrival, and no exterior basement access is available, an interior attack from above may be initiated using closest access to basement stairs. Personnel should avoid working above the involved area.

1.10. Coordinated ventilation at basement fires is critical. Ventilating the basement from above when a lower-level ventilation opening exists, creates a flow path to the upper opening and may result in a sudden increase in fire intensity.
1.10.1. Opening or breaking of basement windows prior to ‘water on the fire’ being announced should only be done to perform a transitional fire attack.

1.11. If unable to access the basement from an exterior position, consider using a cellar nozzle, a piercing nozzle or cutting through the wall, bandboard, or first floor to apply water from the exterior.
1.12. Operating on the floor above the fire prior to exterior water application to the basement shall only occur in extreme situations.
1. Administration
1.1. Purpose: The purpose of this procedure is to identify the response to an alarm or a fire in a high-rise building.

1.2. Responsibility: It shall be the responsibility of each member to know, understand, and utilize these procedures as they apply to the situation at hand. It shall further be the responsibility of all Division Officers to train their subordinates in the proper application of these procedures and to implement and enforce the use of these procedures.
2. Fire Alarm
1.3. The response fora fire alarm shall be two (2) Engines, one (1) Ladder, and one (1) Battalion Chief.
2.1. Level I Staging: Nothing Showing
1.3.1. The Investigation Group will consist of one (1)Engine and one (1) Ladder.
2.1.1. The second engine should stage at the fire department connection.
1.3.2. The crew shall report to the lobby with equipment and initiate Lobby Control.
2.1.2. The Battalion Chief shall assume incident command.
2.2. Level I Staging: Smoke or Fire Showing
1.3.3. If smoke or fire is discovered, Incident Command shall upgrade the assignment to a High-Rise Fire Assignment.
1.3.4. The Investigation Group shall form the Fire Attack Group on the floor below the fire.
1.3.5. The second engine shall report to the Fire Attack Group on the floor below the fire.
1.3.6. The second engine operator shall coordinate with the first engine operator the water supply and series pumping to the fire department connection (see below).
3. Fire Response
3.1. The response for a reported fire in a high rise shall be four (4) Engines, two (2) Ladders, one (1) Rescue, two (2) Battalion Chiefs, one (1) Medic, and one (1) EMS Supervisor.
3.2. Level I Staging: Report of a Fire in a High Rise
1.3.7. All companies shall bring both Passports and their Small Status Board to their reporting location and follow Level III Accountability procedures for High-Rise Incidents (See SOP 02-01-01).
3.2.1. First Engine
1.3.7.1. The crew should report to the lobby and establish the Fire Attack Group.
1.3.7.2. The first engine operator shall coordinate with the second engine operator the water supply and series pumping to the fire department connection.
1.3.7.2.1. The appropriate inlets of the fire department connection shall be connected with high-pressure hose.
1.3.7.2.2. If equipped with a two-stage pump, it shall be in the pressure mode.
1.3.7.2.3. If a fire department connection is not present or OOS, the engine operator shall establish an alternate supply to the building.
1.3.8. First Ladder
1.3.8.1. The interior crew shall join the Fire Attack Group.
3.2.1.1. The first ladder should be positioned where it can be best utilized.
3.2.2. Second Engine
1.3.8.2. The crew shall join the Fire Attack Group.
1.3.8.3. The second engine operator shall coordinate with the first engine operator the water supply and series pumping to the fire department connection.
1.3.8.3.1. The appropriate inlets of the fire department connection shall be connected with high-pressure hose.
1.3.8.3.2. If equipped with a two-stage pump, it shall be in the pressure mode.
1.3.8.3.3. If a fire department connection is not present or OOS, the engine operator shall establish an alternate supply to the building.
3.2.3. Third Engine
1.3.8.4. The third engine shall establish the Lobby Control/Building Systems Group.
1.3.8.4.1. Locate initialAccountability and assume lobby control responsibilities.
3.2.3.1.1. Obtain a large status board for Lobby Accountability.
3.2.3.1.2. Lobby Control may expand as the incident expands.
3.2.4. Fourth Engine
1.3.8.5. The fourth engine should proceed to the floor below the fire and form the Rapid Intervention Team (RIT).
3.2.4.1.1. The crew should bring the following items:
3.2.4.1.1.1. High rise hose pack (150’)
3.2.4.1.1.4. Hand tools
3.2.4.1.2. The RIT should expand as the incident expands.
3.2.5. Second Ladder and Rescue
1.3.8.6. The second ladder andrescue will become the Upper Search and Evacuation (USE) group.
1.3.8.7. The stairwells, the floor above the fire and the top floor will be the first floors to consider when searching.
3.2.5.1. The remainder of the floors will be searched systematically.
3.2.6. Medic
1.3.8.8. If no victims are present or expected, the first arriving medic may be utilized to assist the Lobby Control Group.
3.2.7. EMS Supervisor
1.3.8.9. The EMS Supervisor shall report to the Incident Commander and establish the Medical Branch.
3.2.8. Battalion Chiefs
3.2.8.1. The first battalion chief shall assume a fixed command.
3.2.8.1.1. An exterior CommandPost is desirable.
1.3.8.10. The second battalion chief shall report to the Command Post with full PPE, SCBA, and a Large Status Board, and be prepared to operate in a forward area.
1.3.8.11. The High-Rise Response SOP is a Level I Staging guideline; the Incident Commander may deviate from this procedure in order to accomplish incident priorities.
4. Working Fire Response
1.4. Unless otherwise directed by Incident Command, when a working fire in a high rise is confirmed, the Fire Alarm Office will automatically dispatch the following additional companies:
4.1.1. Two (2) Engines
4.1.2. Two (2) Ladders
4.1.3. One (1) Battalion Chief
4.1.4. One (1) Medic
4.1.5. One (1) EMS Supervisor
4.1.8. Command 18
4.2. Level I Staging: Working Fire Companies
1.4.1. Working Fire companies shall report to the Command Post for assignment based on the incident goals and objectives.
1. Administration
1.1. Purpose: The purpose of this procedure is to identify the responsibilities of command at a fire in a high-rise building.

1.2. Responsibility: It shall be the responsibility of each member to know, understand, and utilize these procedures as they apply to the situation at hand. It shall further be the responsibility of all Division Officers to train their subordinates in the proper application of these procedures and to implement and enforce the use of these procedures.
2. General
2.1. Initiating Command
1.2.1. The first company officer on scene shall assume a fixed command until relieved by a chief officer.
1.2.1.1. He/she shall place a member in charge of their crew or give the remainder of their crew to a group supervisor.
1.2.1.2. Once relieved of command he/she can move up to join their crew or the Incident Commander may reassign them as needed.
2.1.1. An exterior CommandPost is desirable.
2.1.1.1. Command18 should be requested with a working fire.
2.1.2. Asecond alarm shall strongly be considered with a working fire.
2. Command Responsibilities
2.2. The Incident Commander shall be responsible for the following actions:
2.1.1. Develop the incident action plan
2.2.1. Determine the overall strategy
2.2.2. Establish Goals and Objectives
2.2.3. Provide status reports and benchmark completions
2.2.4. Request appropriate resources
2.2.5. Demobilize units after a situation contained
2.2.6. Overall incident safety
2.2.7. Personnel accountability
3. Command Structure
2.2. The Incident Commander shall build a command structure to meet the complexity of the incident.
2.3. The Incident Commander shall designate Section Chiefs, Branch Directors, Division and Group Supervisors.
2.4. Emphasis shall be placed on staffing the Fire Attack Group, Lobby Control Group and Upper Search and Evacuation (USE) Group.
2.5. Based on the incident objectives, the IncidentCommander should consider assigning the second battalion chief to supervise one of the Divisions or Groups.
2.6. Based on need and incident complexity, the Incident Commander should consider establishing the following components in the organizational structure at a high-rise fire:
3.1.1. Fire Attack Group
3.1.2. Lobby Control Group
3.1.3. Systems Group
3.1.4. Upper Search and Evacuation (USE) Group
3.1.5. Rapid Intervention Team (RIT) Group
3.1.6. Resource Group
3.1.7. Medical Branch
3.1.8. Ventilation Group
3.1.9. Utilities/Salvage Group
3.1.10. Stairwell Support Group
3.1.11. Rehab Group
3.1.12. Divisions
3.2. Communications
2.6.1. A high priority should be placed on establishing communications with companies operating inside of the building.
2.6.2. Communications should be established using the most efficient and effective means.
2.6.3. Communications within the building should be established in this order of priority:
3.2.1.1. Radios using TAC channels
3.2.1.2. DIRECT A, B, and/or C
3.2.1.3. Building hand-held fire phones
3.2.1.4. Other means of communication
1. Administration
1.1. Purpose: The purpose of this procedure is to identify the functions of the High-Rise Fire Attack Group.

1.2. Responsibility: It shall be the responsibility of each member to know, understand, and utilize these procedures as they apply to the situation at hand. It shall further be the responsibility of all Division Officers to train their subordinates in the proper application of these procedures and to implement and enforce the use of these procedures.
2. General
1.3. The first two engines and the first ladder will be designated as the Fire Attack Group.
1.3.1. The Incident Commander will designate one of the engine company officers as the Fire Attack Group Supervisor.
1.3.2. The Fire Attack GroupSupervisor assists with line advancement and communicates the ladder companies search progress to Incident Command.
1.4. The Fire Attack Groupwill determine the fire floor via the annunciatorpanel or recon.
1.5. The Fire Attack Group shall designate and announce the attack stairwell and the evacuation stairwell.
1.6. The Fire Attack Group should assemble and initiate the fire attack from the floor below the fire.
2.1. The objectives of the Fire Attack Group will be:
2.1.1. Place an attack line in service
1.6.1. Rescue occupants near the seat of the fire
2.1.2. Recon the fire areas
1.7. All activities of the fire attack group must support the first attack line. The success of the fire depends on the ability of the Fire Attack Group to extinguish the fire.
2.2. Eachengine companyshall bring the following equipment:
2.2.1. High Rise Pack consisting of:
2.2.1.2. 2½” nozzle w/ 1¼” to 1⅛” stacked tip
2.2.2. High Rise Kit consisting of:
2.2.2.1. Inline pressure gauge w/ elbow
2.2.2.2. 18” pipe wrench
2.2.2.3. Fittings and spanners
2.2.2.4. PRV adjustment rod and sockets
2.2.2.5. Door wedges
1.7.1. The second engine shall bring their SmallStatus Board and place it near the standpipe hookup on the floor below the fire for Forward Accountability.
2.3. The ladder company shall bring:
2.3.1. Forcible entry tools, including a hydraulic forcible entry tool
2.3.3. Water can
2.3.4. Pike poles
3. Actions
1.8. The ladder company shall provide reconnaissance information, forcible entry and search and rescue starting in the fire area.
1.9. The engine companiesshall work togetherto get one line in service. The following positions shall be created to assist in moving the attack line:
3.1.1. Nozzleman: Operatesnozzle
1.9.1. Fire Attack Group Supervisor: Supervises and assists handline advancement
1.9.2. Backup Firefighter: Moves hose from the fire floor stairwell to the fire area
1.9.3. Door Firefighter: Works in the stairwell between fire floor and floor below, and assists in moving hose up the stairwell
1.9.4. Control Firefighter: Monitors pressure on the in-line pressure gauge and moves hose from the floor below into the stairwell
1.10. The attack line shall be connected at least one floor below the fire floor with in-line pressure gauge connected directly to the riser.
1.11. The hose line shall be flaked out on the floor below the fire floor with adequate water supply and pressure verified before moving into the fire area.
3.2. Pressure Reducing Devices and Valves
1.11.1. If a Pressure Reducing Valve (PRV) orPressure Reducing Device (PRD) is on the standpipe outlet, the Fire Attack Group Supervisor shall be notified.
1.11.2. If the PRV is adjustable the Fire Attack Group Supervisor should consider increasing the setting if the flow is inadequate.
3.2.1. IncidentCommand shall be notified if a non-adjustable PRV is present.
3.2.2. PRDs shall be removed.
1. Administration

1.2. Responsibility: It shall be the responsibility of each member to know, understand, and utilize these procedures as they apply to the situation at hand. It shall further be the responsibility of all Division Officers to train their subordinates in the proper application of these procedures and to implement and enforce the use of these procedures.
2. General
2.1. Lobby Control will be assigned to the third engine and first medic to arrive.
1.3. The officer in charge of the third engine will become the Lobby ControlGroup Supervisor. As the incident expands the structure of Lobby Control may expand.
2.2. SystemsControl will initially be part of Lobby Control.
1.3.1. A separate Systems Control Group may need to be established at some incidents.

3.1. Lobby Control Functions
3.1.1. Assume control of Lobby Accountability.
1.3.1.1. The crew shall bring their small status board along with forms and pens/pencils.
3.1.1.1. A large accountability board shall be obtained.
3.1.2. Maintain an activity log.
1.3.1.2. Lobby Control establishes a control point to serve as a gateway to access other areas within the building.
1.3.1.3. All companies/equipment that enters the building shall filterthrough Lobby Control.
1.3.1.4. Lobby Control shall record the company designation and assignment for all companies entering the building. Consider using the form ICS 214 for this purpose.

3.2. Systems Control Functions
1.3.2. Systems Control is responsible for evaluating and monitoring the functions of built-in fire protection, life safety, environmental control, communications and elevator systems.
3.2.1.1. Contactthe building engineer or building fire safety director.
1.3.2.1. Gain control of the building communication systems: public address system, hand held fire phones, building Walkie-talkies.
1.3.2.2. Assign firefighter to check the operation of the fire pump and report the pump discharge pressure to the IC.
3.2.1.2. Locate the elevator control room.

1.1. Purpose: The purpose of this procedure is to describe the functions of the high-rise Upper Search and Evacuation (USE) Group.

1.2. Responsibility: It shall be the responsibility of each member to know, understand, and utilize these procedures as they apply to the situation at hand. It shall further be the responsibility of all Division Officers to train their subordinates in the proper application of these procedures and to implement and enforce the use of these procedures.
2. General
1.3. The Upper Search andEvacuation Group shall be established at all working incidents in a high-rise building.
3. Actions
1.4. The second ladder and first rescue will form the Upper Search and Evacuation (USE) Group. The complexity of the incident will determine the final number of crews operating within the USE Group.
1.4.1. The officer in-charge of the ladder will be the USE Group Supervisor, and will report directly to the Incident Commander.

1.4.2. Companies assigned to the USE Group shall bring both Passports and their Small Status Board to their reporting location and follow Level III Accountability procedures for High-Rise Incidents (See SOP 02-01-01).
1.4.3. Crews shall bring the following equipment: thermal imaging camera, forcible entry tools, rabbit tool, 200’ rope, water cans.
1.5. The initial operating location of the USE Group will be dynamic. It shall adjust to the priorities and complexity of the incident, and based on coordination with the Fire Attack Group.
1.6. The USE Group Supervisor should communicate with the Fire Attack Group Supervisor and verify the Tactical Plan, including the verification of attack stairwell and evacuation stairwell(s).
3.1. The priority for the Primary search and evacuation should be:
3.1.1. Attack stairwell
3.1.2. Evacuation stairwell
3.1.3. The floor above the fire
3.1.4. The top floor
3.1.5. Elevators
3.1.6. Other areas
1.7. Emphasis should be made on the control of stairway doors, fire doors, and ventilation openings. Conditions in the attack stairwell should be evaluated as it is searched.
1.8. If the attack stairwell has a roof access door, opening or closing of this door shall be coordinated with the Fire Attack Group Supervisor.
1.9. All essential reports, findings, and fire extension conditions above the fire floor should be communicated to the Upper Search and Evacuation Group Supervisor.
1.10. Victims removed from hazard areas shall be taken to the Casualty Collection Point (CCP).
3.2. Occupant Evacuation Control
1.10.1. It may not be necessary to remove occupants on all floors (especially in residential buildings), and self-initiated evacuation should be controlled to the extent possible.
1.10.2. Occupant evacuation control should be accomplished with the use of an in-house public address system or intercom.
1.10.2.1. Announcements should be made to all floors.
1.10.2.2. An evacuation order shall be issued only to those floors in immediate danger, or those affected by smoke.
1.10.2.3. If a protect-in-place strategy is decided, then this announcement should be communicated to the occupants in these areas.
3.2.1. Attack stairwells should not be used for evacuation.
