1.1. Purpose: The purpose of this procedure is to identify considerations for highrise Ventilation.

1.2. Responsibility: It shall be the responsibility of each member to know, understand, and utilize these procedures as they apply to the situation at hand. It shall further be the responsibility of all Division Officers to train their subordinates in the proper application of these procedures and to implement and enforce the use of these procedures.
2. General
1.3. Establishing the Ventilation Group should be considered at incidents requiring multiple resources to effect building ventilation.

1.4. Ventilation procedures will be implemented and evaluated by the Incident Commander based on the type of building, location of the fire, and information from personnel operating in the hazard zone.
1.5. Initial ventilation priority shall be given to coordinating the shut-down and/or operational control of the heating, ventilation, and air conditioning (HVAC) system.
1.5.1. Building engineer or maintenance personnel shall be utilized to achieve this objective.
1.6. Effective ventilation, specifically above the attack stairwell and in the evacuation stairwells, is dependent on the following factors:
1.6.1. Location of the fire and extent of smoke conditions
1.6.2. Building and fire floor layout
1.6.3. Wind velocity and direction
1.6.4. Accessible horizontal and vertical openings (e.g., stairwell exterior openings and roof access).
2.1.1. Smoke stratification and stack effect
2.1.2. Carbon monoxide levels on upper floors
1.7. All ventilation shall be coordinated with fire attack. Uncoordinated ventilation may result in an undesirable flow path.
1.8. Breaking window glass on upper floors of a high-rise building can be extremely injurious to bystanders and firefighting personnel and should be avoided.
1.8.1. If breaking glass is necessary, it should be coordinated with Incident Command and safety precautions should be taken in the areas that will be affected by falling glass.

1.1 Purpose: The purpose of this procedure is to identify responsibilities of companies responding to “High” and “Low” Risk Advanced Life Support (ALS) Incidents of Chest Pain (CP) and Difficulty Breathing (DB).

1.2 Responsibility: It shall be the responsibility of each member to know, understand, and utilize these procedures as they apply to the situation at hand. It shall further be the responsibility of all Division Officers to train their subordinates in the proper application of these procedures and to implement and enforce the use of these procedures.
1.3 Definitions: Call types for “Chest Pain” and “Difficulty Breathing” will now be triaged as “High” or “Low” based on specific call-taker criteria. 2 Response for “Low-Risk” Call Types
1.4 Criteria: Patient age less than 50 years, with no high-risk symptoms
2.1.2 Response: One (1) Medic Unit.

2.1.2.1 Arrival: The Medic crew will perform a scene size up before or while initiating patient contact. The Paramedic shall initiate and complete a full patient assessment. The crew should determine if additional resources are needed, and request those resources as appropriate.
2.1.2.2 Complete all required documentation per Division policy.
2.4 First Responder:
2.4.1 An Engine or Rescue shall be sent at the request of the responding Medic crew or the FAO to meet defined City of Columbus response times.

2.4.2 If the Engine or Rescue Company arrives on the scene first, the paramedic(s) will proceed into the scene along with a reasonable number of crew members, usually three is sufficient. The crew should carry in the appropriate medical equipment using the information from the original dispatch message, suggestions from the paramedic, and the directions of the officer. The driver shall generally remain with the apparatus and monitor the talkgroup being used. 3 Response for “High-Risk” Call Types
3.1 Criteria: Patient age greater than 50 (or <3 for DB) weight >300 lbs., non-ambulatory, 3rd floor or higher, or high-risk symptoms (diaphoretic, color change, cardiac history)
3.1.2 Response: One (1) Medic Unit and One (1) Engine or one (1) Rescue.

3.1.3 Arrival: The Medic crew will perform a scene size up before or while initiating patient contact. Paramedic shall initiate and complete full patient assessment. The crew should determine if additional resources are needed, and request or cancel those resources as appropriate.

3.1.4 If the Engine or Rescue arrive on the scene first, the paramedic(s) will proceed into the scene along with a reasonable number of crew members, usually three is sufficient. The crew should carry the appropriate equipment using the information from the original dispatch message, suggestions from the paramedic, and the directions of the officer. The driver shall generally remain with the apparatus and monitor the talkgroup being used.
3.1.4.1 Complete all required documentation per Division policy.

1.1 Purpose: The purpose of this procedure is to identify procedures for companies responding to Basic Life Support (BLS) incidents.
1.2 Definition: Basic Life Support Incidents (BLS) are patient events that historically do not require invasive clinical intervention or transportation to the Emergency Department.

1.3 Responsibility: It shall be the responsibility of each member to know, understand, and utilize these procedures as they apply to the situation at hand. It shall further be the responsibility of all Division Officers to train their subordinates in the proper application of this procedure and to implement and enforce the use of these procedures. 2 Response
2.1 Calls for service that the Fire Alarm Office (FAO) determines through specific call taker criteria are low acuity in nature, will get a response of one non-transport ALS apparatus.
2.1.1 Run type examples” Personal assists, tasered persons, law enforcement requests for detainee evaluation, person down, etc.
2.2 One (1) Engine or (1) Rescue.
2.2.1 Signal “X” response should be utilized.

2.3 Paramedics and EMT’s will use medical protocols, directives (both written and verbal), bulletins, and other pertinent division information to make the following decisions based on sound medical care. The goal of the decision-making process shall be to do what is best for the patient, as well as the residents of the City of Columbus as a whole.
2.3.1 Based on the above criteria, the crew will do one or more of the following:

1. Administration

1.1. Purpose: The purpose of this procedure is to identify functions of companies dispatched to water rescue incidents. Rescue Technicians may function to their respective level of training as it relates to NFPA1670 unless otherwise noted. Non-rescue technicians will be limited to shore-based rescue operations only, unless it is critical to the operation.

1.2. Responsibility: It shall be the responsibility of each member to know, understand, and utilize these procedures as they apply to the situation at hand. It shall further be the responsibility of all Division Officers to train their subordinates in the proper application of these procedures and to implement and enforce the use of these procedures.
2. Definitions

1.3. Delta-P – One of the most dangerous hazards to rescuers are known as "Delta P" hazards. Delta P, or differential pressure, presents a unique and potentially fatal hazard to rescuers. The differential pressures occur when two bodies of water intersect, each with a different water level, such as the water levels at a dam, sewer system, or culvert drain.
1.4. Flood Water – Any area or body of water in an area that does not normally hold water. Examples are streets, neighborhoods, parking lots, underpasses, etc.
1.5. Moving Water – Defined in NFPA 1670 as water moving at a rate greater than 1 knot. 1 knot is equal to 1.15 mph or 1.85 km/hr.

1.6. Reach, Throw, Row, Go – The four sequential steps in water rescue with progressively more risk to the rescuer. Specifically, a “go” rescue involves physically entering the medium (e.g., in the water or on the ice). NFPA 1670 3.3.104.
1.7. Static Water – Water that consist of non-moving bodies of water. Examples are ponds, lakes, floods and reservoirs.
2. Response

2.1. A water incident shall be determined by the Fire Alarm Office based upon caller information. Water incidents may include the following, but is not limited to boat responses, swift water rescue, jumper over water, etc.
3. Boat Operations

2.2. In moving water, the boat crew will consist of two rescue technicians. If it is a moving water operation, preference will be given to rescue technicians trained to the water rescue technician level. The boat crew will not exceed two (2) rescue technicians, unless it can be reasonably explained that it is critical to the operation. In static water (lakes, ponds, floods, and reservoirs) the boat crew size can be increased to accommodate DART/Dive operations and or transportation of personnel determined by the I/C Rescue assigned to boat operations.

2.3. While DART divers can dive from inflatable watercraft, offshore dive operations utilize the Connector boats for bestpractice. Consider calling a connector boat if timelines allow early into the incident.

2.4. Conversely, Connectorboats are not suited forfast moving water or launching or loading in remote locations by hand. Consider the need for inflatables or “Jon” boats. The I/C rescue can advise via radio if other watercraft are better suited for the type of water rescue. Best choices are Inflatable, Jon Boat or Connectors.
4. Personal Protective Equipment

2.5. Rescue technicians operating in or on the water shall wear Type 5 PFD equipped with cutting tool, water rescue helmet, safety glasses, gloves, dry suit, boots, throw bag, and chemical light stick for night time identification.
2.6. If a static body of water has ice in or on it, an ice suit, PFD and helmet shall be worn. ICE Suits shall not be used in moving water orfor wading rescues.
2.7. Shore based personnel operating within 15’ of the water, shall wear a PFD, helmet, safety glasses, gloves and be equipped with a throw bag.
4.1. During cold weather, a Coast Guard approved float coat may be used.
2.8. DONOT WEARTURNOUT GEAR ON WATER RESPONSE UNLESS IT IS NECESSARY FOR PROTECTON FROM COLD WEATHER!
3. Types of Incidents
4.2. Static Water
3.1.1. First arriving companies should conduct a scene size up and coordinate all incoming companies.
3.1.2. In case of flood incidents, consider evacuationand shelter in place versus rescue until needed resources arrive.

3.1.3. If victims are visible and needing immediate rescue, members may enact a rescue plan based on Reach, Throw, Row, and Go to the level of their training and available PPE/equipment. Go rescue techniques will only be performed by rescue technicians who have been trained to the swift water technician level according to NFPA 1670.
3.1.4. If victims are not visible, witnesses should be held on scene. Separate and interview them regarding victim locations, names, or other information.
3.1.5. Once DART/Dive operation enacted, all otheroperations in the areawill cease. All work conducted in the area will be coordinated with the DART/Dive supervisor and the Incident Commander.
4.3. Moving Water
3.1.6. First arriving companies should conduct a scene size up and coordinate all incoming companies.
3.1.7. In case of flash-flood incidents, consider evacuation and shelter in place versus rescue until needed resources arrive.

3.1.8. If victims are visible, members may enact a rescue plan based on “Reach, Throw, Row, and Go” to the level of their training and available PPE/equipment. Go rescue techniques will only be performed by rescue technicians who have been trained to the swift water technician level according to NFPA 1670.
3.1.9. If victims are not visible, witnesses should be held on scene.Separate and interview them regarding victim locations, names, or other information.
3.1.10. If a DART/Dive operation is enacted all otheroperations in the area will cease. All work conducted in the area will be coordinated with the DART/Dive supervisor and the Incident Commander.

3.1.11. When operations are underway in or on moving water, safety precautions will be utilized and shall include downstream safety personnel with throw bags and upstream spotters with radios. A safety boat staffed and operational in the water and/or tensioned diagonal can be added if necessary.

3.1.12. Go rescue techniqueswill only be performed by rescue technicians who have been trained to the swift water technician level according to NFPA 1670. If a GO rescue is utilized, a tag line will be attached to the swimmers Type 5 PFD attachment ring with a LOCKING carabiner or directly tied to the ring. Non- Locking carabiners will NOT be used. It is NOT acceptable to attach a rope to anyone in water rescue ops by any other means. The tag line must be manned at all times.
4.4. Ice
3.1.13. First arriving companies should conduct a scene size up and coordinate all incoming companies.
3.1.14. If victims are visible, members may enact a rescue plan based on “Reach, Throw, Row and Go” to the level of their training and available PPE/equipment.
3.1.15. If victims are not visible, witnesses should be held on scene. Separate and interview them regarding victim locations, names, or other information.
3.1.16. If a DART/Dive operation is enacted, all otheroperations in the area will cease. All work conducted in the area will be coordinated with the DART/Dive supervisor and the Incident Commander.
3.1.17. If a rescuer enters the water in Ice rescue PPE, a tag line will be attached to the Sternal attachment point on the ice suit and must be manned at all times.
4.5. Flood Water
3.1.18. In case of flood evacuations, consider evacuation and shelter in place versus rescue until needed resources arrive (in peril vs. uncomfortable).

3.1.19. If wading rescues are utilized, rescuers should identify and avoid drain culverts, storm drains, open manholes and any hazard where Delta-P conditions could exist. At least one crew member should utilize a probe pole to sound the terrain immediately in front of the traveled route.
3.1.20. If evacuating multiple residents, an attempt should be made by the IC to obtain names and addresses of evacuees.

3.1.21. Rescuers should give consideration to avoiding or controlling utility and gaseous hazards such as natural gas, propane, CO and electrical energy from both normal power grids and home generators.
1. Administration
1.1. Purpose: The purpose of this procedure is to identify actions to be taken at suspected explosive incidents to allow for the safety of members.

1.2. Responsibility: It shall be the responsibility of each member to know, understand, and utilize these procedures as they apply to the situation at hand. It shall further be the responsibility of all Division Officers to train their subordinates in the proper application of these procedures and to implement and enforce the use of these procedures.
2. Definition
2.1. Report of a possible explosive device and/or package.
3. Arrival of First Company
1.3. Set up Incident Command at least 300 feet from the location of the suspected device, preferably behind shielding, such as a building, bridge, or wall.
3.1. Give a radio report and direct incoming companies.
3.2. Do not touch, move, ordisturb the suspected device.
3.3. Evacuate the area.
1.4. Setup a hazard zone perimeter of at least 300 feet. CPD can be utilized to secure the area.
3.4. Support the Bomb Squad.
4. Engine Company
1.5. Shall be in position to lay hose lines for exposures and protection of personnel at the direction of the Incident Commander.
5. Medic
5.1. Shall be dedicated to the EMS needs of the Bomb Squad only.
1.6. Additional EMS resources shall be determined and requested by the Incident Commander.
6. Precautions
1.7. Only Bomb Squad personnel and those requested by BS supervisor or Senior Technician shall be allowed to enter the hazard zone.
6.1. No pagers, radios, or cellular phones are to be permitted in the hazard zone.
6.2. Firefighters are not to be used in the search of a suspected device.
7. Media Information
1.8. The Battalion Chief in charge of the scene, orthe PIO, will be responsible to provide media with appropriate information.
1.9. All information regarding the device shall be verified through the BombSquad Supervisor or the Senior Bomb Squad Technician.
2. Bomb Squad Information
2.1. If available, the following information shall be obtained and given to the Bomb Squad upon their arrival.
7.1.1. Exact location of the suspected device.
7.1.2. Description of the suspected device.
7.1.3. Site or floor layout.
7.1.4. Location and number of persons who have not been evacuated.
1. Administration
1.1. Purpose: The purpose of this procedure is to identify activities in the response to Carbon Monoxide alarms.

1.2. Responsibility: It shall be the responsibility of each member to know, understand, and utilize these procedures as they apply to the situation at hand. It shall further be the responsibility of all Division Officers to train their subordinates in the proper application of these procedures and to implement and enforce the use of these procedures.
2. Response
1.3. The FAO will try to determine if an activated CO alarm includes symptomatic victims.
1.3.1. If symptomatic, an appropriate medical response and the closest Columbus ladder company will be dispatched on emergency.
1.3.2. If no symptoms, the closest Columbus Ladderand Rescue Companywill be dispatched on a service run.
3. Investigation
3.1. Medical aid shall be rendered if necessary.
3.2. CO Readings:
1.3.3. First reading shall be taken outside, at least 10 feet away from the structure and any known source of CO such as vehicle exhausts, etc. This reading shall be recorded.
3.2.1. Second reading should be taken just inside the structure.
1.3.4. Monitor CO Detector while checking all suspicious areas and record. If at any time CO readings rise above safe levels (35 ppm or greater) leave structure and return wearing and operating SCBA.
3.3. An attempt should be made to find the source of the CO.
3.3.1. Repairs shall be left to the responsibility of the property owner.
3.3.2. Turn thermostat up to get furnace to start operating.
1.3.4.1. If called to a check a specific room, normally the child’s, go to that room and check air register.
1.3.4.2. Explain to resident thatall rooms would get same readings from ductwork if the furnace is the source.

1.3.5. Turn hot water tank heat setting up so hot water tank will begin operating. After checking for CO, return to original setting. You may have to turn on hot water in sink to get tank to begin heating.
1.3.6. If a gas appliance is suspected, shut the gas off to the appliance, ventilate the area and recheck. Any time gas is shut off, the Gas Company shall be notified.
1.3.7. In multi-family dwellings, if the source of CO cannot be found in the occupancy, attempt to check surrounding occupancies.
1.4. If the difference between any inside reading and the outside reading is Less than 15 PPM:
1.4.1. Advise the occupant that the instruments have detected a level of CO that is not ordinarily considered dangerous to healthy adults.
1.4.2. Advise the occupant ofsymptoms of CO poisoning and to call 911 if symptoms present themselves or the CO detector reactivates.
1.4.2.1. Early warning signs of CO poisoning are headaches, nausea, dizziness, shortness of breath and confusion.
1.5. If the difference between any inside reading and the outside reading is Greater than 15 PPM but Less than 35 PPM:
1.5.1. Advise the occupant that the instrument has detected a level that is above normal and may be dangerous.
3.3.3. Attempt to find and eliminate the source of CO.
1.5.2. Ventilate the area untilCO readings are less than 15 PPM above the outside reading.
1.5.3. Advise the occupants that they may reoccupy the premises at their discretion.
3.4. Ifthe difference between any inside reading and the outside reading is Greaterthan 35 PPM:
1.5.4. Advise the occupant that the instrument detected a dangerous level of CO.
1.5.5. Advise the occupant to leave the premises immediately.
1.5.6. Attempt to find and eliminate the source of CO.
1.5.7. Do not allow occupant reentry until the sourceof CO has been found and eliminated and CO level is below 35 PPM.
1.6. Under all circumstances, advise the occupant to check the CO alarm according to manufacturer’s recommendations and to call 911 if the alarm reactivates or if symptoms become present.
3.4.1. Never indicate that the detector may have malfunctioned.
3.4.2. Never guarantee the safety of the premises.
3.4.3. Never use gas powered fans to ventilate.
3.5. Gas Company
1.6.1. The Gas Company shall be requested anytime the CO level is above normal and a gas appliance is suspected.
1.6.2. UnderNO circumstances should repairs to gas appliances be attempted by Fire Division Personnel.
1.7. Form FP-356 shall be completed on all incidents and the pink copy left for building occupant/owner, white copy attached to white NFIRS-1, yellow copy attached to yellow NFIRS-1.

1.1. Purpose: The purpose of this document is to provide a guideline for the mitigation of spills of common fluids (e.g., gasoline, motor oil, transmission fluid, anti-freeze, hydraulic oil, diesel fuel, etc.) in quantities less than 25 gallons, that do not enter a waterway, body of water, drainage ditch, or storm sewer.

1.2. Responsibility: It shall be the responsibility of each member to know, understand, and utilize these procedures as they apply to the situation at hand. It shall further be the responsibility of all Division Officers to train their subordinates in the proper application of these procedures and to implement and enforce the use of these procedures.
2. Small Spill Mitigation (less than 25 gallons)
1.3. Flushing of vehicle fluids shall no longer be performed except in the instances of life safety of either the patients or the rescuers.

1.4. Spills of common fluids (e.g., gasoline, motor oil, transmission fluid, antifreeze, hydraulic oil, diesel fuel, etc.) in quantities less than 25 gallons, that do not enter a waterway, including a storm sewer, may be handled in the following manner:
1.4.1. Confine the fluid usingstandard dam and diketechniques using available materials.
1.4.2. Use an absorbent to soak up the product, DO NOT FLUSH WITH WATER. The residue is not a hazardousmaterial and may be disposed of as any solid waste.

1.4.3. For trailing spills in the roadway, use absorbent to soak up the product, and let the traffic disperse the absorbent. Be aware that the road may be slippery and appropriate action may be needed. The Street Department can assist with this.
1.4.3.1. Oil-Dry, dry sand, and cellulose absorbents are all good for this type of incident.
1.4.4. At a Vehicle Accident, the wrecker driver is responsible for cleaning up the debris, including the absorbent.
3. Other Spill Mitigation (more than 25 gallons)

1.5. Spills of over 25 gallons, or of any quantity that enters a waterway, any body of water, drainage ditch, or storm sewer, require the immediate notification of the Ohio EPA (1-800- 282-9378) and Franklin County EMA (614-469-9700). Clean up will be under their direction.
3.2. Releases from underground storage tanks also require the notification of the Bureau of Underground Storage Tanks (1-800-686-2878).
3.3. Clean-up of all materials is the responsibility of the owner of the released product.
Section 1 Administration

1.1 Purpose: The purpose is to identify response procedures for first alarm companies to a report of an odor of natural gas or natural gas leak and define what constitutes a major gas emergency, along with other important definitions. Also to outline initial actions, safety considerations, and special circumstances for responding to natural gas emergencies.

1.2 Responsibility: It shall be the responsibility of each member to know, understand, and utilize these procedures as they apply to the situation at hand. It shall further be the responsibility of all Division Officers to train their subordinates in the proper application of these procedures and to implement and enforce the use of these procedures.
Section 2 Definitions & Safety Considerations
2.1 Natural Gas
2.1.1 Characteristics:
o Physical Property: It is lighter than air and disperses quickly outdoors.
o Accumulation: Inside buildings, it can accumulate in "dead air" spaces such as attics and under staircases.
o Safety Hazard: Extinguishing burning natural gas is generally discouraged, as it converts a visible fire into an invisible explosion hazard.
2.1.2 Physical Properties of Natural Gas:
o Flammable Range: 5% to 15%
o Lower Explosive Range (LEL): 5% (50,000 ppm)
o Upper Explosive Range (UEL): 15% (150,000 ppm)
o Ignition Temperature: 1,163°F
o Vapor Density: .057 to .062 (Lighter than air)
2.2 Liquified Petroleum Gas (Propane)
2.2.1 Characteristics:
o Physical Property: LPG is a gas at normal room temperatures and atmospheric pressures. It will liquefy under moderate pressure, rapidly vaporizing upon release of this pressure
o Accumulation: LPG accumulates in low lying, subsurface or below grade areas.
2.2.2 Physical Properties of LPG.
o Flammable Range: 2% to 10%
o Vapor Density: 1.5-2.0 (Heavier than air).
2.3 Minor Gas Emergency:
2.3.1 Natural gas leak that is not believed to pose an imminent threat to life safety.
2.4 Major Gas Emergency is defined as follows:
2.4.1 Serious damage to major components of the gas infrastructure including main distribution lines, gas service lines and meters.
2.4.2 Detection of 10% Lower Explosive Limit (LEL) or greater, either outside or inside a structure.
2.4.3 Detection of 20% LEL or greater in an unvented subsurface structure (i.e., manholes, sewers, etc.).
2.4.4 Presence of gas in two or more subsurface structures (i.e., manholes, sewers, etc.).
2.4.5 Indications of gas migrating into a building from an outside source.
2.4.6 Gas leaks inside of a structure, and the controlling valve cannot be located or is inoperable
2.4.7 Gas leaking or present inside a wall in a structure.
2.4.8 Gas detected on the outside of any structure, locked or unlocked, believed to be coming from inside the structure.
2.5 General Safety Considerations
2.5.1 Personnel Limits: The number of personnel entering the hazard zone to assess the situation should be kept to a minimum.
2.5.2 Approach Pattern: When possible, personnel should approach structures from the corners rather than the center.

2.5.3 Odorant Failure: Further from the leak source that natural gas has travelled, the more dangerous the situation is. Never rely solely on the smell of gas (mercaptan), as it can be filtered out when passing through the ground (soil) or traveling long distances underground.
2.5.4 Fire Management: Fires should be managed by stopping the flow of gas and eliminating all sources of ignition.
2.5.5 Do Not Extinguish: Under most circumstances, burning gas should not be extinguished.

2.5.6 Main Valve Caution: Responders must differentiate between curb/service valves and main valves. Closing a main valve has far greater ramifications; if you are unsure of the valve type, do not close it.
2.5.7 Consult with gas company personnel to identify the location of any leaks. They can provide additional monitoring instruments to detect gas leaks.
2.5.8 Only the gas company can safely plug or squeeze off Distribution or Service Mains.

2.5.9 Use only intrinsically safe equipment when possible. When forcible entry is required in an explosive environment it should be accomplished using equipment and techniques that will limit the chance of causing a spark.
2.5.10 Maintain awareness/accountability for utility workers working in the hazard zone.
2.5.11 When performing a risk assessment, always fall back on Life Safety.
2.5.12 When operating in the Hazard zone use an intrinsically safe radio.

2.5.13 If gas accumulation is suspected, use caution and discretion when shutting off electric power from an external breaker outside the hot zone or leak area while firefighters or members of the public are still inside the building (be aware of backup power systems, i.e. Generators). Natural ventilation is always preferred in the defined leak area. Be patient when using natural ventilation, do not rush to go in and check readings.
Section 3 Response
3.1 Initial Actions
3.1.1 First Arriving Company

3.1.1.1 The first arriving fire company shall park upwind at a safe distance of 300 feet and avoid parking over manhole covers or other subsurface openings. They will provide the initial radio report and perform a sizeup. The initial Company Officer shall assume Incident Command and designate a staging area for other incoming apparatus.

3.1.1.2 If the situation is identified as a major gas emergency, immediately notify the gas and electric company, establish a hot zone (the initial area should be 150 feet or 1-2 houses in all directions), and begin rapid evacuations of the hot zone. Evacuations should start nearest the leak and move outwards.
3.1.2 Additional Arriving Companies

3.1.2.1 Additional arriving apparatus should position themselves 300 feet upwind. It may be necessary for companies to stage at various locations, including downwind, to block traffic. In such cases, continuous air monitoring outside the vehicle using a Natural Gas (NG) monitor is essential to ensure that neither the vehicle nor its occupants are in an Immediately Dangerous to Life or Health (IDLH) environment, as well as to observe any changing conditions.
3.1.2.2 The first arriving Ladder or Rescue company will conduct the initial investigation and size-up when possible or act as directed by the IC.
3.1.2.3 Engine companies should prioritize securing a water supply and deploying handlines for crews, utility workers, and exposure protection.
Section 4 Operations
4.1 Gas Leak Investigation- No Fire or Explosion
4.1.1 Ensure all personnel are equipped with full protective clothing, including Self-Contained Breathing Apparatus (SCBA), prior to investigation.
4.1.2 Monitor the environment with your combustible gas meter(s) as you approach the area.

4.1.3 When communicating natural gas readings to the Incident Commander, specify the reading, location of the reading, indicate whether they were taken near a gas appliance, and report if the levels are rising, falling, or steady.

4.1.4 Evacuate individuals based on the major gas leak criteria (Section 2.4). Evacuation is mandatory when 10% of the Lower Explosive Limits (LEL) is detected on any Fire Division gas meter. Evacuation is mandatory for fire division personnel when 20% LEL is read except for known life safety mitigation.
4.2 Conducting a Rapid Evacuation of a Structure:

4.2.1 Knock on doors (do not use doorbells) and move from door to door to alert occupants. The intent is to alert occupants to self-evacuate immediately due to the potential for a natural gas explosion.
4.2.2 Advise occupants not to turn lights on or off, use cell phones or any other electronic devices.
4.2.3 If no one answers the door to an area or apartment, members should move on to the next door.
4.2.4 Forcible entry should only be accomplished for a known life hazard and should not be attempted to access areas that show no signs of being occupied.

4.2.5 Discretion should be made when deciding to use an elevator for the evacuation of those with special needs or those requiring other assistance. (Elevator location in respect to location of leak, Level of NG in proximity of the elevator etc.). Elevators create electrical arcs whenever they are activated by the call button or signaled to move.
4.2.6 Attempt to locate the source of the gas and shut it off. If it is an appliance, shut the valve to it. Any time gas is shut off, including even one appliance, the gas company must be notified.
4.2.7 Check all gas appliances, even if you have found what you thought was the source
4.3 Fire or Explosion
4.3.1 Arriving on scene of an explosion, natural gas should be considered a potential cause.

4.3.2 Look for signs of a gas leak (i.e., the smell of gas, flames emerging from cracks in the ground or around foundations, bubbling in puddles). Do not attempt to extinguish flames coming up through the ground. (See 2.2.1 Safety Hazard).

4.3.3 Systematically check the area using combustible gas meters. Start close to the explosion site and take multiple readings. If gas is detected, widen the area of inspection until the readings return to zero.
4.3.4 Always remain aware of the possibility of additional explosions. Secure gas and eliminate all potential ignition sources (preferably from outside the hot zone) to the affected area.
Section 5 Special Circumstances
5.1 Excavation Responses
5.1.1 When a gas line has been struck by a boring machine, backhoe or trencher. Nearby structures and below grade areas should be checked.
5.2 Locked Building with a suspected natural gas leak
5.2.1 Remote shut off ignition sources. (See 2.5.13)
5.2.2 Do not immediately force entry, conduct risk assessment and coordinate with gas company.
5.2.3 Evacuate the Hot Zone prior to forcible entry.
5.2.4 Consider forcing both front and rear doors at the same time.

5.2.5 Allow time for natural ventilation to take place prior to rechecking levels. Continue natural ventilation until source of leak is confirmed and gas levels have dissipated to an acceptable level.
1 Administration
1.1 Purpose: To identify responsibilities of companies responding to vehicle accidents.

1.2 Responsibility: It shall be the responsibility of each member to know, understand, and utilize these procedures as they apply to the situation at hand. It shall further be the responsibility of all Division Officers to train their subordinates in the proper application of these procedures and to implement and enforce the use of these procedures. 2 Actions
1.1 Vehicle accidents will generally be classified as one of the following:
2.1.1 Vehicle Accident with Injury.
2.1.2 Vehicle Accident with possible entrapment or High Risk.
2.1.2.1 High risk incidents may include, but not be limited to, accidents involving elevation change of more than 15 feet, high speed, multiple victims, heavy vehicles, etc.

2.2 Extrication companies will be any company that carries extrication tools and is trained to use them. Extrication companies may be any apparatus type included in the CAD. 3 Upgrading the Assignment
3.1 Any extrication requiring multiple hydraulic rescue tools to be operated simultaneously will be upgraded to a high risk incident immediately.

3.2 Any extrication requiring the use of stabilization equipment exclusive of step chocks will be upgraded to a high risk incident immediately. Columbus Division of Fire S.O.P. 02-13-14 Rev. 05/20/2025 1 of 3 Columbus Division of Fire S.O.P. 02-03-14 Rev. 05/20/2025 2 of 3
3.3 Whenever three or more medic vehicles are assigned, the FAO will dispatch EMS-10.
3.4 Any incident that meets the criteria of a Mass Casualty Incident shall be upgraded accordingly. Refer to SOP #02-03-24. 4 Operations
4.1 Incident command will be established on all auto accident responses and all personnel will operate under the principals of the incident command system consistent with SOP 01-03-01.

4.1.1 The 1st arriving officer will assume command by giving a brief descriptive radio report. The brief initial radio report will only be required for auto accidents when three (3) or more fire apparatus are responding. The officer will then size-up the scene to determine resource needs and perform the following:
4.1.2 Declare a working incident.
4.1.3 Request additional specific resources (additional Medics, CPD, Electric Co., Etc.)
4.1.4 Declare a situation contained with only the needed resources tied up. This informs resources still responding to cancel their response and return to service.

4.1.5 Radio report examples for incidents involving three(3) or more apparatus: “E3 on scene. This accident is on 71 south bound, south of Greenlawn Ave. We have two cars involved, heavy damage to both vehicles, make this a working extrication and add two additional Medics for a total of three,” or “Columbus Fire from Command, send one additional Medic for a total of two, we have a situation contained, tie up Engine 3, Medic 3, and the 2nd Medic.”
4.2 Equipment arriving before the rescue or extrication company will leave ample space for them to get into the scene and work from the vehicle.
4.3 Medical Operations will be per SOP 02-03-05, ALS Response. Upon arrival, the EMS field supervisor will be in-charge of all aspects of patient care.
4.4 Incident command will be established on all incidents consistent with SOP 01-03-04. Columbus Division of Fire S.O.P. 02-03-14 Rev. 05/20/2025 3 of 3
4.5 Engine company responsibilities and duties at the scene include:
4.5.1 All fire personnel not in turnout gear shall wear reflective vest, helmet and gloves when operating on the roadway.

4.5.2 Protection of all fire and civilian personnel at the scene. This may initially require the use of the apparatus and/or flares to block the accident scene. Ensure the wheels are turned in an appropriate direction to avoid the accident scene in the event the apparatus is struck. Consider requesting additional resources as blockers (additional apparatus, police, freeway safety patrol, etc.)
4.5.3 Extending hose lines and/or extinguishers to the scene for fire protection as needed.
4.5.4 Having at least two personnel in full PPE per SOP 01-04-01.
4.5.5 Searching the scene for additional victims. Consider thermal imaging cameras as conditions warrant.
4.5.6 Supporting medic and rescue operations as needed.
4.5.7 Requesting the FAO to notify law enforcement immediately when it is necessary to entirely close a major roadway.

4.5.8 Restoring full or partial traffic movement as soon as safely possible. Vehicles involved in an accident, including those with minor injuries, may be moved as necessary to restore or improve traffic flow. In some cases, this may be prior to the arrival of the law enforcement officers.
4.5.9 Other actions as necessary.
4.6 Rescue and/or extrication company responsibilities and duties at the scene include:
4.6.1 Determining the victim’s survivability.
4.6.2 Securing the rescue area, including stabilization of all vehicles.
4.6.3 Containing or stopping a fuel release.

4.6.4 Packaging, treatment, and protection of the victim prior to extrication. The in-charge rescue, most senior, or highest-ranking rescue technician shall be responsible for directing extrication operations under the direction of the incident commander.
4.6.5 Other actions as necessary.

1. Administration
1.1. Purpose: To provide guidance regarding strategy and tactics at occupancies that are identified as vacant premises.

1.2. Responsibility: It shall be the responsibility of each member to know, understand, and utilize these procedures as they apply to the situation at hand. It shall further be the responsibility of all Division Officers to train their subordinates in the proper application of these procedures and to implement and enforce the use of these procedures.
2. Intent

1.3. It is the intent of this policy to establish procedures to minimize the possibility of serious injury or death in vacant premises through appropriate risk assessment. While the intent of this policy is to offer guidance and a standardized response involving vacant premises with emphasis on safety, the Incident Commander is granted flexibility in the application of the SOP due to circumstances that may be unique to a given incident.
3. Definition
3.1. A vacant premise is defined as:
1.3.1. Temporarily unoccupied buildings, structures, premisesor portions thereof, including tenant spaces.
1.4. Buildings, structures and premises for which an owner cannot be identified or located are considered Abandoned Premises. An Abandoned Premise is a type of Vacant Premise.
4. Attack Precautions

1.5. Initial arriving companies, who observe and identify a working fire in a vacant premise, will notify the FAO and the incident commander of this information upon arrival. Prior to the initiation of an interior attack in a vacant premise with no civilian life safety threat(s), personnel must psychologically adjust to a “NO RUSH” approach, as the greatest life hazard is that of the fire personnel who are entering the premise. In this instance, a slower and more cautious approach to conducting operations is appropriate. More time than usual should be devoted to the size-up of vacant premises.
1.6. The structural stability of the vacant premise or parts of the building will be the most important aspect in determining the initial attack strategy, either offensive or defensive.

1.7. Vacant premises promote the rapid spread of fire, both vertically and horizontally. Doors, windows, and partitions which all normally restrict the spread of flames are often times missing. In addition, possible collapse and extension to exposures requires the rapid application of water to achieve timely fire control and extinguishment.
1.8. The I/C should attemptto minimize the number of personnel in the hazard zone at all times based upon the hazard profile for any given incident.
2. Possible Hazards
2.1. Possible hazards to consider for vacant premises include, but are not limited to, the following:
2.1.1. Structure may already be in imminent danger of collapse
4.1.1. Damage from previous fires
2.1.2. Holes in floors
2.1.3. Missing or weakened stairs, stair treads, and railings
4.1.2. Unstable front or rear porches, stairs or fire escapes
2.1.4. Holes in roof, open, missing or broken skylights
2.1.5. Open and/orunprotected vertical and/or horizontal voids
2.1.6. Breached or missing fire walls
2.1.7. Weakened parapets
2.1.8. Sagging floors, roofs and or roof beams
4.1.3. Missing girders and or floor beams
4.1.4. Missing and/or eccentrically loaded columns
4.1.5. Structurally significant cracks in masonry walls
2.1.9. Unusually heavy water load on roof due to poor drainage
2.1.10. Structure may have “CONDEMNED” signs displayed
3. Marking System for Vacant Premises

3.1. Any vacant or abandoned buildings or structures determined to be unsafe relating to structural or interior hazards shall be marked according to the conditions encountered. The identification marking of such premises will be accomplished by using placards with a minimum size of 24"x 24" with a red background, white reflective stripes and a white reflective border. Identification placards will be located on the front of the structure and be visible from the street.Additional placards shall be applied to the side of each entrance to the structure and on penthouses.Placards shall bear the date of their application to the building and the date of the most recent inspection.
3.2. For the purpose of this policy, premises meeting the criteria to be defined as vacant shall have one of the following classifications:
3.2.1. This symbol (Figure 1) shall mean that the structure had normal structural conditions at the time of marking. Figure 1. Normal Structural Conditions at the Time of Marking

3.2.2. This symbol (Figure 2) shall mean that structural or interior hazards exist and interior fire-fighting or rescue operations should be conducted with extreme caution. Figure 2. Structural or Interior Hazards Exist (diagonal hash may run in either direction)
3.2.2.1. If offensive operations are undertaken in a vacant premise that has the symbol containing one diagonal hash (Figure 2), the following actions should be considered:
4.1.5.1.1. Ventilation shall be coordinated with the fire attack.
3.2.2.1.1. Two means of egress shall be maintained on every floor of the structure.
3.2.2.1.2. Identified hazards shall be communicated to all personnel on the scene.
3.2.2.1.3. Minimal personnel should be utilized for fire control efforts within the structure.
3.2.2.2. It is important to remember that a premise identified with one diagonal hash can, over time, deteriorate and become more dangerous.

3.2.3. This symbol (Figure 3) shall mean that structural or interior hazards exist to a degree that consideration should be given to limit firefighting to exterior operations only, with entry only occurring for known life hazards. Figure 3. Consider Exterior Operations Only
4. Vacant Marker Hazard Identification Symbols
4.1. The following symbols shall be used to designate known hazards on the vacant building marker:
4.1.6. R/O – Roof open
4.1.7. S/M – Stairs, steps, or landing missing
4.1.8. F/E – Avoid fire escapes
4.1.9. H/F – Holes in floor
4.2. An example of the hazard symbols used with marking systems are provided below (Figure 4): Figure 4. Example Hazard Symbol Marking System
4.1.10. R/O or “Roof open” will always be located in the upper quadrant.
4.1.11. H/For “Holes in floor” will always be located in the lower quadrant.
4.2.1. S/M or “Stairs, steps orlanding missing” will always be located in the left quadrant.
4.1.12. F/E or “Avoid fire escapes” will always be located in the right quadrant.

4.3. Markings will be placed on the placard that will indicate the date the building was initially inspected on the bottom left side, and the last time the building was inspected on the bottom right side (Figure 5). Figure 5. Date Markings
5. Safety
5.1. The life safety hazard at a vacant premises is almost solely that of members of the Division of Fire.
5.2. At all times, operations are to be conducted in a disciplined and planned manner with emphasis on the safety of operating personnel.

5.3. Because vacant premises tend to have low victim potential, they should be searched within the limits of safety using a reasonable number of personnel after premises conditions and size-up have been evaluated.
5.4. The intent of this SOP is to minimize the total risk and exposure of fire personnel in response to vacant premises on-scene operations.
5.5. Initial arriving companies, who observe and identify a vacant premises, will notify the FAO and the Incident Commander upon arrival that the premise is vacant.
5.6. Premises identified in this manner may require defensive firefighting tactics and the protection of exposures only, with an emphasis on minimizing risk to firefighting personnel.
5.7. Unmarked vacant premises shall be approached with the same degree of extreme caution as marked structures.
1. Administration

1.1. Purpose: The purpose of this procedure is to provide basic knowledge to assist members when responding to electrical emergencies and establish basic guidelines and procedures in the handling of incidents involving electrical hazards.

1.2. Responsibility: It shall be the responsibility of each member to know, understand, and utilize these procedures as they apply to the situation at hand. It shall further be the responsibility of all Division Officers to train their subordinates in the proper application of these procedures and to implement and enforce the use of these procedures.
2. Overview

1.3. An electrical emergency is present where an incident or fire involves any energized electrical equipment or facility with an immediate threat to life or property due to fire, damage, or malfunction.
3. General

1.4. The safest and most preferred method in which electrical emergencies can be handled is to have the electricity shut off by qualified utility company personnel before attempting to extinguish fire, rescue a victim, or come in contact with energized electrical equipment.
1.5. ALL electrical wires and equipment shall be considered energized and dangerous. Any victims, vehicles, structures, etc. in contact with electrical equipment should also be considered energized.
1.6. If no life hazard exists, identify/evacuate hazard zone and protect exposures from a safe distance while awaiting utility company arrival.
1.7. If an immediate life hazard exists and utility personnel are not on the scene, a thorough risk assessment should be conducted prior to attempting any rescue.

1.8. When a life hazard exists or a structure is threatened as a result of an electrical emergency, consideration should be given to upgrading the assignment to include a Battalion Chief if not already assigned.

1.9. When dealing with electrical distribution equipment (e.g., transmission lines, transformers, etc.), be aware of “reclosers.” They are similar to a circuit breaker in that they open the circuit when a fault is detected, but unlike a typical breaker it will reclose the circuit after a predetermined amount of time. It can repeat this cycle several times before it locks itself open. This is one of many reasons to not make contact with a wire because it is nearly impossible for us to determine that the wire is de-energized or that it will stay that way.
1.10. Keepaerial devices and ground ladders a minimum of 10’ from all overhead wires.
1.11. CO2 or dry chemical extinguishers should be used for small electrical fires if extinguishment must be performed prior to utility company arrival.

1.12. If, as a last resort, water must be used, it should be delivered in the form of a 30-degree fog pattern with at least 100 psi nozzle pressure from as great a distance as possible. Refer to 3.4 above when making this determination.

1.13. Water should typically only be used in this manner to protect exposures. Be aware of water runoff and keep personnel at a safe distance. Do not attempt to extinguish transformer fires until power is confirmed off by utility company.

1.14. If an apparatus comes in contact with live wires remain in or on apparatus if possible. If necessary, jump from vehicle, feet together, making sure not to touch vehicle and ground at same time. Then shuffle with feet close together to a safe area (approx. 30 feet away).
1.15. Service wires should only be cut by properly trained personnel using only the approved equipment.

1.16. The cutting of “drip loops” should only be attempted at one- and two-family residential structures due to the higher voltages present at multi-family and commercial structures. This procedure shall be performed by CFD Rescue or Ladder personnel in required PPE (turnout gear and lineman’s gloves) after all other attempts to control power have failed. (e.g., individual breaker/fuse, main breaker at panel).

1.17. When requesting a utility company, provide all visible information from the pole or equipment to the FAO. Be aware that many poles in Columbus are shared byAEP and Columbus Power. Therefore, it may be necessary for both utility companies to respond.

1.18. When dealing with solar panels, be aware that shutting down power to building/equipment supplied by solar power, the panels themselves remain energized and cautionmust be used when working around this equipment.
1.19. Be aware that shutting down the main power may trigger backup power sources, such as generators and battery rooms, which could re-energize equipment.
3.1. Electrical PPE and equipment:
3.1.1. TAC Sticks – Engines, Ladders, and Rescues
1.19.1. Polypropylene Rope –Engines, Ladders, andRescues; should be stored in a sealed bag and shall be considered a single use life safety rope (exchange if opened)
1.19.2. Lineman’s Gloves – Ladders and Rescues; leather outer with rubber liner shall be stored in sealed bag and shall be tested twice a year scheduled by Tools and Equipment (exchange if opened)
1.19.3. Hot Stick Cable Cutter – Ladders and Rescues; should be stored in canvas bag and shall be tested every other year scheduled by Tools and Equipment
1.19.4. Telescoping Hot Stick Hook – Rescues; should be stored in protective tube or canvas bag and shall be tested every other year scheduled by Tools and Equipment
3.1.2. Electrical helmet with flash protection – Rescues
3.1.3. Dielectric boot covers – Rescues
4. Operations

1.20. The following emergency types provide direction for handling specific incidents. The items contained within are not all-inclusive. Many of the items in Section 3 will also be applicable, but not specifically mentioned in each incident type.
4.1. Wires Down
1.20.1. Enter scene with caution, performing initial scene size up from apparatus cab.
4.1.1. Avoid placing personnel or apparatus underwires or equipment.

1.20.2. Identify/evacuate the hazard zone of all bystanders, personnel and, apparatus (at least oneunbroken span between poles on either side of break, preferably on other side of street out from under potentially involved equipment.
1.20.3. Attempt to determine utility provider. May have to use adjacent pole to avoid hazard.
4.1.2. Request utility provider and ETA from FAO.
1.20.4. Utilize “TAC Stick” to check surrounding area for energized fences, structures, autos, etc.
4.1.3. Use scene tape and/orflares to mark hazard zone perimeter.
1.20.5. If available, CPD can be left in charge of scene where CFD resources are no longer needed (e.g., no obvious hazards present).
4.1.4. Do not leave a hazardous scene unattended.
1.20.6. During storm conditions, an alternate approachmay be implementedby Emergency Services Deputy Chief dependent on resources available.

1.20.7. If wires, utility pole, light pole, or illuminated signs are down and in contact with a vehicle and a viable victim is present, have victims remain in vehicle until power is cut off by utility company, if possible. Do not allow personnel to touch victim and/or vehicle that is in contact with energized equipment.

1.20.8. Ifimmediate lifesaving intervention is required and to be performed, a downed wire on a vehicle, person, structure would be most safely handled by CFD Rescue personnel using a fully extended telescoping hot stick with required PPE (turnout gear, lineman’s gloves, boot covers). Refer to 3.4 when making this determination.

1.20.9. If immediate lifesaving intervention is required and a telescoping hot stick is not available, a polypropylene rope as described in 3.17 may be the safest option. This would be accomplished by first throwing a length of rope UNDER THE WIRE to a second FF on the opposite side. The second FF then tosses the rope back over the top of wire to first FF who then pulls both ends of rope to move wire off of vehicle, victim, or structure. Place as much distance as possible between yourself and the wire when moving it. Any member involved in this procedure shall be in full turnout gear with Lineman’s Gloves. Refer to 3.4 when making this determination.
4.2. Pole Fire/Pole Transformer Fire
1.20.10. Identify/evacuate the hazard zone of all bystanders, personnel and apparatus (two poles away from affected pole).

1.20.11. Extinguishment efforts should be avoided until utility company confirms power is off. However, having a charged hose line available as exposure protection from a safe distance should be the primary focus.
1.20.12. Be aware of the possibility of a transformer fire causing an overcurrent situation to the area or an explosion that could affect exposures.
4.3. Substation Fire
4.3.1. Setup upwind and uphill; establish a safe perimeter, protect exposures.
1.20.13. Do not enter or discharge extinguishing agents into substation. Equipment is high voltage and extremely hazardous.
1.20.14. After approval from utility company to enter is obtained, extinguishment can take place with the minimum personnel and equipment necessary to safely perform job.

1.20.15. Much of this equipment contains large amounts of oil for cooling, a Class B foam may be appropriate for extinguishment. Even though most equipment with oil containing PCBs has been removed from service, ALL oil should be presumed contaminated with PCB’s until proven otherwise.
4.4. Underground Vault/Vault Room Fire
1.20.16. Approach from and setup upwind and uphill, establish a safe perimeter, protect exposures and consult utility company.
4.4.1. Life safety rescue should not be attempted.
4.4.2. Stay clear of vault covers, metal grating and manholes.
4.4.3. Request electric company. Specify to FAO that a vault is involved.
1.20.17. Check adjacent exposures for involvement (vapors, fire, smoke, CO) and evacuate as necessary.
1.20.18. These emergencies shall be considered confined space incidents and shall be handled as if they are oxygen deficient or explosive atmospheres.
1.20.19. Do not enter or attemptextinguishment until go ahead is given from utility company.

1.20.20. If go ahead is given by utility company to flow water, the preferable method is laying an open butt 3” line near the opening. Then securing it by tying off or laying a heavy object over the hose and finally removing all personnel from line before slowly opening discharge and allowing water to flow into and flood the area.
1. Administration

1.1. Purpose: This standard operating guideline is intended to establish guidelines for providing rapid, non-destructive entry into certain structures, while providing maximum security for property owners.

1.2. Responsibility: It shall be the responsibility of each member to know, understand, and utilize these procedures as they apply to the situation at hand. It shall further be the responsibility of all Division Officers to train their subordinates in the proper application of these procedures and to implement and enforce the use of these procedures.
2. RapidKeyEntry ProgramComponents and Definitions
1.3. Rapid Key Entry System – A series of security entry devices that are opened with a key. This allows the Division of Fire quick access with no damage to the property.
1.4. Key Secure – The unit that is installed on the fire apparatus that holds the keys in a locked state until needed. The firefighter’s individual PIN is needed to release the keys for use.
2.1. Mechanical Key – The hard cut, traditional key.

1.5. Electronic Key – Key featuring three (3) digits, #1, #2, and #3. After removing the electronic key from the Key Secure, enter the division’s key security code immediately prior to inserting the electronic key into the building’s Key Box. The security code will not be published in thisSOPfor security reasons.
1.6. Key Box – The box at the building that the building’s keys are safely stored in until needed. They include elevator and entry boxes.
1.7. Otherentry items used for the system are padlocks, key switches, power shut down boxes and cabinets. Anyone wishing to order these items should contact the FPB.
3. Procedures
3.1. Mobile Data Computers
1.7.1. In the remarks on the MDC, there will be a notation that the address has Rapid Key Entry System. Further information will be accessed by pushing the hazards button.
3.2. Storage
1.7.2. The Officer is ultimately responsible for security of the keys in the Key Secure Unit on the apparatus.
1.7.3. The electronic and mechanical keys shall be secured in the Key Secure. The keys are not to be removed and left unsecured.

1.7.4. If you are changing over to a reserve apparatus and it has a Key Secure, transfer the keys. If there is not a Key Secure on the reserve apparatus, keep your keys secured in your original apparatus key secure.
1.7.5. The Keys shall be returned to the vehicle KeySecure Unit after eachuse and re-secured.
3.3. Usage
1.7.6. The Rapid Key Entry System shall only be utilized for official department emergency operations, where waiting for a key holder is not advisable as determined by the Incident Commander.
1.7.7. Buildings utilizing the Rapid Key Entry System should have a red sticker on the entry door indicating a key box is available for use for entry.

1.7.8. The Rapid Key Entry System shall not be used to access occupancies for non-emergency duties such as building inspections and/or familiarity inspections, even if given permission by the responsible party unless the responsible party accompanies CFD personnel.
1.7.9. At no time shall the Rapid KeyEntry System be used to gain access to occupancy due to lock-out.

1.7.10. When the key box is opened, the number of set(s) of keys shall be noted, and keys to the occupancy retrieved. The Officer shall be responsible for the security of the key box during its use. Do not leave the entry key box open or unsecured at any time.
1.7.11. The Incident Commander shall be responsible for ensuring that all occupancy keys are returned to the key box, and it is secured before leaving the site.
3.3.1. Keys from the key box are not to be permanently removed or copied.
1.7.12. The member completing the fire or EMS report will document in the narrative that the key box was used for entry.

1.7.13. The key secure unit will “lock out” for five (5) minutes after five (5) invalid PIN attempts. If your PIN does not work after two (2) attempts, have someone else enter their PIN to release the key. This will prevent a “lock out” from occurring.

1.7.14. When the key secure is “locked out,” the light display behind the number keypad will continuously flash for five (5) minutes. No entries can be made till the lock out ends. This is for security reasons.
1.7.15. Any issues with the key secure unit or questions with the Rapid KeyEntry System, contact the FPB.

1.7.16. If a civilian contacts a station for access to the Knox Box to update keys, have them contact the FPB. For accountability reasons, ES Companies are not to gain access to Knox boxes for non-emergency means or lock up a new box.
1.7.17. If a key switch is used to open a gate or for door access, it must be placed back into normal operation mode prior to leaving the site.
1.7.18. If at any time the key secure is locked up and not responding, press and hold the arrow key for ten (10) seconds. This will reset the key secure.
3.4. Missing Key

1.7.19. Upon discovery of a missing Key, ES-2 shall be notified immediately, who will notify the Assistant Chief of the Fire Prevention Bureau. All required documentation regarding missing division equipment shall be completed and forwarded through channels.
3.5. Mutual Aid Entry for Key Boxes

1.7.20. The Division has agreements with MutualAid Departments to allow joint entry into key boxes. Acurrent list is kept on the Division webpage. The link is called Knox Joint Entry and is found under the Division Information section. This list is updated as needed.
1. Administration
1.1. Purpose: The purpose of this procedure is to provide direction for practical and safe response to incidents involving elevators.

1.2. Responsibility: It shall be the responsibility of each member to know, understand, and utilize these procedures as they apply to the situation at hand. It shall further be the responsibility of all Division Officers to train their subordinates in the proper application of these procedures and to implement and enforce the use of these procedures.
2. General

1.3. The number and variety of elevators being installed across the city has increased over the years. Due to the expansive technology and increased response to incidents involving elevators, this procedure has been created. Extreme caution and the safety of all persons shall be the highest priority on all incidents.
2.1. SOPs to reference:
1.3.1. 02-03-21 – Lockout/Tagout SOP
2.1.1. 03-05-05 – Rope Rescue SOP
2.2. Response:
2.2.1. Initial dispatch involving an elevator entrapment will receive:
2.2.1.1. One (1) Engine
2.2.1.2. One (1) Ladder
2.2.1.3. One (1) Heavy Rescue
1.3.1.1.1. A township Heavy Rescue may be used, but,a CFD Heavy Rescue will always respond.
1.3.2. The response may be upgraded to a Rescue Response by the Fire Alarm Office or responding companies if additional information is available.
1.3.3. In the event on scene companies upgrade the incident to a “working incident”, consider upgrading to a “Rescue Response” depending on the extent of the incident.
2.2.2. The highest-ranking officer on the scene will be the incident commander.
2.3. Apparatus Responsibilities
2.3.1. First Arriving Apparatus
1.3.3.1. Give initial size-up, establish command, establish accountability, and direct all incoming companies.
1.3.3.2. Investigate and gatherthe following information (tasks may be delegated):
2.3.1.1.1. Location and number of persons trapped.
1.3.3.2.1. Medical needs (if any)of persons trapped. If medical needs are identified, request an appropriate EMS response.
2.3.1.1.2. Description of events that led to the entrapment.

1.3.3.3. Confirm elevator technician has been notified and determine ETA. If the total time of entrapment and ETA of technician is less than one (1) hour with no medical needs noted, considerwaiting for the elevator technician.
1.3.3.4. If an elevator technician has not been notified, consider requesting one through the following methods:
2.3.1.1.3. The property manager
2.3.1.1.4. Use the elevator phone or call button by the occupant
1.3.3.4.1. Call the FAO and give the name of the company and a phone number if available
2.3.1.2. Identify type of elevatorinvolved (hydraulic, traction, MRL, etc.).
1.3.3.5. Consider use of the State of Ohio Elevator Database for elevator information (https://icsearch.com.ohio.gov/Elevator).
1.3.3.6. Identify location of control room or main power disconnect. Consider assistance from building supervisor or maintenance to find the above location.
1.3.3.7. Locate all potential keys that may be required for extrication (e.g., hoist- way door keys, fire service keys, control room keys etc.).
2.3.1.3. Considerall appropriate tools for forcible entry and extrication.
2.3.2. Engine Company
2.3.2.1. If first to arrive, follow “first arriving apparatus” guideline.

1.3.3.8. If an entrapment is confirmed, send at least (1) member to the elevator control room or main power disconnect to prepare for lockout / tagout procedures. Preference shall be given to members with working knowledge of elevators. Membershall have a radio and monitor the assigned talk group.
1.3.3.9. If keys are not available to the control room, consider forcible entry with appropriate tools.
2.3.3. Ladder Company
2.3.3.1. If first to arrive, follow “first arriving apparatus” guideline.
1.3.3.10. Assign crew to work with the rescue company /RS-10 and report to the floor in which the occupants are trapped.
1.3.3.11. Assure all appropriate equipment (Irons, pike poles etc.) and keys are taken.
2.3.4. Rescue Company
2.3.4.1. If first to arrive, follow “first arriving apparatus” guideline.
1.3.3.12. Report to the floor in which occupants are trapped. Work under the direct supervision of RS-10 in coordination with the ladder company and elevator technician (if on scene).
2.3.4.2. Assure all appropriate equipment and keys are taken.
2.3.5.1. If first to arrive, follow “first arriving apparatus” guidelines.
2.3.5.2. Reports directly to the incident commander.
1.3.3.13. Establish the Rescue Group (forward operations) and report to the floor in which occupants are trapped.
1.3.3.14. Establish an operation plan in coordination with rescue and ladder crews through coordination with incident commander. Also coordinate with the elevator technician if on scene.
2.3.6. All Additional companies
2.3.6.1. Will be directed as needed by the incident commander.
3. Operations
3.1. Non-Technical Extrication
1.3.4. Assure all above procedures are complete. The following steps shall be completed in this order:
1.3.4.1. Communicate with occupants to assure the elevatordoor is in the closed position.
3.1.1.1. Assure all hoist-way doors are in the closed position.
1.3.4.2. Have occupants confirm that the emergency stop has not been activated.
3.1.1.2. Have occupants press and hold the (door open) button.
1.3.4.3. Attempt to call the elevator to the floor in which it is stalled orback to the lobby.
3.1.1.3. Attempta Fire ServicePhase 1 recall.

1.3.5. If the above steps do not work, the Incident Commander shall order the power (with the exception of the lights to avoid panic) to the elevator in question to be temporarily shut down for at least 30 seconds in an attempt to “hard reset” the elevator. Turning the power back on for the “hard reset” procedure shall only be performed by the order of the incident commander and shall only be attempted one (1) time. In the event this procedure does not remedy the situation, shut down the power to the elevator (with the exception of the lights, if possible) and perform lockout/tagout procedures. Refer to the lockout/tagout SOP.

1.3.6. At no point will any member assume that the power is off to an elevator. Consider alternate energy sources. Lockout/Tagout procedures shall be performed prior to any attempt to manually extricate an occupant from an elevator.
3.2. Manual Extrication
1.3.7. In the event the above procedures were unsuccessful and lockout / tagout procedures are in place, a manual extraction may be performed.

1.3.8. Identify the keyhole location within the hoist-way door. If there is not a keyhole at the hoist-way door in question, send a representative to the hoist-way doors above or below until a keyhole is found. Create a templateof the existing keyhole and mark the hoist-way door in question to drill your own keyhole.

1.3.9. Once the hoist-way door is open, size up the situation. If the elevator is more than 2 feet above or below the landing, or brake slippage is a concern,the elevator shall bemechanically secured unless section3.2.4 applies. The procedure to manually secure the elevator shall be performed by the Rescues only. Only trained rescue technicians may enter an elevator shaft. Refer to SOP 03-05-05.

1.3.10. If the elevator in 3.2.3 is hydraulic or MRL, the use of the hydraulic bleeder valve or MRL keys may be used if conditions warrant to move the car to the nearest landing. This decision shall be made by the Incident Commander in consultation with RS-10, rescue crews and the elevator technician (if on scene). The member performing this procedure shall have a thorough knowledge of this procedure and must have a portable radio in direct contact with the incident commander. This procedure shall be done with the elevator car door in the closed position.

1.3.11. In the event the elevator is unable to be lowered, assure the gap between the elevator and the landing is blocked to prevent occupants and/or rescuers from becoming caught or falling between the two.
3.3. Shaft-Way Rescue (through the hatch)

1.3.12. An elevator shaft-way rescue shall only be performed by trained rescue technicians. Refer to SOP 03-05-05. Consider setting up rope operations 2 floors above the elevator in question. Have medics standing by at the first floor located above the elevator for patient care if needed.
1.3.13. Extreme caution shall be used when entering the shaft-way. All power to adjoining elevators shall be locked out prior to entry.
1.3.14. Many elevators are being built with battery units within the shaft or on top of the elevator. Extreme caution shall be used around all backup power sources within these units.
1.3.15. Any occupantbeing removed from the elevator in a shaft-way rescue shall be secured with a rescue harness and separate safety line.
