3.4.2.3. Assign 1 member on the surface to continuously monitor the air monitor readings with any tunnel entry. Each entry team shall also have 1 member assigned the recorder position.
3.4.2.4. Ensure all forms are distributed and filled out appropriately.
3.4.3.1. Establish EMS Branch
3.4.3.2. Establish and oversee Rehab
3.4.4. Engine or ladder:
3.4.4.1. Ensure lock out, tag out procedures (or equivalent) are performed and maintained on any masked incident, or any other incident where power is shut down. Coordinate with on-site electrician.
2.2.4.1. Set up and establish a Decon corridor, if needed.
2.2.4.2. Follow Decon flow charts.
2.2.5. All other companies:
3.4.4.2. Level II stage (SOP 02-02-05) at Station 25 unless an alternate staging location is determined.
2.2.5.1. Assist operations as determined by the Incident Commander.
3.4.4.3. Tunnel Team members will coordinate with their officers and report to the Tunnel Branch Officer.
3. Staffing
3.1. Staffing on Masked incident

3.4.5. Initial rescue team will consist of five (5) Tunnel Rescue Technicianswith a minimum of 1 being a paramedic. The entry team leader will be identified by the Incident Commander. This may be by rank or experience level.
3.4.5.1. All members, priorto entry and when exiting the tunnel, will have vitals and EKG taken.
3.4.5.2. Primary entry team will coordinate with the on-site rescue team/construction crew to perform rescue.
3.4.5.3. Determine type of incident and specialized equipment needed (intrinsically safe).
3.4.5.4. Each member will have one (1) 4-hour SCBA. One (1) additional 4- hour SCBA will be carried with the entry team for emergency/rescue use for a total of six (6) SCBAs.
3.4.5.5. Each SCBA will be completely tested prior to use in the tunnel and members will assure all oxygen cylinders are full (3,000 psi). Refer to flow charts.

3.4.6. Standby rescue team will consist of five (5) Tunnel Rescue Technicians with a minimum of 1 being a paramedic. The standby team leader will be identified by the Incident Commander. This may be by rank or experience level.
3.4.6.1. Each member will have one (1) 4-hour SCBA. One (1) additional 4- hour SCBA will be carried with the standby team for emergency use for a total of six (6) SCBAs.
3.4.6.2. Each SCBA will be completely tested prior to use in the tunnel and members will assure all oxygen cylinders are full (3,000psi). Refer to flow charts.
3.4.6.3. Standby crew will be 90% ready, and a standby location will be established in close proximity to the collar. Consider a temperaturecontrolled location out of the elements.
3.2. Staffing on No Mask incident
3.4.7. Initial rescue team will consist of an appropriate number of Tunnel Rescue Technicians, a minimum of one (1) shall be a paramedic.
3.4.8. Initial rescue team will collect enough personalescape bottles and proceed into the tunnel.
3.4.9. The standby rescue team will consist of five (5) tunnel rescue technicians 90% ready with a minimum of one (1) being a paramedic.
4. Operations
3.5. All members entering below grade into the tunnel for any incident shall be Tunnel Rescue certified. If an SCBA is required, it must be full (3,000 psi).

3.6. All power to the tunnel shall be locked out and tagged out (or equivalent) prior to entry into the tunnel on a Mask incident except for the power to the ventilation system. Power to ventilation may be reversed in coordination with onsite construction crew. Power may remain on in a No Mask incident. Coordination shall be made with the construction crew to maintain the lock out/tag out procedure if needed.
3.7. Entry into the tunnel will only be initiated if the Incident Commander, Tunnel Branch Officer, and the Tunnel Rescue Team members determine entry can be performed safely.
3.8. The Division of Fire “Confined Space Rescue Permit” form ES-223 shall be completed by a designated member for any entry into the tunnel.

3.9. All entry will occur with continuous air monitoring in place throughout the incident. A minimum of3 multi-gas meters will be required on all entrywithin the tunnel. One team member will be assigned the “recorder” position. Readings will be recorded frequently. All readings will be performed in the same sequence for every check.

3.9.1. Elevated atmospheric readings (by interior crews or member monitoring readings from the surface) at any time will require additional protection and the incident to be upgrade to a masked incident. Masked incidents will require flash protection. Refer to SOPs 01-07-03 and 02-03-09.
3.10. Members shall not make entry into the tunnel if there is a fire. BIO PAK 240Rs are not rated for firefighting operations.

3.11. All masked incidents will use the 40/60 rule (40% in, 60% out). Entry will be limited to 1 hour 42 minutes or once the first SCBA on the team reaches 1,800 psi.At this point, all members will begin their exit from the tunnel. Verify time on P-400 prior to entry.
3.12. Any incident involving flooding will be a masked incident. At any point water levels rise to the level of your knees, allmembers must evacuate the tunnel.
4.1. LevelIII accountability will be in effect on all tunnel incidents.
3.13. All deceased victims will be brought to the shaft area and all will be removed at the same time.
4.2. In the event of a mayday:
4.2.1. The standby crew will be activated immediately.
3.13.1. All additional Tunnel Team members in the city will respond to the incident.
3.13.2. In the event more members are needed, the Class -1 call in will be initiated.
3.13.3. Any mayday incident will initiate ES-1, ES-2, ES-3 and RS-1 to respond if not already on scene.
5. Communications

3.14. On No Mask Incidents, power may be maintained within the tunnel and radios, cell phones and mine phones may be accessible. Determination shall be made prior to entry on which system will be used. One member on the surface will monitor the mine phone system at all times.
3.15. On Mask Incidents, communications will not be available. A strict time schedule shall be followed.
4. Conclusionof Incident

4.1. All members exiting the tunnel will decon and report to Rehab for evaluation. (02-01-08). A member who has made entry into the tunnel on a masked incident will not be allowed to re-enter the tunnel for a minimum of 6 hours. If the incident is prolonged, consider a class-1 call-in of required tunnel team members.
4.2. Establish PAR on the incident scene.
4.3. All tunnel equipment will be returned to an operational state of readiness and returned to service.
5.1. Assure that the scene is secured and turned over to the responsible party.

4.4. After the incident, all members will meet and critique the incident. All Tunnel Team Members active in the incident will write an RT-154 describing what they did on the incident and send them through the rescue chain of command to RS-1.
4.5. If the incident occurred outside of the LOT, a rescue will be responsible for returning the equipment to the LOT trailer.
4.6. Assure all NFIRS reports are complete and submit a copy of the ES- 223 through the Rescue chain of command to ES-1.
1. Administration

1.1. Purpose: To control the hazardous energy of machines, equipment and utilities during an emergency incident in which the unexpected start of and/or activation could cause injury to victims and/or rescuers.

1.2. Responsibility: It shall be the responsibility of each member to know, understand, and utilize these procedures as they apply to the situation at hand. It shall further be the responsibility of all Division Officers to train their subordinates in the proper application of these procedures and to implement and enforce the use of these procedures.
2. Definitions
1.3. Energy Sources – Electric, Hydraulic, Mechanical, Pneumatic, Chemical, Thermal or other energy, which if not controlled could create a hazardous condition.
1.4. Hazard – Any device, machine or incident that creates a life safety factor that, if not controlled, could exacerbate the incident or potentially harm the patient and responders.

1.5. Safe Condition Check (Verification of De-energization) – The inspection or test of a system or component, performed by the appropriate personnel to ensure that the hazardous energy or materials are controlled to prevent injury or accident.
3. Procedures
3.1. Procedures for shutdown (refer to OSHA 29 CFR 1910.147):

1.5.1. Consult with company / contractor to determine all energy sources and proper procedures for removal of energy sources along with expert consultation on said hazard. Consider detrimental effects of removing energy source.

1.5.2. Disconnect or isolate the hazard from the energy source(s). Assure properPPEand procedure when removing energy source as determined by NFPA 70. (Full fire gear for flash protection, facing away from the energy source).

1.5.3. Assure one (1) member with a radio remains at the energy source to maintain lockout procedures. This procedurewill typically be controlled by the Engine crew; however, alternate crews may be used at the discretion of the Incident Commander.
3.1.1.1. Coordinate lockout / tagout procedures with facility staff / workers.

1.5.3.1. If more than one (1) energy source, ensure one (1) member with a radio maintains lockout procedures at each location. Consider alternate energy sources such as; generators, solar panels, batteries, hydraulics, compressed air or gas, etc.
1.5.4. If a lockout / tagout kit is available, the devices may be used, however, a member with a radio will remain at each energy source.
1.5.4.1. All lockout / tagout devices, if used, must be used in accordance with manufacturer’s recommendations.
1.5.4.2. The use of a facilities lockout / tagout device is appropriate as long as the Division of Fire maintains complete control of the device.
1.5.4.3. Once lockout / tagout (or equivalent) has been performed, this shall be aired over the radio to the incident commander.

1.5.5. Release, restrain, or otherwise render safe allpotential stored or residual energy. If the possibility exists for re-accumulation of hazardous energy, ensure one (1) member with a radio is assigned to regularly verify that such energy has not accumulated to hazardous levels.
1.5.6. Perform and verify a “Safe Condition Check” prior to entering the hazard zone.
1.6. Procedures for releasing the system to the proper authority:
1.6.1. Assure the incident is contained and all victims and rescuers are out of the hazard zone. The Fire Department will maintain complete control of the incident until this is complete.
1.6.2. Communicate and coordinate the exchange of control with the proper authority (e.g., facility personnel, maintenance technician).

1.6.2.1. In the event the proper authority is not on the scene. Assure the power remains off to the hazard and an out ofservice tag will be left on the power source. If a tag is not available, mark the hazard out of service with scene tape.
1.6.3. Do Not leave locks on devices when clearing the scene. Considerrequesting prevention 18 or OSHA representatives for violations.
1. Administration

1.1. Purpose: The purpose of this procedure is to identify the process in the event Prevention 18 (P18) becomes overwhelmed with fire systems out of service calls due to an extreme weather situation or major power outage.

1.2. Responsibility: It shall be the responsibility of each member to know, understand, and utilize these procedures as they apply to the situation at hand. It shall further be the responsibility of all Division Officers to train their subordinates in the proper application of these procedures and to implement and enforce the use of these procedures.
2. Process
1.3. P18 will communicate through the FPB Chain of Command (COC)to implement Fire Watch Storm.
2.1. FPB OIC or P18 will inform ES2 that Fire Watch Storm is being implemented.
1.4. Once Fire Watch Storm has been implemented, if a company officer determines a fire suppression/alarm system is impaired, then the company officer or IC shall complete the following:
1.4.1. Attempt to notify the key holder or responsible party for the property that the building will need to be on fire watch.
1.4.2. If a responsible party is on scene, complete the Emergency Impairment Fire Watch Order, leave a copy with the responsible party and send a copy to FPB.

1.4.3. If a responsible party is not on scene, complete the Emergency Impairment Fire Watch Order, write N/A on the occupant signature line, and post a copy in a conspicuous area such as the front door or the main entrance. If possible, post the paperwork in a location protected from the elements/weather. Send the top copy to FPB.
1.4.4. When back in quarters, fill out the FP-320 Fire Watch Storm form andhit submit. This will send it to FAO@columbus.gov.
1.4.5. The person responsible for the NIFRS report shall document the fire watch details on the NFIRS report.

1.4.6. CFD officers should use discretion based on the building demographics. Is the building occupied? Are the residents ambulatory? Is the property a high hazard building? If there is a question of appropriateness for fire watch then pass concerns up the chain of command.

1.5. The FAO will enter the property information on the Fire Watch Storm record template (located in the common shares folder). Additional alarms to properties on this list shall require an ES response, however the response may be downgraded to a single company response. The ES Company may respond signal X.
1.6. The FAO Lt. will email the list to CFDFireReferral@columbus.gov at 0800 and 2000 to maintain a current list.
1.7. P18 or FPB personnelwill follow up with the appropriate fire watch oversight and proper documentation.
3. Demobilization
1.8. Demobilization of Fire Watch Storm will occurwith consultation between P18, FPB COC, and ES Command Staff.

1.8.1. The Fire Watch Storm Process shall not be implemented as a measure of convenience, rather it may be implemented to ensure properties are appropriately placed on fire watch should their fire suppression or fire alarm system be compromised due to an extreme weather event ormajor power outage. These orders for fire watch must be in compliance with Ohio Fire Code Section 901.7.
1. Administration
1.1. Purpose: The purpose of this procedure is to describe the actions taken when responding to a fire alarm.

1.2. Responsibility: It shall be the responsibility of each member to know, understand, and utilize these procedures as they apply to the situation at hand. It shall further be the responsibility of all Division Officers to train their subordinates in the proper application of these procedures and to implement and enforce the use of these procedures.
2. General
2.1. Alarm Panel General Controls:
1.2.1. Acknowledge – Silences the audible alarm at the Fire Alarm Control Panel (FACU) only.
1.2.2. Silence – Silences the notification devices in the building (e.g., horn alarm).

1.2.2.1. If a building is actively being evacuated, do not silence the alarm until crews can ensure no hazards are present. The notification devices are designed to continually run to get all occupants out safely.
1.2.3. Reset – Resets the fire alarm system. This should not be done until an investigation by CFD personnel occurs, preferably by a person responsible for the occupancy.
2. Actions
2.2. Upon arrival, perform an on-scene radio report as outlined in SOP 01-02-03.

2.1. After completing a 360°, attempt to gain access to the building. If the building is locked, attempt to contact a building representative on site, request a key holder, or utilize the building's Knox Box key if present.
2.2. Upon entry, send crews to locate the main FACU and determine what initiating device triggered the alarm.
2.3. Investigate the activated initiating device prior to attempting to reset the alarm system.
2.4. Mitigate any hazards in the affected area and reset any initiating devices (e.g., ventilate smoke, reset the fire alarm pull station, etc.).
2.5. Once the area is cleared and thoroughly investigated, attempt a reset at the main FACU.

2.6. After the fire alarm activation investigation is complete, the Fire Company Officer(s) may assist the responsible person at the occupancy in resetting the alarm. The CFD Officer may attempt a reset if a responsible person is not on the scene.
2.7. If unable to reset the FACU, contact Prevention 18. Do not place the system in “test”. If a fire suppression/detection system is non-operational contact Prevention 18 for assistance.
2.8. If a wet or dry system activates, contact Prevention 18 for assistance and guidance. Do not attempt to reset the entire system on your own.
2.9. If an alarm system is not functioning correctly, in addition to Prevention 18, instruct the building owners to contact their alarm service provider.
2.10. Afterthe incident, thoroughly document the incident in the appropriate fire reporting software.
1 Administration
1.1 Purpose: The purpose of this procedure is to establish standardized guidelines on response to a Mass Casualty Incident (MCI) based off number of victims.

1.2 Defining MCI: A mass casualty incident (often shortened to MCI) describes an incident in which emergency medical services resources, such as personnel and equipment, are overwhelmed by the number and severity of casualties. 2 Levels of Mass Casualty Incidents
1.3 MCI Level 1
• 5-9 Victims.
• At least (1) victim with immediate or delayed priority injuries.
• Dispatch 5 Medics, 2 Engines, EMS 10 and 1 Battalion Chief.
• May choose to use triage tags/patient tracking system.
2.1 MCI Level 2
• 10-19 Victims.
• Additional dispatch of 5 Medics (10 total), 3 additional apparatus (total 2 Engine + 3 E, L) 1 EMS Officer, MC850 and ES2.
• FAO notifies COTS HIL, EMS 10 calls COTS HIL from scene.
• FAO goes into EPTP moves medics not involved in MCI away from trauma centers or hospitals that will be receiving these patients.
• Must use triage tags/patient tracking system.
1.4 MCI Level 3
• 20 or more Victims.
• Additional dispatch of 5 Medics (15 total), 3 more additional apparatus (total 2 Engines + 6 E, L) 1 EMS Officer and 1 Battalion Chief.
• COTA requested through the FAO.
• If more than 40 victims consider MC 29, temporary shelter and activate COTS MCI resources.
• Medics shall respond back to staging location after transporting to the hospital.
• Must use triage tags/patient tracking system. 2 General

2.1 The original run shall be made a “Working Incident” and placed on a battalion talk group. To ensure an appropriate assignment is filled out and only companies assigned to this run are on the channel. An added benefit to operating on one BN# talk group is the IC can transmit vital information over the BN# ATG.

2.2 MCI should be requested as an “Associated event” and placed on BN# EMS channel the additional TAC channels can be used as triage and transport groups. Companies dispatched on the MCI (BN# EMS channel) should be prepared to assist with EMS functions.
2.3 Associated event allows the original dispatch to still be upgraded. Also allows two different tablet command managers. One for the primary incident and one for the MCI.

2.4 In the event of an MCI 1 the EMS officer should contact hospitals directly to see what their capabilities are for this event. If operating at an MCI 2 or 3 then EMS 10 shall call COTS Healthcare Incident Liaison (HIL). (EMS 10 has the number in their phone, or contact FAO for number)

2.5 At large-scale or complex incidents, the number of Divisions and/or Groups may create a significant span-of-control problem. When this occurs, consideration should be given to the implementation of Branches. Branches are also of great value when large numbers of resources are committed to specific functional activity. A good example would be a fire incident with a major EMS problem. A Medical Branch could be implemented to alleviate these problems.

2.6 A Mass Casualty Incidents may require a separate staging area for transport vehicles. In such cases a Staging Area Manager will need to be designated and relay this information to The Incident Commander and the Fire Alarm Office.

2.7 If any Physicians report to the emergency scene, they will be directed to work in conjunction with the Medical Branch Director. The Medical Branch Director and the Treatment Group Supervisor will be guided by the recommendations of the physician relating to medical treatment.
2.8 The Transportation Group Supervisor or medical group must keep a record of all victims transported by recording the triage tags serial number and to which hospital each victim was transported.

2.9 Early notification to the HIL and area hospitals is very important, but just as important is an “all clear” from the scene. This allows them to plan for reestablishing the scheduled surgeries that were put on hold due to the MCI. 03-01-01.t: Bomb Squad Operations – Table of Contents
p: 1. Administration

1.1. Purpose: The purpose of this procedure is to provide a Table of Contents of the Standard OperatingProcedures utilized by members of the BombSquad. Certain information is confidential and will be restricted to personnel on a need-to-know basis.

1.2. Responsibility: It shall be the responsibility of each member to know, understand, and utilize these procedures as they apply to the situation at hand. It shall further be the responsibility of all Division Officers to train their subordinates in the proper application of these procedures and to implement and enforce the use of these procedures.

1. Administration
1.1. Purpose: The purpose of this procedure is to identify the role of the Bomb Squad, the selection of members, and the training requirements.

1.2. Responsibility: It shall be the responsibility of each member to know, understand, and utilize these procedures as they apply to the situation at hand. It shall further be the responsibility of all Division Officers to train their subordinates in the proper application of these procedures and to implement and enforce the use of these procedures.
2. General

1.3. Duties: The Bomb Squad Standard Operating Procedures provide general procedures for safe operation of the Division of Fire Bomb Squad Unit and its response to hazardous devices and explosive emergencies. The Bomb Squad’s duties include the following (but are not limited to):
1.3.1. Investigate, render safe and/or dispose of suspected hazardous devices, incendiary devices, explosives, explosive materials, pyrotechnics and ammunition.

1.3.2. Coordinate with other local, state, and federal partners to investigate, perform diagnostics and potential render safe operations in chemical, biological, radiological, nuclear, and explosive (CBRNE) events.
1.3.3. Provide legal, safe transportation and disposal of explosives and other items as listed above.
2.1.1. AssistFire Investigations Unit with bombing crime scene investigations.
2.1.2. Collect and preserve evidence.
2.1.3. Prepare and provide courtroom testimony.
2.1.4. Store,maintain and inventory Bomb Squad equipment and explosives.
1.3.4. Provide technical support to special operations as determined by the Fire Chief.
2.1.5. Provide dignitary protection (VIP) as determined by the Fire Chief.
2.1.6. Prepare and participate in explosive related training programs.
1.3.5. Maintain and be familiar with a library of FBI technical and intelligence publications, NBSCAB Bomb Tech Wiki, Federal Explosives Laws and Regulations, and other explosive related materials.

1.3.6. Maintain professional and training liaison with other Bomb Squads, explosive detection canine units, special weapons and tactics (SWAT) units,military EOD units, as well as local, state, and federal agencies.
1.3.7. Compile and report technical data on explosive devices and incidents to the Bomb and Arson Tracking System (BATS).
1.3.8. Develop emergency response plans for bombthreats and explosive related incidents.
1.3.9. Develop and promulgate bomb threat awareness and safety programs for public and private organizations.
2.1.7. Report found or recovered military ordnance to military EOD units.
3. Chain of Command
3.1. The Columbus Division of Fire Chain-of-Command shall prevail.
3.1.1. Exceptions:

1.3.9.1. Incident commander shall control the scene of operations with any assistance and information necessary from the Bomb Squad unit. However, the ultimate disposition of the suspicious/hazardous device or item encountered and tactics employed in the render safe operation of the suspicious/hazardous device or item at the scene shall rest with the senior Bomb Squad Technician as established by the Hazardous Devices School graduation. The Bomb Squad Commander or his designee shall be responsible for the conduct of the Bomb Squad unit.

1.3.9.2. Control of all operations at incidents outside the City of Columbus shall be guided by any existing written mutual aid agreement. When no written agreement exists then the ranking Columbus Fire Division official shall be in charge of approving scene operations. However, the ultimate disposition of the suspicious/hazardous device or item at the scene shall remain with the senior technician, as established by Hazardous Devices School graduation. The Bomb Squad Commander or his designee shall assume responsibility for the conduct of the Bomb Squad unit.
4. Personnel Selection
4.1. PersonnelSelection – A candidate for the Bomb Squad must:
1.3.10. Have a minimum of three (3) years fulltime experience in a public safety department.
4.1.1. Have five (5) years retainability within the Columbus Fire Division.

1.3.11. Be a willing volunteer to engage in basic bomb technician training, including six (6) week basic training at the FBI Hazardous Devices School.Attendance to the course will be at the direction of the Fire Chief.
1.3.12. Be recommended to the Fire Chief by the Selection Review Panel. The members of the Selection Review Panel include the Bomb Squad Commander and the three (3) Bomb Squad Supervisors.
1.3.13. The recommendation of the Selection Review Panel shall be contingent upon past and present work performance as well as the following:
4.1.1.1. Be or are willing to become a Rescue Technician.

1.3.13.1. Be or are willing to become a Hazardous Materials Technician per 29 Code of Federal Regulations (CFR), section 1910.120(q) (6) (iii), Emergency Responder to Hazardous Materials Technician for CBRNE Incidents. Training that meets the National Fire Protection Association (NFPA) 472 standards will also satisfy this requirement.
1.3.13.2. Individuals assigned tothe BombSquadStation will be given preference.
1.3.14. Meet FBI Bomb Data Center application requirements (e.g., physical examination, arrest check, etc.). Applicant must meet all eligibility requirements for an FBI “Secret” level clearance.
2. Training
4.2. On-the-JobTraining

2.1.1. The trainee must remain active within the Bomb Squad in order to be selected to attend the Hazardous Devices School (HDS). Inactive members may be removed at the discretion of the Bomb Squad Commander.
2.1.2. TheBomb Squad Commander shall, from the list of eligible candidates, recommend to the Fire Chief trainees to attend HDS.
4.3. TechnicianTraining: Initial Bomb Technician training
2.1.3. The bomb squad member will satisfactorily complete the FBI Hazardous Device School (HDS).
2.1.4. The bomb squad member will complete an on-the-job training program and yearly proficiency evaluations under the supervision of experienced technicians and the Bomb Squad Supervisors.
4.4. Continuing Education

2.1.5. It shall be mandatory that each technician will participate in a minimum of forty (40) hours of explosive related training annually to include the safe use of live explosive through practical applications. The time spent on bomb runs can be counted as part of this requirement.
2.1.6. Complete 16 hours minimum practical exercise/training (monthly) within the department.
2.1.7. Each technician must attend the forty (40) hour HDS Recertification Course every three (3) years or as soon as the HDS Recertification Course schedule allows.
2.1.8. Each technician must show proficiency with the following safety equipment each year:
4.4.1.1. The portable X-Ray machine (X-Ray procedures and developing film)

1. Administration
1.1. Purpose: To establish guidelines for Columbus Fire participation in a BioWatchActionable Result (BAR). These procedures are to be considered sensitive and not released to the public.

1.2. Responsibility: It shall be the responsibility of each member to know, understand, and utilize these procedures as they apply to the situation at hand. It shall further be the responsibility of all Division Officers to train their subordinates in the proper application of these procedures and to implement and enforce the use of these procedures.
2. Definitions

2.1. BioWatch – BioWatch is a federally-managed, locally-operated, nationwide bio- surveillance system designed to detect the intentional release of select aerosolized biological agents. The program operates in more than 30 high threat metropolitan areas across the country and is utilized to supportNational Special Security Events like the Super Bowl, national party conventions, and the Presidential Inauguration.

2.2. BAR – BioWatch Actionable Result. This means one of the BioWatch detectors has detected the DNA of one of the detectible substances. A BAR doesnot necessarily indicate a terrorist or man-made release.A BAR requires a response by the local BioWatch Steering committee to verify the initial test result.
2.3. CMMRS – Columbus Metropolitan Medical Response System
3. Introduction and Background

3.1. Columbus Fire participates in the CMMRS BioWatch steering committee. HazMat 1 and the Special Operations DeputyChief are part of the BioWatch Steering Committee and Response Plan. BioWatch uses ten (10) detectors and tests for 5 different agents in the central Ohio area. Seven (7) of the ten (10) detectors for central Ohio are located at CFD fire stations. The location of each detector is considered FOR OFFICIAL USE ONLY (FOUO) and is not to be published or shared with anyone without an official need to know. Each detector is visited on a daily basis by Ohio EPA.
4. BAR Notification

4.1. Upon notification to the BioWatch public health officer of a BAR, the public health officer will call the FAO and ask to talk with ES-2. ES-2 will be told the location of the BAR detector. ES-2 can then contact HazMat-1 at 774-0550 and/or the Special Operations Chief for additional details. Due to the testing procedures that take place, the notification of a BAR usually happens in the evening.
2. ES-2 Responsibilities

4.2. If a BAR is received for one of the detectors located at a CFD fire station then ES-2, HazMat1 and/or The Special Operations Deputy Chief will contact that fire station and explain to the Officer In-Charge what can be expected to occur at that sensor in the next few hours. Any questions can then be directed to HazMat1 and/or The Special Operations Deputy Chief. If a BAR is received for a detector not on CFD property then ES-2 has no other responsibilities.
3. BAR Activities

4.3. The BioWatch detector that tested positive will be visited by an Ohio EPA Sampling team. The team will wear level C protective clothing and retrieve additional samples from the unit and adjacent areas. These additional samples will be further tested by the Ohio Department of Health to verify the initial results. The BioWatch advisory committee meets on a conference call to determine local response actions.
4. Confirmationof aBAR

4.4. If a BAR is confirmed, then steps will be taken by Columbus Public Health to give prophylaxis to all firefighters and their immediate family members that worked at that station for at least 48 hours prior to the BAR. The BioWatch advisory committee will determine, with assistance from local, state, and federal partners, any additional requirements for the protection of our personnel and the public health.
1. Administration
1.1. Purpose: To establish guidelines for Threat Level Staging. These procedures are to be considered sensitive and not released to the public.

1.2. Responsibility: It shall be the responsibility of each member to know, understand, and utilize these procedures as they apply to the situation at hand. It shall further be the responsibility of all Division Officers to train their subordinates in the proper application of these procedures and to implement and enforce the use of these procedures.
2. Introduction and Background

2.1. Columbus Fire uses traditional staging of equipment on gas leaks (SOP 02- 03-13), multiple alarm fires (SOPs 02-02-05 and 02-02-06), HazMat incidents (SOP 03-03-02), etc. The purpose of traditional staging is to allow the first in company or incident commander time to investigate an incident, determine the additional needs of that incident and how best to deploy companies. Traditional staging hasall companies staging in one given area. Threat Level Staging is designed to eliminate the potential that a secondary device could be deployed and take out multiple companies. Threat Level Staging is to be used on any incident where a threat of violence to firefighters is perceived by the FAO or the initial company or companies responding to or on the scene.
3. Threat Level Staging

3.1. Threat Level Staging is a response mode where companies will stage in various locations instead of in one announced location. Upon notification that Threat Level Staging should be utilized, all companies responding to the scene should pull to the side of the road or pick another convenient area no closer than ¼ mile from the incident, stop, and maintain staging there. They should announce that they are “threat level staged”. Companies should stage in a variety of locations but not within 100 yards of another responding company.
4. Uses of Threat Level Staging

4.1. Threat Level Staging should be utilized whenever a threat is known (preplanning or intelligence that gives us reason to believe that firefighters could be endangered), for reports of known terrorist incidents, and/or explosions in large venues (e.g., Red, White and Boom, Nationwide Arena, malls etc.).

1.4.2. Evaluations monitors members’ medical fitness for continued participation.

2.1.3. Number of personnel being sent.

1. Administration
1.1. Purpose: The purpose of this procedure is to provide guidelines for a safe response by the Columbus Division of Fire to a hazardous materials incident.

1.2. Responsibility: It shall be the responsibility of each member to know, understand, and utilize these procedures as they apply to the situation at hand. It shall further be the responsibility of all Division Officers to train their subordinates in the proper application of these procedures and to implement and enforce the use of these procedures.
2. Responders
1.3. ColumbusDivision of Fire members will respond in these capacities, as determined by their level of training:

1.3.1. First Responder Operations Level: All Columbus Division of Fire personnel are trained to a minimum of First ResponderOperations Level. Operations level personnel are expected to take defensive actions, without trying to stop the release, for the purpose of protecting persons, property, and the environment. Their function is to contain the release from a safe distance, keep it from spreading, and protect exposures.
2.1.1.1. The standard assignment for a HazMat Incident will include:
2.1.1.1.1. Three (3) Engines
2.1.1.1.2. Two (2) Ladders
2.1.1.1.3. One (1) Rescue
2.1.1.1.4. Two (2) Battalion Chiefs
2.1.1.1.6. One (1) EMS Coordinator
2.1.1.1.7. Air Supply
2.1.1.1.9. HazMat 4 (Rescue, Medic, HazMat)
1.3.1.1. First Arriving Unit: Establishes the basic incident command structure upon which safe operations are founded. Actions should include:
2.1.1.1.10. Response:
1.3.1.1.1.1. Always approach from upwind and uphill if possible. Do not drive through vapor clouds. Avoid rushing in before sizingup the situation. What is at risk? Life, property, or environment?
1.3.1.1.1.2. Determine and announce a safe staging area for all other responding units. Avoid staging too close to the hazard.
2.1.1.1.11. Isolation of the Scene:
1.3.1.1.1.3. Isolate the hazard and deny entry of unprotected personnel into the hazard area. Avoid exposure to all chemicals and vapors.

1.3.1.1.1.4. Perform rescue of victims while wearing full structural firefighting protective clothing. Do not enter visible vapor clouds for rescue purposes. Turnout gear is not chemical protective clothing. The use of turnout gear (SFPC) into a hazardous atmosphereshould be limited to a “quick in-andout” to execute only a life-saving rescue.
1.3.1.1.1.5. Perform “emergency decon” while wearing turnouts by flushing victims and rescuers with water and removing their outer layer of clothing.
2.1.1.1.12. Evaluation of the Scene:
1.3.1.1.1.6. Gather information from any and all possible sources, including:placards; MSDS sheets; occupancy; container shape, color, markings, etc.
2.1.1.1.12.1. Determine what chemical(s) is (are) involved.
1.3.1.1.1.7. Consult the Emergency Response Guidebook (ERG)for “Initial Isolation” and/or “Evacuation Distances.”
1.3.1.1.1.8. Determine what resources are needed and direct their placement.
1.3.1.1.1.9. Separate contaminatedand deconned individuals, including rescuers, until evaluation by the HazMat team or EMS.
2.1.1.1.12.2. Take protective action:
1.3.1.1.1.9.1. Evacuation: This is the best protective action, if time permits. Consider evacuation if flammable vapors (massive fire and/or explosion) or long-term vapors are present.
1.3.1.1.1.9.2. Shelter-in-place:When evacuation isn’t an option due to greater risk to accomplish or lack of time. The following situations may justify shelter-in-place:
1.3.1.1.1.9.2.1. Short-term incidents
2.1.1.2.3.6.2.2. Short-term vapor clouds
2.1.1.2.3.6.2.3. Greaterhazard to movepeople
2.1.1.2.3.6.2.4. Impractical to move
1.3.1.1.2. Mitigation of the spill:

1.3.1.1.2.1. Perform “Operation’s Level” defensive actions to control, confine, or contain the product. Keep the product out of the sewers, storm-drains, or waterways. The following defensive actions should be considered:
2.1.1.1.12.2.1. Damming (overflow or underflow)
2.1.1.1.12.2.2. Diking (to retain fluids)
2.1.1.1.12.2.3. Diversion (to redirect fluids to a more desirable location)
2.1.1.1.12.2.4. Absorption
2.1.1.1.12.2.5. Removal of all ignition sources
2.1.1.1.12.2.6. Application of Firefighting Foam to reduce vapors
2.1.1.1.12.2.7. Water streams to cool containers
2.1.1.1.12.2.8. Withdrawal (for possible BLEVE or explosions)
2.1.1.2. Remaining assigned companies report to Staging for direction:
2.1.1.2.1. Engines and ladders prepare to assist as needed.
1.3.1.1.3. Rescue prepares to assist the hazardous materials branch officer with entry and back-up duties.
1.3.1.1.4. Medic and EMS coordinatorprepare to treat decontaminated patients.

1.3.2. On-scene incident commander: Assumes control of the incident. Must possess minimum training at the first responder operations level with additional knowledge of state, local, and federal response plans (first arriving Battalion Chief).

1.3.2.1. If the B/C is preceded to the scene, he/she will establish communications with the incident commander and prepare to formally assume command of the incident by announcing via radio his identification and the location of the new command post.

1.3.2.2. On “working incidents,” the B/C will ensure that the Health Department, Ohio EPA, and Franklin County EMA have been notified.Other considerations would be Sewers and Drains and the Street Department.

1.3.3. Hazardous Materials Technician: HazMat techs respond to a hazardousmaterials incident in an offensive manner for the purpose of stopping the release. Upon the arrival of HazMat 4, the officer will:
1.3.3.1. Report to, and obtain briefing from, the incident commander. The officer of HazMat 4 will normally become the hazardous materials branch officer.
1.3.3.2. Size-up the HazMat site, ensuring that the on-scene units have not become dangerously close to the hazard and that they have not become contaminated.
1.3.3.3. Ensure the following zones are established:
1.3.3.3.1. Hot Zone: Only entry and back-up crews may enter.
1.3.3.3.2. Warm Zone: The decontamination corridor. This area is only for those in direct support of the entry and back-up crews.
1.3.3.3.3. Cold Zone: The staging area where personal protective clothing is not needed.
1.3.3.4. The positions identified in the HazmatStaffingSOP, will be assigned to HazMat techs, under the direction of the hazardous materials branch officer:
2.1.1.2.2. Lead tender/timer
2.1.1.2.3. Research officer and assistant officer
2.1.1.2.4. Decon officer
2.1.1.2.5. HazMat EMS
2.1.1.2.6. Entry and back-up teams
2.1.1.2.7. HazMat safety officer
2. Incident Termination
2.2. At conclusion of successful mitigation of hazard:
2.1.1. Have the responsible party, or the EPA, contact a clean-up contractor.
2.1.2. Debriefing: All personnel should be informed of the materials that were involved and what the health hazards are, the symptoms of exposure, and when and where they should receive treatment.
2.1.3. Gather information for reports:
2.1.3.1. The first assigned Battalion Chief will assure the NFIRS-1 report is completed.
2.1.3.2. HazMat officer will complete NFIRS-HMI when HazMat 4 is on the scene. Will also collect and submit cost recovery information.

1. Administration

1.1. Purpose: To provide general explanations of the various components, staffing, and training of the Columbus Division of Fire Hazardous Materials Team that meets OSHA 29 CFR 1910,120 “Hazardous Waste Operations and Emergency Response”regulations, as well asaddresses NFPA 471,472, and 473.

1.2. Responsibility: It shall be the responsibility of each member to know, understand, and utilize these procedures as they apply to the situation at hand. It shall further be the responsibility of all Division Officers to train their subordinates in the proper application of these procedures and to implement and enforce the use of these procedures.
2. Componentsofthe HazardousMaterials Team:
2.1. Personnel:
2.1.1. Qualifications and Training:

1.2.1.1. All personnel comprising the “HazMat Team”must be journeymen and hazardous materials technicians with current HazMat physicals. They may be assigned anywhere in the Division. Members interested inbecoming HazMat techs shall write a letter to the captain at Station 4 requesting the appropriate 36 hours of training meeting OSHA 1910.120 (q)(6)(iii). If accepted, they also must receive a minimum of 8 hours of refresher annually.

1.2.1.2. Members assigned to the Station 4 HazMat team must have the same qualifications and must receive 36 hours of refresher annually leading to attaining NFPA Standard 472, Chapter 4: “Competencies for the Hazardous Materials Technician”.

1.2.1.3. Paramedics assigned to Station 4 will attend the National Fire Academy course titled “Advanced Life Support Response to Hazardous Materials Incidents”, or similar courses aimed at attaining NFPA 473 standards.
1.2.1.4. HazMat technician officers assigned to Station 4 will attend courses aimed at attaining NFPA Standard 472, Chapter 7: “Competencies for the Hazardous Materials Branch Officer.”
1.2.1.5. HazMat technician officers not assigned to Station 4 shall attend training aimed at attaining NFPA Standard 472, Chapter 8: “Competencies for the Hazardous Materials Branch Safety Officer.”
1.2.2. Job descriptions and minimum daily staffing positions (10) atStation 4 (all personnel are HazMat technicians):
1.2.2.1. Hazardous Materials Branch Officer (1): The officer (or FF tech working out of class fora maximum of 4 hours) of HazMat 4, under the direction of the Incident Commander, is responsible for:
1.2.2.1.1. The coordination of theHazMat branch and the assignment of personnel roles within that branch.
2.1.1.1.1. Safe entry and operations within the hot and warm zones.
1.2.2.1.2. Determining the safest level of chemical protective clothing ensembles to be used in the various zones.
1.2.2.1.3. Recommendations to the incident commanderforthe safe mitigation of the incident.
1.2.2.2. Lead tender/timer (1): Under the direction of the HazMat branch officer, is responsible for:
1.2.2.2.1. Following the lead tender/timer checklist and current “dress-out” procedures.
1.2.2.2.2. Proper set-up of the dress-out area.
1.2.2.2.3. Assigning other companies’ personnel to serve as tenders for entry and back-up teams.
1.2.2.2.4. Dressing-out entry and back-up teams in the recommended chemical protective clothing ensemble.
1.2.2.3. Decon coordinator (1): Under the direction of the HazMat branch officer, is responsible for:
1.2.2.3.1. Coordination of the decon group and directing additional personnel in the decontamination of the entry and back-up teams.
1.2.2.3.2. Set-up of the decon area.
1.2.2.3.3. Assuring the decon group is wearing the recommended chemical protective clothing ensemble.
1.2.2.3.4. Assisting in decontaminating the entry teams.
1.2.2.4. Research Officer (2): Underthe direction of theHazMat branch officer, is responsible for:
2.1.1.1.2. Following the research checklist.
1.2.2.4.1. Identification of the hazardous properties of the chemical(s) involved by being able to access information from both hard copy and electronic information reference sources.
2.1.1.1.3. Notification of outside agencies needed for assistance.
2.1.1.1.4. Connection to internet for electronic research abilities.

1.2.2.5. Entry team (2 members): Under the direction of the HazMat branch officer, shall be responsible for the safe entry into the hot zone for the purpose of identifying and mitigating the HazMat incident.
1.2.2.6. Back-up team (2 members): Under the direction of the HazMat branch officer, shall be responsible for the safe and expedient rescue of downed entry team members.
1.2.2.7. HazMat EMS officer (1): Under the direction of the HazMat branch officer, is responsible for:
1.2.2.7.1. Following the EMS checklist and the “Emergency Treatment Post Exposure” section of the Protocol for Medical Evaluations for Members of the HazMat and Bomb Squads.
2.1.1.1.5. Pre-entry and post-entry evaluations.
2.1.1.1.6. Treatmentof HazMat techs exposed to hazardous chemicals.
1.2.2.8. HazMat Safety Officer (Not a Station 4 minimum staffing position): Under the direction of SO-2, and following the safety officer’s checklist, is responsible for:
1.2.2.8.1. Ensuring the safety of the personnel in the hazardous materials branch.
1.2.2.8.2. In some instances, he/she may accompany the entry team to maintain safe operations within the hot and warm zones.
2.2. Billing:
1.2.3. The HazMat branch officer shall be responsible for submitting an itemized bill to the CFD Business Office within ten business days for any billable HazMat incident.
1.2.4. The Division of Fire will follow the current procedures on “Cost Recovery” as outlined by the Franklin County EMA:
1.2.4.1. The Division of Fire shall bill for any and all supplies used and equipment destroyed on a HazMat incident.
1.2.4.2. The Division of Fire may bill for any overtime personnel required to mitigate the HazMat incident.
1.2.4.3. The Division of Fire will bill for on-duty personnel when the time onscene exceeds two hours.
2.3. Equipment:
1.2.5. Supplies: The captain at Station 4 shall be responsible for the ordering and replacement of all equipment and supplies assigned to HazMat 4.
1.2.6. Air monitors: The captain at Station 4 shall be responsible for all air monitors assigned to HazMat 4.
2.3.1.1. Station 4 personnel shall calibrate their air monitors at least monthly.
1.2.6.1. All use of air monitors shall be logged on the Air Monitoring Log assigned to each air monitor at Station 4.
1.2.6.2. All personnel using air monitors in potentially hazardous atmospheres must understand their proper use and limitations.
2. Chain of Command

2.1. The Columbus Division of Fire chain of command shall prevail until such time that the incident is contained and control of the scene is turned over to another agency. The officer in charge of HazMat 4 shall report to the Incident Commander and obtain a briefing. On working incidents, he/she will normally become the hazardous materials branch officer.

2. Procedures
2.1. Placement and Operation

1.1.1. The UDR-13BR radiation unit shall be placed in the cab of all engine, ladder, and rescue companies. Upon declaration of an "orange" or '"red" terrorism threat level, they will be placed on the waist strap of the incharge position SCBA.The unit should also be utilized on any report of or actual explosion.

1.1.1.1. The unit will normally be carried in the sleep mode this will allow the unit to "wake up" every 5 minutes, vibrate, and give a current rate reading, then return immediately to sleep mode. Batteries will last approximately 1500 hours (two months) in this mode.
1.1.1.2. Personnel can change batteries by replacing the four (4) AAA batteries in the unit.

1.1.1.3. Each day, the officer or in-charge person will verify that the unit is in the sleep mode. A unit that is found running in the “ON” position can be placed back in “OFF" button simultaneously until "SLP" appears, then release, and the unit should go back into the sleep mode.
2.2. Activation

1.1.2. The unit should be taken out of the sleep mode by pressing the "ON/OFF" button for any suspicious incident (e.g., an explosion, the presence of radioactive placards orlabels, or concerns that the incident might involve terrorism). This will give full time detection of radiation levels on the scene.
1.1.3. After the situation is contained and the scene has been evaluated, return the unit to the sleep mode.
2.3. “RATE” Alarm Procedure

1.1.4. The "RATE" alarm is set to alarm when radiation rates exceed 10 milliRad per hour (10 mR/hr). When a "RATE" alarm is sounded, all crews will immediately cease all non-essential or non-life saving activities and back out from the area until the alarm stops. No activity will take place in an area where a rate alarm is sounding with the exception of rescuing viable victims.

1.1.5. Under certain circumstances, people and/or animals who have recently received radioactive medications and/or tests will set off the rate alarm of the UDR-13BR. If appropriate, interview anyone involved with the scene to verify that this is not the cause of the alarm.
2.4. “DOSE” Alarm Procedure

1.1.6. The “DOSE" alarm is set to alarm when the total dosage of radiation that the unit receives exceeds one (1) rem. Under normal conditions, the "DOSE" alarm will never be exceeded without the "RATE" alarm sounding first. The total ''DOSE" is accumulative in the unit from the minute it is first turned on until it is reset. The Office of Research and Development will reset the dose level in the first quarter of the year.
1.1.7. Contact HazMat 4 for instructions immediately whenever a dose alarm is activated on just one unit at a scene.

1.1.8. If multiple units are giving a “DOSE” alarm, all crews will immediately cease all non-essential or lifesaving activities and back out from the area until the rate drops below 1 mR/hr. Incident commanders will establish an evacuation perimeter around the site and attempt to investigate the cause of the radiation and/or alarm. Consult the Emergency Response Guidebook for appropriate isolation distances. If no legitimate reasons can be determined for the presence of radiation, a HazMat response will be requested (the HazMat branch officer will assist in determining the origin and, if needed, contact the appropriate radiation responders at the state and/or federal level).
2.5. Repair and Calibration

1.1.9. All units found to be defective or in need of repair shall contact the Logistics Center at extension 75480 for evaluation and disposition. The Logistics Center will check calibration once every 18 months. Those that are out of calibration will be sent to a facility to be recalibrated.

1. Administration
1.1. Purpose:Mutual Aid HazMat team responsesoutside of Franklin County. These procedures are to be considered sensitive and not released to the public.

1.2. Responsibility: It shall be the responsibility of each member to know, understand, and utilize these procedures as they apply to the situation at hand. It shall further be the responsibility of all Division Officers to train their subordinates in the proper application of these procedures and to implement and enforce the use of these procedures.
2. Introduction and Background
1.2. HazMat 4 is considered a Type I HazMat team by State of Ohio standards. The City of Columbus has agreed that these assets can be used regionally for mutual aid responses.

1.3. The HazMat Team is equipped with a primaryvehicle, HazMat 4 (HZ4), and a second similarly-equipped vehicle, HazMat Support Unit 4 (HSU4). These vehicles can be used in tandem at one large incident or separate at two different incidents.
3. Mutual Aid Request

1.4. The Fire Alarm Office will be the initial contact for all HazMat mutual aid requests. Upon receipt of a request for a HazMat team mutual aid response the FAO will obtain a contact number for the Incident Commander/dispatch center requesting the mutual aid, or connect them directly to Station 4. The FAO will inform the Incident Commander/dispatch centerthat HZ4 will contact them directly. The FAO will then contact the HazMat officer at Station 4 with the contact information.

1.5. The HazMat officer at Station 4 will gather information on the request, such as location and type of incident. He/she will determine the urgency of the needed response and possible duration of the response. The HazMat officer will then contact ES-2 with recommendations on the appropriate response and/or for permission to respond.

1.6. The HazMat officer will again contact the Incident Commander/dispatch center with the answer from ES-2 on if and how the HazMat team will respond. At this point the HazMat officer will determine which MARCSradio communications channel will be utilized for contact as the team approaches the area. Directions to the affected area will also be determined.
4. Response Options
1.7. Upon receipt of a request for mutual aid the HazMat officer shall determine the best response option from the following:

1.7.1. Option 1 – An immediate emergency response to include HZ4, Medic 4, and Rescue 4. This should be limited to responses in which response time is critical and the length of time needed will be limited (less than 12 hours). HSU4 will remain behind to be staffed by other on-duty HazMat techs or by special called off-duty Station 4 HazMat techs. One HazMat officer and three HazMat firefighters will be moved up to station 4 or called in. ES- 2 will determine if a call in is needed.

1.7.2. Option 2 – A delayed response in which off-duty crews (preference will be given to Station 4 assigned personnel) will be called in to staff HZ4 and Medic 4 (one HazMat officer and nine HazMat firefighters). This response should be able to leave Station 4 within one hour from the request. An offer to contact off-duty HazMat technicians for ES-2 will be made by the HazMat officer. Personnel responding must be capable of remaining on the mutual aid scene for a maximum of 24 hours. This response would be used any time that a concern that a second incident is likely and/or the duration of the response could be greater than 12 hours. The HazMat Support Unit would be left behind to be staffed by the onduty crew.
5. HazMat Team Mutual Aid Responses SOP
1.8. HazMat 4 will follow the standard HazMat team SOP (SOP 03-03-02)while operating at any mutual aid response.
1.9. The HazMat officer must collect information on howand who to bill for the incident from the Incident Commander prior to leaving the scene.
1.10. Regularand timely updates to Columbus Fire (ES-2, Special Ops 1, and/or HazMat 1) should be made by the HazMat officer.
1. Administration
1.1. Purpose: The purpose of this procedure is to provide guidelines for a safe response to a suspected radiological event by first responders.

1.2. Responsibility: It shall be the responsibility of each member to know, understand, and utilize these procedures as they apply to the situation at hand. It shall further be the responsibility of all Division Officers to train their subordinates in the proper application of these procedures and to implement and enforce the use of these procedures.
2. Procedure
2.1. Responder Levels

1.2.1. First Responder Operations Level – Firefighters will be trained at the minimum to the First Responder Operations Level. Operations level personnel are expected to take defensive actions without trying to stop the release, for the purpose of protecting persons, property, and the environment. Their function is to contain the release from a safe distance, keep it from spreading, and protect exposures.

1.2.2. Hazardous Materials Technician – All HazMat team personnel will be trained to the Hazardous Materials Technician Level. HazMat Technicians respond to a hazardous materials incident in an offensive manner for the purpose of stopping the release.

1.2.3. On-Scene Incident Commander – Assumes control of the incident beyond the first responder awareness level. This individual must have minimum training at the first responder operations level with additional knowledge of state, local, and federal response plans.
2.2. Level I Staging for a Radiological Event
2.2.1. First Arriving Unit
2.2.1.1. Response

1.2.3.1.1. Approach from upwind and uphill if possible. Do not drive through vapor or dust clouds.Avoid rushing in before sizing-up the situation. Determine if the risk is life, property, or environment?
1.2.3.1.2. Establish command. Determine and announce a safe staging area (minimum of ¼mile away, approximately2.5 city blocks) for all other responding units. Avoid staging too close to the hazard.
2.2.1.2. Isolate the scene
1.2.3.1.3. Isolate the hazard anddeny entry of unprotected personnel into the hazard area. Avoid exposure to all chemicals and vapors.

1.2.3.1.4. Perform rescue of victims while wearing full structural firefighting protective clothing (SFPC). DO NOT enter visible vapor/dust clouds for rescue purposes. The use of SFPC into a hazardous atmosphere should be limited to a “quick in-and-out” to execute only a life-saving rescue. Additional personnel should not enter the hazard area without being ordered to do so, if help is needed for rescue, request assistance through the incident commander.

1.2.3.1.5. Responders shall wear full structural firefighting protective clothing while performing “emergency decontamination” procedures.Victims and rescuers will be decontaminated, before removing their outer layer of clothing.

1.2.3.1.6. Time in the “Hot Zone” for rescue should be limited to the use of one SCBA air bottle. After using the initial air bottle, the rescuer shall exit the “Hot Zone” area, be decontaminated, and evaluated by EMS.
2.2.1.3. Evaluate the Scene

1.2.3.1.7. Initially a 330-foot minimum hot zone around suspected device or area shall be secured if no radiation meters are present on the scene. This information can be found in the Emergency Response Guidebook (guide 163) for “Initial Isolation” and/or “Evacuation Distances" for radiological incidents.

1.2.3.1.8. If the Canberra UDR-13 radiation pagers are available, turn them on and use them in the “rate mode” to establish a hot zone perimeter at the1000mR (1R)/hr point. The command post can be established in any area with less than 10mR/hr.

1.2.3.1.9. If the 715 survey meter is available, it can be used just like the Canberra UDR-13. Turn it on and use it to establish a hot zone perimeter at the 1000mR (1R)/hr point. The command post can be established in any area with less than 10mR/hr.
2.2.1.3.1. Gatherinformation from:
2.2.1.3.1.1. Occupancy
2.2.1.3.1.2. Container shape
2.2.1.3.1.3. Markings or colors
2.2.1.3.1.4. Placards or labels
2.2.1.3.1.5. Shipping papers
2.2.1.3.1.6. MSDS sheets
2.2.1.3.1.7. Victim signs and symptoms
2.2.1.3.2. Try to determine the hazard(s) involved.
1.2.3.1.10. Determine whatresources are needed and direct their placement.
1.2.3.1.11. Separate decontaminated rescuers and victims for triage, treatment, and transportation by EMS units and/or the Hazmat team.
2.2.1.3.3. Take protective action.
1.2.3.1.12. Evacuationmay be the best protective action if there is enough time. Consider evacuation when the following are present:
2.2.1.3.3.1. Flammable vapors presence (massive fire or explosion)
2.2.1.3.3.2. Long-term vapor presence
1.2.3.1.13. The following situations may justify sheltering in-place:
2.2.1.3.3.3. Short-duration incidents
2.2.1.3.3.4. Short-term vapor clouds
2.2.1.3.3.5. Greater hazard to attempt to move people
2.2.1.3.3.6. Impractical to move people
2.2.1.4. Mitigation

1.2.3.1.14. Perform "operation level" defensive actions to control, contain, or confine the product. Keep the product out of the sewer, stormdrains, and waterways. The following defensive actions should be considered:
2.2.1.4.1.1. Damming (overflow or under flow)
2.2.1.4.1.2. Diking to retain liquids
2.2.1.4.1.3. Diversion to redirect liquids to a more desirable location
2.2.1.4.1.4. Absorption
2.2.1.4.1.5. Removal of all ignition sources
2.3. Incident Commander
1.2.4. For“working radiological incidents”ensure that the following organizations are notified:
2.3.1.1. Hospital Incident Liaison (the HIL)
2.3.1.2. Ohio Department of Health – Radiation Protection
2.3.1.3. Franklin County Emergency Management & Homeland Security
2.3.1.4. Central Ohio Poison Control
2.3.1.5. Ohio EPA
2.3.1.6. ColumbusPublic Health/Franklin County Board of Health

1.2.5. Be advised, the Columbus Fire Alarm Office can activate their Radiation Incident Notification Group to notify hospitals in Franklin County as well as the organizations listed above that a radiological event is in progress.
2.3.2. Other considerations for notification include:
2.3.2.1. Sewers & Drains and Streets Departments
2.3.2.2. 52ndCivil Support Team – WMD
2.3.2.3. FBI, if it is a suspected terrorist incident
1.2.6. Consider the declaration of a Medical Emergency if more than 5 victims are involved.
1.3. Remaining Engines and/or Ladders
2.3.3. Follow standard staging procedures from a designated “safe” area.
1.4. Rescue Company
1.4.1. Report to the staging area and be prepared to assist the hazardous materials branch officer with entry and back-up duties.
2.4. Medic Transport Unit and EMS Officer
1.4.2. Report to the staging area and be prepared to triage, treat and transport decontaminated victims.

1.4.3. Ensure that hospitals have been notified to expect victims of a radiologicalevent. Include, if possible, the type of radiological hazard, number of victims, the extent of on-scene decontamination, and the estimated time of arrival.
1.5. Arrival of HazMat Team/Bomb Squad
1.5.1. The officer of the Hazmat/Bomb Squad will report to and obtain briefing from the Incident Commander.
1.5.2. Besides utilizing the standard operating procedures of the HazMat team and/or the Bomb Squad, consider the following:
1.5.2.1. Using the UDR-13 pagers or the 715 Survey meter, set-up proper zones, or verify that proper zones have been established:
2.4.1.1.1. Hot Zone – Perimeterat 1000mR (1R)/hr
1.5.2.1.1. Warm Zone – The decontamination corridor. This area is only for those in direct support of the entry and back-up teams.
1.5.2.1.2. Cold Zone – The Command Post established at an area of a level less than 10 mR/hr.
2.4.1.2. While completing a contamination survey inside hot zone:
2.4.1.2.1. Wear Level B or LevelC PPE as appropriate
2.4.1.2.2. Use dosimeters to monitor dose rate of all entry team members
2.4.1.2.3. Maximum dose 5000 mrem
2.4.1.2.4. Check dosimeters every 15 minutes
2.4.1.2.5. Document each entry team member’s received dose
1.5.2.1.3. Calculate entry time and/ortime remaining based on “dose rate” (1000mR(1R)/hr for 5 hours = 5000mrem dose)
1.5.2.1.4. Use Contamination monitor (LUDLUM MODEL 3 SURVEY METERwith MODEL 44-9 PANCAKE DETECTOR)to identify contamination and “hot spots” (concentrated contamination)
1.5.2.1.5. Start on x100 scale, then move to lower scales until readings are seen
1.5.2.1.6. Use a sweeping motion, < 2 inches from ground or individual, moving across at less than 4 inches per second
1.5.2.1.7. Identify areas of contamination in units of CPM (counts per minute)
2.7.2.2.11. Use audio to help guide to highest readings (if desired)
2.7.2.2.12. Read the instrument dial; multiply the highest value by the instrument setting (x1, x10, x100) (e.g., 2000 CPM on x10 setting = 20,000 CPM)
2.7.2.2.13. Document Dose Rate and Contamination survey results on a simple diagram showing landmarks, readings,and distances.
2.4.1.3. Radioactive material Identification:
1.5.2.1.8. If the instrumentation is available, use the Isotope Identi-Finder to establish isotope. Inform all previously notified agencies and the Incident Commander of results.
2.5. Terminating the Incident
2.5.1. Gather information for reports and documentation.
1.5.3. Document all responders and the amount of time estimated that they spent in the Hot Zone.

1.5.4. During the debriefing, all personnel should be informed of the material(s) that were involved and what the health hazards are, the symptoms of exposure, and when and where they should receive treatment.
2.5.2. Critique the incident.
