1. Administration
1.1. Purpose: To establish standard guidelines for incidents involving confined space rescue.
1.2. Scope:The procedures below shall apply to all Division of Fire personnel while on-duty and involved with confined space rescue incidents.

1.3. Responsibility: It shall be the responsibility of each member to know, understand, and utilize these procedures as they apply to the situation at hand. It shall further be the responsibility of all Division Officers to train their subordinates in the proper application of these procedures and to implement and enforce the use of these procedures.
2. Permit Required and Definition

1.4. The basis for all confined space rescue operations is OSHA Regulations Standard 29 CFR 1910.146 Permit-Required Confined Spaces regulating entry into confined spaces for general industry and the rescue service (see
Section 5 Permit and Approval below, and CFD Confined Space Rescue Permit elsewhere).

1.5. For the purpose of emergency response, a confined space is defined as: A space large enough for personnel to physically enter, and a space with limited entry and egress, and a space not designed for continuous employee occupancy.
1.6. The atmosphere within a confined space shallbe considered hazardous until proven otherwise.
2. Command, Initial Actions, and Further Assessment
2.1. Establish Command
2.1.1. Followcurrent Columbus Fire Standard Operating Procedures.
2.1.1. Determine if this will be a RESCUE or RECOVERY.
2.1.2. Identify and communicate the hazards, critical factors, and needs.
2.1.2. Isolate immediate hazard areas, secure the scene, and deny entry forall non-rescue personnel.
2.2. Initial Actions

2.1.3. Initial Engine, Ladder, and Medic companies SHALL NOT enter a confined space as theyare not usually equipped to safely do so; however non-entry retrieval of victims is permitted if it is safe to do so.

2.1.3.1. If possible, establish communications with the victim(s) and determine if a non-entry retrieval can be made. Non-entry retrieval may include actions such as passing a ladder or other items in to a space to provide a means of self-egress for conscious persons, operating with caution a retrieval system already in place, utilizing a pike pole or other means to drag a person to safety, etc.

2.1.4. Companies who arrive first at a confined space incident shall recon the area without making entry into the confined space, in full turnout gear, breathing from SCBA and using multi-gas monitors. Companies should make note of multi-gas monitor readings.

2.1.5. Secure a witness or responsible party to assist in gathering information to determine exactly what happened. If no witnesses are present, personnel may have to look for clues on the scene to determine what is likely to have happened.
2.2.1. Ifa confined space entry is indicated, establish control zone perimeters:
2.2.1.1. Hot Zone – Rescue Team Members only
2.2.1.2. Warm Zone – Rescue Team and Attendants
2.2.1.3. Cold Zone – EMS, Safety, Command, Support personnel
2.3. Further Assessment
2.1.6. Secure the existing Confined Space Entry Permit, and any other relevant information including diagrams for entry and egress locations.
2.1.7. Determine what products and materials may be present and conduct hazard assessments.
2.3.1. Identify other potential hazards including engulfment, entanglement, etc.
2.3.2. Ensure adequate EMS for victims and personnel.
2.3.3. Determine potential need for decontamination.
2.1.8. Assess on-scene capabilities and request additional resources as needed.
3. Planning and Preparations
3.1. Atmospheric Monitoring
2.1.9. Determine what atmospheric hazards might be present by testing for oxygen level, flammability, and toxicity using a multi-gasmonitor or other suitable equipment.

2.1.10. Atmospheric monitoring shall be done prior to and throughout all entry operations. All readings shall be communicated to the Rescue Team Leader and recorded on the Rescue Permit at least every 5 minutes.
2.1.11. Readings must be obtained by personnel with a thorough knowledge of atmospheric monitoring.
2.1.12. Preference should be given to the monitors from Rescue and Hazmat companies, which have a peak hold setting as well as a pump and extension tubing for sampling at a distance.
2.1.13. The hazards identified and the results of atmospheric testing will determine if entry can be made and the proper level of PPE to be worn by rescuers.
2.1.14. The rescuers should not enter a known flammable atmosphere. If a flammable atmosphereis detected at any time, the rescuers shall exit the space as soon as possible.
2.1.14.1. A flammable atmosphere is defined as any atmosphere that contains 10% or more of the Lower Explosive Limit (LEL) for any substance.
3.2. Ventilation
2.1.15. Consider appropriate ventilation for incident; positive and/ornegative pressure, entry and/or exhaust, and their affects to the scene and atmosphere.
2.1.16. Always ventilate the confined space; unless flammable gases are detected and doing so would potentially increase the hazards.
3.2.1. Provide for ventilation to the general area if necessary.
3.3. Additional Preparations
3.3.1. Ensure the structural stability of the confined space and surrounding area.
3.3.2. Implement Lock-Out/Tag-Out procedures, if applicable.
2.1.17. If any product is in or flowing into the confined space it shall be secured via blanking and blinding if possible.
3.4. Planning for Rescue Entry
2.1.18. Review conditions and information. Determine if there is a justifiable need to proceed with entry and rescue operations.
3.4.1. Reevaluate initially established control zones, and adjust as needed.
2.1.19. In conjunction with qualified rescue personnel develop a detailed plan of rescue operations.
2.1.20. All entry operations shall be conducted under the direction of a Company Officer and/or In-Charge Rescue personnel.
2.1.21. Assign and verify key rescue operations personnel including Safety Officer(s), Rescue Team Leader(s), Entry Team members, Backup Team members, Attendants, and supporting personnel as needed.
2.1.22. The rescue plan shall be discussed so that all involved personnel are aware of the plan, the hazards, and means of communication.
2.1.23. Assign and communicate tasks and areas of responsibility to all involved personnel.
2.1.24. The Safety Officer and Rescue Team Leader shall make sure all Entry and Backup Team personnel have appropriate PPE, and that equipment and personnel are checked prior to entry.
4. Permit and Approval

2.2. The Division of Fire form “Confined Space Rescue Permit” form ES-223 shall be completed by the Rescue Team Leader prior to entry in to a confined space, with the Atmospheric Monitoring portion of the Permit filled out at fiveminute intervals.

2.3. The Confined Space Rescue Permit is used to record incident information including location, hazard assessment, assignments, pre-entry checklist, ventilation plan, communication plan, and atmospheric monitoring.
2.4. The Safety Officer shall be responsible for seeing that the Confined Space Rescue Permit is followed.
2.5. Once approved, each permit is only valid for one hour. If more than one-hour elapses, all plans and information must be reviewed, updated and reapproved.
5. Entry Equipment
5.1. Entry equipment includes, but is not limited to:

2.5.1. A retrieval system with a back-up system shall be readied and in place. This may include a vertical or horizontal haul system constructed of ropes, pulleys, and other hardware, with a minimum of a 2:1 mechanical advantage. Entry shall not be made unless a means to retrieve rescuers is established.

2.5.2. Any entrant entering the space shall wear a class III harness, with a tag line of 1/2” life safety rope, secured to the dorsal attachment point on the harness, or at another point which presents a profile small enough for the successful removal of the entrant. Wristlets may be used if they are the safest and most effective alternative.

2.5.3. Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) shall include, at a minimum, helmet, gloves, proper footwear, goggles, Nomex or PBI clothing or jumpsuit orturnout gear as appropriate. Additional PPE may be indicated by the hazard and atmospheric assessment.

2.5.4. Supplied Air Breathing Apparatus (SABA) or Self-Contained Breathing Apparatus (SCBA) shall be utilized by all entry and back-up personnel, unless normal atmospheric conditions can be confirmed throughout the confined space. SABA is the breathing apparatus of choice. Any airline that is used must be purged for 1 minute prior to users going on air.
2.5.4.1. If SCBA must be used, personnel shall maintain line of sight and exit the confined space prior to low air alarm activation.

2.5.4.2. If any portion of a Self-Contained Breathing Apparatus (SCBA) must be removed to enter or access a part of the confined space, Supplied Air Breathing Apparatus (SABA) shall be used instead of SCBA.

2.5.5. Electronic communication equipment used bypersonnel to enter the confined space shall be intrinsically safe. If this equipment is not available,entry personnel may use a tag-line for communication or a message relay person.
2.5.6. Intrinsically safe lighting equipment shall be required for entry personnel. If this equipment is not available, entry personnel may use chemical light sticks.
2.5.7. An additional multi-gas air monitoring device that monitors oxygen levels, flammability, and toxicity for the entry team.
6. Entry, Exit, and Termination
6.1. Entry
2.5.8. The Incident Commander, Safety Officer, and all members of the Rescue Teams must agree that conditions are safe to proceed before Entry is initiated.

2.5.9. During Entry Operations the Rescue Team Leader shall closely monitor conditions and personnel involved in the rescue and keep the Incident Commander or other supervisor as assigned, informed of conditions, progress and any concerns.
6.2. UponExit
2.5.10. Immediately after egress, victim(s) care, with all treatment information, should be transferred from the Rescue Team to EMS.
6.2.1. Ensure the safety/accountability of all personnel.
6.2.2. All victim(s) shall be decontaminated as needed before transport.
6.2.3. Personnel shall be decontaminated as needed.
2.5.11. All personnel who entered the confined space and any others showing signs of stress shall be medically evaluated by EMS before returning to service.
2.5.12. In case of a fatality, consider leaving everything in place until cleared by investigators.
2.5.13. Consider the potential risks involved and as appropriate remove toolsand equipment used in the rescue/recovery, decontaminate as needed and return to proper apparatus.
6.3. Terminating the Incident
2.5.14. Considerand take appropriate actions regarding the emotional state, mental health and religious needs of victim’s family, co-workers, emergency responders, and affected community.
6.3.1. Consider a Post Incident Critique.
6.3.2. Ensure that the scene is secure.
6.3.3. Turn the scene over to the responsible party.
2.5.15. Upload the Confined Space Rescue Entry permit, Form ES-223, and attach to the NFIRS report or submit a copy to ES1.
1. Administration
1.1. Purpose:To establish guidelines for incidents involving rope rescue.

1.1. Responsibility: It shall be the responsibility of each member to know, understand, and utilize these procedures as they apply to the situation at hand. It shall further be the responsibility of all Division Officers to train their subordinates in the proper application of these procedures and to implement and enforce the use of these procedures.
2. Definitions and Standards
2.1. Definitions

1.1.1. Rope Rescue is defined as any rescue effort that requires rope, rigging, and/or rope rescue equipment to safely gain access to and remove patients from hazardous geographic areas with limited access; such as in or around water, various buildings, towers and other structures, construction sites and other areas.
1.1.2. Rope rescues are divided into two general categories: Low Angle and High Angle.
1.1.2.1. Low Angle Evacuations are those of less than 40º inclination, utilizing a single-rope belay, with the majority of weight on the ground. Involves less risk.
1.1.2.2. High Angle Evacuations are considered those from 40º to 90º, utilizing a two-rope system, with the majority ofweight on the rope. A much greater risk.
1.1.3. CFD issued device is any device approved bythe Columbus Division of Fire for use on emergency scenes.
1.1.3.1. CFD issued devices will be issued by In-service training after the appropriate training has been issued.
2.2. Standards
1.1.4. National Fire Protection Association (NFPA) standards shall provide the basis for all CFD Rope Rescue training & tactics as applicable.
3. Command,Size-Up, and Initial Actions
3.1. Establish Command
3.1.1. Follow current Columbus Fire Standard Operating Procedures.
3.1.2. Initiate Command and conduct Size-Up.
3.1.3. Identify and communicate hazards, critical factors and needs.
3.1.4. Establish control perimeters; Hot, Warm, and Cold zones.
3.1.5. Conduct Initial Actions as may be done safely.
3.2. Size-Up
3.2.1. Secure witnesses and/or responsible party.
3.2.2. Determine location, number, and condition of victims.
3.2.3. Determine and make clear if operating in rescue orrecovery mode.
3.2.4. Request utility company(s) to respond as needed.
1.1.5. Attempt to make contact with the victim(s) and evaluate their level of consciousness and medical condition(s).
1.1.6. Assess on-scene capabilities. Determine the need for and request additional and/or outside resources as needed.
3.3. Initial Actions
3.3.1. Address all hazards as able.
1.1.7. Initial attempts can be made to access victims from a position of safety that does not include fall hazards.

1.1.8. Personnel working within six feet (6’) of an edge or climbing a non-fireservice ladder for access above or below grade will utilize travel restriction or fall protection equipment/systems as appropriate.

1.1.9. Make an effort to prevent the victim(s) from falling any further. If the victim is conscious, this may be completed by simply lowering a rope that can be attached easily to them or their system.
1.1.9.1. Take up the slack and connect stabilization rope(s) to the most secure anchor point available.
3.3.2. Clearthe general area, make it as safe and approachable as possible.
3.3.3. Stand by for the arrival of sufficiently trained and equipped personnel.
4. Planning and Preparations
4.1. Planning for Rescue Operations
4.1.1. Assessand address utility company and other hazards.
1.1.9.2. Have a representative from all involved utility and hazard related companies present if possible.
4.1.2. Develop a rescue plan and a back-up plan.
4.1.3. Select optimum routes for rescue access and egress.
4.1.4. Identify proper Personal Protective Equipment (PPE).
4.1.5. Identify and stage equipment.
5. Equipment
1.2. All rope rescue operations considered high angle evacuations shall utilize a dual rope technique main line and belay line. This will be accomplished with two CFD issued progress capture devices.
1.2.1. All rope rescue operations shall use ½-inch (12.5 mm) diameter rope for the main line and belay line.
1.2.2. The main line and belay lines for high angle evacuations shall run through CFD issued progress capture devices.
1.2.3. The main line and belay line will be attached to independent anchor systems. If circumstances permit, main line and belay line should be attached to two separate anchors.

1.3. Edge protection shall be utilized where needed to help protect against abrasion and cutting where the rope is in contact with abrasive surfaces, corners and edges.Edge protection is a key factor in rope rescue safety.
1.4. Rope rescue operations considered low angle shall utilize a minimum of one rope as a belay line.
1.4.1. The line/s for low angle evacuations shall be run through CFD issued progress capture devices.

1.5. For high angle evacuations from confined spaces working from an Artificial high directional (AHD), a CFD issued lowering device shall be used as the main line and a belay line ½-inch (12.5 mm) may be run through CFD issued progress capture devices.

1.6. For the purposes of gaining access to an area, ascending or descending will utilize dual ½-inch (12.5 mm) ropes (main line and belay line). The ropes shall be run through division issued devices. This is not permitted for confined space entry or for performing any work while on the main and belay lines.
6. RopeRescue Operations
6.1. All non-essential personnel shall stay out of the rigging and operations areas.
1.7. The Incident Commander, Safety Officer, and all members of the Rope Rescue Team(s) must agree that conditions are safe to proceed before a rope rescue is initiated.
1.8. All stages of the rescue operations shall be communicated to the Rescue Team Supervisor for logging of times, benchmarks and coordination.

1.9. The Rescue Team Supervisor shall closely monitor conditions and personnel involved in the rope rescue and keep the Incident Commander or other supervisor as assigned, informed of conditions, progress and any concerns.
6.2. Rescuers shall determine and utilize the best patient packaging option.
6.3. Upon completion of the rescue, transfer patient(s) to EMS personnel.
7. Terminating the Incident
1.10. Upon completion of the rescue, ensure all personnel are safe and accounted for.
7.1. Recoverand secure all ropes and equipment as appropriate.
7.2. Reviewoperations and conduct a post incident critique.
1.11. Secure the scene. If possible, have responsible party secure entry points to assure no additional entry.
7.3. Return companies to service.
1.12. In-Charge Rescue personnel are to complete the incident report rescue section.
1.13. An After-Action Report shall be completed for such event by the Incident Commander or designee from the incident.
1. Administration
1.1. Purpose: To standardize bailout (ladder and rope) training fall protection across the Division of Fire in accordance with PERRP/OSHA requirements.

1.2. Responsibility: It shall be the responsibility of each member to know, understand and utilize these procedures as they apply to the situation at hand. It shall further be the responsibility of all Division Officers to train their subordinates in the proper application of these procedures and to implement and enforce the use of these procedures.
2. Definition and Standards

1.3. It is the policy of the Division of Fire to provide the necessary safety equipment in accordance with PERRP (Public Employment Risk Reduction Program) and OSHA (Occupational Safety and Health Administration) guidelines to all employees.
1.3.1. Division of Fire employees have the responsibility to be aware of and understand the proper procedure for use of this safety equipment.

1.4. Belay device – A mechanical device used to act as a brake on a rope in the event of fall, so as not to free fall and to slow the firefighter’s descent in a controlled manner in the event of a fall.
1.5. Travel restraint – A system used to limit the movement of an individual so they are not capable of falling out, from, or over an edge, window, or wall opening.
1.6. Anchorage – A secure point of attachment for equipment such as lifelines, lanyards, or deceleration devices.
3. Bail Out Kits and Harnesses
1.7. Bail out kits have been created to ensure all necessary safety equipment is available for crews performing bail out training. These kits will be housed at Tools and Equipment.
3.1. All components must be accounted for prior to signing out the kit.
3.2. Belay/bail out kits will include the following equipment:
3.2.1. 100 ft. of PMI rope
3.2.2. 3 carabiners
3.2.3. 2 pieces of webbing for anchors
3.2.4. Rescue 8
3.2.5. 1 single pully
1.7.1. A variety of harness sizes will be available at Tools and Equipment and signed out as needed.
3.3. Check out/in procedures:
3.3.1. Request will be handled by Tools and Equipment.
1.7.2. Kits must be signed in/out. The form will be maintained by Tools and Equipment.
1.7.3. The lead instructor should inspect/inventory equipment and rope before leaving with equipment and before returning.
1.7.4. Tools and equipment will inventory all kit contents, and inspect the rope on return to tools and equipment.
2. Procedures
3.4. General Overview

2.1.1. When performing any rope/ladder bail out training ≥4 feet above the ground/lower level, members performing the evolution must be in a fall protection harness and on a manned belay line attached to the appropriate anchorage. Instructors demonstrating techniques must also be in a fall protection harness and on a manned belay line if performing a bailout.

2.1.2. When an instructor is in a location that causes or has the potential to cause them to lean out a window or over an edge that is ≥4 feet above the ground/lower level, members must be on a travel restraint to keep them from falling out or off the elevated position. In addition, instructors must be on a travel restraint if they will be near an opening where the inside bottom edge of the opening is <39 inches above the walking surface and the outside bottom edge of the opening is ≥ 4 feet above the ground/lower level, to protect from falling, regardless of whether the instructor may lean out the window or over an edge.
2.1.3. Members (instructor, participants, etc.) performing the drill, regardless of experience level, are required to wear appropriate fall protection.

2.1.4. Prior to training, requests for bail out kits need to be completed. If no kits are available and coordination can be made with a CFD Rescue, then suitable equipment may be substituted from the rescue. At no time should you separate the rescues from their equipment and reduce their available cache. If the rescues cannot attend the training and provide the necessary equipment, then members must wait for the availability of the bail out kits.
2.2. Overhead anchors must be attached to a suitable anchor point in line with the direction of decent down the ladder.
2.2.1. Bottom anchors must be attached to a suitable anchor point in line with the direction of rope travel.
2.2.2. Belay lines must be serviceable ½-inch rope that is provided in the kits. Rope should be kept clean and properly washed and dried if it becomes dirty.
2.2.3. Rescue 8 and munter hitch are the two preferred methods for decent control. This enables the userto allow for rapid movement, but affords the belay person the ability to manage decent control.
2.2.4. Examples of not meeting the requirements: Firefighters may not use their body as a means of friction for belay. Firefighters may not hand hold the belay rope without a belay / friction device.
2.2.5. Firefighter operating the belay line must be attentive and ready to stop the rescuer from falling at all times.

2.2.6. Instructors at the window – The instructors operating at the window opening will be responsible for ensuring that the members performing their bail out procedure are wearing the appropriate fall protection harnessand are attached into the belay system. This includes ensuring that the carabiner of the belay kit is attached to the appropriate connection point on the fall protection harness.
1. Administration
1.1. Purpose: To provide basic operating guidelines for the CFD personnel responding to a civil disturbance. This includes all Task Force Operations.

1.2. Responsibility: During a period of civil disturbances the role of the Columbus Division of Fire does not change. The Columbus Division of Fire is responsible for providing fire protection and emergency medical care to the citizens. It shall be the responsibility of each member to know, understand, and utilize these procedures as they apply to the situation at hand. It shall further be the responsibility of all Division Officers to train their subordinates in the proper application of these procedures and to implement and enforce the use of these procedures.
2. Responses to Incidents
2.1. Administration Staff

1.2.1. As soon as a civil disturbance or the potential for one exists and it is decided that the City of Columbus Emergency Operations Center (EOC) will be staffed, the Fire Chief or his directed alternate will report. All Assistant Chiefs (with the exception of ES-1) will report to the Department Operation Center (DOC) and follow procedures set forth in the Division of Fire Disaster Plan. ES-1 will report to the incident or area command post. All other Administrative Staff report as directed in the Division of Fire Disaster Plan.
2.2. Command Staff
2.2.1. All Battalion Chiefs will be notified of the affected areas by the FAO.
2.2.2. All Battalion Chiefs should be assigned a driver/aide.
2.3. Company Assignments to Incidents
1.2.2. Once trouble areas are identified by the police, or by fire companies in the area, the following actions may be taken:
2.3.1.1. Area command will be established by direction of ES-2.
2.3.1.2. Single company response in trouble areas will be stopped.
2.3.1.3. Task Force response procedures will go into effect.
3. Actions in Major Disturbance Areas

1.3. As a civil disturbance escalates, the need to change from traditional fire suppression strategies will be required. If areas become too hostile, fire personnel and apparatus will be withdrawn from the fire stations in those areas to staging areas in safe locations. TaskForces will be assembled and will be dispatched from designated staging areas.
3.1. Task Force Operations

1.3.1. Task Forces shall be assembled with equipment and personnel from CFD and CPD. The specific make up of Task Force Teams shall be determined by the type of incident. However, these guidelines should be followed:
3.1.1.1. Fire Suppression Task Force
3.1.1.1.1. One (1) Fire Department Battalion Chief with driver/aide
3.1.1.1.2. Two (2) Engines
3.1.1.1.3. One (1) Ladder
3.1.1.1.4. One (1) CPD Cruiser or wagon
3.1.1.2. EMS Task Force
1.3.1.1.1. Two (2) EMS Transport Medics with additional 3rdman added for manpower to each Transport Medic
1.3.1.1.2. One (1)EMS Officer (Lt. or Capt.) and/orBattalion Chief with driver/aide
3.1.1.2.1. One (1) CPD Cruiser or wagon

1.3.2. Task Forces shall be identified by the battalion chief or EMS officer number (e.g., a Task Force led by Battalion 3will be called “Task Force 3” or a Task force led by EMS-13 will be designated “Task Force 13”).
1.3.3. Task Force units will be used within the incident boundaries only. They will not be used to respond to incidents outside this defined area.

1.3.4. When actively engaged in firefighting and/or EMS activities, and supplementalforcesare available, Task Force units should be rotated from active to standby at periods of time determined by the Area Command.

1.3.5. Unless instructed to do otherwise, Task Force units operating should utilize the most direct route to the incident using the perimeter of the incident scene boundaries whenever possible. Do not respond through known hostile areas.

1.3.6. CFD units brought in from outside the area should be paired with local units. This will help those not familiar with the area and have access to knowledge that could affect operations and safety. Automatic/Mutual Aid companies will not be part of a Task Force Team within a disaster or civil disturbance area.

1.3.7. Basic Task Force personnel and equipment may be supplemented by additional personnel and apparatus or equipment, depending upon the resources that have been deemed as necessary to deal effectively with the existing situation (e.g., heavy-duty road clearing vehicles, military or additional police escorts, water tank apparatus, etc.).
1.3.8. Task Force Locations
1.3.8.1. Task Forces will be assembled in staging areas outside the trouble area boundaries.
1.3.8.2. There may be more than one staging area, if the incident boundaries are significant. The staging area(s) will be located preferably in close proximity to the Area Command Post.
1.3.9. Dispatching Task Forces
1.3.9.1. The FAO shall notify the Area Command via radio of the type and location of the fire or incident.
1.3.9.2. The Area Command will notify the Staging Area Manager who will deploy the appropriate Task Force to the incident.
1.3.10. Task Force Support
1.3.10.1. If and when available,CPD will be assigned to escort task forces into incident scenes.
1.3.10.2. Logistical support for the task forces shall be provided at the staging area(s) (e.g., fuel, air bottles, food, toilet facilities, etc.).

1.3.10.3. A minimum of (1) Rescue Company will be held at each staging area to be utilized for the purposes as Rapid Intervention (10-3 or Maydays), additional manpower, or take the place of a ladder company when that resource is depleted.
3.2. Abandoning Areas
1.3.11. The Fire Chief or Area Command shall make the decision on whether fire personnel and equipment will be pulled out of an area. Factors involved in this decision include police action.
3.2.1.1. Is the Police Department pulling out?
3.2.1.2. Is violence being directed toward the Fire Personnel or apparatus?
3.2.1.3. Even though the police are in the area, is there enough control?
4. Personnel Safety
1.4. During periods of civil disturbance, members shall take all necessary precautions to protect themselves.
4.1.1. All members (including drivers) shall follow these guidelines:
1.4.1.1. Fire company personnel shall wear turnout gear to, during, and upon returning from incidents.
1.4.1.2. EMS personnel shall wear Ballistic Vests at all times when operating within the civil unrest areas.
1.4.1.3. Helmets shall be worn upon exiting apparatus by fire and EMS personnel.
1.4.1.4. Members shall conduct themselves in a manner that will not result in a hostile confrontation.
4.1.1.1. Do not use hose streams or tools as weapons.
1.4.1.4.1. EXCEPTION: As a last-ditch defense while making an escape and firefighters lives are being threatened.
4.1.2. Response Safety
4.1.2.1. Keep all windows rolled up.
1.4.1.5. Emergency warning lights should be kept on at all times when serving in an affected area. This will help locate companies calling for emergency assistance.
4.1.2.2. Hose beds are to remain covered at all times.
1.4.1.6. Fire extinguishers shall be kept with members inside cab when responding to, or returning from calls. These are to be used in the event the apparatus is fire bombed.
1.4.1.7. Place all tools and equipment carried on the outside of apparatus in compartments or under cover.
1.4.1.8. Size-up the area that you are responding into.Be alert fortraps or ambushes.
4.1.2.3. Back into dead end streets.
4.1.3. Fire Ground Safety
1.4.1.9. Scenes should be approached with attention to emergency exit in case evacuation of area is ordered.
1.4.1.10. Park apparatus in a manner that will provide as much personnel protection on the scene as possible. Keep all vehicles close to each other.

1.4.1.11. DO NOT park pumpers a block away from the fire, with only one member attending it. If possible, conduct forward lays only, pumping in series with both engines placed in close proximity to each other.
1.4.1.12. DONOT leave members by themselves to catch hydrants away from the apparatus.
1.4.1.13. No member shall be positioned at the tip of aerial ladders. Personnel are permitted to be in Tower Buckets.
4.1.3.1. Abandoning an incident scene:
1.4.1.13.1. The Incident Commander has the authority to abandon a fire scene if they feel the safety of members are jeopardized or are in imminent danger.
1.4.1.13.2. All members shall pickup equipment and leave the scene as quickly as possible.
4.1.3.1.1. All members and apparatus shall leave at the same time.
5. FireFighting Operations
5.1. Changes in Tactics
1.4.2. Fire incidents shall have task force assignments dispatched in the following order of priority:
5.1.1.1. Occupied dwellings or buildings with immediate hazard to life.
5.1.1.2. Vacant buildings with occupied exposure buildings.
5.1.1.3. Multiple buildings on fire.
1.4.2.1. Vital public utilities (e.g., Columbia Gas facilities, electric substations, telephone switching buildings, etc.).
1.4.2.2. Response to the following incidentsmay be reduced, or stopped in the TROUBLE AREAS ONLY:
5.1.1.3.1. Fully involved buildings with no exposure problems
5.1.1.3.2. Garages with no exposures
5.1.1.3.3. Vehicle fires
5.1.1.3.4. Dumpsters, grass, or rubbish
1.4.3. During periods of civil disturbance consideration must be given to changing fire suppression tactics.
5.1.1.4. Quick knock down of fires is paramount.
5.1.1.4.1. Use of aerial ladders, and/or deck guns as much as possible.
5.1.1.5. Overhaul shall be non-existent or kept to a minimum.
5.1.1.6. Do not reload hose.
1.4.3.1.1. Roll hose lines or throw them on the hose bed and leave the area as soon as possible.
1.4.3.1.2. When companies arrive in safe areas, staging or fire stations, reloading the hose beds will take place.
1.4.3.2. Fire investigations WILL NOT be conducted within hostile area boundaries.
1.5. Terminology
1.5.1. In addition to the standard terminology the following terms will help maintain accurate communications:
1.5.1.1. Firefighter shot – A firefighter has been hit by gun fire.
1.5.1.2. Firefighter injured as a result of – A firefighter has been injured due to something other than gun fire. A description of the injury and its cause shall be given.
1.5.1.3. Company under fire – The reporting company is being shot at.
1.5.1.4. Shots being fired in the area – Self-explanatory.
6. Integrated Task Force Operations
1.6. Multiple Agency and Command Structure

1.6.1. When setting up the command structure for dealing with a civil disturbance, the use of “unified command” concept allows for joint management of the entire situation by the leaders of each of the agencies involved. During a civil disturbance, agencies will be faced with many different types of emergency situations. By utilizing unified command, there will be no disputes as to which agency is in charge. The different agencies will be operating as one.
1.6.2. The Incident Command System will be utilized forArea and Incident Operations.

1.6.3. The Incident Area Command Post designation will be the fire station (district) number where the Incident Area Command Post is located (i.e., The Area Command set up at E. 12th and N. High St. will be called “Area 7”. When a working incident is declared within the Area Command, the designation will be “Command” followed by the Task Force Number. For instance, Task Force 3 is functioning at a working fire on Chittenden Ave. The incident will be designated as “Command 3”. “Command 3” will report to “Area 7”).
6.1. Task Force Staging Areas

1.6.4. When a civil disturbance escalates to violence in a wide area and cannot be controlled by the available number of law enforcement personnel, staging procedures shall be established. Police, Fire, EMS, and other essential agencies shall deploy personnel and apparatus to designated staging areas.

1.6.5. Company officers from CFD and Patrol officers from CPD shall report to the Staging group supervisor. The initial Staging group supervisor(s) will be appointed by the Area Incident Commander then when available, all staging responsibilities will become the responsibility of the Administrative Investigations Unit.
1.6.5.1. The Staging Area(s) will operate as follows:
1.6.5.1.1. Assemble task forces in accordance with established department guidelines (SOPs) and follow the guidelines set forth in the Division Disaster Plan.
1.6.5.1.2. The Staging group supervisor shall evaluate the incident information provided by the Area Command Post and deploy the task force accordingly.
6.2. Response
1.6.6. All units shall respond in convoy fashion. Convoys shall be set up as follows:
6.2.1.1. CPD cruiser or wagon in front
6.2.1.2. Battalion Chief and/orEMS Officer
6.2.1.3. Fire and/or EMS apparatus
6.2.1.4. Additional CPD unit (if available)
6.2.2. TEAMS SHOULD STAY TOGETHER AT ALL TIMES!
1.7. Operations
1.7.1. No matter what type of incident, time is a critical factor. Utilize emergency procedures and protocols based upon departmental procedures.
1.7.1.1. Once on the scene the police shall secure the area as best as they can. Access to the roofs of nearby buildings can be gained by using fire division aerial ladders.
1.7.1.1.1. Police Task Force personnel will be responsible for perimeter security and the overall security for fire and EMS personnel resulting from a civil disobedience.
1.7.1.2. Fire and/orEMS personnel shall expedite their operations.
1.7.1.2.1. EMS shall place patients into Medics as quickly as possible, provide treatment and move out of the area.
1.7.1.3. EMS Task Force shall stay together.
1.7.1.3.1. When the Medics transport the patient(s), all police and fire will depart with the Medic.
1.7.1.3.2. Patients will be transported to designated casualty collection points UNLESS the EMS officer in-charge determines that immediate hospital care is required.
1.7.1.3.3. Casualty collection points are established under EMS procedures, outside the trouble areas and away from the staging area.
6.2.2.1.1. These areas will have triage and treatment capabilities.
1.7.1.4. The ranking fire and police officers at the scene will stay together for both communications and scene supervision.
1.7.1.5. Fire Task Forces will go in together and come out together with the following exceptions:
1.7.1.5.1. If there is a critically injured individual (a civilian or task force member)thatrequires immediate transport, theTransport Medic and one (1) police unit will leave together.

1.7.1.5.2. The remaining EMS and Police units will return to the staging area and either be reassigned to a new Task Force by the Staging Area Manager or wait until the original medic and police unit return to staging.
6.3. Safety
6.3.1. ALLCOMPANIES THAT ENTER TOGETHER WILL LEAVE TOGETHER.
1.7.2. CPD UNITS WILL NOT LEAVE FIRE AND EMS UNITS AT AN INCIDENT SITE.
1.7.3. If it is determined by the Task Force Chief or EMS Officer that the area must be abandoned:
1.7.3.1. The police, fire, and EMS officers will announce this over their radios and assure the Area Command is informed.
1.7.3.2. The drivers of the fire apparatus will sound their air horns for a period of 10 seconds. This will be followed by 5 seconds of silence and another blast of 10 seconds.
1.7.3.3. All personnel will report to their company officer or EMS officer in preparation for a PAR to be conducted by the Task Force Chief.
1.7.3.4. After PAR is confirmed, evacuate and leave immediately.
1. Administration

1.1. Purpose: Area Commands are particularly beneficial to incidents that are typically not site specific, are not immediately identifiable, are geographically dispersed, and evolve over longer periods of time (e.g., public health emergencies, earthquakes, tornadoes, civil disturbances, etc.). Incidents such as these, as well as acts of biological, chemical, radiological, and nuclear terrorism, require a coordinated intergovernmental, nongovernmental, and private-sector response with large-scale coordination typically conducted at a higher jurisdictional level. Area Command is also used when a number of incidents of the same type in the same area are competing for the same resources, such as multiple hazardous material spills or fires.

1.2. Responsibility: It shall be the responsibility of each member to know, understand and utilize these procedures as they apply to the situation at hand. It shall further be the responsibility of all Division Officers to train their subordinates in the proper application of these procedures and to implement and enforce the use of these procedures.
2. General
2.1. When should Area Command be initiated?

1.2.1. Area command should be initiated when several incidents within close proximity are using similar and limited critical resources. An example would be multiple dumpster fires in the OSU campus region or a civil disturbance concentrated in one or several areas of the city.
1.2.2. Difficulties are encountered with inter-incident resource allocation and coordination.
1.2.3. When coordination and delivery of critical resources becomes difficult to manage from a remote location (agency EOC or FAO).
2.2. Who will establish anArea Command?
1.2.4. Area command can beestablished by a CFD Battalion Chief upon approval of the on-duty Deputy Chief.

1.2.5. Once established the Area Commander will allocate the resources necessary to deal with the event. This will be coordinated by establishing a talkgroup directly with the FAO that disseminates the information directly to the Area Commander.
2.3. How will resources be managed?
1.2.6. The Area Commander will assign resources to a talkgroup and monitor their progress and assign the resource to another incident within his/her command area when that resource becomes available.
1.2.7. Once resources are assigned to Area Command, they will remain under its control until demobilized.
1.2.8. Whennecessary, the Area Commander can create division or group supervisors to maintain span of control.
1.2.9. The Area Commander will coordinate the demobilization of all assigned resources.
1. Administration

1.1. Purpose: The Columbus Division of Fire is committed to providing predetermined resources for all large venues/events occurring within the City of Columbus throughout the year. Significant events include: OSU sporting events, Red, White, and Boom, marathons, and POTUS visits. In order to provide the proper span-of-control as well as coordination with on-duty resources, the Division has set the standard for the command levels for all events based on the number of spectators/participants at each event and the threat level at the time of the event. The higher the participant and threat level the higher the command level will be present.

1.2. Responsibility: It shall be the responsibility of each member to know, understand and utilize these procedures as they apply to the situation at hand. It shall further be the responsibility of all Division Officers to train their subordinates in the proper application of these procedures and to implement and enforce the use of these procedures.
2. Command Levels
1.3. Level 1

1.3.1. Any venue with an expected attendance over 150,000 participants or a venue with a known high-risk assessment will be commanded by a minimum of a Deputy Chief with an Assistant Chief or Fire Chief available to respond with a 30-minute maximum ETA.
1.4. Level 2

1.4.1. Any venue with an expected attendance between 25,000 and 150,000 participants or a known moderate level risk assessment will be commanded by a minimum of a Battalion Chief with a Deputy Chief available to respond with a 15-minute maximum ETA.
2.1. Level 3

1.4.2. Any venue with an expected attendance of less than 25,000 participants with a low or minimal threat level assessment will be commanded by a Company Officer with a Battalion Chief available to respond with a 15- minute maximum ETA.

p: Section 1 Administration

1.1 Purpose: To implement, outline and standardize evidence room procedures for the collection, analysis, retention and disposition of evidence from fire, explosives, and Haz-mat investigation scenes.

1.2 Responsibility: It shall be the responsibility of each member to know, understand, and utilize these procedures as they apply to the situation at hand. It shall further be the responsibility of all Division Officers to train their subordinates in the proper application of these procedures and to implement and enforce the use of these procedures.

1.3 Policy: The Columbus Division of Fire will follow all applicable laws and standards relating to the collection, storage, analysis, retention, and disposition of evidence collected at the scene of a fire, explosion, or Haz-mat incident.
Section 2 Procedure
2.1 Collection & Storage

A. Members of the Fire & Explosives Investigations Unit (FEIU) or Bomb Squad shall collect property that will be used as evidence during the course of fire, explosives, and/or Haz-mat investigations. Other Division members shall secure the scene until the arrival of the FEIU or Bomb Squad.
B. Movement of evidence, once entered into the BEAST, must have a chain-of-custody label attached.
C. The evidence technician or a qualified substitute will assign a property number to each piece of evidence.
A. Evidence not sent for analysis will be stored in the appropriate bin.
B. Evidence must have a completed evidence sticker on it.

D. Explosive or potentially energetic materials (other than undamaged, commercially packaged, fireworks) will be transported immediately from the scene to the Bomb Range for storage, until testing, and then retained until it is deemed no longer useful to the court. Once an official determination is made by the court to allow its destruction, it will be destroyed by the Bomb Squad.
E. Haz-mat (white powders, unknowns, etc.) will be appropriately packaged by CFD Haz-Mat personnel and transported to the Health Department Lab for testing and storage when deemed necessary.
F. All digital evidence that is collected will be placed into the Incident Folder on a secured drive for permanent retention with all investigative documents and photos.
2.2. Analysis

A. Evidence that will be transported to, and tested at, either the Columbus Division of Police lab, the State Fire Marshal lab, or the Ohio Bureau of Criminal Investigation lab will be placed in bin X. Required paperwork, including a chain of custody, must be completed and attached to the evidence before the evidence will be transported and tested.

B. The evidence technician or a qualified substitute will transport evidence on a weekly basis to either the Columbus Division of Police (CPD) lab, or the State Fire Marshal (SFM) lab, or the Ohio Bureau of Criminal Investigation (BCI) lab unless otherwise needed on a more frequent basis.
C. The evidence technician will log and shelve evidence returned from either the CPD, SFM or BCI labs.

D. The evidence submittal and return receipts generated by either the CPD, SFM or BCI lab will be placed in digital format in the K: drive with an email notification to the primary investigator, K-9 handler, other agencies (police or fire), and other involved parties as to the results.
2.3 Retention of Non-Biological Property

A. The lead investigator will be responsible for determining the level of offense/potential offense, thereby determining the retention period for property obtained by the Fire Investigations Unit during the course of an investigation.

B. When the investigator determines that property is evidence of the commission of a crime, but no arrest has been made, the statute of limitations listed below will be used as a guideline to determine the retention period.
1. Aggravated Arson resulting in death: No limitation period.

2. Aggravated Arson resulting in serious injury: 20 years, unless the investigator determines that the victim’s injuries are such that death may result from the fire, explosion, or Haz-Mat at some time beyond 20 years.
3. Aggravated Arson resulting in no death or injury: 20 years
4. Felony Arson: 6 years
5. Other Felonies: 6 years (except for sections 2909.22, 2909. 23, 2909.24, 2909.26, 2909.27, 2909.28, & 2909.29 of the Revised Code)
1. Misdemeanors: 2 years
6. Minor Misdemeanors: 6 months

C. When arrest, prosecution, or trial occurs, property used as evidence will be retained until the property no longer has evidentiary value or there is no other justifiable need for the property. The investigator may need to contact the prosecutor to assist in determining if the property has evidentiary value based on case status and applicable appeal timeframes

D. When the investigator has not made a determination regarding criminal conduct, evidence will be retained for a minimum of three years. Depending on the circumstances of the particular investigation, the investigator may elect to retain the evidence for a longer period of time.

E. When the investigator determines that a fire or explosion was accidental, the property may be returned to the owner as soon as the property no longer has evidentiary value. When the property remains unclaimed, it will be retained for a period of three years.
2.4 Retention of Biological Evidence

A. “Biological evidence” (DNA) means any item that contains identifiable biological material that was collected as part of a criminal investigation and that reasonably may be used to incriminate or exculpate any person for an offense or delinquent act. This includes evidence (other than soil samples collected for the purpose of accelerant testing) that contains biological material, such as clothing, cups, household material, or cigarettes upon which biological material is present.

B. Biological evidence must be retained for the crimes listed below. While the Fire Investigations Unit does not directly investigate these crimes, the Fire Investigations Unit may be conducting an investigation and obtain biological evidence of the following crimes. In those circumstances, the Fire Investigations Unit must retain the evidence for the listed retention periods or release custody of the evidence, to include a chain of custody, to the law enforcement agency that will investigate the following crimes.
1. Aggravated Murder
2. Murder
3. Voluntary Manslaughter
4. Involuntary Manslaughter
5. Aggravated Vehicular Homicide, Vehicular Homicide, and Vehicular Manslaughter.
6. Rape
7. Sexual Battery
8. Gross Sexual Imposition
9. Attempt to Commit Rape
2. Domestic Violence
C. Biological evidence will be retained for the period of time that the offense or act remains unsolved for the following offenses:
1. Aggravated Murder
3. Murder
D. Biological evidence will be retained for thirty (30) years for the following offenses if the offense or act remains unsolved:
1. Voluntary Manslaughter
4. Involuntary Manslaughter
2. Aggravated Vehicular Homicide, Vehicular Homicide, Vehicular Manslaughter
3. Rape
4. Sexual Battery
5. Gross Sexual Imposition
6. Attempt to Commit Rape

E. Biological evidence will be retained in cases where a person is convicted of or pleads guilty to one of the offenses listed in (2.4)(B) of this procedure for 30 years or until the latest period of time that the person is:
1. Incarcerated
7. Under community control sanction
2. Under any order of disposition for the offense
8. Under judicial or supervised release for the offense
9. On probation or parole for the offense
10. Under post-release control for the offense
11. Involved in civil litigation
3. Subject to registration requirements under sections 2950.04; 2950.041; 2950.05; and 2950.06 of the Revised Code.
F. Biological evidence may be disposed of prior to the expiration of the time period listed in two circumstances.

1. When an offender is found guilty of one of the offenses listed in (2.4)(B), a written notice of intent to dispose of the biological evidence must be provided by certified mail to the following: a. The offender, and a. The attorney of record for the offender, and b. The Ohio public defender, and b. The county prosecutor, and c. The Ohio Attorney General If no response has been received within one (1) year after the letter was sent, the biological evidence may be disposed. If any of the parties listed above request its retention, the biological evidence will be retained.

2. When an offender pleads guilty or no contest to one of the offenses listed in (2.4)(B), biological evidence can be destroyed five years after the plea and any appeal timeframes from the plea have been exhausted, unless the offender requests retention and a court finds good cause to retain the evidence.
2.5 Disposition of Property
A. Annually, for each item of property for which the investigator is responsible, the investigator will make one of the following determinations:
1. Release to Owner: The property is no longer needed as evidence and may be released to the owner.
2. Dispose of Property: The property will be disposed of when the property is no longer needed for evidence and is either contraband or ownership cannot be determined after reasonable effort.
3. Hold for Evidence: The property still has evidentiary value for an investigation or the case is still pending in court.
B. The Fire Investigations Unit will make reasonable efforts to locate persons entitled to possession of the property to effectuate its return.

C. For all property that is not claimed by an owner, or for property that has been forfeited, the Fire Investigations Unit will seek permission from the Franklin County Municipal Court to dispose of the property.
1. Property will be disposed of by the Fire Investigations Unit as needed.
2. The order granting disposition will be maintained by the Fire Investigations Unit for a period of 5 years.
D. For all property disposed of, the Fire Investigations Unit will maintain a record with the following elements:
1. Date the property was acquired;
12. Description of the property;
13. Date the property was disposed;
14. Manner the property was disposed;
15. Financial records for any property that was sold; and
16. Name of any person who received the property.
Section 3 Disposal/Destruction of Evidence Process

3.1 Once a piece, or list, of evidence is identified for disposal or destruction, that item or list will be designated Exhibit A and will be signed and notarized by the FEIU Captain or Lieutenant for attachment to an “Entry for the Disposition of Property” form for presentation to the court.

3.2 The paperwork from 3.1 is sent to the CFD Legal Advisor along with a “Motion for the Disposal of Certain Property Held in Custody by the Division of Fire” form, and a “Memorandum in Support” form for signatures by the Legal Advisor (City Attorney).

3.3 All of the completed paperwork from 3.1 and 3.2 is then transported to the Municipal Courthouse for approval by signature of the Duty Judge. Then the signed paperwork is filed with the Clerk of Courts to receive a Court Case #.

3.4 Once all paperwork is completed and filed with the court, the FEIU Captain or Lieutenant will work with the Evidence Technician to determine the best course of disposition or disposal for each piece of evidence. Then the Evidence Technician will follow the decided upon course of action.
Section 4 References
Section 5 Review
5.1 This S.O.P. shall be reviewed at least once every three years, or within a shorter period of time as is necessary.

03-08-01.t: Dive and Rescue Team (DART) Standards and
p: 1. Administration
1.1. Purpose: The purpose of this procedure is to explain the standards and certifications the Columbus Division of Fire Dive and Rescue Team (DART) will operate within.

1.2. Responsibility: It shall be the responsibility of each member to know, understand and utilize these procedures as they apply to the situation at hand. It shall further be the responsibility of all Division Officers to train their subordinates in the proper application of these procedures and to implement and enforce the use of these procedures.
2. Procedures
2.1. Minimum Training Requirements:

1.2.1. The DART team will train and operate under the training and safety standards for Public Safety Diver Training, as issued under the Public Safety Divers Association. All divers operating as a Public Safety Diver for the team will be trained to the PSD level one certification or equivalent.
2.1.1. This training level requires:
1.2.1.1. Completion of the International Association ofDive Rescue Specialist (IADRS) swim test
2.1.1.1. Recreational advanced open water card by a national agency
2.1.1.2. Successful completionof the PSDA level one course or equivalent
2.2. Yearly Recertification Requirements:
1.2.2. Each DART dive team member will keep and maintain a logbook of each dive completed.
1.2.3. Each DART level one public safety diver will be required to meet the recertification requirements for the Level One card by November of each calendar year.
2.2.1. Each diver must complete:
2.2.1.1. IADRS swim test, per NFPA 1006 standards
2.2.1.2. 16 hours of continuing education credit
2.2.1.3. Six (6) fully dressed public safety dives
1.2.3.1. Yearly medical evaluation perthe RecreationalScuba Training Council (RSTC) standards
1.2.4. Continuing Education Credits can be in watertraining, lecture, or other training approved by the DART Commander.
2.3. Lack of Continuing Education Credits

1.2.5. It is the responsibility of each diver to ensure the needed continuing education credits are completed to renew. Members not meeting these requirements, byOctober first of each year, will be placed in a non- diving capacity until the requirements are met.

1.2.6. If these requirements are not met within a reasonable period of time, the diver may be removed from the DART roster. Divers on sick leave, injury leave, or military leave will not be subject to these requirements until they return to active duty within the Division of Fire.
1. Administration
1.1. Purpose: To explain the proper equipment needs of the DART team so that each diver is properly protected from contaminated water, communication is provided, and thermal protection is adequate.

1.2. Responsibility: It shall be the responsibility of each member to know, understand and utilize these procedures as they apply to the situation at hand. It shall further be the responsibility of all Division Officers to train their subordinates in the proper application of these procedures and to implement and enforce the use of these procedures.
2. Dive Equipment
2.1. Minimum team equipment, to be worn on all submersions:
2.1.1. AGA mask
2.1.2. Drysuit
2.1.3. Two (2) cutting tools, with a knife optional if properly stowed
2.1.4. Team BCD with weight harness if needed
2.1.5. 80 cubic ft. steel SCUBA tank

1.3. Other equipment, such as the communication system or ropes and harnesses, may be omitted if deemed OK by the dive supervisor. Recreational equipment may be used if within the scope of the training. Recreational gear is usually shunned, but some evolutions may require it.
2.2. ANY rescue operation will commence with the diver wearing:
2.2.1. AGA mask, with communication system in place
1.3.1. Drysuit – Under 60-degree water insulation mandatory, over 80-degree water insulation optional or restricted
2.2.2. Fins
2.2.3. Team BCD with weight harness if needed
2.2.4. 80 cubic ft. steel SCUBA tank
2.2.5. Pony bottle
2.3.7. Two (2) cutting tools
2.3.8. Body harness attached to a proper tender line
2.4. Anyrescue operation will commence with the tender wearing:
2.4.1. At least a PFD or float coat
2.4.2. Dressed for the weather (hot/cold)
2.4.3. Tenders will have in their control:
2.4.3.1 Tender report
2.4.3.3 Clipboard
2.4.3.4 Timing device
2.4.4. Necklace style tug card and tender checklist
1. Administration
1.1. Purpose: To detail the requirements to provide safe training and operational environments for each member of the DART team, including shore support personnel.

1.2. Responsibility: It shall be the responsibility of each member to know, understand and utilize these procedures as they apply to the situation at hand. It shall further be the responsibility of all Division Officers to train their subordinates in the proper application of these procedures and to implement and enforce the use of these procedures.
2. Procedures
2.1. Training Ratios:
2.1.1. The PSDA allows for the following student to instructor ratios:
2.1.1.1. Classroom – 30/1
2.1.1.2. Confined water/pool sessions – 8/1
2.1.1.3. Water with 20ft. or more visibility – 4/1
2.1.1.4. No visibility – 2/1
2.2. Training Safety

1.2.1. All open water training evolutions will be done with a backup diver dressed and ready to respond, or each diver has a dive partner in close proximity at all times, and communication between the partners is maintained.
1.2.2. All shore personnel shall wear a PFD while within 15 feet of the water’s edge.
1.2.3. Dive Supervisors overseeing the training shall also have the following equipment ready at all time in a close proximity to the diver entry point:
2.2.1.1. Oxygen equipment
2.2.1.2. Throw bags or retrieval equipment
2.2.1.3. Whistles or warning horns
1.2.4. In the event of a training accident, all other dives shall be aborted until the hazard or accident has been mitigated.

1.2.5. Dive physiology presents the possibility of specialized treatments, such as recompression chamber treatment. Dive supervisors will contact the Diver’sAlert Network (DAN) upon recognition of any barotraumas related injury, and be guided by Division EMS protocol and DAN recommendation.
1. Administration
1.1. Purpose:To explain and detail the responsibilities of a Dive Supervisor.

1.1. Responsibility: It shall be the responsibility of each member to know, understand and utilize these procedures as they apply to the situation at hand. It shall further be the responsibility of all Division Officers to train their subordinates in the proper application of these procedures and to implement and enforce the use of these procedures.
2. DiveSupervisor Duties and Responsibilities
2.1. Dive Supervisor Responsibilities on DART runs:
1.1.1. Deem the appropriate scene search measures,giving consideration to water conditions, scene safety, victim timeline, and diver staffing.
1.1.2. Controls the operational parameters of the dive, but operates and reports to the Incident Commander on scene.
1.1.3. Acts as the DART liaison to the Columbus Police Underwater Search and Recovery Unit (USRU), and provide information to USRU, both in person and over the proper radio channels.
1.1.4. Ensure that all divers are satisfactorily rehabilitated post dive, and that all equipment is returned to an operational state.
2.2. Day to day Dive Supervisor Responsibilities:
1.1.5. Supervise and ensure training evolutions are completed eachmonth as set by the Dive Commander.
1.1.5.1. Coordinate with each Battalion Chief orES2 to enable DART training, with staffing concerns taken into account.
1.1.6. Devise and update a dive response each day in the city, taking into account staffing and equipment concerns.
2.2.1. Address any operational concerns made known.
2.2.2. Any other duties given by the DART commander.
1. Administration
1.1. Purpose: To explain and detail the typical dive response from the DART team.

1.2. Responsibility: It shall be the responsibility of each member to know, understand and utilize these procedures as they apply to the situation at hand. It shall further be the responsibility of all Division Officers to train their subordinates in the proper application of these procedures and to implement and enforce the use of these procedures.
2. Procedures

1.3. A member may make a rescue attempt alone, if necessary, in an emergency situation ONLY if he feels that the dive can be done with reasonable safety, there is no current, overhead environment, a definite point last seen is obtained,and the delay would definitely result in death ratherthan the rescue of the drowning victim.Automobiles must not be penetrated, but searched by reaching only. This shall be followed with a written report to the Dive Commander.
2.1. Rescue timeline:
1.3.1. DART operations maycommence when a victim is believed to be submerged for less than 60 minutes.
1.3.2. The Dive Supervisor must make a rescue or recovery decision before divers are committed to the water.

1.3.3. In normal response, a rescue attempt will be done when the timeline submersion is under 60 minutes, and rescue operations will normally be converted to recovery operations at the 60-minute mark. Witness interviews and triangulation are crucial, and should be undertaken by the first arriving fire unit.
1.4. Dive Crew Requirements:

1.4.1. Each normal rescue mission should be comprised of a minimum of (3) dive Personnel. Responses from different geographical areas of the City may entail waiting on the proper staffing to start a dive. SAFETY must be paramount.
1.4.1.1. Under no normal circumstances should a dive commence with only one diver on scene.
1.4.2. The team shall consist of:

1.4.2.1. One (1) Dive Supervisor – The Dive Supervisor is responsible for the dive operation, safety, pattern selection, diverrehab, and equipment use. A Dive Supervisor can be used as a tender, but a dedicated tender should be deployed specifically as soon as practical.
1.4.2.2. One (1) Primary Diver – The diver who enters the water first is the primary diver.
1.4.2.3. One (1) Backup Diver – The backup diver will be positioned in an area to be able to directly respond to the primary diver if requested. This may be on the shore or in the water.

1.4.2.4. One (1) Dive Tender, if applicable – The tender will control the communications and rope for the primary diver. Divers, both primary and backup, should have tenders assigned to them for the duration of the mission. The tender also helps dress and undress the divers, does final checks, and monitors the divers while underwater. A Dive Tenderdoes not have to have dive cards or qualifications, but must have completed CFD Tender training to function as one on a scene.
2.1.1. Additional Personnel:
1.4.2.5. Safety Diver – A 3rd, dressed diver, in another backup position. This diver may be staged with the full-face mask off, and assumes the role of backup diver if the backup diver deploys.
1.4.2.6. Secondary tender – Anothertender added to the crew, usually with the backup diver.
1.4.2.7. Additional public safetydivers – As dive needs increase, additional divers will stage at the DART truck, and be guided by the Dive Supervisor.
2.2. Shore support needs:
1.4.3. Any time the DART team is on an actual rescue mission, an ALS medic unit and crew will be standing by with gear at the shoreline, or closest point.
1.4.4. Trainings may not require an ALS unit, and the instructor or dive supervisor before the training will decide the requirement of an ALS unit.
3. DART Member Responsibilities
1.5. Daily Checks – Each day, a memberof the DART team shall be assigned to the staffing at Station 2, or wherever the DART truck is stationed. This member will be responsible for the following:
3.1.1. SCUBA equipment
1.5.1.1. Air pressures, full face masks, weight systems, communication systems, drysuits, etc.
3.1.1.1. Extra SCUBA bottles
3.1.1.2. Reports
3.1.1.3. DART truck morning checks and readiness
1.5.2. Any piece of equipment needing repair or attention will be reported to the Dive Supervisor on duty that day and properly tagged.
1.5.3. Transporting the DART truck to a dive scene, and coordinate its location with the Dive Supervisor.
1.5.3.1. In the event of the member being assigned to another run, all efforts will be made to use another firefighter at the station to transport the truck to a dive scene.
1.5.3.2. In the event the entire station is tied up, the Dive Supervisor will call on the closest member to deliver the DART truck.
2. Communication During Responses
2.1. DART members may or may not be required to respond to a dive run.Staffing of divers will be scattered throughout the city, and the plan the Dive Supervisor initiates must consider this.
2.2. Upon receipt of a waterrescue response, boatrun, etc., the Fire Alarm Office will announce the run on all station PAs and 10 Fire.

2.2.1. The divers will then respond with their apparatus, and mark enroute on the assigned fireground. The Dive Supervisor will monitor the radio on the assigned fireground and cancel any diver not needed.
2.2.2. The Dive Supervisor will also monitor Talkgroup 8 P/F, in order to facilitate communications with the CPD USRU.

03-08-06.t: Scene Security and Transfer to CPD
p: 1. Administration
1.1. Purpose: To detail the process of securing and transferring a dive operation or dive scene to the Columbus Police Underwater Search and Recovery Unit (USRU).

1.2. Responsibility: It shall be the responsibility of each member to know, understand and utilize these procedures as they apply to the situation at hand. It shall further be the responsibility of all Division Officers to train their subordinates in the proper application of these procedures and to implement and enforce the use of these procedures.
2. Transfer of the Scene to thePolice Recovery Unit
2.1. Police Notification
1.2.1. DART supervisors will notify the USRU upon receiving notification of a run that the supervisorbelieves there will be DART members committed.

1.2.2. The USRU team may be dispatched through their dispatchers, and can be reached normally on radio channel 8 P-F. USRU dive unit liaisons will be in contact and the DART team will be guided by their input.
2.2. Scene Preservation
1.2.3. If a rescue is made, the victim receives priority, but efforts must be made to preserve the scene for USRU.

1.2.4. Notification will be given via radio to USRU of victim transport ASAPover 8 P-F. The DART team shall continue with information gathering, and the dive supervisor in charge of the DART operations will be required to supply all information to the arriving USRU divers.

1.2.5. All witnesses should be asked to stay on scene, and a CPD officer can be assigned to them if needed. In the event of a witness leaving before the underwater unit arrives, all pertinent contact information should be recorded and left with the USRU Diver in charge.
3. Recovery Mode
1.3. The Police Unit will do all underwater investigations, car or body recoveries, and recovery of any evidence they deem necessary.
1.4. The DART team may be used as a support group to USRU, but once a declaration of victim recovery has been made,USRU will then assume and command the dive operations.
1.4.1. Upon moving to a recovery operation, DART members will exit the water, and standby away from the hot zone, and standby for the arrival or input of USRU.
1.4.2. The shoreline will be processed as part of a potential crime scene, and if possible, all members should retreat to a location that preserves the shore, but allows contact with the scene.

1.4.3. If a recovery operation is determined, or other reasons will not enable the DART team to recover the victim in rescue mode, the DART diver will mark victim location with a pelican buoy beside the victim; all divers will exit the water, and then be guided by the USRU upon their arrival, or radio input.

1.4.4. Scene security is a crucial part of scene preservation, and DART members should consider utilizing scene tape or apparatus to form a “hot” zone. DART and CFD personnel should remain outside this hot zone unless needed. Joint operations may be necessary, and training between both teams is encouraged. The DART team may be requested to stand by or participate in CPD missions, but will normally stay ready to respond, unless approved by ES-2.
4. Non-Human Recoveries
1.5. Any car, body, or unusual object found on a search pattern or training evolution will be marked by Pelican buoy, and the Police unit notified as soon as possible.

1.6. USRU will make the final decision as how to handle the situation. The buoy should be left where needed or deployed even if the DART team goes in service. USRU can recover when done, and return it to the DART truck.
5. Victim Recovery from Automobiles, Trucks, Etc.

1.7. If a victim is recovered from an auto without the auto being brought to shore, the vehicle will remain in the water where found, and no other DART members will disturb the vehicle, except to search for possible victims.
1.8. NO vehicle may be removed at any time, UNLESS a victim is known to be pinned by such a manner as to need hydraulic rescue tools to free the victim.

1.9. If a vehicle has to be removed from the water to extricate, all efforts will be made to document as much as possible for later investigations by CPD, including statements from Heavy Rescue Personnel if the car was manipulated in the course of the extrication.
2. Floating Deceased
2.1. Floating deceased will be considered beyond the scope of rescue, and become crime scenes for the Police Unit.

2.2. Efforts may be made to secure the body, but only if not doing so will result in the body being lost. A floating deceased on calm water should only be guarded by personnel in boats if able, and the point where the body was first seen should be marked by a pelican buoy and/or triangulation if possible.
2.3. If currents will cause the body to be lost downstream, DART personnel should stabilize the body with as little interference as possible, and wait on the CPD Unit to handle the scene.
1. Administration
1.1. Purpose: To explain and detailoperations involving special dive operations, such as ice and current diving.

1.2. Responsibility: It shall be the responsibility of each member to know, understand and utilize these procedures as they apply to the situation at hand. It shall further be the responsibility of all Division Officers to train their subordinates in the proper application of these procedures and to implement and enforce the use of these procedures.
1. Procedures

1.3. Each DART member will have the right to decline any dive they feel is beyond the scope of their training and capabilities, and no diver shall undertake any of the following types of dives without proper training.
1.1. Ice Diving
1.3.1. Ice diving requires special training and procedures, and is considered to be very dangerous, and this danger is even worse in blackwater conditions.
1.3.1.1. No dive will be made under any circumstances without the diver being tethered on a life safety rope attached to the diver’s harness with a locking carabineer.
1.3.1.2. Any diver under the ice shall have an ice diving certification, except while ice dive training.
1.1.1.1. Redundant air supplies will be used on all ice dives.
1.3.1.3. All divers must have obtained an ice diving certification before diving in an ice rescue response.
1.3.2. Ice diving operations in current and no visibility water are extremely hazardous, and the Dive Supervisor will have the right to abort or stop operations.
1.2. Boat Diving and Operations
1.3.3. Normal boat operations will entail non-running motors, when the diver is below surface.
1.3.4. A boat may slowly idle in to another boat anchored and being used as a dive platform, but only on the verbal or signed permission of the dive tender.

1.3.5. Static line operations in rivers may be conducted with the rescue or engine personnel moving the boat, as well as controlling the lines, but the tending shall be done by a certified DART tender.
1.3. Current Diving

1.3.6. Currents of more than 3 knots estimated, will not support safe dive operations, and normally will not be undertaken. In currents of 1 to 3 knots estimated, all efforts will be made to dive from a static line and boat-based control.
1.3.7. If at any time the Dive Supervisor feels safety is at risk, the dive will be terminated.
1.3.8. Upstream lookouts and downstream safetypersonnel should be in place and have communication with the Dive Supervisor.

1.3.9. At NO TIME will a diver dive into an area where there is a known water intake, dam grate, storm grate, culvert with 3 knot or greater estimated current flow, overhead environment or under a vehicle.
1.3.9.1. All efforts will be made to maintain a database of such hazards, and will be kept in the DART vehicle for reference. Delta P phenomenon shall be noted and kept in the preplans.
1.4. Contaminated Water Diving
1.4.1. No diver, at any time, may dive in any known contaminated waters.

1.3.10. Sewers, cesspools, and chemical tanks present a hazard DART is not prepared to submerge in, and require the use of true hazardous materials equipped teams, usually a commercial diving company.

1.3.11. Normal scope of DART operations will have a chance of being exposed to small amounts of contaminants, such as gasoline or oil from a submerged car, or storm runoff, but DART gear can be used in such situations, and will provide the diver an acceptable level of protect.

1.3.12. Normal decontamination or washing should take place after diving waters that the Dive Supervisor deems it necessary, and will be mandatory in automobile work, or work with a runoff exposure hazard.
1.5. Overhead Environment Diving

1.3.13. Overhead environments are defined as such space that the diver cannot ascend to the ambient environment directly. These present a special hazard to DART divers, and divers shall be prohibited from diving under any overhead environment.

1.5.1. Ice diving when properly equipped shall be exempt from this rule.
