1. Administration
1.1. Purpose:To identify Research and Development Committee assignments, duties, responsibilities and conflict of interests.

1.2. Responsibility: It shall be the responsibility of each member to know, understand and utilize these procedures as they apply to the situation at hand. It shall further be the responsibility of all Division Officers to train their subordinates in the proper application of these procedures and to implement and enforce the use of these procedures.
2. General

1.3. The Division of Fire operates on the premise that the people who work on, or have a special insight on, a particular subject are generally the most knowledgeable as to appropriate product design. These selected members will represent the Division’s best interest in each respective committee.
3. Committee Assignment
1.4. Research and Development (R&D) committees are formed based on the need to develop specifications for a Columbus Fire requirement, such as a fire apparatus.
1.5. R&D committees are not limited strictly to apparatus and can be formed to address special needs, with the approval of the Fire Chief.

1.5.1. Members wishing to serve on a R&D committee should submit a RT-154 through their chain of command to the Fire Chief. Members should specify which specific committee they wish to serve on, as well as a summary of all experience and knowledge pertaining to that committee.
1.5.2. The Fire Chief will review all requests to serve as a member of an R&D committee. The approved RT-154 will be sent to the R&D Captain and kept on file.
1.5.3. If the committee is full, requests will be held by the R&D Captain until a vacancy exists. Their name will be added to the waitlist for that specific committee.

1.5.4. When an opening occurs, the Support Services Assistant Chief, Support Services Battalion Chief, R&D Captain, along with recommendations from the committee itself, will select the most qualified member on the waitlist to serve on the committee.
1.5.5. If a member wishes to no longer participate on a committee, the member will submit a RT-154 to the Fire Chief asking for removal.
1.6. The R&D Captain will maintain a listing of all current committees and members.

1.7. Committees will normally meet at least once annually. However, R&D may determine a meeting may not be necessary. For example, if an apparatus is not determined to be in need for several years, there is no reason to hold a committee meeting for an apparatus that will not be built for an extended time. A meeting summary will be kept on file with R&D.

1.8. Typical committees will be chaired by the R&DCaptain or designee, and be made up of six (6) Emergency Service Members, one (1) Local 67 Representative, and one (1) Fleet Representative for all vehicles.

1.9. Overtime or compensatory time may be approved for committee activities at the discretion of the Fire Chief or their designee. Committee activities will strive to meet during normal business hours.

1.9.1. Members that need to attend a committee activity that requires overnight stay, will apply forSpecial Duty. If a member is on platoon duty, they may request up to 12 hours of Special Duty prior to the date of travel. On the day or return, if it is a member’s unit work day, they may request special duty for the entire day as well. This will make sure that member is capable of meeting the travel needs. Members designated as Special Duty WILL NOT receive overtime or compensatory time.
1.10. At times, travel may be limited due to expenses or Division manpower needs. If travel is needed, the R&D Captain will have the final say of the members chosen to go.
4. Duties
1.11. Research and Development committees are given the task to study a particular product and recommend specifications to provide for safe and efficient Division operations.
1.12. Each committee will use the previous specifications, plus any directions given by the Fire Chief, to begin their review.
1.13. If the Division does not intend to purchase a specific product, the committee’s recommendations will be kept on file until the appropriate time.
1.14. The committee assistsat pre-construction conferences, and will be used as a technical resource group during and after construction.
1.15. All written and oral communications regarding committee activities to vendors or contractors will be coordinated through the R&D Captain.

1.16. Working relationshipsdo occur with vendors. However, committee members WILL NOT directly contact vendors or contractors regarding committee matters, without the permission of the R&D Captain or their designee.
1.17. The R&D Captain or designee can recommend through the chain of command to remove a member from a committee for violating a provision of this SOP or for a lack of participation.
1.18. Members will treat everyone with respect at all times. Being disruptive or representing the Division in a negative way will be grounds for removal from the committee.
1.19. Committee members will not engage in the practice of lobbying other city agencies and/or elected officials outside of the chain of command.
1.20. Committee members will abide by all City Work Rules, Division SOP’s and policies while representing the City of Columbus Division of Fire.
5. Conflict of Interest

1.21. No committee member may be currently associated in any way, with any product manufacturer, organization or business that represents any product manufacturer or other equipment vendor. A public official has a “conflict of interest” when his or her ability to be an objective decision-maker is impaired by his or her own interests, or the interests of family members or business associates. A request to serve on a committee will be considered confirmation by the member that this condition is satisfied.

1.22. Per the State of Ohio Ethics Commission, having a conflict of interest is not illegal. In fact, conflictsare normal because public servants have families and friends, and may have businesses, professions, investments, property interests, and other connections to their communities. Any of these connections could result in a conflict of interest for the official. The issue is how the public servant responds to his or her conflict of interest. A public official has a “conflict of interest” when his or her ability to be an objective decision-maker is impaired by his or her own interests, or the interests of family members or business associates. Remember, how one acts with a conflict of interest decides if a law has been broken or not.

1.23. If a member feels a conflict of interest could or does exists, the committee member shall notify the R&D Captain immediately in writing, documenting the issue. The member will not be considered part of an active committee until the conflict is resolved and they are found to not be in violation.

1.24. All R&D committee members WILL BE required to complete at a minimum one online training session. This session is the State of Ohio Ethics Commission Conflicts E-Course. This will be assigned by the Training Bureau on Vector Solutions. When finished, make sure to check the box stating “I have read the information and watched the video in its entirety”. Failure to complete this course will be grounds for removal from a committee.
1. Administration
1.1. Purpose: The purposeof this procedure is to identify the course thatmust be followed during the Apparatus Specification and Bid Process.

1.2. Responsibility: It shall be the responsibility of each member to know, understand and utilize these procedures as they apply to the situation at hand. It shall further be the responsibility of all Division Officers to train their subordinates in the proper application of these procedures and to implement and enforce the use of these procedures.
2. General

1.3. The Fire Chief directs the Research and Development Captain to produce current specifications for the type of apparatus the Division intends to purchase. The Chief may give the Captain additional guidelines and parameters to follow. The current specifications will be the starting point.
1.4. The R&D Captain will work with the appropriate apparatus committee to develop changes to the previously used specifications, applying the guidelines and parameters given by the Chief.

1.5. The recommended changes are then presented to the Chief in accordance withSystems Manual Sec. 326.00-326.18, with each recommended change, its description, and justification, followed by an “Approved” and a “Disapproved” checkbox and a blank line for the Fire Chief’s initials. The recommended changes are also incorporated into a complete draft specification.

1.6. The Chief then forwards the recommendations and draft specifications to the Apparatus Specification Evaluation Committee for review and recommendation. This committee, chaired by the R&D Captain, includes the Support Services Assistant Chief, a Fire Maintenance Shop representative from Fleet, and the Fire Division Safety Officer. This committee will make recommendations to the Fire Chief following Systems Manual Sec. 326.00- 326.18, and the checkbox format described above.
1.7. The Fire Chief accepts or rejects the recommended changes and sends the results to R&D for preparation of the final bid document. R&D also prepares a potential bidders list.
3. Bid Process
1.8. The Fire Chief sends the bid documents and potential bidders list to the Safety Director, who reviews them, then forwards them to City Purchasing.
1.9. CityPurchasing sends the specifications to Fleet and EBOCO for review and comment, then asks the Division to make any necessary modifications.
1.9.1. After the specifications meet the approval of Purchasing, Fleet, and EBOCO, Purchasing advertises a request forbids, notifies know potential bidders, and sets Bid Opening date.

1.10. Bidders submit their bids to City Purchasing prior to the Bid Opening date. Each bidder responds to line items in the specifications, indicating that they agree to comply with each line item, or that they will not comply. The specifications ask the bidder to describe exactly what they propose to substitute for any item to which they choose not to comply.
1.10.1. On the Bid Opening date, Purchasing opens all the bids. Purchasing then reviews each submitted bid to verify compliance with City Purchasing requirements.
1.11. City Purchasing sendsall the received bids, along with their review comments to the Division’s R&D Captain.

1.12. The Bid Evaluation Committee, chaired by the R&D Captain, and including the Support Services Assistant Chief and the Division Safety Officer, analyzes the bids for compliance with the written specifications. Items of bidder noncompliance are evaluated to determine the acceptability of any proposed substitute items.

1.12.1. The Bid Evaluation Committee completes the analysis of the bids by weighing such additional factors as applicable local bidder preferences (City Code 329.06) and the impact of financing terms required by the various bidders (e.g., partial payments or prepayments). Any comments from Purchasing are also considered. Based on the completed analysis, theBid Evaluation Committee makes a recommendation to the Fire Chief. Their final recommendation to the Chief must include a detailed explanation of the criteria they used as well as a listing of the actual bid prices submitted by each bidder.
1.12.2. The Fire Chief reviews the recommendations, selects the best bidder, determines the quantity to be purchased, and directs the Administrative Manager to prepare the contract legislation.

1.13. The Fire Chief forwards the legislation to the Safety Director, who reviews it and submits it for legislative approval to EBOCO, the City Auditor, and the City Attorney. It is then presented to the City Clerk for consideration on a future City Council agenda.

1.13.1. After the legislation is passed and the contract is officially awarded, a preconstruction conference is scheduled with the builder to discuss unsettled specification items and possible alterations in vehicle design.

1.13.2. There are usually minor adjustments to the specified design. Fire vehicles are very technologically complex pieces of equipment and each vehicle is constructed with building materials and components provided by many manufacturers. As each manufacturer attempts to improve his or her product, they make slight changed in the way it fits on the completed vehicle. Since our purchase process takes many months to complete, we often discover during the pre-construction meeting that several of the items we specified are no longer available exactly as we specified them. Occasionally our own procedures or methods have changed requiring an alteration in design. This is true for nearly every apparatus purchase.

1.13.3. If the design changes are substantial, or there is any financial impact, the Division goes back through the Safety Director, to City Council to amend the contract. If the changes are not substantial, and there is no financial impact, a letter of agreement is sent between the Fire Chief and the builder describing the exact changes agreed upon.

1.14. Visits to the manufacturer’s facilities to inspect the apparatus for contract compliance prior to delivery will be made by members of the Apparatus Acceptance Committee. The committee will consist of the R&D Captain and/or his designee, Support Services Assistant Chief, and a representative from Fleet. All travel will be conducted within the guidelines described in the apparatus specifications and in accordance with the current Division procedures as established by the Administrative Manager.
1.15. Questions that cannot be resolved will be forwarded to the Fire Chief. The Chief will have the issue researched by the R&D Captain and will make a final decision based upon this research.
1. Administration
1.1. Purpose: The purpose of this procedure is to identify the course thatmust be followed to field-test and evaluate any new product.

1.2. Responsibility: It shall be the responsibility of each member to know, understand and utilize these procedures as they apply to the situation at hand. It shall further be the responsibility of all Division Officers to train their subordinates in the proper application of these procedures and to implement and enforce the use of these procedures.
2. General

1.3. Request for field-test and evaluation of any new products must be submitted to the Fire Chief for approval. These requests may be initiated by the Division, Local 67 of the IAFF, or the manufacturer, or distributor directly.

1.4. Once a determination has been made by the Fire Chief that a field-test evaluation will be conducted, a minimum of two (2) items will be submitted for evaluation. At the manufacturer or agent’s discretion, more items may be submitted, but in no instance shall there be less than two. The test items shall be delivered to the Division’s Research and Development Captain.

1.5. Research and Development will obtain items for evaluation, design the evaluation forms, and select the Division members to conduct the evaluations. The evaluations will be for a specific time period. Written evaluation forms must be submitted monthly. If the Collective Bargaining Contract grants Local 67 the right to approve the quality of the items, the Union will be given the opportunity to select half the evaluators.
1.6. When the evaluation is set to begin, a memo which will include the names of the evaluators will be sent to the Fire Chief, Division Safety Officer, and Local 67.

1.7. Evaluation periods will run for a pre-determined time frame agreed to by the manufacturer’s agent and the Division. At the end of the field-test, the product and the final evaluation forms will be returned to Research and Development. Any evaluations not returned on time and satisfactorily completed, and the party responsible will be assumed to have no opposition to the product.
1.8. Once the appropriate committee has analyzed the evaluations, a copy of the results will be forwarded to the Fire Chief, Local 67, the Division Safety Officer, and the individual evaluators.
1. Administration
1.1. Purpose: To identify the Division’s policy for the use, care and maintenance of Division Cellular Telephones and Pagers.

1.2. Responsibility: It shall be the responsibility of each member to know, understand and utilize these procedures as they apply to the situation at hand. It shall further be the responsibility of all Division Officers to train their subordinates in the proper application of these procedures and to implement and enforce the use of these procedures.
2. Use, Care, and Maintenance

1.3. Cellular phones and pagers are the property of the Division of Fire. Their primary use is for official Division business. The number and duration of all cell phone calls shall be kept to a minimum.
2.1. General Guidelines
1.3.1. Members of the Division of Fire shall devote their full time and attention to the business of the Division while on duty.
1.3.2. All cellular phones, pagers and other like items, that are carried while on duty, shall be set to vibrate rather than produce an audible alert.
1.3.3. The Division will assign, reassign, orremove equipment and adjust calling plans as needed to meet the changing needs of the Division.
2.1.1. Bureau heads may reassign equipment to meet the needs of their bureau.
2.2. Acquisition of cell phones or pagers
1.3.4. Cell phones and pagers are assigned to specific positions. The assignment of this equipment will be for the enhancement of service within the Division and to the public.
1.3.5. Members assigned to a position or assignment that they feel requires a cell phone or pager shall submit a request through their chain-ofcommand to the Fire Chief.
1.3.6. Members desiring to update their equipment shall submit a request through their chain-of–command to the Fire Chief.
1.3.7. Approved acquisition requests will be sent to the Telephone Equipment Coordinator. The coordinator will contact the individual to set up an appointment for distribution and training.

1.3.8. Upon reassignment from a position that was issued a phone and/or pager the reassigned member shall turn in their electronic equipment to their supervisor. The supervisor will issue the equipment to the member’s replacement, to another member of their bureau or return it to the Telephone Equipment Coordinator.

1.3.9. Members that feel that they no longer have a need for their pager and/or cell phone will discuss the issue with their supervisor. If the supervisor is in agreement, the equipment will be given to the member’s bureau head. The bureau head will either reassign the unit within their bureau or return it to the Telephone Equipment Coordinator.
2.3. Maintenance of cell phones and pagers
1.3.10. Lost, stolen, destroyed,missing, or equipment damaged beyond repair requires the submittal of form ET-68.
1.3.11. Equipmentneeding repaired, or programmingwill be taken to the Telephone Equipment Coordinator.
1.3.12. Batteries for the pagers may be obtained from supply. The Telephone Equipment Coordinator will exchange batteries for the cell phones.
1.3.13. Cell phones are issued with a personal battery charger. Recharging of batteries will be in accordance with the manufacturer’s recommendation.
1.4. Use of cell phones
1.4.1. Cell phones are the property of the Division of Fire and their primary use is for official Division business. The number and duration of all calls shall be kept to a minimum.
1.4.2. Monthly cellular phone bills listing airtime and use charges of both incoming and outgoing call is monitored and will be forwarded to the Division Bureau Heads.
1.4.3. It is the responsibility of the Bureau Heads to monitor the expenditures for cellular phone usage by personnel within their bureau.
1.4.4. The billing cycle is the 17th of each month. Members are encouraged to monitor their own use and reset their “minutes used” timer each month.
1.4.5. It is recommended that members use the “Direct Connect” walkie-talkie feature when possible. The Direct Connect feature does not use cellular minutes.
1. Administration
1.1. Purpose: To set criteria for field installation of the McGard hydrant lock device by the Water Division for illegally opened fire hydrants.

1.2. Responsibility: It shall be the responsibility of each member to know, understand and utilize these procedures as they apply to the situation at hand. It shall further be the responsibility of all Division Officers to train their subordinates in the proper application of these procedures and to implement and enforce the use of these procedures.
1. General
1.1. Criteria for installation of the hydrant locking device will be as follows:
1.2.1. Total of three (3) illegalhydrant openings documented by the Embers Reporting System in a seven (7) day period.
1.2.2. Total of four (4) illegal hydrant openings documented by the Embers Reporting System in an eight (8) hour period denotes priority installation.

1.3. When the above criteria are met the company officer responding to the hydrant flowing incident will transmit the following information to the FAO. The FAO will in turn relay the information to the Water Division.
1.3.1. The make of hydrant is required so the correct lock configuration can be installed. Makes of City of Columbus hydrants are: Mueller, Eddy, Darling, A.P. Smith/Michigan Valve, or Kennedy.
1.3.2. If a hostile environment is encountered at the hydrant flowing scene, the Police must secure the area for Water Division personnel to install the hydrant lock.
1.3.3. The FAO will advise the on-scene fire company of the estimated arrival time of the Water Division to install the locking device.
1.3.4. Response from WaterDivision personnel will be based on the following time periods:
1.3.4.1. Weekdays 0730 to 1530 normal work hours (priority period for lock installation)

1.3.4.2. Night hours 1530 to 0730, weekends/holidays are on-call basis. If hydrant openings meet priority installation criteria (4 times in an 8- hour period) a lock could be installed during this time period. NOTE – Refer to Bulletin 05-046 for police enforcement of hydrant flowing, ifWater Division installation of the hydrant lock is not available. Refer to SOP 01-05-03 for fire response to hydrant flowing runs.
1. Administration

1.1. Purpose: To provide sufficient guidelines which will facilitate the proper process of placing hydrants “in” and “out” of service as well as documenting routine repairs needed using a web-based tracking system.

1.2. Responsibility: It shall be the responsibility of each member to know, understand and utilize these procedures as they apply to the situation at hand. It shall further be the responsibility of all Division Officers to train their subordinates in the proper application of these procedures and to implement and enforce the use of these procedures.
2. Overview

1.3. The Water Web will be utilized for placing hydrants out of service, tracking repair of hydrants by the Division ofWater, performing maintenance follow-up checks, and creating out of service hydrant lists.
3. Accountability
1.4. The Company Officerutilizing the Water Web tracking system shall be responsible to:
1.4.1. Ensure that any hydrant found in the need of repair or placed completely out of service is entered into the Water Web reporting and tracking system.
1.4.2. Check the status of hydrants in their first-in district daily and assign personnel to perform any needed inspections.
1.4.3. Ensure that follow-up inspections are properly documented within the Water Web Tracking System.
1.4.4. Create an “Out ofService” Hydrant List for their First-in District on a daily basis.
1.5. TheStation Captains utilizing the Water Web tracking system shall be responsible to:
1.5.1. Perform the duties of the Company Officer, outlined above, and shall additionally audit the performance of other units to ensure compliance with this policy.
1.6. The Battalion Chiefs utilizing the Water Web tracking system shall be responsible to:
1.6.1. Audit the performanceof their stations to ensure compliance with this policy.
3.1. The Fire Alarm Office (FAO) shall be responsible for:
1.6.2. Making proper notification of the first-in station of the need to verify any report of an out of service hydrant received by the FAO.
4. Procedure
4.1. Flagging Hydrants for Repair:

1.6.3. Fire Alarm Office – When the Fire Alarm Office is notified of a hydrant that is in need of repair or is unserviceable from the public; they shall notify the officer of the first-in station of the location of the hydrant and reported problem. The station officer, or designated representative, shall physically inspect the hydrant to determine the EXACT hydrant, by hydrant number, and the extent of the problem. Upon returning to quarters, from inspecting the hydrant, the member who performed the inspection shall make the proper entries in the Water Web tracking system and the daily log.

1.6.4. Station Level – When performing routine hydrant inspections of your district and you encounter a hydrant in need ofrepair or is unserviceable, this information shall be entered into the Water Web tracking system and the daily log.
4.2. Verify Repaired Hydrants:

1.6.5. Each morning between the hours of 0800 and 1000 the Company Officer of each station shall review the list of hydrants in their First-in District that are ready to be verified. If hydrants are found needing verification, the Company Officer shall assign the appropriate personnel to perform the required inspection and make the proper entries in the Water Web tracking system and the daily log.
1.6.6. Verification of hydrants shall be done following the guidelines contained with the Systems Manual and SOPs.
4.3. Out of Service Hydrant List:

1.6.7. Each evening between the hours of 1800 and 2000 the Company Officer of each station shall review and print copies of the Out of Service Hydrant list for their First-in District. A copy of the “Out of Service” Hydrant List shall be placed on each engine and ladder company in their station.
5. Water Web System Technical Support

1.7. When the end user encounters a problem with the Water Web system, it is their responsibility to start the troubleshooting procedure. If the problem involves application operational procedures, such as “How do I search for hydrants needing inspected?” or “How do I print an OOS list?”, it is up to the end user to educate themselves as to how to properly operate the application that they are using. This can be accomplished through manuals, on-line help systems (“WaterWeb”from the Intranet Page), attending training sessions, or by scheduling an appropriate time for training with the Water Web Coordinator.
1.8. There are a few potential errors that could be encountered while using or attempting to use the Water Web system.

1.8.1. If the problem is WaterWeb application related, take note of specificerror messages encountered, determine if the problem is repeatable or intermittent, and under what circumstances the error appears. Be prepared to answer questions regarding any recent changes to your system prior to the error, if the error has occurred before, and under what circumstances the error occurs.

1.8.2. If the problem is not Water Web application related, the end user should first verify that all connections are secure, take note of specific error messages encountered, determine if the problem is repeatable or intermittent, and under what circumstances the error appears. Be prepared to answer questions regarding any recent changes to your system prior to the error, if the error has occurred before, and under what circumstances the error occurs.
5.1. Troubleshooting:
5.1.1. Log out and log back in.
5.1.2. Log out and restart your computer and try again.
5.1.3. Contact the Water Web Coordinator as listed on the Intranet page.
1.8.2.1. The WaterWeb Coordinatorwill contact the City of Columbus Division of Water or DOT Technical Support as needed.
6. System Outages

1.9. Anytime the Water Web system is down, the responsibility to complete the reports will not change. During system outages maintain a written report and when the system is back online you will need to complete the reports, in a timely manner, on the Water Web system.
1. Administration
1.1. Purpose: To provide a definition of the Division’s Standard Operation Procedures and Protocols.

1.2. Responsibility: It shall be the responsibility of each member to know, understand and utilize these procedures as they apply to the situation at hand. It shall further be the responsibility of all Division Officers to train their subordinates in the proper application of these procedures and to implement and enforce the use of these procedures.
2. Standard Operating Procedures

1.3. Standard Operating Procedures/ Protocols (SOPs) are a set of organizational directives that establish a standard course of action. Utilization of SOPs provides consistency and effectiveness of the Columbus Division of Fire during emergency operations and day-to-day activities.
1.4. Allmembers are expected to know, understandand operate according to these procedures as the situation demands.
1.4.1. SOPs shall be written,applied to all situations, enforced, integrated and coordinated with all other directives.
1.4.2. SOPs are a set of written directives that are flexible and expandable, that deal with routine operations.
1.4.3. SOPs are a collection of directives, which have evolved through experience. They become a tool, with provisions for newmembers to learn from and experienced members to build upon.
2.1.1. An SOP follows a never-ending cycle:
2.1.1.1. Establishment or Revision of the Standard Operating Procedures
2.1.1.2. Training in the Standard Operating Procedures
2.1.1.3. Application of the Standard Operating Procedures
2.1.1.4. Review of the Standard Operating Procedures
2.1.1.5. Revision of the Standard Operating Procedures
1.5. SOPs provide a structured guide for training. Operations at emergency incidents validate SOPs.
1.5.1. SOPs, which are enforced and performed aswritten, strengthen the organization.
1.5.2. SOPs, as written, can be viewed in the light of post analysis. The determinationof training needs and/orpossible revisions can be made during an incident critique.
1.5.3. The Division’s SOP philosophy is “enforce it, revise it, or eliminate it!” Proposed revisions or deletions shall be addressed using the Division’s “SOP Evaluation” procedures.

1.5.4. Enforcement of SOPs is generally viewed as educational in nature. A disregard for SOPs without extenuating circumstances may subject a member to discipline. Enforcement of safety issues is critical to the wellbeing of all personnel.
1.5.5. All SOPs are to be enforced unless the Fire Chief authorizes a change or elimination.
1. Administration
1.1. Purpose: The purpose of this procedure is to describe the formatting of the Columbus Division of Fire’s Standard Operating Procedures and Protocols.

1.2. Responsibility: It shall be the responsibility of each member to know, understand and utilize these procedures as they apply to the situation at hand. It shall further be the responsibility of all Division Officers to train their subordinates in the proper application of these procedures and to implement and enforce the use of these procedures.
2. Header
2.1. The format of all the Division of Fire’s SOPs will be the same general style.
1.3. The Office of Research and Innovation, R&I, will review the correctness of the Division’s SOPs header information prior to printing.
1.4. The Division’s SOP Header template will be used as the header for the first page of the SOP.
1.5. The SOP subject title is to be short and concise, generally limited to six words or less.

1.6. The SOP numbering system is as follows: S.O.P.Number 99-99-99.99 Vol-Ch-Cat.Sub Example: S.O.P. 07-02-23 Volume 07: EMS Protocol Chapter 02: AdultMedicalProtocols Category 23: Hypothermia Subcategory: To be used as necessary to further define a category
1.7. Confidential information such as Bomb Squad TechnicalProcedureswill be marked RESTRICTED, and distribution will be limited to “need to know” individuals.
1.8. The Fire Chief’s signature will indicate approval. The Medical Director will cosign medical care protocols.
1.9. Issued (mm/dd/yyyy) will be the date the provisions were originally implemented.
2.2. Revised (mm/dd/yyyy) will be the date the SOP was last revised.
2.3. Reviewed (mm/dd/yyyy) will be the date the SOP was last reviewed.
2.3.1. Accreditation recommends review at least annually.
3. Body
3.1. AllSOP submittals must contain the following information:
1.9.1. PURPOSE: The Purpose is a short, one- or two-sentence summary of the purpose of the SOP.
3.2. The body of the SOP will be submitted using the following guidelines:
1.9.2. The SOP body is to be in a numeric outline format. Numbers will identify major headings. This SOP is outlined in the proper format. We will no longer use Roman Numerals.
1.9.3. Print type is Arial, Justified, 12 point and single-spaced.
1.9.4. Section titles are Arial 14 point, bold.
1.9.5. The body should be concise and to the point. It should be remembered that SOPs are not training manuals.
1.10. An effort should be made to keep the SOP as short as possible. If longer, consideration should be given to dividing the SOP into separate, appropriately titled SOPs.
1.11. Bold or ALL CAPS may be used for emphasis of a point, however, excessive use renders an SOP somewhat difficult to read and it loses its effectiveness.
1.12. The SOP shall be submitted in Word as an email attachment to R&I. The SOP template may be found in Division Homepage, Resources, Division Forms, SOP Draft Template 2021.
2. Footer
3.3. The Divisions SOP Footer Template will be used on each page of the SOP.
2.1. Footer information will include Department Name, SOP Number, Revision date and page number (x of y) format.
3. Revisions

3.1. When making updates or revisions to SOP, request unprotected document from R&I. All changes or revisions must be tracked. Go to “Review” tab; click “Track Changes” on. Make all corrections or revisions.
3.2. Submit all changes through the chain of command for review and comment.
3.3. The SOP shall be submitted in Word as an email attachment to R&I.
1. Administration

The Division manuals contain established policies, operating procedures, protocols, orders, rules, regulations, and otherrelated information. A comprehensive index of the subjects contained in the SOPs as well as various sections of the Systems Manual are contained in the INDEX volume of the SOPs.

1.2. Responsibility: It shall be the responsibility of each member to know, understand and utilize these procedures as they apply to the situation at hand. It shall further be the responsibility of all Division Officers to train their subordinates in the proper application of these procedures and to implement and enforce the use of these procedures.
2. Distributionof Manuals

1. Administration
1.1. Purpose: To describe the steps in the approval process for new SOPs.

1.1. Responsibility: It shall be the responsibility of each member to know, understand and utilize these procedures as they apply to the situation at hand. It shall further be the responsibility of all Division Officers to train their subordinates in the proper application of these procedures and to implement and enforce the use of these procedures.
2. SOP Development

1.2. Adherence to these guidelines will ensure that the individuals responsible for administration and enforcement of Standard Operating Procedures have verified the correctness of the SOPs and that the SOPs adequately describe the methods to obtain the desired outcome.
2.1. Submittal

1.2.1. Any employee who sees a need for the establishment of a new Standard Operation Procedure or Protocol may submit the suggested information through their chain of command, to the appropriate Assistant Chief.
1.2.1.1. The employee shall advise the Chief if the new procedure has an effect on, or impacts any existing SOPs.
1.2.1.2. Receipt of the submittal will be acknowledged by the Assistant Chief’s office.
1.2.2. The Draft SOPs shall be prepared on plain paper following the procedures described in the Division’s SOP 04-02-02 (SOP – Format).
2.1.1. Each SOP shall begin with a clear, concise purpose.
2.2. Review

1.2.3. The appropriate Assistant Chief shall forward copies of the proposal to the individuals/groups that may be affected by the procedure, for their review and comments. If necessary, a review committee may be formed.
1.2.4. The original proposal, along with the review comments attached, will be forwarded to the Fire Chief for a preliminary review.

1.2.5. If, in the Fire Chief’s opinion, the proposal does not meet the immediate needs of the Division, the proposal will be filed for future reference. The submitter will be notified of this decision through their chain-of-command.
1.2.6. If the Fire Chief approves the concept, the proposal will be returned to the Bureau Head for a concise review and processed into a finalized document.
2.3. Processing

1.2.7. The Bureau’s staff shall review the content, consistency and compatibility with existing documents when preparing their finalized document. Existing documents, which are affected by the new SOP, will be addressed and included as part of the submittal package for the Fire Chief’s review.
2.3.1. The Bureau’s staff shall process the final SOPutilizing Microsoft Word.
1.2.8. The submittal packagewill be distributed to the other Assistant Chiefs for their review. This portion of the review process is to eliminate conflicts between bureaus.

1.2.9. The Bureau will submit the SOP to the Fire Chief, through the office of Research and Development, in electronic copy format. The SOP submittal will be printed in its entirety within the body of a bulletin. The bulletin will include any information needed to introduce the SOP to the members or to further explain the intent of the SOP.
1.2.10. The bulletin will be reviewed by R&D to ensure that the SOP is consistent with the Division’s format and style.
2.3.2. R&D will submit the SOP bulletin to the Fire Chief.
2.4. Approval
1.2.11. Upon approval by the Fire Chief the new SOP will be issued as a bulletin. This will provide for timely distribution and give an opportunity to identify minor errors or omissions.
2.5. Printing

1.2.12. An approved copy of the SOP will be printed, or made available electronically, approximately 60 to 90 days after the effective date. Distribution will be in accordance with the Division’s Distribution Policy.
1. Administration
1.1. Purpose: To describe the evaluation and review process for existing Division of Fire Standard Operating Procedures and Protocols.

1.2. Responsibility: It shall be the responsibility of each member to know, understand and utilize these procedures as they apply to the situation at hand. It shall further be the responsibility of all Division Officers to train their subordinates in the proper application of these procedures and to implement and enforce the use of these procedures.
2. Evaluation
1.3. The Division of Fire’s SOPs follow a never-ending cycle: Establishment, Training, Application, Review and Revision. This SOP describes the revision and review process.
2.1. Revisions
1.3.1. Proposed revisions to an existing SOP will follow the same general procedures as required for submittal for a new SOP.
2.1.1.1. Any employee may propose a revision.
1.3.1.1. The proposal shall state if the proposal has an effect on or impacts any other SOP(s).
1.3.1.2. The proposal shall be submitted through the chain-of-command to the appropriate Assistant Chief.
1.3.1.3. The Assistant Chief will process the proposed revision in accordance with the review, processing, and approval procedures outlined in the SOP dealing with SOP proposals.
2.2. Bi-Annual Review
1.3.2. The review of existing SOPs is an ongoing process. Bureau Heads will ensure that all SOPs that pertain to their Bureau are revised as needed and reviewed at least every two years.

1.3.3. The review is to evaluate the SOPs overall effectiveness and that the objective of the SOP is being met. This is in accordance with the Division’s SOP philosophy: “enforce it, revise it, or eliminate it.”
1.3.4. The Assistant Chief will process any proposed revisions in accordance with the review, processing, and approval procedures outline in the SOP dealing with SOP proposals.
2.3. Revised SOPs

1.3.5. Revised SOPs shall have the revised sections notated with a single vertical line in the right margin parallel to the section(s) in which a change has occurred. A sample notation line is to the right of this section. This will enable personnel to quickly identify and follow changes to the Division’s operating procedures.
1.3.6. Subsequent revisions will have the previous vertical notation lines removed and new revision notation lines added. Columbus Division of Fire | S.O.P 04-03-01 1 of 2
1. Administration
1.1. Purpose: To provide timely and sensitive notification to Division members about a life-threatening injury or death of an immediate family member.

1.2. Responsibility: It shall be the responsibility of each member to know, understand and utilize these procedures as they apply to the situation at hand. It shall further be the responsibility of all Division Officers to train their subordinates in the proper application of these procedures and to implement and enforce the use of these procedures.
2. General
2.1. The following are guidelines to follow when a Division member’s immediate family member has a life-threatening injury or has died.

2.1.1. In the event that an on-duty Division member’s immediate family member has sustained a life-threatening injury or has died, every attempt will be made to notify the affected member in a timely and sensitive manner.

2.1.2. In the event that a family member suffers a life-threatening injury or death within the Division’s response jurisdiction these guidelines provide for a timely and sensitive notification of the affected member.
3. Initial Responsibilities
3.1. In the event that a Division member becomes aware of a Division member’s immediate family member who has a life- threatening injury or who has died DO NOT attempt to contact the member.

3.1.1. Notify the FAO Lt. immediately when aware of, or on the scene of a crisis that involves a family member of a Division member. Use discretion by not revealing identifications using radio frequencies. The preferred method of notification is telephone.
3.1.2. Provide pertinent information to the FAO regarding the family member and any information about the Division member.

3.1.3. The Fire Alarm Office will notify the on-duty Deputy Chief of the incident, if the member is assigned to Emergency Services, and will notify the appropriate Bureau Head if assigned to 40 hours. Columbus Division of Fire | S.O.P 04-03-01 2 of 2
4. Notification
4.1. The on-duty Deputy Chief or the Bureau Head shall:
4.1.1. Determine the circumstances and obtain as much information as possible. Notify the Lead Shift Peer, a Division Chaplain and/or Family Support Liaison, if appropriate.

4.1.1.1. A Family Support Liaison and/or Division Chaplain can provide moral support and comfort to member and assist in getting answers to their questions. The liaison should be the most appropriate person available to perform this role without regard to rank. The liaison will be relieved of other duties to the extent necessary to fulfill this responsibility.
4.1.1.2. The Lead Shift Peer may be a valuable asset. They may recommend personnel to act as, or to assist the Family Support Liaison.
4.1.2. If the member is unaware of the situation, determine the best method of delivering the information taking into consideration the time of day, location, etc.
4.1.3. For a death:
4.1.3.1. Determine a course of action that combines a prompt, but appropriate notification.

4.1.3.2. If the member is on duty the member’s Battalion Chief / Section Head should assist in determining the appropriate notification procedures. The support of the Lead Shift Peer, a Division Chaplain and/or Family Support Liaison, should be considered.
4.1.4. For a life-threatening injury:
4.1.4.1. Determine a course of action that combines a prompt, but appropriate notification.

4.1.4.2. If the member is on duty notify the member’s Battalion Chief/Section Head and have them contact the member’s immediate supervisor to discuss an appropriate course of action, i.e. providing immediate transportation to the family member’s location, etc.
4.1.5. Notify the FAO of the actions taken.
4.2. The Fire Alarm Office will notify the following personnel of the situation and actions taken by the Deputy Chief or the Bureau Head:
4.2.1. Fire Chief
1.1.1. Administrative Chief
1.1.2. Bureau Head of member
1.1.3. Deputy Chief of Member, if applicable
1.1.4. Public Information Officer
1.1.5. Members Support Supervisor
1.1.6. Local 67 President

04-03-02.t: Death or Serious Injury of Member
p: 1 Administration

1.1 Purpose: This procedure provides guidelines for the notification and support of family members in the event an employee is seriously injured or dies in the line of duty. It establishes a priority for notification of family and division members and steps for conducting the notification.

1.2 Responsibility: It shall be the responsibility of each member to know, understand, and utilize these procedures as they apply to the situation at hand. It shall further be the responsibility of all Division Officers to train their subordinates in the proper application of these procedures and to implement and enforce the use of these procedures. 2 General

2.1 The overriding philosophy of the Columbus Division of Fire is that the first priority following a line of duty serious injury or death - after caring for the victims - is the swift, compassionate notification of the injured or deceased member's family and the extension of assistance and support to them. In this context, a serious injury is defined as one that is life threatening, or that will disable the employee for a substantial period of time. 3 Initial Responsibilities

3.1 Immediately upon becoming aware that an employee has been seriously injured or died, the following should occur: The Battalion Chief or other ranking person at the scene of the injury or death should immediately notify the on-duty Deputy Chief. The Deputy Chief becomes the point of contact for making necessary assignments to address the situations.
3.2 The Lead Shift Peer can be a valuable asset to the Deputy Chief. They may recommend personnel to act as, or to assist the Family Support Liaison.
3.3 Deputy Chief’s duties:
1.1.1 Notify Fire Chief and Administrative Assistant Chief.
1.1.2 Notify all on-duty Battalion Chiefs via conference call.
1.1.3 Notify the Public Information Officer.

3.3.1 Have the Fire Alarm Office (FAO) notify the Members Support Unit Supervisor to activate Lead Shift Peer and the Chaplains. Have the FAO direct all calls about the incident to the PIO, as appropriate: news media, public, etc.
1.1.4 Assign a two-person Notification Team.
1.1.5 Assign a Hospital Liaison, if applicable. Consider EMSO.
1.1.6 Assign a Family Support Liaison.

3.3.2 The Deputy Chief will assign someone to write a Public Address announcement for all stations and to be used for an all-user email to confirm the details of the loss to all CFD employees with the confirmed details of the employee death. The Deputy Chief and/or the Fire Chief should approve the memo before it is read as a Public Address message and sent to every station and bureau via e-mail and/or hard copy. See section 3.9.2.

3.3.3 If the family of the employee does not live in or near Franklin County, measures must be taken to have someone in the employee's hometown make the notification. Unless a clergy person or someone else with a relationship with the family is known to the Deputy Chief, or is on record in the employee's personnel file, the fire department in the family's city of residence is probably the most appropriate source to ask to make the faceto-face notification. In that case, the Deputy Chief or designee should stand by and prepare to take a phone call from the family as soon as the notification is made.
3.3.4 The Deputy Chief should select and immediately dispatch a two-person team to travel to the employee’s hometown to meet with the family, if appropriate.
3.4 Hospital Liaison:

3.4.1 If a member has been seriously injured, an EMS coordinator will be assigned to the hospital to keep the Deputy Chief informed of the status of the member. He may be relieved of duty when the family and the Family Support Liaison arrive at the hospital.
3.4.2 The Family Support Liaison will keep the Division informed of the family’s needs, concerns, and the status of the member.
3.5 Notification Team:

3.5.1 Ideally, the team will consist of a Division Chaplain and a Chief Officer. Two Officers will be sent if the Chaplain is delayed or not available. The Deputy Chief, if available, should be one of the team members.

3.5.2 Division Human Resources shall be the primary point of contact for obtaining a member’s emergency contact information. During Human Resources non-working hours, emergency contact information may be accessed through Dayforce.
3.5.2.1 Access to emergency contact information is restricted to the rank of Battalion Chief and above and shall be used only for legitimate emergency purposes, including:
• Line-of-duty injury or illness
• Medical emergency or incapacitation
• Death notification or critical incident
3.5.2.2. Emergency contact information shall not be accessed for routine, administrative, or non-emergency purposes.
3.5.3 For an employee's family who lives within Franklin County, the goal is to make the notification within two hours of the Deputy Chief learning of the injury or death.
3.5.4 If more than one employee has been injured or died in an incident, duplicate teams will be assigned to each affected family.
3.5.5 Chief Officers and Chaplains assigned to notification teams should wear dress uniforms if at all possible.
3.5.6 If the two members of the team do not leave from the same location, they should meet near the family's home or the site where they expect to find the family member to be notified.

3.5.7 When the team members have met and are prepared to proceed, the Chief Officer should speak by phone - not over department radio channels – with the Deputy Chief to get the most up to date verified facts about the incident.
3.5.7.1 Attempt to answer the questions, who, what, where, when, why, and how.
3.5.7.2 Information regarding precipitating or causal factors, or information that is not verified, should not be provided until an investigation has been completed.
3.6 Notifying the Family:
3.6.1 The team members should rendezvous near the family’s home, or notification site. If in Franklin County, a medic unit should stand by at the rendezvous location.

3.6.2 The roles of the team members should be coordinated prior to arrival at the notification site. The person who will make the notification should make introductions at the door and ask to come in. In most cases, if a Chaplain is part of the notification team, he or she should make the notification.

3.6.3 Because the appearance of a CFD Chief Officer at the home of an employee, or at the workplace of an employee's spouse will likely cause alarm, the information about what has transpired should be given as rapidly as possible.
3.6.4 If the notification occurs in a home, try to bring together all family members present.

3.6.5 It is best to give all the important information as soon as possible and in one or two brief sentences. For example, "Your husband responded to a major fire today and was trapped when a roof collapsed. I am sorry to tell you that he (is critically injured or has died.)”
3.6.6 The notification team will offer to drive the family to the hospital if appropriate.
1.2 Family Support in the event of death:

3.6.7 After the family has been notified, some time may be needed, as the shock subsides, to discuss details and plan for what is next. Let them know that the Members Support Unit team as well as EAP are available.
3.6.8 Do not overwhelm them with information. People react differently in such occasions, and they will ask you what they want to know.

3.6.9 Ask the family members if there is someone you can call for them. Encourage them to let you do this. Let them know they can count on the Division’s support to help them get through the trying days to come.
3.6.10 Unless the family desires otherwise, the notification team will remain with the family until the Family Support Liaison arrives.
3.6.11 The Notification Team Chief Officer will notify the Deputy Chief when all necessary notifications have been made.

3.6.12 Sometimes the Deputy Chief or another member will know of relationships between the families of employees. In these cases, it may be appropriate to send a third person, without regard to rank, with the notification team. That person will wait in the car until the notification has been made and then be invited to join the family.
3.7 Family Support Liaison:

3.7.1 The Family Support Liaison should be the most appropriate person available to perform this role without regard to rank. The liaison will be relieved of other duties to the extent necessary to fulfill this responsibility.
3.7.2 Prior to leaving for the hospital or the family's home, the liaison will notify his or her Supervisor that he/she has been assigned that function.
3.7.3 The Family Support Liaison will provide moral support and comfort to the family and assist in getting answers to their questions.

3.7.4 In the days that follow, it will be the responsibility of the liaison to communicate to the Division the family's needs and concerns. The Family Support Liaison must be sensitive to the family's need to grieve privately and use discretion in when to leave them.
3.7.5 When leaving, the Family Support Liaison will make sure family members know how to reach him/her and will establish a time to contact them in the future.
3.8 Notifying Others of the Incident:
3.8.1 When the death or serious injury of an employee occurs, the Division should notify certain people before they learn of it through the news media.

3.8.2 After the family, the first people to be informed are on-duty Division employees. Cautionary reminder: Please do not share information on social media until a formal notification from the Division, ex. identity of member has taken place. This will ensure the family is notified properly and false information is not shared on social media. See Section 3.3.8
3.8.3 Others who must be notified immediately upon a death are:
1.2.1.1 Public Information Officer
1.2.1.2 Mayor and City Council
1.2.1.3 Safety Director
1.2.1.4 IAFF, Local 67 President
1.2.1.5 Safety Officer
1.2.1.6 Chief investigator Note: This is not necessarily an exhaustive list, the Administration must consider if anyone else needs specific notification.
1.3 Public Notification:

3.8.4 The Deputy Chief will inform the Fire Chief and the Public Information Officer (PIO) when the next of kin and on-duty Division members have been notified of the death, and that the information may be released to the public.
3.9 Division Condolences:

3.9.1 As soon as it is deemed appropriate, and in no case more than 24 hours after the employee death, the Fire Chief, or in his/her absence the Administrative Assistant Chief should visit the family. Guidance will be offered by the Family Support Liaison about when and where such a meeting should take place. Columbus Division of Fire | S.O.P 04-03-03 | Rev. 04/17/2026 1 of 3
1. Administration

1.1. Purpose: The purpose of this procedure is to provide interested members with information regarding the application process for criteria for membership in; and responsibilities to the Division Peer Support Team.

1.2. Responsibility: It shall be the responsibility of each member to know, understand and utilize these procedures as they apply to the situation at hand. It shall further be the responsibility of all Division Officers to train their subordinates in the proper application of these procedures and to implement and enforce the use of these procedures.
1. General

1.3. Mission Statement Provide a confidential, safe, non-judgmental, network of support for members to connect with trained peers who understand the unique stressors of the work environment and can act as a bridge to additional resources if the need is recognized.
2. Team Organization

1.4. Members Support Office schedules and organizes training for new and current peers, coordinates 40hr peers and Lead shift peers, oversees and coordinates Chaplains, and maintains overall records of Peer Support activities. Ensures the professionalism and responsibility of all Peer Support members.

1.5. Lead Shift Peer coordinates requests for Peer Support deployments on assigned unit, assists the Members Support Office with training and daily station visits, maintains Peer roster of assigned unit. Each unit should have a Lead peer and 3-4 Alternate Lead Peers.
1.6. Peer Team consists of Division members from any rank, trained to the standard in Section 5 that handles on duty after hours critical issues and assist the Members Support Office when needed.

1.7. EAP/Mental Health Professional provides guidance to the Leadership Team and professional support during Peer Team activations. These individuals should have at least a master’s degree in psychology, social work, psychiatric nursing, or mental health counseling. They must be trained in crisis intervention and post-traumatic stress. Mental Health Professionals assigned to the Peer Support Team are encouraged to ride along on CFD apparatus to become familiar with personnel and duties of ES personnel. Columbus Division of Fire | S.O.P 04-03-03 | Rev. 04/17/2026 2 of 3
1.8. Chaplain Team provides spiritual support and guidance. (See Chaplain team S.O.P. 04-03-09 for additional details)
3. Peer Team Requirements
1.9. All interested candidates for the Peer Team shall be in good standing with the Division of Fire and be free of discipline or investigations (the Focus) for 1 year.
1.10. All interested candidates for the Peer team must have completed the apprenticeship program, obtaining journeyman status.
1.11. All candidates must participate in the Peer team selection interview.
1.12. All Candidates must complete a 16-hour CFD approved Peer Class, as directed by the Members Support Office.
1.13. All candidates are expected to attend regular scheduled Peer Support Team functions or CE events for continuing education.
4. Peer Team Training
1.14. The selection process starts with the recommendations from current members of the Peer team.
1.15. Interested members who choose to volunteer as a Peer team member shall submit their request through their chain-of-command to the Members Support supervisor.

1.16. A committee comprised of Members Support office personnel and EAP clinicians will interview and evaluate applicants. Division members applying for team membership will receive consideration for the following factors:
1.16.1 The ability to maintain confidentiality
1.16.2 Personal experience with crisis, trauma, and behavioral health
1.16.3 Motivation to become a team member
1.16.4 Willingness to volunteer some time as a team member
1.16.5 Willingness to attend required training, including continuing education and team meetings
1.16.6 Willingness and ability to listen without making judgments
1.16.7 A genuine interest in helping their fellow firefighters
2. Selection Process

1. Administration

1.1. Purpose: To assist in the identification of critical incidents faced by personnel that cause them to experience unusually strong emotional reactions. These incidents can have the potential to interfere with their ability to function, either at the scene of an incident or sometime after the incident has concluded. Once a critical incident is identified, initiate the appropriate type of management assistance.

1.2. Responsibility: It shall be the responsibility of each member to know, understand and utilize these procedures as they apply to the situation at hand. It shall further be the responsibility of all Division Officers to train their subordinates in the proper application of these procedures and to implement and enforce the use of these procedures.
1. General
1.3. Critical Incident - Any unusually challenging incident that has the potential to create significant human distress, physical or psychological, and can overwhelm one’s usual coping mechanisms.
1.4. Critical Incident Stress Management (CISM) - A comprehensive, phase sensitive, and integrated, multi-component approach to crisis/disaster intervention.
1.5. Members Support Unit – Includes a supervisor and assigned personnel that are peer-support trained, that lead in the management of and response to critical incidents.
2.4 Peer Team- A designated group of Columbus Division of Fire members who have been trained in CISM recognition and management.
2. Management Types
2.1. The type of response conducted depends on the circumstances of the particular incident. The following types are the most commonly used either singularly or in combination:

2.1.1. On-Scene or Near-Scene Management: On-Scene consultation by a Peer team member should be considered a resource available for some critical incidents of extreme magnitude when time and circumstances permit. Team members should be considered a resource available to command officers. In these situations, team members can observe and be Columbus Division of Fire | S.O.P 04-03-04 | Rev. 04/17/2026 2 of 3 alert for acute stress reactions. In addition, team members will provide support and encouragement, be available to help resting personnel deal with stress reactions, and allow for expression of feelings and reactions when appropriate. Peer support team members providing this service are not to be involved in operational functions.

2.1.2. Initial Defusing: This confidential discussion occurs shortly after the incident (possibly several hours, but normally within the same work shift). It is a spontaneous, informal, non-evaluative discussion, provided by one or more Peer Support Team members. It provides updates and status reports on the incident and related injuries, encourages discussion of reactions as indicated and provides resources for those involved in the incident.

2.1.3. Formal Debriefing: A strictly confidential, supportive, and educational discussion process designed to accelerate normal recovery of individuals who have been exposed to highly abnormal incidents. This is a confidential, non-judgmental discussion of involvement, thoughts, and feelings resulting from the incident and includes discussion of possible stress-related symptoms. Ideally, it should be conducted within 24 to 72 hours of the critical incident. This will be conducted by members of EAP, Members Support Unit/Peer Team and Chaplain Team.

2.1.4. Follow-up: This follow-up may be done informally and may occur weeks or months after the incident, if necessary. Its purpose is to assist members after the incident with any issues or problems that were not initially resolved, i.e. delayed or prolonged stress reaction. The follow-up may be held with the entire group present or only a portion of the group.
3. Debriefing Facilitation
3.1. Will include a clinician from EAP familiar with the Columbus Division of Fire operations to help facilitate debriefing, as well as members of the Division trained in the management process.
3.2. A debriefing is not group therapy. It is an opportunity for personnel to discuss their feelings and reactions, in order to reduce the stress resulting from exposure to critical incidents.
3.3. Each debriefing has educational elements designed to help the participant recognize, prevent, and mitigate stress reactions.
3.4. Debriefing is not a tactical critique. Operations or performance on scene will not be discussed at any time during the debriefing.
3.5. Note taking or recording during the debriefing will not be permitted to ensure confidentiality.

3.6. Individuals not involved in the critical incident will not be allowed to attend the debriefing under any circumstances. Strict Confidentiality is of the highest priority. Columbus Division of Fire | S.O.P 04-03-04 | Rev. 04/17/2026 3 of 3
2. Initiating Peer Support

3.7. The Members Support Unit/Peer Team is activated by calling the Members Support unit office from 0700-1600, the Lead shift Peer from 1600-0700 or the on-duty Deputy Chief (ES2). Whenever the assigned Peer Team response requires the release of on-duty Peer Team personnel, the on-duty Deputy Chief shall be notified. A Peer Team member will contact the requesting person to get further details. The Lead Shift Peer will assist in determining the recommended level of Peer Team intervention.

3.8. Evaluation of the need for a CISM session may be very obvious or less clearcut. The following are general considerations that may aid in determining the need for some form of debriefing, or simply a referral:
5.2.1 The number of individuals who participated in the event and may be negatively affected.
5.2.2 The type of symptoms being reported by participates in the event.
5.2.3 Changes in behavior by participating in the event.
5.2.4 Regression in behavior by participants in the event.
5.2.5 Determine if group members are having problems with acute or delayed stress and if they would benefit by speaking with peers.
5.2.6 Determine if group members are asking for information on stress management or if a formal debriefing is necessary.
3.9. Following evaluation, it is important to note that services are offered freely
3.10. The following types of incidents will almost certainly involve the Members Support Unit/Peer Team in some manner:
5.4.1 Line of Duty death, or serious injury of a firefighter*
5.4.2 Mass casualty incidents*
5.4.3 Suicide of a firefighter*
5.4.4 Death or serious injury of a civilian resulting from emergency operations (e.g. auto accident involving Division vehicle, etc.)
5.4.5 Death of a child, or violence to a child by an adult.
5.4.6 Loss of life to a civilian following extraordinary and prolonged rescue attempt.
5.4.7 Incidents attracting unusual, critical, or extensive news media coverage.
5.4.8 Any incident charged with profound emotion.

5.4.9 Any incident in which the circumstances are so unusual, or the sights and sounds so distressing as to produce a high level of immediate or delayed emotional reaction. *Note: Attendance at debriefings for these types of incidents is strongly encouraged for all working at the scene of the incident. If an individual believes the process may be harmful to him/her, he/she should speak with EAP, a Peer Team member, or member from Chaplain Team.

1.1. Purpose: The purpose of this procedure is to identify the procedures to use during hot and cold weather emergencies.
