1. Administration
1.1 Purpose: To establish procedures for Fire Investigators authorized to carry firearms.

1.1 Responsibility: It shall be the responsibility of each Fire Investigator to know, understand, and utilize these procedures as they apply to the situation at hand. It shall further be the responsibility of all Fire Investigator supervisors to train their subordinates in the proper application of these procedures and to implement and enforce the use of these procedures.
2. Definitions
2.1 Primary Service Firearm
1.1.1 The Division-issued Smith & Wesson model M&P 2.0 9mm full-size auto pistol.
2.2 Alternate Firearm

1.1.2 A Division-issued or privately-owned firearm authorized for carrying instead of the primary service firearm, provided applicable Division of Police qualification standards are met. A list of approved firearms is available at the Police Ordnance Unit.
1.1.3 The Division-issued Smith and Wesson model M&P 2.0 9mm compact auto pistol is an authorized alternate firearm.
1.1.4 The Division-issued Remington 870 shotgun may also be carried if the annual Division of Police qualification standards are met.
2.3 Off-duty/Back-up Firearm

1.1.5 A Division-issued or privately-owned firearm authorized for carrying during non-work hours or in addition to the primary service firearm/approved alternate firearm during work hours, provided applicable Division of Police qualification standards are met. A list of approved firearms is available at the Police Ordnance Unit.
3. Policy Statements Division issued firearms shall be kept in a safe condition and secured from unauthorized access, misuse, or theft at all times.

1.2 The Fire Chief will designate Fire Investigators authorized to be issued a Division firearm, or to possess and use a firearm or any other type of force while on-duty. An authorized list will be periodically reviewed and updated at least annually for any change in status.

1.3 Assigned Fire Investigators, without authorization to carry a firearm prior to June of 2012, shall be required to complete and pass the Peace Officer Basic Training requirements as set forth by the Ohio Peace Officer Training Commission through the Columbus Division of Police Training Academy.
1.3.1 Fire Investigators authorized to carry a firearm must successfully complete any training requirement designated by the Fire Chief, including annual refresher training.

1.4 Fire Investigators shall annually meet Division of Police qualification standards with any firearm they intend to carry while on-duty or off-duty. This does not apply to personal rifles, shotguns, and/or handguns used for recreation purposes.
1.4.1 Fire Investigators shall annually meet all Division of Police qualification standards with all Division of Fire issued firearms.
1.4.2 For Division issued firearms, Fire Investigators shall be allotted a monthly maximum of 200 practice rounds provided by the City.
1.4.3 Only Division of Police Ordnance Unit personnel may repair or alter any issued firearm.

1.4.4 Testing, evaluating, and any required “breaking in” of all firearms, chemical agents, intermediate weapons, and any accessory to these weapon systems are to be conducted under supervision by the appropriate Division of Police Training Bureau personnel.
1.5 Fire Investigators shall use Division-approved weapons only when reasonable and within policy.
3.1 Fire Investigators shall not use any weapon for a retaliatory or punitivepurpose.

1.5.1 All confrontations between Fire Investigators and suspects where a firearm is deployed, with intent to use, must be reported in writing to their immediate supervisor and forwarded through the chain of command to the Fire Chief. This documentation is required in all such circumstances, regardless of whether an action-response to resistance/aggression investigation is required.
3.2 Fire Investigators shall not carry personally-owned shotguns or rifleson-duty.
3.3 Carrying Loaded Firearms

1.5.2 Fire Investigators shall carry a loaded, authorized firearm at all times with the following exceptions: 1) When it would be a violation of law. 2) When it would be impractical. 3) When ordered not to by a competent authority, such as a court, or not permitted to by Division Policy or restrictions. In the State of Ohio, an establishment serving the public cannot prohibit or restrict sworn personnel from carrying an authorized firearm on the premises.
3.3.1 Off-dutyFire Investigators are not required to carry a firearm.
1.5.2.1 Off-duty Fire Investigators carrying an authorized firearm shall have it within their immediate control unless it would be a violation of law or this policy.
1.5.2.2 Fire investigators shall carry off-duty firearm(s) authorized for carry in a concealed manner.

1.5.2.3 ObtainingAuthorization to Carry an Alternate and/or Off-dutyFirearm: Fire Investigator: 1) Complete a Firearms Qualifications form, S-70.102, listing the information specific to the firearm. Forms are available from the Ordnance Unit. 2) Submitthe firearm to Ordnance Unit personnel forinspection. 3) Qualifywith the firearm on the OPOTA pistol qualification course. Ordinance Unit & Investigations Supervisor: 1) Issue authorization foran approved firearm asappropriate. 2) Maintain a list of personnel who have qualified with an alternate and/or off-duty firearm and the specific type of firearm. Note: Justification for not carrying a firearm while on duty shall be required. In the State of Ohio, an establishment serving the public cannot prohibit or restrict sworn personnel from carrying an authorized firearm on the premises.

1.5.3 When required or authorized to carry a firearm, Fire Investigators shall carry and use only those firearms and ammunitions that have been approved by the Chief of Police, and with which they have satisfied the qualification standards established by the Division of Police and the Ohio Peace Officers Training Commission.
1.5.4 Fire Investigators shall carry only the Division issued firearms while on- duty, unless otherwise approved by the Fire Chief.

1.5.5 All Fire Investigators authorized to carry a firearm shall also carry their Division issued badge, law enforcement identification credentials, issued authorized firearm, spare magazine with issued duty ammunition, and handcuffs at all times while on-duty.

1.5.6 When not wearing a Division issued uniform, the Division issued badge shall be worn so that it is visible in the center of the chest, or concealed as necessary. When wearing the ballistic vest, the badge shall be clipped to the front outside of the ballistic vest, or worn on a neck chain outside of the ballistic vest.

1.5.7 Fire Investigators shall not carry a loaded firearm within a court building or courtroom when attending court on any personal/private matter unless prior approval is obtained from the Judge, Magistrate, or Jury Commissioner (if on jury duty).
1.5.8 Fire Investigators shall return all issued firearms to their immediate supervisor when they depart the unit, relinquish the firearm for any reason, or are otherwise ordered.

1.5.9 Carrying or using a firearm while under the influence of alcohol or drugs, or consuming alcohol at a D-permit establishment or in an open-air arena for which a permit of that nature has been issued, is a violation of law.
1.5.10 Fire Investigators may use an approved rail-mounted light and holster for Division issued pistols, upon training and qualification conducted by Division of Police Ordnance Unit personnel.
3.3.2 Shotgun
1.5.10.1 Fire Investigators shall annually complete a familiarization class and qualification with the shotgun.
1.5.10.2 Only Fire Investigators who have successfully completed annual qualification training with the shotgun shall be permitted to carry one.
1.5.10.3 Fire Investigators who have not qualified with a shotgun shall not deploy, carry, or use the shotgun except under the most critical circumstances.
2.10 Authorization to carry an alternate firearm may be terminated at any time.
2.11 Failure to Qualify with a Firearm
2.11.1 Failure to qualify with the primary service firearm by satisfying the firearms qualification standards as established by the State of Ohio:

2.11.1.1 Fire Investigators who fail to qualify with the primary service firearm in three attempts during the first qualification session of each required course/phase shall receive a written order under the authority of the Fire Chief from their immediate supervisor to: (A) Surrenderall Division issued firearms. (B) Mark out-of-service with the Fire Alarm Office. (A) Not to take any law enforcement action, on or off-duty (may work in the Fire Investigation offices). (C) Not carry any firearm on oroff-duty. (D) Notifytheir supervisor of the date of their next qualificationsession.

2.11.1.2 Failure to Qualify with an Approved Alternate and/or Off-dutyFirearm (A) Sworn personnel who fail to qualify in three attempts during the first qualification session with the approved firearm are prohibited from carrying the firearm until qualifications are met. (B) Sworn personnel who fail to qualify with their approved firearm shall surrender the firearm to Ordnance Unit personnel if the firearm is City- owned. (C) Sworn personnel shall be allowed a total of three qualification attempts per day during normal Ordnance Unit hours until qualifications are met. Note: If the Fire Investigatoris asked, by Ordnance Unit personnel, to sign a written order from the Chief of Police explaining the restrictions of their service, they are to comply.

3.10.2 Fire Investigators shall be allowed a total of three qualification sessions of three attempts each. Personnel failing to qualify by the completion of these sessions shall receive a written order advising them that they have seven days in which to qualify on their own time. Failure to qualify during that time shall be cause for disciplinary action and/or adjustment of work assignment, as determined by the Fire Chief.

3.10.3 Fire Investigators who fail to qualify in three attempts during the first qualification session shall be provided remedial training prior to any further attempts to qualify. This training can range from verbal instruction up to and including regimented firing of the qualification course. The contents of the remedial training will be at the discretion of the Ordnance Unit personnel based on the needs of the involved Fire Investigator. Fire Investigators that have failed to qualify by the conclusion of the first session will be scheduled to attend firearm technical skills development.
3.10.4 Fire Investigators who fail to qualify with the Division issued alternate firearm or shotgun must surrender the firearm to their immediate supervisor.

3.10.5 The supervisor shall place a copy of the written order in the Fire Investigator’s firearms file and forward the original written order through the investigator’s chain of command to the Fire Chief.

3.10.6 Investigators shall be given the opportunity to qualify up to three approved alternate or off-duty firearms. An annual maximum of 450 rounds shall be provided by the City for the purpose of qualifying with those approved firearms. Once personnel have qualified, no more rounds shall be allocated for that firearm.
3.11 Carrying Firearms Aboard Aircraft and into Secured Areas inAirports
3.11.1 The carrying of Division issued firearms aboard aircraft and into secured areas of airports will follow the policies and procedures as set forth by local, state and federal regulations.
3.11.2 Fire investigators shall not carry a firearm on their person into secured areas of airports or aboard an aircraft.
3.12 Carrying Firearms While Off-Duty
3.12.1 Fire investigators, while on-duty or off-duty, shall only enforce arson and arson related crimes.

3.12.2 The responsibility for a safe response is shared by all parties in situations involving fire investigators encountering an individual claiming to be an offduty, undercover, or a plain-clothed law enforcement officer. The challenging personnel have a responsibility to use reasonable tactics and sound judgment in approaching the situation, whereas the challenged individual has the responsibility for a safe response to the challenge.
4. Procedures
1.6 Firearms Qualifications
4.1.1 Division of Police Ordnance Unit
4.1.1.1 Formulate firearms training and qualification standards.
1.6.1.1 Advise Investigations Unit supervisorof firearms training and qualification schedules.
4.1.2 Investigation Supervisor
1.6.1.2 Ensure all Fire Investigators under your command are scheduled for each phase of qualification.
1.6.1.3 After each phase, review the circumstances of each individual who has failed to successfully complete the particular phase.
1.6.1.4 Ensure appropriate remedial training and follow procedures for failure to qualify.
1.6.1.5 Notify the Bureau Head of the schedule and results of the qualification process.
4.1.3 Fire Investigators
4.1.3.1 Attend firearms qualification phases as scheduled.
1.6.1.5.1 If there is a legitimate conflict preventing attendance, advise the unit supervisor who approved the schedule.
1.6.1.5.2 If there is no legitimate reason for failing to appear at the scheduled time, reschedule qualification times on your own time within 30 calendar days.
1.6.1.5.3 Failure to qualify when one is physically able, may result in discipline, including surrender of Division issued firearms and reassignment of work duties.
4.2 Obtaining Temporary/ReplacementFirearms
1.6.2 Contact the immediate supervisor to schedule a time for the issuance of a temporary firearm.
1.6.3 Immediately return the temporary firearm to the immediate supervisor when the primary Division issued firearm is returned.

1.7 Loss or theft of a Division issued firearm or other law enforcement equipment will be immediately communicated to the immediate supervisor and through the chain of command to the Fire Chief. An RT-154 must be completed documenting the details surrounding the lost or stolen firearm and sent to the Fire Chief by the first work day following the incident. A police report shall also be filed.

1.8 The Fire Chief will designate a Firearms Officer who shall maintain current records of all Fire Investigators authorized to carry firearms, as well as inventory and maintenance records of all weapons pursuant to this policy.
1.9 Fire Investigators shall wear the Division issued ballistic vest when serving arrest warrants, search warrants, are armed in a Division uniform, or when designated by the immediate supervisor.

1.9.1 Planned high-risk warrant, surveillance, or other activity will require notification to the local law enforcement agency having jurisdiction prior to the scheduled event. Whenever possible, any required dynamic entry to support an investigation is to be coordinated and performed with the appropriate supporting agency tactical team.

1.1 Pursuant to Ohio Revised Code 2744.07(A)(1), defense will be provided by the Columbus City Attorney’s Office for an employee in any civil action to recover damages for injury, death, or loss to persons or property allegedly caused by an act or omission of the employee.
1.2 Pursuant to Ohio Revised Code 2744.07(A)(2), the City Attorney's Office does not have a duty to provide defense to Division personnel in a civil action in the following circumstances:
1.2.1 The act or omission occurred while the employee was not acting in good faith.
1.2.2 The act or omission occurred while the employee was acting manifestly outside the scope of the employee's employment or official responsibilities.
1.2.3 The civil action or proceeding is commenced by or on behalf of a political subdivision.
1.3 In order for the City Attorney’s Office to provide representation, a written request must be received from the involved personnel.

1.4 Personnel who are represented by the City Attorney’s Office may also retain private legal counsel to assist in defending a civil or criminal action. Private legal counsel will be at the involved personnel’s personal expense.

1.5 Division Personnel Named as a Defendant in a Civil Action Should:

2.1.1.2 Attach a copy of all papers served, including envelopes within which any legal papers were contained.
2.1.1.3 If desired, request City Attorney representation, and agree to assist the City Attorney.
2.1.1.4 Advise if private legal counsel will also be retained.
2.1.1.5 Include the best time during normalbusinesshours to be contacted in the event additional information is needed.
1.6 City Attorney for the Division of Fire.
1.6.1 Notify the City Attorney’s Office and the Fire Chief of all lawsuits involving Division personnel.
1.6.2 Immediately notify personnel who will not be represented by the City Attorney’s office. Personnel may assume City Attorney representation unless notified otherwise.
1.6.3 Upon request, provide the Fire Chief with the appropriate information concerning Division or employee-related lawsuits.

1.1 Purpose: It is the policy of the Columbus Division of Fire to utilize a professionally trained canine team to assist the daily operations of the Division. The purpose herein is to establish guidelines for the supervision, operation, evaluation and utilization of the Division’s Accelerant Detection Canine Team. The canine is a City of Columbus asset and a working canine. The training and safety of this canine is the sole responsibility of the handler.

1.2 Responsibility: It shall be the responsibility of each member to know, understand, and utilize these procedures as they apply to the situation at hand. It shall further be the responsibility of all Division Officers to train their subordinates in the proper application of these procedures and to implement and enforce the use of these procedures. 2 Definitions
2.1 Accelerant Detection Canine
1.2.1 A working-class canine which has been procured and specially trained to execute a number of specific tasks utilizing the canine’s keen sense of smell.
2.2 Canine Handler
1.2.2 A firefighter who has been specially trained in the care, handling, and training of a canine for accelerant detection.
2.3 Canine Team

1.2.3 A firefighter and canine, which together have completed the “Columbus Fire Canine Accelerant Detection Program” and have obtained certification as an Accelerant Detection Canine Team. 3 General and Staff Supervision

1.3 The accelerant Detection Canine Teams report to the Fire & Explosive Investigation Unit (FEIU). The team will be under the supervision of the Fire & Explosive Investigations Unit chain of command. 4 Shift Hours

1.4 The shift hours of members assigned to the Canine Unit are subject to change to meet the demands of the Division Canine Unit. Members who are responsible for the training and maintenance of a canine will primarily be assigned to a thirty- five (35) hour, five-day workweek. One hour a day of the five-day workweek will be allocated for weekend training and maintenance of the canine.
1.5 The Canine handlers cannot work Emergency Services overtime or special duty due to the fact they must care for the canine at all times.
1.6 All vacations are to be submitted and approved before scheduling to avoid any unforeseen conflicts.
1.7 Any vacation longer than three consecutive days, where the canine is not going to be with the handler, may require the canine to stay with a member of the canine unit.
4.1 Any canine leaving the state will require approval from the Fire Chief.
4.2 The handler shall notify their chain of command for any extended leave. 5 Essential Functions
1.8 The foundation in which this canine was trained is vital to its performance. All adjustments must be approved by the trainer and documented in the handlers’ training records.
1.9 The canine team is a tool to be used by the fire investigator to detect the possible presence of ignitable liquids.
1.10 Maintain the canine in such physical condition so as to perform the required task of the position.
5.1 Conduct daily training as to maintain the canine in good working order.
5.2 Maintain canine certification as required.
5.3 Conduct canine operations as required.
5.4 Collect and process evidence.
5.5 Prepare and present canine reports for court presentation.
5.6 Testify in Municipal, State, and Federal court as required.
1.11 Assist other agencies as required. 6 Authority to Act

1.12 Pursuant to Chapter 3737.24 of the Ohio Revised Code and City Code 1925.04, all fires that occur within the jurisdiction of the Columbus Division of Fire shall be investigated. The investigation will determine the cause, origin, and circumstances of every fire or explosion in order to determine whether a fire or explosion was the result of an accident, carelessness, or design. 7 Training
7.1 Education Requirements
7.1.1 Training Required
1.12.1 Canine handlers shall acquire the following training within a reasonable time period upon being assigned to the FEIU:
7.1.1.1 Ohio Fire Academy Basic Fire Investigation Course.
1.12.1.1 Fire Academy Advanced Fire Investigation Course.
7.1.1.2 NationalFire Academy Evidence Collection Course or similar (IAAI).
7.2 Continuing Education
1.12.2 Canine handlers should complete a minimum of twenty-four (24) hours continuing education a year in the area of accelerant detection canines.
1.12.3 Canine handlers shall locate and enroll in seminars, training, and classes as needed to maintain education hours.
1.12.4 Canine handlers shall meet all annual certification testing standards set for the position.
1.12.5 Canine handlers will be able to maintain any Fire Division qualifications they hold, but they will be inactive during the time they are with the Canine Unit.
1.13 In-Service Training
1.13.1 Canine handlers shall maintain all training hours required for Division personnel.
1.13.2 Canine handlers may be required to attend other courses relating to current trends and techniques as directed by the FEIU Captain.
1.13.3 Canine handlers shall complete daily canine training/exercises as required through the food reward system.

1.13.4 Non-Fire Department personnel will not work the dogs. Family members who have been trained by the handler or canine trainer, may be permitted with the permission from the Fire Prevention Bureau Assistant Chief.
1.13.5 Develop adequate training locations and provide training to Division personnel and outside agencies.
7.2.1 Maintain training logs and all other required documentation.
1.13.6 Handlersmust not take the canine to any other trainer for any reason. 2 Canine Care

2.1 The immediate care and safety of the canine will be the sole responsibility of the handler. It shall be the responsibility of the canine handler to keep his/her canine in such physical condition as to perform the duties expected.
7.3 Housing
2.1.1 The canine will live at the handler’s residence and be a socially interactive member of the family.
7.3.1 Housing areas will be clean and sanitary (home, kennel, vehicle, etc.)

2.1.2 The canine will be kept in its crate during the night time hours, when company comes to the handler’s residence, and any time the handler leaves their residence and does not take the canine with them.
7.3.2 All canines will be controlled anytime they are in the office.
2.1.3 The only toys to be in the crate with the canine is a Benebone or an agreed upon toy with the trainer – NO SOFT TOYS.
2.1.4 The handler is required to abide by all Ohio dog laws as per Chapter 955 of the Ohio Revised Code.
2.1.5 Never take your canine off lead unless it is in an enclosed, controlled area, during a training scenario or if the situation reflects that need.
2.1.6 There is to be no sharing of toys.
2.1.7 The handler will be required to demonstrate safe handling skills and current record keeping.
7.4 Control
2.1.8 The canine will be secured at all times, on duty or off duty via leash, crate, kennel, or vehicle.
2.1.9 Canine handlers must maintain close control of their canines at all times. The handler must remember that there are individuals who do not care for animals and should consider their feelings.
2.1.10 Canines shall never be allowed to run loose unless engaged in agencyauthorized training or exercise.
7.5 Feeding

2.1.11 The canine has been conditioned through a praise and food reward system. It is the handler’s responsibility to maintain the feeding regiment as required through the Columbus Division of Fire K-9 Training Program.
2.1.12 Daily training must be performed 1-4 times/365 days a year per CFD food reward training program.
2.1.13 Food will be provided by the City of Columbus through a purchase order account with a local pet supplier.
2.1.14 The canines will ONLY be fed and administered the food and supplements the Division and Division’s veterinarian has deemed prudent and healthy for the canine.
7.6 Veterinary Procedures
2.1.15 The medical needs of the canine will be provided by the City through a designated veterinarian.
2.1.16 A purchase order account will be established between the City of Columbus and the designated veterinarian.
2.1.17 It is the responsibility of the handler to schedule and maintain annual office visits at the veterinarian’s discretion.

2.1.18 In an emergency situation, the canine may be treated at any emergency care facility. The canine trainer needs to be contacted immediately for instructions and to give consent to the facility. In such cases, notification shall be made through the chain of command.
2.1.19 All emergency situations will be reviewed by the chain of command as to negligence on part of the handler.
7.7 General Care
2.1.20 It will be the handler’s responsibility to perform routine care and grooming as to maintain the canine in good condition.
2.1.21 The City of Columbus will provide general care equipment through a purchase order account with a local pet supplier.
2.1.22 The canine will be examined by the handler daily, to include eyes, ears, mouth, nostrils, feet and general body condition.
2.1.23 The canine will be groomed daily.
2.1.24 Nails will be trimmed as needed.
7.7.1 Teeth will be maintained and brushed as needed.
7.7.2 The canine will be bathed as needed.

2.1.25 The ideal weight for the canine shall be maintained, which has been established by a veterinarian and the trainer. If at any point the canine’s weight is at a level (high or low) that affects the canine’s health or ability to work, immediate steps will be taken to determine the cause and correct the problem.
7.7.3 All canines will be weighed and reported on each Monday. 8 Public Relations
8.1 K9 handlers shall abide by the Division social media policy.
2.2 As a representative of the City of Columbus and Division of Fire, the handler must conduct themselves in a professional manner and exhibit good citizenship at all times.
2.3 In public, the canine must be secured at all times, no off-lead walks, breaks, etc.
8.2 The canine must be under control, no jumping, barking, etc.
2.4 The canine handler, is required to interact with the general public. The handler should be professional and courteous.
2.5 Relieve the canine in designated areas only.
2.6 The handlermust retrieve all of his/her canine’s feces.
2.7 The handler must remember that there are individuals that are not canine friendly. The handler must consider their feelings.
2.8 Requests for canine team demonstrations shall be approved through the FEIU Captain.
2.9 Because of the unpredictability of children, demonstrations for children will be at the discretion of the individually assigned handler.
2.10 A canine handler can terminate a demonstration if in that handler’s opinion the circumstances so dictate. 3 Vehicles
3.1 The canine handler will be assigned a vehicle that is specially equipped for canine operations.
3.2 Handlers will be provided take home vehicles equipped with a containment system, heat alarm system, and tinted windows.
3.3 The center divider, behind the front seats in the vehicles, will remain closed at all times.
3.4 Itis the handler’s responsibility to maintain the vehicle in good working order.
3.5 It is the handler’s responsibility to maintain regular service intervals.
3.6 The handler must abide by all Division guidelines pertaining to take home vehicles.
3.7 The handler is responsible for maintaining the vehicle in a clean and sanitary condition.

3.8 The vehicle will be parked at the handler’s residence when not in use. A locked garage is the preferred location. However, a driveway may be utilized. The vehicle will not be parked on the street on a regular basis.
3.9 Any time a K-9 vehicle leaves a surrounding county, it must be reported to the supervisor.

3.10 If the handler is out of service for an extended period of time, the K-9 vehicle is to be parked and plugged in at Groves Road or other location to keep it charged and to be used as a backup. 4 Equipment
4.1 Condition of Equipment
4.1.1 The handler is responsible for the care and condition of all equipment issued to them for the training and control of the canine.
4.1.2 NoK-9 training equipment will be changed orabandoned withoutapproval of the K-9 trainer (i.e., collar, harness, etc.)
4.1.3 All equipment should be inspected periodically and kept in good working condition.
4.1.4 Any lost or damaged equipment will be reported through the chain of command.
4.1.5 All requests for canine supplies will be turned into the Lieutenant prior to the end of the month.
4.1.6 The supplies will be logged in and out on the Supply Smart Sheet to help maintain accountability and inventory.
4.2 Training Aids
4.2.1 Training aids will be distributed to the handler as required. Itisthe handler’s responsibility to secure and maintain the aids at all times.
4.2.2 Each training aid container will be labeled with pertinent contact information. 5 Deployment

5.1 The canine team will respond in a modified, specially equipped vehicle. The canine team will be “on call” during normal off-duty hours. The team’s services may be requested at any time and shall not be compensated unless actually called out.
5.2 Call-Out Procedures
8.2.1 By the On-Scene Investigator.
5.2.1 By the Incident Commander. In this case, an Investigator must be enroute or on the scene. 6 Fatalities
6.1 The canine team will be called out automatically by the Alarm Office on all fatal fires. 7 Mutual Aid
7.1 When requested to jurisdictions other than the City of Columbus, the following procedures must be adhered to:
7.1.1 The incident scene must be secure as the canine handler will have to answer to the basic rules of evidence and authority under constitutional law in order to conduct a canine search.
7.1.2 Notifythe FEIU Captain/Acting Officer and obtain ES-2 approval.
8.2.2 Once approval is granted, notify the FAO of response.
7.1.3 If no Columbus Fire incident number has been assigned to the incident, the handler must obtain one.
7.1.4 If an incident is assigned to the handler, it is his/her responsibility to complete all appropriate paperwork.
7.1.5 A completed canine report, evidence collection form and/or laboratory analysis results should be forwarded to the lead investigator.
8.2.3 Handlermust maintain original copies of all forwarded documentation.
8.2.4 Notify the FAO when team is BIS. 8 Incident Authority
8.1 The I/C is in charge of the entire incident; however, direct scene authority is given to the Fire Investigator.
8.2 The canine handler is in charge of his/her canine and will ultimately decide if the canine will be utilized. 9 On-Scene Operations
9.1 Arrival
8.2.5 Notify the FAO, Incident Commander and Fire Investigator of arrival.
8.2.6 Coordinate pertinent information with the on-scene Fire Investigator.
9.2 Assess information
8.2.7 Determine the nature and scale of the incident.
9.2.1 Conduct a threat analysis (actual danger, no immediate danger) identify/ prioritize hazard.
8.2.8 Conduct a needs assessment (nature of support, number needed).
8.2.9 Don personal protective equipment as needed.
9.3 Scene Control
9.3.1 The canine team must answer to the basic rules of evidence and authority under constitutional law prior to conducting all canine operations.
9.3.2 All incidents shall be evaluated for safety by the handler prior to introducing the canine into the area.
9.3.3 The decision to utilize the ADC at an incident shall remain with the canine handler.
9.3.4 The operational environment should be void of distractions. All fire personnel should be removed from the main fire area and all extended operations ceased during the canine investigation.
9.4 Define the Mission
8.2.10 Determine the expectations of the canine team.
9.4.1 Considerthe capabilities/limitations of the canine.
8.2.11 Considerthe resources needed to complete the mission.
9.5 Developa Plan
8.2.12 Define a concise course of action.
9.5.1 Advise the I/C and Investigator of the decision as to the utilization of the canine team.
9.6 Implementation
8.2.13 Canine Operations:
9.6.1.1 Should be organized and systematic.
9.6.1.2 Should be slow and methodical.
9.6.1.3 Should emphasize quality over quantity.
9.7 Actionon Find
8.2.14 Reward the canine. Mark the area of interest and continue search.
9.7.1 Upon completion of the search, return the canine to the vehicle and proceed with evidence collection if applicable.
9.7.2 Once evidence is collected, the handler shall verify that the proper sample(s) have been collected.
9.7.3 Layering of debris may require the team to re-visit a search area multiple times at different intervals.
9.7.4 When the canine mission is complete, notify the I/C and/or Investigator of the results.
8.2.15 Collect and process evidentiary items. 10 Response Action Guidelines

10.1 The canine team may be used in a variety of situations involving no, moderate or extensive fire damage. The handler should determine the specific mission to be accomplished. The mission should be within the limitations and capabilities of the canine. If necessary, inform on scene personnel of said limitations and capabilities.
10.2 Structures

10.2.1 The canine team will be utilized in a variety of situations involving structures of all types. The size of the structure and level of fire damage will vary. The handler will conduct canine operations accordingly.
8.2.16 Procedures
10.2.1.1 Scene must be secure
10.2.1.2 A Fire Investigator should be on the scene.
10.2.1.3 Notify FAO upon arrival.
10.2.2 Handler Actions
10.2.2.1 Locate investigator or I/C and obtain pertinent information and determine the specific mission.
10.2.2.2 Conduct a safety walk through of the operational environment prior to introduction of the canine.
10.2.2.3 Develop a search plan accordingly.
10.2.2.4 The operational environment should be void of distractions. All personnel should be removed from the area and all operations ceased during the canine investigation.
10.2.2.5 Focus and motivate the canine prior to entering the search area.
10.2.2.6 Acclimate the canine to the search area with a general walk through prior to initiating the “seek” command.
10.2.2.7 Beginthe search from the least burned area tothe most burned area.
10.2.2.8 Conduct a systematic and thorough search pattern.
10.2.2.9 Areas shall be searched no more than three times.
10.3 Vehicles
10.3.1 Procedures
10.3.1.1 Scene must be secure.
10.3.1.2 A Fire Investigator should be on the scene.
10.3.1.3 Notify the FAO upon arrival.
10.3.1.4 Avoid contact with areas of ignitable liquid run-off.
8.2.17 Handler Actions
10.3.1.5 Locate Investigator or I/C and obtain pertinent information and determine the specific mission.
10.3.1.6 Conduct a safety walk through of the operational environment prior to introduction of the canine.
10.3.1.7 Determine the accessibility of the vehicle’s interior.
10.3.1.8 Pre-plan search accordingly.
10.3.1.9 Focus and motivate the canine prior to entering the search area. Interior inaccessible items may be removed from the interior and worked by the canine team to the exterior of the vehicle.
10.3.1.10 Underside ground area may be searched by relocating the vehicle.
10.3.1.11 Areas shall be searched no more than three times.
10.4 Articles
10.4.1 The team may be utilized to conduct an article sniff. This situation may occur when the team is requested to work over an individual item(s).
8.2.18 Procedures
10.4.1.1 Utilize more than one article.
10.4.1.2 Articles shall be placed at ground level, in a line, approximately 3-4 feet apart.
10.4.1.3 Be cautious of bio-hazard material. (Bodily fluids)
8.2.19 Handler Actions
10.4.1.4 Don sterile latex gloves when handling items.
10.4.1.5 Examine items for safety.
10.4.1.6 Place items in clean unused evidence cans or on a clean surface prior to working the canine over them.
10.4.1.7 Focus and motivate the canine.
10.4.1.8 Work the canine into the wind over all articles no more than three times.
10.5 Open Areas
8.2.20 Procedures
10.5.1.1 The handler should obtain pertinent information as to the nature of the search and expectations of the canine team.
10.5.1.2 The area to be searched should be evaluated for safety by the handler prior to the introduction of the canine.
10.5.1.3 Be cautious of unrestrained canines in the area.
10.5.1.4 Establish the perimeter of the area to be searched and plan the search accordingly.

10.5.1.5 Large areas may require the handler to grid sections of the search area. Outer boundaries will require marking system (landmarks, flags, cones, etc.) in order for the handler to maintain an organized and systematic search pattern.
17.5.2 Handler Actions
17.5.2.1 Focus and motivate the canine.
17.5.2.2 Search into the wind.
17.5.2.3 Utilize a grid search pattern. If there is a change in wind direction, the handler may have to grid search on both the length and width of the search area.
10.6 Crowds
8.2.21 Procedures
10.6.1.1 The handler should obtain pertinent information as to the nature of the search and expectations of the canine team.
10.6.1.2 A safety check of the area should be completed prior to introducing the canine. Particular attention should be given to unrestrained canines in the area.
10.6.1.3 Work into the wind.
8.2.22 Handler Actions
10.6.1.4 Focus and motivate the canine.
10.6.1.5 Don food pouch, give “seek” command and inconspicuously walk through the crowd.
10.6.1.6 Do not allow the canine to jump up on anyone.
10.6.1.7 Note area(s) of canine interest and/or indication(s).
10.7 Line-Ups
8.2.23 Procedures
10.7.1.1 It is the handler’s responsibility to answer to the basic rules of evidence and authority under constitutional law in order to conduct a line-up sniff.
10.7.1.2 Juveniles should have a legal guardian present.
10.7.1.3 Utilize at least three (3) individuals for the procedure.
8.2.24 Handler Actions
10.7.1.4 Thoroughly explain the procedure for a canine line-up sniff to all participants as well as legal guardians if applicable.
10.7.1.5 Obtain consent from all participants as well.
10.7.1.6 Place participants in the standing position approximately 3-4 apart with hands at sides.
10.7.1.7 Work the canine over all participating individuals no more than three (3)times.
10.7.1.8 Do not allow the canine to jump up on anyone.
10.7.1.9 Note area(s) of canine indication(s).
10.8 Fatalities
8.2.25 Procedures
10.8.1.1 Be aware of bio-hazard material.
10.8.1.2 Monitor the canine closely to avoid direct contact with victim(s) (chewing, licking).
10.8.1.3 If victim(s) removed prior to arrival, do not allow the canine to lick, eat or chew on area where victim was located.
10.8.1.4 Use caution placing hands near the canine’s muzzle area (biohazard).
10.8.1.5 Use caution handling items that have come in contact with bodily fluids (victim’s clothing).
8.2.26 Handler Actions
10.8.1.6 Obtain pertinent information including location of victim(s). If victim(s) were removed prior to arrival, identify the previous location(s).
10.8.1.7 Conduct a safety walk through of the search area. Identify bio-hazard areas and plan the search accordingly.
10.8.1.8 Focus and motivate the canine.

10.8.1.9 Conduct recommended search pattern. Observe the canine for signs of stress and address accordingly. 10.8.1.10Bio-hazard evidentiary items should be collected and packaged according to suggested practices.
10.8.1.11 Upon completion, the canine should be thoroughly cleaned. 11 Scene Documentation
11.1 Record Time of Arrival
8.2.27 Document pertinent information prior to leaving the scene:
11.1.1.1 Incident number.
11.1.1.2 Address.
11.1.1.3 Dispatch time.
11.1.1.4 Scene upon arrival.
11.1.1.5 Procedure taken.
11.1.1.6 Evidence collection.
11.1.1.7 Departure time.
11.2 Response Action Documentation
11.2.1 A canine report (FI-49) must be completed on all incidents involving the canine team.
11.2.2 An evidence collection form (FI-7) must be completed on all evidentiary items collected by the canine team. 12 Evidence Procedures
12.1 It is the responsibility of the handler to properly gather and preserve evidentiary samples in which canine indications are given.
12.2 Packing:
8.2.28 Liquids
12.2.1.1 Glass vials provided by the Division should be used for the preservation of liquid samples.
12.2.1.2 Samplingequipment shall not be used for more than one(1) sample.
12.2.1.3 Bodily fluids should be collected in a manner consistent with acceptable practices.
8.2.29 Non-Liquids
12.2.1.4 Non-liquid material that is to receive laboratory analysis is to be packaged in clean, unused metal cans supplied by the Division.
12.2.1.5 Large items that will not fit in a metal can should be properly sealed in nylon bags designed for fire debris. These bags are supplied by the Division.
12.2.1.6 Earthen material should be refrigerated prior to transport to a laboratory facility.
12.3 Latent Prints.
12.3.1 Evidentiary material that is to be involved in latent print analysis shall be transported in containers as to preserve the integrity of the print(s).
12.4 Incendiary/Explosive/Dangerous Ordinance.
12.4.1 Devices used as incendiary devices shall be rendered safe prior to recovery and storage.
12.4.2 Noperson shall attemptto render safe any suspected orverified explosive device or dangerous ordinance. Notify the Bomb Squad.
12.5 Evidence Integrity.
12.5.1 All samples indicated on by the canine must be confirmed through laboratory analysis.
8.2.30 Establish and maintain a chain of custody for all evidence collected.
12.5.2 A FI-7 (evidence collection form) shall be completed on all collected evidence.
8.2.31 Evidence collection methods shall be consistent with accepted practices.
12.5.3 Collected evidentiary items shall be logged into and secured within the Division’s evidence room as soon as possible.
12.5.4 Any time evidence is removed, released, or destroyed from the evidence room, it shall be documented appropriately. 13 Rules for Division Employees
13.1 No firefighter or Division employee shall do any of the following without permission of the handler:
8.2.32 Approach or have any verbal or physical contact with the K-9.
8.2.33 Feed the canine.
8.2.34 Strike, discipline or give the canine any command.
8.2.35 Tease or agitate the canine.
8.2.36 Play with the canine.
8.2.37 Enterthe canine vehicle.
8.2.38 Remove the canine from any area of confinement.
8.2.39 Horseplay with the handler in the presence of the K-9. 14 Canine Bites and Injuries
14.1 Whenever a canine has bitten or scratched an individual or has alleged to have done so, whether on or off duty, the handler shall do the following:
8.2.40 Provide immediate medical attention.
8.2.41 Request EMS support if needed.
8.2.42 Notify the FAO (obtain an incident number)
8.2.43 Notify FEIU Captain.
8.2.44 Notify CPD (complete a police report).
8.2.45 Obtain witness information (Name, address and phone number).
8.2.46 Prepare and submit a RT-154 detailing the incident.
14.2 After Action Response
8.2.47 Supervisory review of the incident.
8.2.48 K-9 trainer review of the incident.
8.2.49 Handler is advised as to summation of review.
8.2.50 Handleris advised to corrective and or preventative measures.
8.2.51 If required, disciplinary action taken.
8.2.52 Fire Chief notified as to action taken. 15 Retirement of the K-9
15.1 The Public Safety Director must be notified prior to retirement of the canine. A canine handler may apply to take possession of his or her canine.
15.2 The canine is retired from duty or relieved due to injury/illness.
15.3 The handler is transferred, promoted or retires and a decision is made to retire the canine.
15.4 To take possession and transfer ownership, the handler will purchase the canine from the City of Columbus for a stipulated fee.
15.5 Once the transaction has been completed, the handler will assume financial responsibilities and liability in the continued care and maintenance of the canine.
15.6 If the canine is not retained by the assigned handler, Public Safety Director will be notified and the proper procedures will be followed to place the canine in a suitable home.
15.7 Allequipment assigned to the retiring canine will be returned to the Canine Unit. 16 Removal of Canine
16.1 If the guidelines of this policy are not followed the handler may face discipline and/or removal of the canine.
1 Administration
1.1 Purpose: To establish procedures for all Fire Investigators involving the use of License Plate Readers (LPR) and LPR databases.

1.2 Responsibility: It shall be the responsibility of each Fire Investigator to know, understand, and utilize these procedures as they apply to the situation at hand. It shall further be the responsibility of all investigation supervisors to train their subordinates in the proper application of these procedures and to implement and enforce the use of these procedures. 2 Introduction

1.3 License Plate Readers (LPR) use digital cameras affixed to a vehicle or in a stationary location to quickly photograph a large number of vehicle license plates, convert the information to digital text, and store the information in a computer database. The date and time the license plate was captured is documented by a Global Positioning System (GPS) within the LPR unit, which then stores the location where the license plate was encountered. This provides an invaluable database to Division of Fire FEIU personnel for use in investigations, crime analysis, or locating vehicles or persons.

1.4 LPRs also compare captured license plate numbers against a hot list to identify vehicles that may be stolen, contain a wanted or missing person, have a terrorist alert, or have been identified as a vehicle of interest. When a license plate is identified as being on the hot list, the LPR generates a hit alert notifying the officer who then may use the information to investigate further. NOTE: An LPR does not have a direct link to the NCIC/LEADS system; therefore, the information on a hot list is not provided in real time and the NCIC/LEADS data on a hot list could be over 24 hours old. Data entered manually into a LPR could be up to four days old.
1.5 The following LPR systems are currently used by the Division of Police:
1. ELSAGLPR (Mobile)
2. Flock Safety LPR (Stationary)
3. Vigilant LPR (Stationary)

1.6 All of the LPR data gathered by the Division of Police is transferred to and stored in computer servers maintained by the Franklin County Sheriff's Office (FCSO), Flock Public Safety, or Motorola/Vigilant. These servers also contain LPR data gathered by other local agencies, national agencies, and commercial businesses. LPR data gathered by the Division is stored for a minimum of 30 days and can be accessed through a web-based interface. The web interface varies based on the vendor, and the retention period varies based on the owner of the data. ELSAG is administered by the FCSO Information Technology Section, Flock is administrated by Flock Public Safety, and Vigilant/LEARN is administrated by the CPD PoliceNET Unit.

1.7 Alert hits are specific to only the LPR system that detects the noted license plate. Additionally, license plate numbers manually entered into a LPR will only produce an alert hit for that LPR. 3 Definitions
1.8 Alert Hit An audible and/or visual signal given by the LPR indicating a possible match between a captured license plate number and a license plate number contained on the hot list.

1.9 License Plate Reader (LPR) A system that uses a digital camera, computer, and software to photograph and convert identifying markings on a license plate to digital text, store the information in a database, and compare captured license plate numbers against a hot list.

1.10 Hot List A data set of identified license plate numbers gathered from NCIC/LEADS that is periodically downloaded onto the LPR server and accessed after the LPR operator has logged on or turned on the unit. It is then used to compare against captured license plate numbers in order to generate an alert hit. This includes license plate numbers entered manually into the LPR.

1.11 LPR Data Any information including license plate numbers, location, date and time a license plate number was captured, or any photographic image of a license plate and/or vehicle generated by means of an LPR.

1.12 Active Hit Protocol Guidelines established to ensure sworn personnel react to correctly detected license plates and reduce the risk of taking enforcement action on a misread or incorrect license plate. 4 Procedures – LPR Use and Data Access
1.13 Only Division of Fire FEIU personnel properly trained on LPR policy and operations may operate an LPR.

1.14 Division personnel shall only access or use LPRs, LPR data, or hot list data for official law enforcement purposes. Division personnel shall not disseminate LPR Data or hot list data to any non-law enforcement personnel or entity.
1.15 Sworn personnel manually entering a license plate number into an LPR shall list the reason the license plate was entered and include his/her name and badge number.

1.16 Before taking any enforcement action based on an alert hit, sworn personnel shall confirm the license plate captured in the photograph is the license plate on the hot list. FEIU Personnel shall never initiate a traffic stop, and if a license plate match exists, CPD shall be utilized to conduct a lawful stop when legally allowed to do so. Note: Some numbers and letters are commonly misread by an LPR (for example, "0" may be read as "O" and "X" may be read as "K").

1.17 Sworn personnel shall confirm an alert hit is still active in NCIC/LEADS at the earliest reasonable opportunity. If there is time to do so, personnel should validate the information on the alert hit through NCIC/LEADS to ensure the alert is still active before Requesting CPD to conduct a traffic stop and/or make a detention.
1.18 Sworn personnel shall reduce the risk of taking enforcement action on a misread or incorrect plate by following the below Active Hit Protocol:
1. Visually verify the license plate being scanned matches the translation given by the LPR and check for misreads.
2. Confirm the state on the scanned license plate matches the state listed on the hot list source.
3. Conduct a records check on the license plate and ensure it is wanted and in the system.
1. Administration
1.1 Purpose: To provide intervention to at risk fire curious or fire setting youths by means of referral, assessment, education, and interaction.

1.2 Responsibility: It shall be the responsibility of each member to know, understand, and utilize there procedures as they apply to the situation at hand. It shall further be the responsibility of all Division Officers to train their subordinates in the proper application of these procedures and to implement and enforce the use of these procedures.
2. Mission Statement

1.3 Our mission is to prevent and reduce youth fire setting behavior through assessment, education, and intervention. We aim to empower our young individuals and their families with the knowledge and skills necessary to promote safe behaviors and positive decision making. By collaborating with community partners, we strive to create an environment that promotes fire safety awareness, emotional well-being, and personal growth. Ultimately providing community risk reduction.
2. Procedures
2.1 Anytime there is a fire involving a youth, the following information is needed by the Youth Fire Intervention Specialist to follow up on cases involving youth offenders:
• Name
• Sex
• Race
• Date of birth
• Parent or guardians name, address, and phone number(s)
• Other close relative’s name, relationship, andphone number(s)
2.2 Requests for a child to become involved in theYouth Fire Prevention and Intervention Program can be accomplished by:
• A parent phone call oremail to the program
• Franklin County Juvenile Court System
• A mental health professional
• Franklin County Children’s Services (FCCS)
• Post fire referrals by the Fire Investigation Unit
• Anyfire department personnel (preferably through a fire investigator)

2.3 A child that enters the Youth Fire Prevention and Intervention Program will be assigned to work with a Youth Fire Educator who will complete the initial interview and evaluation process. After the completion of the initial parent and child interview process, an evaluation is made as to whether or not the child needs only education, or if a referral to another agency is necessary, such as:
A. Mental Health Professionals
B. Franklin County Children Services
C. Otheragencies dedicated to dealing with youth

D. Various other Family orSocial Services (food, clothing, housing, etc.) Education information sessions are conducted to provide the child with protective and preventative measures with regard to fire safety education. Each session will usually be one on one (or along with parent or guardian), and last approximately one hour and can be conducted for up to six one-hour sessions.

2.4 The Coordinator shall keep records of all youth involved in the program. The records will be held confidential and secure. The Coordinator will also have records for data collection purposes. The data collection will maintain a system for tracking referrals, assessments, interventions, and outcomes.

2.5 The Coordinator shall attempt to obtain follow-up information. The follow-up information will help monitor progress of the youth’s behaviors and help with outcome evaluation. The outcome evaluation will measure the effectiveness of the intervention program and help improve the program where necessary.

2.6 The Youth Fire Prevention & Intervention will be staffed with one Program Coordinator and Educator and other interested Division members. All staff are to undergo regular training on fire safety, intervention techniques, and mental health awareness. Any team meeting and educator training will be done while in on-duty status.

2.7 The YFP&I Coordinator should develop community partnerships with other fire departments, schools, and community organizations for resources and support. It is also important for the coordinator to promote public awareness of the program.

2.8 Division members who are interested in volunteering for the YFP&I Program shall submit an Official Intra-Divisional Communication (form RT-154), requesting that they be included in an upcoming session. This request shall be addressed to the Fire Chief, and processed through proper channels. Included in this communication will be the requesting member’s full name and Division I.D. number, current assignment and unit designation. 1. Administration
1.1. Purpose: To provide the process of reporting a false alarm to the City of Columbus Licensing Section to aid in the reduction of false alarms.

1.2. Responsibility: It shall be the responsibility of each member to know, understand and utilize these procedures as they apply to the situation at hand. It shall further be the responsibility of all Division Officers to train their subordinates in the proper application of these procedures and to implement and enforce the use of these procedures.
1. False Alarms

1.3. When an automatic fire, medical or other detection or notification system is activated, the Columbus Division of Fire responds to protect the lives and property of the citizens of the city. This rapid response requires the Columbus Division of Fire to place numerous emergency vehicles on the street which inherently increases the dangers to members of the Columbus Division of Fire and to the citizens of the city. Although the Columbus Division of Fire supports and encourages the use of automatic fire, medical or other detection or notification system to discover a fire or other emergency in its early stages, multiple malfunctions of these systems result in increased dangers and unnecessary expense. In order to recoup the cost of responding to false alarms, and provide incentive to reduce the number of false alarms the following SOP is provided to work in conjunction with the City of Columbus Licensing Section requirements.

1.4. The City of Columbus is using an alarm tracking and processing software called CryWolf. The software allows a streamline method to track false alarms, process invoices, collect payment and simply false alarm management.
1.4.1. The software as an automated interface with the CAD system for daily transfers of alarm incident data, permit status, and alarm system contacts between CryWolf and the CAD system.

1.4.2. The software requires the flagging of false alarms in the CAD system is based upon the final disposition code of the incident that must be selected when the fire or EMS company, responsible for the incident report, clears themselves from the incident.

1.5. False alarm means the activation of an alarm system through mistake, mechanical failure, malfunction, improper installation or design, lack of proper maintenance, or negligence of the alarm user, its employees or agents.
1.5.1. A call for a response that is canceled by the FAO prior to the arrival of the Division of Fire shall not constitute a false alarm.
1.1. Each false alarm notice shall constitute a separate occurrence.

1.6. The Division of Fire shall report all false alarms to the City of Columbus Licensing Section, through the MDC and CAD system. The City of Columbus Licensing Section has the ability to dismiss false alarm occurrence based upon the following guidelines:
1.6.1. Equipment malfunctions, with written verification from the alarm company that such malfunctioning equipment has been repaired
1.1.1. Acts of nature such asearthquakes, flood, orwinds greater than fifty-nine (59) mph
1.1.2. Verifiable power outages greater than four (4) hours
1.1.3. Vandalism, if a proper police report was filed at the time the crime occurred
1.2. Equipmentmalfunctions do not include the following:
1.2.1. Low battery
1.2.2. Improper use of alarm system by the user
1.2.3. Faulty, defective, or malfunctioning equipment
1.2.4. Impropermonitoring by the alarm dealer
1.2.5. Impropermonitoring by the alarm monitoring company
1.6.2. Alarm activations that occur while alarm agents are repairing, servicing, or testing the alarm system

1.7. Non-system smoke and carbon monoxide alarms are exempt from the false alarm guidelines. This includes, but is not limited to, battery power and 110 volts single station and multi-station alarms (not monitored).
2. Notification
1.3. False Alarm Notice Door Hanger

2.1.1. Prior to clearing an incident involving a false fire alarm, medical alarm, or any other automatic alarm that summons a response of the Division of Fire, the officer, acting officer, or paramedic shall complete a “False Alarm” notice and leave the notice with the occupant. If there is no occupant, leave the notice on the main entrance door to the building.
1.3.1. Complete the following fields on the False Alarm Notice:
2.1.1.1. Date – Today’s Date (MM/DD/YYYY)
2.1.1.2. Officer/Firefighter Name – Company officer or in-charge person name
2.1.1.3. Badge No – FDID number (e.g., Z001)
2.1.1.4. Assignment No – Apparatus ID (unit)/shift (e.g., E23/1 Unit)
2.1.2. False Alarm Notice Door Hangers may be ordered with other Division of Fire forms through monthly form requests.
1.4. MDC Final Disposition of Incident

2.1.3. It is imperative, for proper notification of the City of Columbus Licensing Section, that a final disposition code be used when clearing an alarm incident. The unit that will be completing the incident report will be responsible to select the proper disposition code on the MDC before placing themselves in-service.
1.4.1. The following are the types of final disposition codes to be used:
2.1.3.1. F = Fire Usethis code for all responses to fire or hazmat related incidents.

2.1.3.4. A = Alarm Use this code for alarms that were canceled prior to arrival of the Division of Fire or for alarms determined not to be a false alarm (e.g., activation for a valid condition).
2.1.3.5. NA = Nuisance Alarm Use this code for false alarms as defined in 2.3 above.
1.5. Fire Incident Report

2.1.4. A NFIRS incident report must be completed for all alarm incidents. Please remember that these reports may be scrutinized by the City of Columbus Licensing Section and the alarm user, its employees or agents in determining if a false alarm occurred. 1. Administration
1.1. Purpose: The purpose of this procedure is to describe the Columbus Division of Fire’s Standard Operating Procedures and Protocols for conducting school fire drills.

1.2. Responsibility: It shall be the responsibility of each member to know, understand and utilize these procedures as they apply to the situation at hand. It shall further be the responsibility of all Division Officers to train their subordinates in the proper application of these procedures and to implement and enforce the use of these procedures.
1. School Fire Drills

1.3. The purpose of conducting school fire drills is to evaluate the proficiency of students and school staff members to safely leave an occupied building in the shortest possible time without confusion.

1.4. To alleviate the potential fear and anxiety of students and school staff members, it is the policy of the Division of Fire to notify the principal or person in charge of the educational institution immediately prior to conducting the fire drill. The principal or person in charge shall be allowed to make a public address announcement to all occupants, stating that the fire department will be conducting a fire alarm drill.
1.5. As a consideration to the students, companies should avoid scheduling at the following times:
1.1.1. Avoid scheduling during proficiency and standardized testing.
1.1.2. Avoid scheduling around lunch periods.
1.1.3. Verify lunch periods and testing schedules with the school before activating the alarm.
2. Proceduresof Drill
1.6. The School Fire Drill Inspection Report is to be printed prior to conducting the drill and is to be thoroughly completed immediately after conducting the drill.

1.6.1. The officer in charge shall then review the completed School Fire Drill inspection report with the responsible party, addressing general observations, satisfactory performance, and areas where improvements are needed.
1.6.2. The responsible party is to be afforded an opportunity to make a copy of the School Fire Drill inspection report, if desired.
2.1.1. The “Remarks” section is to be used to identify any of the following:
2.1.1.1. Schoolalarm system is not working properly.
2.1.1.2. When a building is no longer operating as a school.
2.1.1.3. General observations by crew.
